Inside this lecture, I'm going to teach you about primitive data types inside Java programming language. Why should we use primitive data types? Usually any programming language it should capable of processing lot of data based upon our business logic. Suppose think like you have given two numbers to your programming language based upon your instructions are based upon your logic. It should be able to do addition, multiplication, division. So regardless of how complex the operation is going to be, your programming language should be capable of accepting the data, processing the data, and returning that data once the program is executed.

Since we are going to provide lot of data to our programming language, we should use these primitive data types to store that data inside them. Inside Java anytime if you want to store data, there are two types of data types. One is Reference types, the other one is Primitive types. Inside this section, we are going to discuss in detail about all the Primitive data types available. Because these primitive data types are most basic and natural entry into the Java programming language.

Using these primitive data types, only we can store simple data like numbers, whereas with the reference data types we can store complex data. Think like you want to store a details of a person, so the person will have a name, age, gender, address. Can't we have a single data type using which we can store any kind of data?

But before that, here you may have a burning question saying that why should I use primitive data types?

So it is going to completely depend on your business logic that you have written. But working with computers is not going to be super easy. Because programming language is a contract between a developer and a computer saying that we both are going to follow the so and so syntax, so and so rules. So I hope you are now clear like why we need primitive data types. So let's try to understand more details about this primitive data types in the next lecture as well. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

So if you want to store that total number of goals using your Java programming language, do you think storing them in long or int or short is going to make sense? Off course not, because the maximum number of goals that a particular team may have is maybe 10 or 20. or best case it may be 100. If you go with the long, your Java is not going to complain anything. It is going to work very similarly but behind the scenes you are going to waste a lot of memory inside your computer. lectures.title: [Java 7] Using underscore in numeric literals
lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, I'm going to show you under which scenarios we can use underscore special character while we are trying to define numeric literals with the help of int, float, double, byte, short, long. So regardless of whatever primitive data type that you are trying to use to declare numeric values in all such scenarios, we can use underscore to improve the readability of the code. So let's try to understand more details about this. In some scenarios we are going to mention very big numbers, which is very hard for the developers to read.

Suppose if you have eight digit number or nine digit number, the developer has to count how many numbers are there inside your Java code manually by putting some efforts. So to improve the readability in these kind of scenarios, Java allows you to mention underscore in between your numbers, and your compiler is also not going to complain anything. So underscore is not a number and it is a special character. Your Java compiler will not throw an error. Behind the scenes your Java compiler is going to remove these underscore values by the time your Java code is converted into the machine code. Inside the Java source code, you will be able to see underscore, but the machine code will not have these underscore, because in between, the compiler is going to do the magic of removing these underscore value.

So these underscore values is going to simply improve the readability of your variable declarations and initialization. Here you can see I'm trying to define a variable num of type int. If I don't mention these underscore values it will be very tough for other developers, including me also, to understand what is the total value of this number or how many zeros are there inside my number. So in future, whenever you see some developer using underscore values inside their numeric, please don't scratch your head by thinking like how this is possible, because this is a feature available inside the Java programming language. But there are some rules and regulations that we need to follow while you are trying to define this underscore value inside a numeric value.

So let's try to understand what are those rules. The very first rule is the underscore value is not allowed at the beginning or at the end of a number. Suppose if we want to create a number six, we can't create a number underscore six and six underscore. And in the case of decimal numbers the underscore is not allowed adjacent to your decimal point, either before decimal point or after decimal point the underscore value is not allowed, and very similarly, when we try to create long numbers will mention the suffix as l, and for float numbers will mention the suffix as f, so the underscore is not allowed just after the suffix or just before the suffix value.

And at last, when you try to represent your numbers using the string format using underscore values is not allowed. I know we are yet to discuss about what is string data type in the coming lectures we are going to discuss about it, but for now, please note that when you try to define your numeric values using String data type in such scenarios we are not allowed to use underscore value. I hope this is clear. Now let's see the demo of these underscore inside numeric values by going to the jshell.

Here I'm going to create a variable with the name num of data type int. For this first I'm going to assign a value with one, and after one I'm going to mention some zeros. So in total I have mentioned seven zeros. So if you try to define this way you can see it is very hard for someone to read your value. Whereas if I try to change the same numeric value by mentioning underscore values at different places, then this is going to be super easy for other people to read my numeric value.

So if I try to execute this, you can see by the time I get output, all the underscore values are being removed by the Java compiler. You may have a question can I use some other special character in the place of underscore? Let's try with comma. So if I try to use commas which is other than underscore, you can see we are getting a compilation error. That means we are allowed only to use underscore only. Now let's try to test some negative scenarios.

For negative scenarios I'm going to mention underscore at the starting of the number which I'm trying to create here. So this is not allowed. And very similarly at the end of the number also it is not allowed. So let me mention the underscore at the end. This is also not allowed. Let me clean my console here. This time I will show for long variable. So for long variable we are going to mentioning underscore just before L is not allowed. Very similarly, just after L also is not allowed.

As a next step, I'm going to create a flot to variable. And inside this float variable I'm going to store a number 3._6f. Do you think this is allowed? Off course this is not allowed because we are not supposed to use underscore adjacent to the decimal point. Even if I try to move these underscore before the decimal point, even this is also not allowed. I hope you are clear about these negative scenarios. Now let me show you an interesting demo, which is not known for many of the Java developers.

Since you are my student, you're going to have the knowledge about the new demo that we are going to discuss. So previously we created a variable by mentioning these underscore value. Sometimes you may want more readability and you can mention underscore values like here I have mentioned three underscore values. Very similarly here also I'm going to mention. So do you think this is allowed or not. Off course please note this is completely allowed inside Java.

So you can use any number of underscore values to improve the readability of your numbers. So these are secret where very few Java developers know. I hope you're happy and clear about all the scenarios that we have discussed. So please note about all the rules that we need to follow while we are trying to use underscore in the numeric literals that we are going to define inside Java programming language. Before we try to close this lecture, I want to highlight that these underscore feature is introduced inside JAVA 7, which means you can use this feature only with the JAVA 7 and above version, but not with the JAVA 6 or JAVA 5.

Off course, these days there is no option for us to use JAVA 6 or JAVA 5, but I just want to let you know in case if someone asks you from which version this feature is introduced, you can answer them from JAVA 7. This underscore feature is introduced for numeric literals. I hope this is all clear to you. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

So what is widening casting? If you are trying to convert a smaller type to a larger type size, such casting, we call it as implicit casting or widening casting.

lectures.text:
So far we have created classes and inside the classes we have declared that Java fields. As a next step, we should try to define methods as well inside the Java class. Before we try to do that, let's try to understand what is a method in Java. Why should we write methods inside Java? We already wrote a main() method in the previous section when we were trying to execute the hello world example. So you have a basic idea on how to write a method. Let's try to revise the same in detail inside this lecture.

A method which we are going to define within a Java class represents the behavior of the objects belonging to that particular class or the behavior of the class itself. In other words, these methods, they are going to serve as a named blocks of code that can be invoked to execute its specified actions. I can handle a particular business use case with a Java logic inside a method, and whatever use case that we are trying to handle with the method, it has to be associated with the given class at the given object of a particular class.

Inside a Car class, I can define methods which are going to handle the logic related to the Car. I should not write the logic related to the Person or a Customer inside the Car class, though technically it is possible and your Java compiler is not going to complain anything about that, but it is always a good practice to define the business logic related to of a class or an object inside its own body. So that's why we are going to follow the same standards throughout this course and in the same process I'm assuming you will also get used to the standard.

Once we define a method inside a class, any other class, or any other entity, they can invoke our method. In such scenarios, whatever business logic we have written inside a method will be executed. So the entity or the component who are initiating our method execution, we can refer them as a caller. And when we define a method, our methods may receive input parameter values from the caller, and in return they can also return a value to the caller.

So there is always a possibility for your method to accept the input and to send the output, whoever is invoking the method by sending the output and receiving the input is completely optional, which means we can write a method with zero input parameters indicating that it is not going to accept any input, and very similarly, we can also mention the return type as void, which means the method is not going to return any output. And inside Java, the methods we should always encapsulate them within the body of a class or an interface.

Where to talk about interface. But if you talk from class perspective, we are always allowed to define our methods inside the body of a class. We cannot really write an method independently without a class. This encapsulation ensures that the behavior defined by the method is closely associated with the structure and purpose of the class to which it belongs. That's what we have discussed previously in the very first point. The return type of a method represents the data type of the value that the method is going to return whenever the method execution is completed, and this return type can be a simple primitive data type like int, float, double or it can be a reference data type like Car or a String.

In cases where a method does not going to return any output to the caller. In such scenarios like we discussed, we need to mention the return type as void, indicating that the absence of a return value to the invoking entity. And when we are trying to define a Java method, we should also give a name to the Java method. Otherwise how the invoking entity is going to invoke our method. That's why we should always give a name to our method and the naming standards that we need to follow while we are trying to define a method name is very similar to the standards that we followed while declaring the variable names our field names.

This means even if our method names, they should follow the camel case style. The very first letter of your method should always start with a small letter, and post that every subsequent word that you are trying to add to your method name should start with a capital letter. For example, here I have defined a method names like moveVehicle(), applyBreak(), getSpeed() and stopVehicle() . So these are all the valid method names which are following the Java standards.

Whereas if I try to define a method name like moveVehicle() vehicle with a random capital letters or small letters like you can see here, this is still going to be a valid method name from your Java compiler perspective, but with this, you're not going to follow the standard of camel case naming conventions, which will make your code as a bad code in front of other developers. Now, since we talked enough details about what is a Java method, let's try to understand how we can declare methods in a Java class, and what is the syntax that we need to follow.

Like you can see here, whenever we are trying to define a method, the very first information that we should provide is modifier. Just like how your class and Java field have a modifier. Very similarly, your method also can optionally have a modifier. This modifiers indicates who can invoke your method. If you start your method declaration with the private, then no one can invoke your method from outside of your Java class. Only the methods which are present in the same class can invoke.

So we're going to talk about modifiers in detail for now, we are going to go with a modifier which is public for all our methods. Even if you don't mention this modifier, your compiler is not going to complain anything because this is completely optional. After the modifier, you need to mention what is the return type of your Java method? The return type means what is the data type of the output that your method is going to return. If you are trying to return an int value, you should mention the return type as int or if you are trying to return an String, then you should mention the String as an return type.

After the return type, you should mention a method name like we discussed previously the method name should follow the CamelCase style, and while you are trying to give a method name, please make sure you are giving a name which is very meaningful. Your method name should give an high level information to the other developers. What exact logic your method is going to execute. So such high level summary your method name should hold. lectures.title: Introduction to method signature
lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, let's try to discuss a very important topic which is method signature. Every Java method is going to have a method signature. And this method signature is very helpful in the concepts of method overloading and overriding that we are going to discuss in the coming sections. So what is a method signature? Each method is going to have a signature. This signature is going to help to uniquely identify a method within a specific context or within a specific class.

So how the method signature is calculated. The method signature is composed of four important elements. What is the name of the method? What are the types of input parameters? What are the number of input parameters and the order of the parameters? Using these four elements, only a method signature is going to be calculated by your Java compiler. Apart from these four elements, we also have other elements like modifier, return types, parameter names and Throws class as part of the method syntax.

But these are not going to be part of the signature of the method. Regardless of which modifier you have mentioned, what is the return type of the method, what are the parameter names that you have discussed, and what is the type of Throws class that you have used? So all these components are not going to be considered to calculate your method signature. And like we discussed, the signatures of a method help us to uniquely identify the methods within a class.

It is not allowed to have more than one method in a class with the same signature. I'm going to show you this in that demo in few minutes with this quick introduction about the method signature now let me give you some method declaration examples and the equivalent method signature. That's why public is ignored, return type int is ignored, only add is considered, and the name of parameters also is not going to be considered. Regardless you mentioned num1, num2 or any other name.

The method signature doesn't care about the parameter names. It is only consider how many input parameters you have, what is the order of parameters and what is the data type of your parameters. lectures.title: Purpose of a return statement in Java methods
lectures.text:
Inside this lecture let me talk in detail about this return statement. As of now, you can see inside the sum() method we are trying to return a variable result, which is going to hold the value that we calculated by adding two input parameters like num1 and num2. Sometimes you may see developers directly mentioning the expression inside the return keyword itself. For example, instead of me writing these two lines, I can try to combine these two lines and write return num1 + num2.

After that, I need to mention the semicolon. You can see this is also completely perfectly fine, because I'm trying to send the output from these additions and the same I'm trying to return to the caller of this method, so this is also perfectly fine. In the coming sections, I'm also going to show you the demo of how to write some complex expressions as part of your return statement. Apart from using these variables and expressions, if needed, we can also directly return a hard coded value like I can say return 30 here this is also completely valid statement because I'm trying to return a hard coded value, which is 30, and this 30 is matching with the primitive data type that I have mentioned here, which is int.

That's why my compiler does not going to throw any errors and simply accept these output. If I try to change this 30 to String value by mentioning double quotes, and you can see my compiler is throwing an error because we're trying to return a String value, whereas the return type of the method is mentioned as int. Since there is a mismatch, you're going to get a compilation error. So let me revert back to the previous code changes. To revert back to the previous code changes, you can always press command+Z inside the mac, whereas inside the windows you can press Ctrl+Z.

So let me press command + Z multiple times so that all the code will be reverted back to the original code that we have written. And the next scenario that I want to discuss here is, if you go to the Car class here, we have a method with the return type as void. That means this method is not going to return anything even in these kind of scenarios also, I can mention the return keyword, but I should not provide any output value or Java expression to the return keyword.

I should simply mention return followed by colon, and this is completely optional, and it is also not a standard to mention this return. This is a bad code practice because it is very obvious for your Java compiler. As soon as it executed the Java statements inside the method body, it has to return back to the caller. That's why we don't have to explicitly mention that return keyword in the scenarios of void methods. You can see I'm also getting an warning saying that return is unnecessary as a last statement in a void method.

So that's why never ever try to mention this, though it is technically possible. So what is the purpose of return keyword inside any Java method? With the help of return keyword, we are trying to give control back to the caller. So when someone invoked our Java method, all the Java code that we have written inside our Java method will be executed. And at last, with the help of return keyword, we are telling to the compiler I am done executing. Please take the control back to the caller method.

If there is an output, the output will be carry forwarded to the caller method. In case of void methods, the control simply return back to the caller method. So that's the purpose of return keyword, and it is also perfectly fine to have multiple return statements inside your Java methods. I know this might be very surprising to you, but when we start writing our Java programming with the help of conditional statements or conditional logic, in such scenario, we can mention the return statements in multiple places inside your Java method.

We are going to discuss about this scenario in the coming sections, when we are enhancing our Java programs with the help of conditional flows or conditional logic. All the points that I have discussed inside this lecture, I have mentioned the same inside this slide for your reference. So please always read these points to quickly brush up your Java knowledge. I hope you are clear with the purpose of return statement in a method. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

So let's try to understand what is the syntax that we need to follow whenever we are trying to invoke a method. Here you may have a question what is the meaning of method invocation? So based upon these parameters, the syntax is going to change. For example, think like you're trying to invoke the sum() method which we have declared inside the arithmetic operations Java class. So here I'm trying to pass two into values like 6, 24. But the same sum() method is present inside some other Java class. Then you have two options based upon the type of the Java method. If the Java method is a non-static Java method where there is no static keyword inside the method declaration, then in such scenarios, you need to create an object of the class where the sum() method is present, where to discuss on how to create an object from a Java class.

For now, let's assume the object variable name is object name. So with the help of the variable name and dot operator, you need to invoke the method sum(). And to this sum() method you need to pass the input parameter values like 6, 24. You can directly invoke the static method sum() with the help of the class name itself.

So the syntax is going to be ClassName.sum(6,24). And at last we need to mention the semicolon. So this is how you're going to invoke the methods. By the time they are trying to invoke the sum() method for the execution of the business logic. So these are the syntax that we need to follow. lectures.title: Let’s say hi to main method again
lectures.text:
Now, since we have gained some good amount of knowledge on Java methods, let's revisit our main method that we have discussed in the previous sections. So we are going to say hi to the main method again. Like we know the syntax of main method is public static void main array of string as an input parameter and inside the method body we can write our business logic. So now it should be pretty clear for you what is the purpose of each word inside your main method declaration.

The purpose of public is it is going to act as a modifier for your method. So mentioning public is very important and mandatory for your main method. This public allow my JVM to access my main method without any issues. If you don't define public for your main method, then your JVM cannot access it since you have not made your method as public. And after public, we should also mention static because we want our JVM to invoke the main method without creating the object of the class.

Like we discussed previously, whenever we want to invoke a static method, we can simply invoke it with the help of class name. So behind the scenes, when we start our Java program where we have a main method declared, the JVM is going to invoke this static main method with the help of class name itself. It does not have to create the object of the given class where the main method is present. This is one of the standardized approach that is implemented by the Java team for the JVM because JVM cannot create the object before invoking a method.

So how come JVM can create an object of a class without invoking a method? So to give that convenience to the JVM, we need to make the main method as static. That means this method can be invoked by your JVM with the help of class name itself and without the need of writing the Java statement to create the Java object. And the return type of the method is void. So void means your method is not going to return anything and the input parameters that we need to send to the main method is array of string values.

So we are going to discuss what is an array in the coming sections. Array of string means we can send multiple string values inside an array and this parameter name is a placeholder. So instead of args, you can define some other parameter name like myArgs. So any name should be fine for your method parameters. As a thumb rule, we just have to make sure the same name we are using inside the method body to refer to the method parameters. Otherwise you are going to get a compilation error.

So with this knowledge, now let's try to create the public static void main method again and let's try to answer some tricky questions. So to create a main method, first I'm going to create a class like we discussed in the previous sections. The class name is going to be HelloWorld. Inside this HelloWorld class, I'm going to create a main method. So to create a main method, the shortcut in IntelliJ is psvm, the public static void main. So once you type this psvm, you can press enter.

And with that, you can see you have an empty main method. And inside this, I want to print the HelloWorld statement. So what is a shortcut for System.out.printerln? S-O-U-T. So if you press enter, you'll get System.out.printerln statement. And inside this, you can simply write HelloWorld string value. So if I try to execute this Java class, you can see I'm going to get an output, which is HelloWorld. Now the tricky question that you may face in interviews is, the interviewer person can ask, can I remove static for my main method or can I remove the public for my main method?

So these kind of tricky questions you may face. So let's try to understand what is going to happen. If I try to remove this static from my main method definition, you can see this is completely a valid method, but my JVM cannot use this main method to start the program. That's why right now you can see the start button also disabled. As soon as I try to bring back the static, you will be able to see that these buttons are enabled. That means my JVM always is going to look for the exact method signature like public static void main string of array.

Here this time I can also show you that I'll try to remove this public and with that you will be able to see all these buttons will be disabled or disappear. So let me remove this. You can see right now this method cannot be used by my JVM to start the program. So let me bring back public. This time I will change this aux to some other name. Instead of aux, I'll just keep it as my aux. With this, it is perfectly fine because parameter names are going to be simply placeholder.

You can give any name. So I can also try to execute this program and you are going to get the same output which is hello world. I hope you are clear with the signature of the public static void main. This is very very important inside Java. Interviewers can confuse you a lot around this method. So please be very very clear around this method. The next question that interviewer may ask you is, can I write multiple main methods inside a same Java class?

The answer is, of course we can write the multiple main methods, but we need to make sure the method signature is not same. For example, if I try to copy the same method, the method signatures are going to be same. That's why I'm getting an error. So what I can do? I can try to create main methods which are not matching with the original main method signature. So here what I can do is, I can try to introduce one more parameter for the same. Let me mention comma followed by float num.

This time you can see there is no compilation error and for this main method, there is no start button, whereas for this main method, there is a start button because this is matching with the main method signature that JVM is expecting. Very similarly, I can also create any number of main methods with different different method signature. Maybe here this time I will try to mention public double main and this main method is not going to accept anything.

It is simply going to return a double value, which is 3.14. So you can see this is perfectly fine. I hope this is clear. Even if interviewer is trying to trick you or trying to confuse you, don't get confused. You can tell him or her confidently saying that, yes, it is absolutely possible to define multiple main methods, but different different method signatures. I hope this is clear. For your reference, I have mentioned the details about these tricky questions around the main method inside this slide.

So please refer the same whenever you have some questions. I hope you are liking the progress that we are making throughout the course. Thank you and I will catch you in the next lecture. Bye.

lectures.text:
Inside this lecture. Let me answer your burning question. What is a Constructor in Java? What is the role that it plays while we are trying to create objects with the help of Java classes and new keyword. Before I try to explain you the formal definition of constructor, first let me give a real life example. Think like you want to construct your own house, our own building. So what are the steps that you follow? First, you're going to have a blueprint or planning for your building.

By taking help from one of the architect, you're going to have a plan for your building. Once the plan is ready, you're going to start the construction. In the construction stage you're going to build the walls, you're going to fit the windows, doors, you're going to build bathrooms, you're going to lay down the tiles. You're going to do some drainage work, electric work, water piping work. So there are so many activities you're going to do as part of the construction.

Once the construction is completed, you're going to get your final output, which is your own house or your own building. If you try to compare the same analogy with the Java whatever blueprint that you have initially inside the building scenario, the same kind of blueprint or template you are going to build with the help of Java classes. And the final output that you got in the building scenario, which is the building itself, it is like a object in the Java world.

So using a plan you're going to build your own house, which is a final output. Very similarly inside Java programming using that Java class, which is a blueprint, I'm going to create as many objects I want. So object is a final output. But in between my class definition and my object to final output, they're going to be an intermediate stage, just like how you have construction stage inside the building scenario very similarly in the Java scenario also we have a constructor.

So there is a similarity like construction stage and the constructor that's why the name constructor came using this constructor we are going to do some initialization activities that we want to take care before my object is completely created by the JVM. These initialization activities are like assigning the data inside my object. So all such initialization activities we are going to do with the help of constructor. I hope you are clear with the high level introduction about the constructor, in Java constructor always going to help you to initialize your object before it is completely created.

Now let's try to discuss the formal definition of constructor. A constructor is a code block that is essential inside Java for creating an object. So what is an object? It is an instance of your class. In other words, we can also call our objects as instance of class, because if the class is a blueprint, object is going to be an instance of that blueprint. So this code block of constructor, it is going to look like very similar to your Java method inside your Java classes.

But there are certain differences, which is going to help you to clearly identify whether a given code block is a Java method or a constructor. So let's try to understand what are those? The very first thumb rule that you need to follow to define a constructor for your Java class is, the constructor name has to be same as your class name. If my class name is Employee, then the constructor name also should be Employee. I cannot choose any other name.

That's a very first rule. And the second rule that we need to follow while we are declaring constructor is, from the constructor, we are not supposed to return any value, not even void. So that's why inside the definition of constructor, we're not going to mention any return type, even void also, we should not mention. So what is the purpose of constructor? When we try to create an object inside Java, the JVM invokes your constructor and it is the developer responsibility to write some initialization logic, like assigning values to the fields of the object.

So all such initialization tasks you need to perform them inside your constructor. But please note that this is completely optional. If you have a business requirement where you want to populate some data, or where you want to perform some activities before your object is completely created, then you can leverage the constructor. You can define your own constructor, and you can write all your business logic. Otherwise, you can simply ignore the constructor itself.

Behind the scenes, your JVM compiler is going to create a default constructor, and this default constructor is not going to accept any parameters, and the body inside the constructor also is going to be empty. We also saw this in the previous lecture. So once the code inside the constructor is executed, your JVM is going to create your object by allocating memory inside your system. So here is a sample class and it's a default constructor. The class name is Employee.

I have defined that by following the syntax public class Employee and inside the class only, just like how we define the methods. Very similarly we can define a constructor, so here I have just mentioned the default constructor. How I'm telling this a default constructor, you can see it is not accepting any input parameters. And at the same time this constructor does not have any business logic. So if your constructor does not have any code and it is not accepting any input parameters, then we can safely call it as a default constructor because it is going to look like the same constructor that is going to be generated by your JVM.

The important thing that I want to observe here is your constructor name has to match exactly with your class name, otherwise you're going to get a compilation error. Like I said before, if you are not defining any constructor inside your classes, Java automatically provide a default constructor with an empty body. And that's what we are trying to invoke here. When I'm trying to create an object of Employee on the right hand side, just after the new keyword, I'm trying to invoke the constructor, which is Employee like you can see here employee and empty parentheses.

So this is how you're going to invoke your constructor which is present inside your Java class. And whenever we are trying to invoke that default constructor our object does not going to have any values. All the fields are going to hold the default values like null, zero, false or blank space in the scenario of char data type. So those are all default values. The reason is when we don't define our constructor, that means we don't want to provide any initialization code.

In such scenarios whatever default constructor is generated by the JVM, the same will be executed and since this default constructor has an empty body, no initialization will happen and your object is going to hold the default values. So if you see here on the right hand side first I'm using that new keyword. The purpose of new keyword or the new operator is, we need to use this to tell to my JVM that I'm trying to create a new object. After the new keyword, we need to invoke the constructor of the class.

So here I'm trying to invoke the default constructor Employee with the blank parentheses. So the combination of your new and default constructor is going to return a reference of the newly created object, the same reference we are trying to catch onto the variable with the name myObj on the left hand side. Whatever default constructor that is going to be generated by the Java compiler, we are also going to call it as no args constructor. It is not going to accept any parameters.

That's why many developers sometimes they'll also call this default constructor as no args constructor, which means no arguments constructor or no parameters constructor and the access level of the default constructor is always going to be the same as the access level of the class. So if you have defined the public as a access modifier for your class, the same modifier will be considered for the default constructor that is going to be generated by the JVM or Java.

So let's try to understand more details about what is a constructor. Like I said before, the constructor they are going to look very similar to method. There are some differences that you can follow to identify whether a particular code is a constructor or a method. Method is a class member, whereas constructor is not a member of the class because it is not a method. The only purpose of the constructor is to be invoked. Whenever we are trying to create a new instance of the class or the new object from the class, like we discussed what kind of code we have to write inside the constructor, we need to focus strictly on initializing the instance variables or the Java fields of the newly created object.

We should always restrict ourselves to the tasks related to the initialization of the variables or any other initialization tasks related to object. And we should also note that whenever we are trying to write some business logic inside the constructor to initialize our object, we should consider that object is not completely created inside the memory. Because it is in the process of getting created, my object is not fully formed. We need to assume this while we are trying to define some logic inside the constructor.

Otherwise we are going to get an unexpected outcomes. Just like how we can create any number of methods inside your Java class. Similarly, we can create any number of constructors inside your Java class, but all your constructors, they are going to have the same name, which is same as your Java class name. Then how we are going to define multiple constructors inside a Java class is by defining the different set of input parameters. I can write a empty constructor, and I can write another constructor, which is accepting two input parameters.

And very similarly, I can write one more constructor, which is accepting only one input parameter. This way, by having different, different set of input parameters, I can write any number of constructors which I can invoke them based upon my scenario. So defining multiple constructors in a same Java class, we call such concept as constructor overloading because we are trying to define multiple constructors in the same Java class that's why we call this scenario as constructor overloading.

We also have concepts like method overloading, which we are going to discuss in the coming sections. Now you can see here this is the general syntax that we need to follow whenever we are trying to create a Java constructor. First you need to mention the modifier, modifier also is optional. After that you need to mention the constructor name. Please note that constructor name should be always same as your Java class name, and after that you need to mention the parentheses and inside the parentheses you can put it as blank without any input parameters or you can define some parameters as well based based upon your business requirement.

And after the parenthesis, I can define Throws class to indicate what kind of exception my constructor logic can throw in the case of any error or runtime exceptions. For now, please don't worry about throws, because we are yet to discuss about the exception handling inside the Java programming. And after the Throws class, you need to define the curly braces, and inside these curly braces you can write all the business logic and these business logic, such as assigning some values to your instance variables present inside the object or performing any other initialization tasks.

I have mentioned all the details about these syntax here itself. You can read them for more details. The same information we discussed just now. With this I'm assuming that you have a good clarity about what is a constructor. In the next lecture, let's try to define some constructors inside our Java classes, and in the same process let's try to explore more about constructor. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.text:
You may have some questions around the written statements usage inside the constructor. Let's try to discuss about written statements inside Java constructors and clarify any doubts that we may have. We know that inside the constructor definition we cannot declare a return type. So these are one of the primary difference between a constructor and a Java method. Your Java methods they can declare what is the return type inside that definition, whereas constructors are not allowed.

This is because we cannot return any value from the constructors. So inside the constructors we are only allowed to write the code which is related to the initialization of the object variables or other initialization tasks related to your current object. With that reason, we are not allowed to mention return statement inside the constructor body as well, though it is technically possible to use a simple return statement without any expression inside a constructor, but doing so is strongly discouraged as it is considered a poor practice.

Let me show you some code screenshots about the return statements inside the constructor. Here in the very first screenshot, you can see I'm trying to return a String value, but do you think this is allowed? Off course this is not allowed. Your code is not going to compile because if you see the constructor definition nowhere we are telling that my constructor is going to return a String data type value. With that reason, the return statement with the Java expression are with a hardcoded value is not allowed inside the constructor body.

Now, the very next question you may have here is can I simply mention only return keyword inside my constructor body? Off course this is allowed. Like you can see here, this is perfectly works. Your code is going to perfectly compile if you simply use the return keyword, but it is not recommended to mention the return keyword inside your constructor body, because it is very obvious at the end of the execution of your constructor body, the JVM is simply going to return the control back to the invoking caller or invoking entity.

With that reason, just like how inside methods we try to avoid mentioning simply return keyword very similarly inside the constructor also, we should avoid mentioning only the return keyword. I hope this makes sense to you. Now let me quickly show you both of these two examples inside the intellIJ. So here I have two constructors. If I try to remove these hardcoded value, the code is going to be compiled, but there'll be some warning saying that return is unnecessary as a last statement in a constructor. So if I try to execute the EmployeeMain, nothing wrong is going to happen.

Your code is going to work perfectly without any issues. I can also show you that by running the program in the run mode. Why I want to run in the run mode. So inside Java there is a difference between a warning and error. With the warning you can still run your programs, so you may face some warnings whenever you are not following some standards. Whereas with error you will not be able to run your program. Until you fix the error the JVM is not going to allow you to run your Java program.

Few lectures back when we were discussing about what is a Java class, I said Java will contain components like fields, methods, constructors, instance initializers, and static initializers. As of now, we discussed about what are Java methods? What are constructors? As a next step, we need to understand what are these instance initializers and static initializers that we can define inside a Java class. Inside this lecture, let's focus on instance initializers.

In Java instance initialization block is a block of code which we can write within a Java class that is going to be executed each time an instance of the class or the object of the class is getting created. The primary purpose of the instance initialization block is to initialize the instance variables of an object, and this block is particularly useful when we want to perform some initialization logic for each object of a class. And here you have a burning question we discussed just now about constructor.

Constructor also is playing the same role. With the help of constructor, we can define some initialization logic for the objects. Then why java is given another approach to initialize my Java variables and to initialize some tasks during the object creation. I'll answer that question in few minutes. For now, let's focus on how to define these instance initialization block. We can define this block within a class, but outside of the methods or constructor.

We should not write this instance initialization block inside Java methods or inside the constructor. We should develop these blocks inside the Java class. But outside of that Java methods and Java constructor. And the very important point that you need to be aware about this instance initialization block is there not going to have any name. We just have to mention the open curly brace and closing curly brace. And within the braces we need to write the logic that we want to be executed as part of this instance initialization block.

Let me show you a sample. This time I have taken the car class that we have. Inside the Car class we have three Java fields with the name, model, color and horsePower. So whatever we have written inside this block, it is going to be executed whenever an object or whenever an instance of the class is getting created. After this, I'm going to create one more object with the name car2. When I try to create these two objects, my instance block will be executed, and for the both objects, we are going to assign the same values like Camry, black and 200. Let me save this file and run this program in a debug mode. As soon as I click on this debug option, you can see the breakpoint stopped inside my instance initialization block. So let me release this breakpoint and this time you can see the breakpoint stopped again. Let me release this breakpoint and you can see that the program execution is completed. Let's try to understand more about this in the next lecture. Thank you. Bye.

lectures.text:
As of now we are trying to create the Java fields inside the class. Here you can see we have fields like model, color and horsePower. So what is the purpose of these fields? These fields allow us to store the unique data, which is specific to each object that we are going to create with the help of a given class. But sometimes you may want to create a field or a variable, which is going to hold the data that is common for all the objects that you are going to create.

For example, for my Car vehicle, I want to create a variable to hold the how many wheels my car is going to have. Obviously the car is going to have four wheels regardless of how many objects that I try to create with the help of Car, I want to have each and every object to have the same data, which is four wheels. So how to handle these kind of data with the help of a Java field? Let's try to understand the same inside this lecture. Inside Java we can create static variables or fields.

As of now we are trying to create normal fields we can also call them as instance fields or non static fields. Because with the fields that we have created so far, we can store the unique data which is specific to each and every instance or object that we are going to create. But with the help of static variables or static fields, we can store the data that is common for all the instances or the objects. So what is a static variable? In Java, a static variable is a variable that belongs to a class rather than a particular instance or object of the class.

How to declare a static variable. We just have to use the ' static ' keyword. For example, if I want to create an variable with the name employer name, I should follow this syntax which is static String EmployerName = Google. equal to Google As of now, we have a class called Employee inside our Java project, and with the help of Employee class, we are trying to create the objects representing various employees. Like their name, like their firstName, lastName, age, gender, but for all the employees, since they are going to work for the same company like Google, we can create an employer name as a static field.

And with that, all the Employee objects that we are going to create, they are going to have the same data under the employerName field. This is very similar to the four Wheeler example that we have discussed for the car scenario. So with the help of static variables, we can store the data that is common to all the objects, such as a constant value or a read only value. In case if you want to access the static variable, we don't have to create an object.

We can simply access the static variable with the help of class name itself. Like what is your class name dot and what is your static field name? We're going to see the demo in few seconds. Whenever we try to create the static variables inside the Java classes, behind the scenes, all the static variables are going to be stored inside a memory called method area or class area. This is an area inside the JVM memory which is going to be shared by all the threads.

So what is a thread inside a Java programming? For example, think like you have deployed your code into a production server and your code is going to be invoked by the thousands of requests coming from the thousands of end users using their own laptops. So each and every user, when they initiate the request to your code, the back end server is going to assign a thread for them. So Java supports multi-threading execution as well. We are going to discuss about threading and multi threading in the coming sections.

Whatever data that we are going to store inside the static variables, it is going to be shared across all the threads. When we try to execute a Java program, JVM first loads the Java class into the memory and it will look for any static variables are present inside the class. If they are present, then it is going to initialize and store them inside the memory called method area class area and the static variables that we store inside these memories, they are going to be remain and available until the program terminates.

Like I said before, since the static variables can be accessed or shared by all the objects of the class, we can access these static variables with the help of the class name without creating any instance or object of a class, the JVM behind the scenes it will ensure that only a single copy of the static variables exist inside the memory, and all the instances are the objects that we create. They will refer to the same single copy available inside the JVM memory.

And here I want to provide an important note. All the objects that we create inside the Java, they are going to be stored inside the heap memory. Whereas the static variables that we are going to create will be stored inside the method area or class area. This method area or class area is very limited in nature compared to the heap memory because usually inside the Java programs we are going to create thousands of objects that's why we will get a lot of heap memory compared to the method area or class area.

So if you try to create too many static variables inside your classes, it may cause out of memory error. But you don't have to worry. This error you will face only if you try to create thousands and thousands of static variables, which will never be a scenario in real projects as well. We are going to talk about the JVM memory, where this objects, variables are going to be stored in the coming lectures. For now, if you try to visualize all this information first like I said, all the static variables are going to be stored in a memory called class area or method area.

So you can see there is only a single copy is going to be maintained by the JVM. If you try to create multiple objects like employee1, employee2, and employee3 all of them, they are going to refer to the same copy of employer name which is available inside the class area. You can see I have created three objects and all these three objects they are going to be stored inside the heap memory. And these objects, they are also going to have unique data under firstName, lastName, age and gender.

But coming to the employerName field, they're not going to store that employerName field and its value inside the heap memory because it's unnecessary and it will be repeated in all the objects. Since it is a common data, a unique copy of this data is going to be maintained in a memory location of class area or method area. The same will be referred by the objects which are created inside the heap memory. I hope you are clear with this theory discussion.

lectures.title: Static Initialization Block in Java class - Part 1
lectures.text:
From this slide we can see a Java class can contain below components like fields, methods, constructors, instance initializers and static initializers. As of now, we discussed everything except static initializers. Let's try to discuss what are the static initializers and what is the purpose of them. So what is a static initialization block? In Java, a static initialization block is a block of code that is going to be associated with a class, rather than the instances or the objects of the class.

Whatever code that we are going to write inside the static initialization block, it is going to be loaded by the JVM. When we try to execute the class for the first time, the primary purpose of the static initialization block is to initialize any static variables of a class. So how to define the static initialization block? It is going to be very simple. First we need to mention the static keyword followed by opening and closing curly braces. They should not be any name to your static initialization block.

And this block we need to create outside of the method and constructors, but inside the Java class. So this is one of the sample reference that you can refer. So there is a class with the name Car. And inside this I have a static variable which I just declared. The static variable name is numberOfEngines. This static variable I want to initialize when I try to execute my class. So how to achieve this with the help of static initialization block, you can see I have defined a static initialization block here and inside the body of this block, I am trying to initialize the numberOfEngines to a value called 1.

So whatever code that we mentioned inside the static initialization block, it is only going to be executed when the class is loaded into the memory of the JVM, which means it is only going to be executed only once, no matter how many objects or instances of the classes are going to be created, similar to instance initialization block the static initialization block also is not going to have any return statement. This static initialization block is very useful in the scenarios where you want to perform one time initialization of the static variables, or when the initialization logic is more complex and cannot be accommodated with a single line, which means I have some complex logic to calculate the value of a static variable, which I cannot achieve with the single line, like here I have a single line like static byte numberOfEngines.

If I want to assign a simple value, I can directly mention here is equal to and what is a value. But in some scenarios, to calculate that initialized value, we need to execute a lot of code. In such scenarios, we can move all such complex initialization logic of the static variable into the static initialization block. If needed you can have multiple static initialization blocks within a class, and all of them are going to be executed in the order in which they appear in the class definition.

Whatever code that we are going to write inside the static initialization block is going to be executed before your main() method. So inside Java, we know whenever we want to start or whenever we want to execute a Java program, we use the main() method. So the code inside the static block is going to be executed before the main() method itself, because the code inside this block is going to be invoked by the JVM when it tries to load the Java class.

Some interviewers, they can ask a tricky question for you. Can I execute a code before the main() method? So that is perfectly possible. You can do that with the help of static initialization block. I'm also going to show you this in the demo. Now very quickly let's see the difference between a static initialization block and the normal instance initializer block. The very first difference is very simple. The static block is going to have the static keyword.

Using the static keyword only, we can difference whether a given block is a static initializer block or the normal instance initializer block. Moving on to the next difference, the static blocks are going to be executed during the class loading, whereas the instance block is going to be executed during the every object creation or every object instantiation. The third difference that we have here is inside the static initialization block, we can refer only the static variables, whereas inside the instance block we can refer both static and non static variables.

And the next difference that we have here is in terms of usage of ' this ' keyword inside the static block, we cannot use the this keyword, because this keyword will come into the picture only in the scenarios of object creation or objects related code. Since static block is specific to the class, we cannot use the this keyword, whereas inside the instance block we can use the this keyword without any issues. The last difference that we have here is, this is very important.

The static block is only going to be executed only once during the lifetime of a Java program and the execution is going to be during the class loading into the memory and just before the execution of the main() method, whereas instance block is going to be executed each and every time you are trying to create an object. lectures.title: Where does Java store classes, objects, variables, methods
lectures.text:
As of now we are trying to create lot many Java classes, Java objects, Java fields, Java methods. We are creating lot of code. But do you know where all these classes, objects, variables, methods are going to be stored inside our system? Let's try to answer the same question inside this lecture. We as humans, we store the information and we try to process the information with the help of our brains. Very similarly, when you write some business logic with the help of Java classes, objects, variables and methods, JVM is going to handle the memory management.

So JVM is like our brain. It is responsible for allocating and deallocating memory for the Java programs. When we try to run a Java program at runtime, JVM is going to create various types of memory in each of the memory it is going to hold different kinds of data. So let's try to understand what are the important types of memories that are going to be created by the JVM. The very first important memory is heap memory. So what is the purpose of heap memory?

Inside this area of memory, only the objects are going to be allocated. That means whenever an object is created, a space for the object is going to be assigned inside the heap memory to store its data. And whenever the object is reclaimed, that means whenever we are done with a particular object, the space occupied by that object is going to be reclaimed by the jvm's " Garbage collector ". Behind the scenes, when we try to run a Java program, a process called Garbage collector is going to run continuously, and the job of this Garbage collector is to free up the memory by deleting the object, which we are no longer being used.

How JVM knows if I am not using a particular object or not, it is going to scan the execution of the program continuously. For example, in the previous lecture we created so many methods like method1(), method2(), method3() and method4(). As of now, you can see I'm trying to create an object inside the main() method. If I try to create the same object inside the method4(), then these variable or these object reference is going to be localized for this method only. You can see the same variable name demo object and creating both in method4() and main() method.

But the compiler is not complaining anything because both of these variables are present in a different scope, which are different methods in this case. But if you try to create another object with the same name inside the same method, you will get an error saying that variable demo object is already defined in the scope. So what is the scope here? Whatever we write inside the curly braces of a method is going to be considered as a local scope for a given method.

That's why creating the objects or creating variables with the same name is not allowed within the local scope. Now coming to the Garbage collection discussion, you can see as of now I have created a object inside the method4(). As soon as I'm done with the method4() execution, the control will go back to the method3(). At that point of time, my Garbage collector know that this demo object is no more used and it is an unused object. That's why behind the scenes it is going to delete these objects, and with that, it is going to free up the heap space for the future objects that we are going to create inside the Java code.

Just like objects, we can also create variables inside the methods. You can see here there is a variable called output inside the method2(). So this variable we call it as a local variable because this variable is going to make sense only within this method. If I try to access this output variable inside another methods, then I'm going to get a compilation error because the output is not going to make sense for other methods. So these kind of local variables are also going to be regularly deleted whenever the method execution is completed.

But please note that Garbage collector is only responsible to clean up the objects. So what are objects object we can only create with the help of reference data types like a Java class. So String also is one of the Java class. So whatever variable that we create with the help of String it is also an object. So my JVM can delete these object whenever I'm done with these method2() execution. But coming to the primitive data types like number here, the Garbage collector is not going to track these because these are only local primitive variables, but not the objects we're going to discuss in few minutes.

Who is going to maintain and delete these kind of variables inside the Java program? I hope you are clear, what is heap memory? Always remember, heap memory means it is a place where Java is going to store all the objects. After heap memory the next important memory that we have is stack memory. This is the area of memory where local variables and method calls are going to be stored. In the previous lecture, I showed a demo of method invocations where all the method invocations are going to be maintained with the help of stack data structure, so all the method invocations with the help of stack data structure is going to be saved inside the stack memory.

So whenever a new method is being called, a new stack frame is going to be created on the stack, which will contain all the methods, local variables and parameters. And whenever the method returns the execution or completes the execution, the stack frame is going to be removed along with the local variables and the parameters. So here you can see we have a local variable which is of type int. So since it is a primitive data type we can call it as a local variable instead of local object.

So whenever we try to invoke the method1(), a stack frame is going to be created inside the stack memory along with the method input parameters method local variables. Once the method is returning the execution or once the method is done with the execution, all the local variables and parameters that we stored inside the stack memory will be deleted along with the stack entry related to this method, always please remember stack memory means it is an area where method calls are going to be stored along with the local variables of a method.

After the stack memory, the very next important memory is method area or class area. This is the place where we are going to store all the class definitions, method definitions and other runtime constants like static variables are going to be stored. We previously discussed objects are going to be stored inside the heap memory. But how JVM is going to remember? What is the definition of a class? What is a method definition or what is a static variables.

So all such information are going to be stored inside the method area. This method area we also call it as class area because inside this memory only we are going to store all the class definitions. And at last the next important memory we have is native heap. This is the area of memory where native libraries and the code are going to be loaded are stored. So what is native code? When we discussed about the compilation and interpretation process of Java, I explained about a process called JIT compilation Just In Time compilation.

So what my JIT compiler is going to do, my JIT compiler is going to identify the hotspots inside my classes and methods, which are going to be executed many times or very frequently all such hotspots bytecode is going to be converted into a native executable code by the JIT compiler, and it is going to cache it inside a memory. And that memory is native heap. So this native heap is going to be used by JVM for runtime memory allocation, and to store some native related libraries and code inside this native heap my JVM is also going to create some objects with the help of native code and native libraries.

But whatever objects that JVM is going to create inside the native heap, they are not going to be tracked by the Garbage collector. My Garbage collector is only going to clean the objects inside the heap memory, but not inside the native heap. As a developer, we don't have to worry much about the native heap because JVM is going to take care of it behind the scenes. Now here you may have a question like how my JVM will have the space or disk space to create all these memories at the runtime.

Let me answer that question. Whenever we try to execute a Java program with the help of a JVM, the JVM is going to receive a portion of memory from the underlying operating system. So based upon that JVM version and the platform that you are trying to run, a portion of memory is going to be received by the JVM like 1 GB or 2 GB. Most of the times these memory is more than enough to run any large amount of Java code. But in some special scenarios where you want to customize this memory allocation to the JVM, you can do that.

But that is a very rare scenario where developers, they are going to increase the space assigned to the JVM by the underlying operating system. With this, I'm assuming you have some good understanding where Java is going to store all our classes, objects, variables, and methods. Please have this information handy always, because in any interview related to Java, there will be definitely questions around the memory like heap memory, stack memory, method area.

With that reason only, I'm trying to share this information with you. Let's continue this discussion around the memory management by JVM in the next lecture as well. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: Introduction to null in Java
lectures.text:
Null has a very important significance inside Java, let's try to understand the same inside this lecture. So what is a null, in Java null is a reserved keyword that denotes a variable or a attribute, but does not reference to any object, which means you only declared a variable by providing a reference data type, but you have not created an object or you have not assigned any object to that variable. In such scenarios, we can say that variable or attribute is going to hold the null value.

So null indicates an absence of an instance or an object associated with a given variable or field. This might be very confusing. Let me give you an example. Here you can see I'm trying to create two variables or attributes or Java fields by using the reference data types. So what are the reference data types I'm trying to use here String and Employee. How I'm saying these are reference data types because String and Employee they both are Java classes.

lectures.title: Object Destruction and Garbage collection in Java
lectures.text:
As of now, we discussed about how to create the objects inside Java. So what is the approach to create objects inside Java? With the help of the new operator and the constructor of the Java classes, we can create any number of objects. So creating of the objects with the help of Java class, in other words, we can call it as object construction. Inside this lecture let's try to discuss about object destruction. Because inside interviews, people may ask you how to destroy an object or how to remove an object inside Java.

In Java, there is no need of destroying the object or removing the object. People can try to confuse you by asking questions like how can I destroy or remove or destruct the object inside Java? So please let them know that there is no such concept, and there is no need for the Java developers to manually delete or remove the objects. If you worked on the languages like C or C++, inside these languages, it is the developer responsibility to destroy the object to clean up the memory.

Otherwise, the program which is written with the help of C or C++ it is going to have some memory leaks and eventually the memory execution will fail. But Java is different. You don't have to stress about manually getting rid of things that you have created like objects, because inside Java we have Garbage collector. So behind the scenes there is a process that is going to run continuously, which is going to keep an eye on all the objects and things that you are trying to create.

If this Garbage collector identifies that a particular object is no more going to be used in such scenarios, the Garbage collection is going to free up the memory that is occupied by the particular object by deleting it. So with the help of Garbage collection in Java, the developers, they never have to worry about destroying the objects. They can always focus on the creating the objects and building the business logic. The memory management inside Java is going to be taken care by the JVM automatically, with the components like Garbage collection. Behind the scenes, this Garbage collection, they are going to follow some algorithms to identify the unused objects.

If we talk about the old JVM's, which Java used to use a decade back, they used to follow an algorithm with the name mark and sweep. By using these algorithm, the Garbage collector process which is going to run behind the scenes, it is going to mark all the objects that were still being used by the JVM. With that, whatever objects which are not marked, the JVM is going to sweep them away and free up the space. But this approach has some issues, like JVM used to take some passes in between the cleanup of the objects.

That's why sometimes the cleaning up the objects is going to take more time, because regularly JVM is taking a pass to overcome this disadvantage in the latest JVM's that are introduced in the latest versions of the Java new Kind of Modern Garbage collectors are introduced, which are smarter, and they can work continuously without causing any delays. These modern Garbage collectors, they are going to divide the memory into multiple sections. For example, they can keep all short lived objects separately in a quicker cleanup area compared to long lived objects.

So these are with the help of modern Garbage collectors nowadays, Java and JVM is doing a great job in terms of object destruction and the memory management at runtime. Sometimes you may end up in a scenario where you want to manually tell to the Garbage collection process to initiate the cleanup as soon as possible. In such scenarios, you can manually initiate this process of cleanup or tell to your JVM to speed up this process by invoking a static method available inside the System class.

So what is this method? GC means Garbage Collector. If you try to invoke this gc() method inside System class, it is going to give a nudge to your Java JVM to clean up the Garbage collection process. But please note that it is not a guarantee that your JVM or Java are your Garbage collection always going to listen for you? It is going to be completely random. Sometimes it is going to simply ignore it if it has some other priorities. Let me show you this Garbage collection invocation manually in the inter-league as well.

You can go to any of the classes that we have created, and inside any of the methods, you can simply invoke the class with the name System. After this class name you can mention dot operator followed by gc(). gc means Garbage Collector. This is a static method. That's why I'm able to invoke it without creating the object of System class. If I go inside the documentation of this GC method by hovering on this method, you can see I'm getting a hyper link because I'm holding the command button inside my mac system.

Whereas inside the windows operating system, you need to hold the control button and hover your mouse onto this gc() method. And with that, you'll be able to see a hyperlink. If I click on this hyperlink, I'll be taken to the System.java class, which is available inside the libraries of the Java. You can also see that documentation of this method which is mentioned on top of this method. There are details about this method. What is going to happen when we call this method?

Inside these commands, they clearly highlighted. There is no guarantee that this effort will recycle any particular number of unused objects. That's why please make a note that System.gc() always will not trigger the Garbage collection process. Sometimes if your JVM has other priorities, it can simply ignore your request. This point is going to be a very important question for the interviews inside the interviews, they can ask you about what is Garbage collection, and once you answer about the Garbage collection, they can also ask you how to invoke the Garbage collection process manually.

But this question you can answer by simply saying that with the help of System.gc()method, I can invoke the process of Garbage collection manually, but there is no guarantee that my JVM or Java is going to accept my request. I hope you are clear about object destruction in Java. In simple words, there is no need of object destruction inside Java, and the Garbage collector is going to take care of it. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.
