In this lecture let's try to talk about the multi line comments approach in Java. Whenever we want to write multi line comments inside Java we should always start with / immediately followed by an asterisk mark. Once you have mentioned these forward slash followed by asterisk mark you can define any number of lines of comments. Once you have mentioned all your lines of comments at the end, you need to close the comments with the help of asterisk followed by forward slash.

So anything that you are going to write in between the starting and the ending of your multi line comment symbols is going to be considered as a comment by your Java compiler, and all the content that you have written inside these comments will be ignored by the compiler. Here you may have a question which is if we already have single line comments, why do we need to follow the multi line comments approach? Let me try to answer the same. In some scenarios, we may not be able to explain the complexity of our Java code within a single line of comment.

In this kind of scenarios we can use multi line comments approach. Apart from explaining complex code of logic, we can also try to document a purpose of a class, a purpose of the method with the help of multi line comments. Apart from documenting, we can also comment multiple lines of code at a time. For example, if you want to comment out entire method, you can comment out with the help of multi line comments. When I say comment you want to temporarily disable or temporarily ignore certain lines of Java code.

So that process we call it as comment. In the previous lecture, when we were discussing about the single line comment, we were able to comment, method invocations or a single line of Java code, but with the help of multi line comments, we can comment multiple lines of Java code at a time. Let's try to understand few examples here around the multiple line comments like you can see here I have a class Customer. If I want to explain the purpose of this class to other developers, or if I want to document the purpose of this class for my future reference, I can achieve that with the help of multi line comments.

Once I'm satisfied with my lines of comments, I need to terminate our closer multi line comments with the symbol asterisk followed by forward slash.

Very similarly, you can also try to document the purpose of a method. So here you can see I have a method with the name calculate rectangle area. So that's what I tried to document with the help of multi line comments.

Very similarly, we can comment entire class or multiple lines of code by following the same syntax. Sometimes you may see few developers they try to achieve the multi line comments with a single line comments. For example, you can see first I have a multi line comment where I'm trying to mention an example of a multiple line comment. The same multi line comments we can also try to achieve with the help of single line comments. So how the developer is achieving here?

He's trying to mention the single line comment symbol at every line of comment. So you may see this kind of strategy as well by few developers. And these strategy may work only for certain limited number of lines of comments. If you have more lines of comments like five lines or ten lines, then always the easiest and recommended approach is to follow the multi-line comments instead of mentioning the single line comment syntax before each line of comment.

I hope you are clear why we should avoid single line comment when you are trying to define multi-line comment. The last point that I want to discuss here is, we can write multi-line comment in the middle of a Java code. This may be surprise for you because for single line command we saw that it is a limitation whenever we try to use a single line comment in the middle of a Java code, it is going to throw a compilation error, whereas a multi-line comment can be written or inserted in the middle of a Java code.

With this, I'm assuming you're clear about what is multi-line comments. The summary is very simple. As of now, we discuss two types of comments inside Java. Now is the time to discuss the last type of comments in Java, which is javadoc comments. lectures.title: Introduction to String Pool in Java - Theory
lectures.text:
In the previous lecture, I told you that String is a special data type compared to other primitive data types that we have in Java. Because string has its own charm and capabilities. Throughout this section, you're going to see and understand the charm of String. And by the end of this section, you're going to agree with me that String is something different compared to other primitive data types. I also told you that we can save data with the help of String data type by using two different approaches.

The very first approach is by simply creating the literal or variable, by following the same syntax of primitive data type. The other approach is we can try to create an object of String class with the help of new operator and the constructor. But here you may have many questions, what is the difference between these two approaches and when to use which approach? That's why inside this lecture, let's try to understand the difference between these two approaches.

Inside the very first approach, we can simply store the data inside the String variable by following the same syntax of primitive data types. Here I'm trying to assign a value hello to the variable str. So the declaration and the initialization is very simple here. So whenever I'm using these kind of syntax to store the data with the help of String data type behind the scenes, Java is going to create an object of the String. Don't assume that since we are using primitive data type syntax to store data here, the str variable is not going to be an object regardless of which approach you're going to use.

Always remember inside Java, the data that we store with the help of String data type is going to store as an object. But when we use these primitive data type syntax approach, there is a concept called String pool come into picture. Whenever you are trying to store data with the help of this first approach. First, my Java JVM will check if there is any memory location where we have stored the same String data. If there is such memory location, then my JVM is not going to create a new object of String.

By this time, it should be pretty clear for you that a String is a combination of multiple characters. For example, if I try to store Java String data inside a String object, my String is going to have multiple characters like j, a, v, a. Sometimes you may have a requirement to fetch a character or to find a character which is available at a specific index inside your String. So what is an index? Index represents the position of the character inside your String data.

To fetch a character from a specific position within a String object, we can use the charAt() method. This charAt() method is a non-static method or an instance method, which we can invoke only by using the object of the String. Here you need to be aware about an important point inside String whenever we want to understand the position of a character, we should always start the index at the position from zero. But not the one. For example, like you can see here, I have a String object which is holding the Java word.

lectures.text:
Searching for a given value inside String is a most common scenario in real projects. For example, think like I have a sentence stored inside a String object. The sentence goes like this my name is Madan. If I want to search this String, if it contains my name which is Madan, I need to search for it. If the name Madan available inside the given String, then it is a match otherwise it is not a match. So how to perform this kind of searching in a given String data, there are multiple approaches to search a given String.

The very first approach is with the help of indexOf() method. indexOf() is a instance method or a non-static method, which we can invoke with the help of String object. To this indexOf() method, you need to pass what you are trying to search and to whatever input data that you have provided to this indexOf() method is going to be searched inside the original String that you have provided, and if there is a match for your given input data, then this indexOf() method is going to return the index number at the position where the given word or given data is available inside the original String.

Here you can see I have an example where inside the original String I stored that data, which is Hello, World!. If I want to understand if my original String as a word world or not, I can use this indexOf() method and to this indexOf() method I can pass the input which is world. Since this world word is available inside my String data, this indexOf() method is going to return the index value at the position where my world word is starting inside my String. We can see what is the index number that we are getting in this scenario as part of the demo.

But how about the negative scenario? Think like whatever input data that you have provided to these indexOf() method is not available inside your original String. In such negative scenarios, the output from the indexOf() method is going to be -1. So whenever you are getting index value as -1, that is an indication to you that given String data is not available inside the original String. So these are very first method which will help you to identify whether the given data is available inside the original String.

The next approach is with the help of contains() method. This contains() method is going to give you an boolean value as an output, just like indexOf() method. This method also is going to accept input data, and if the input data is available inside the original String, you're going to get true. Otherwise you're going to get false. Here inside the example you can see under the third Java statement for the contains() method, I have passed the @ symbol to search if it is available inside the original String.

So inside the original String. Since I don't have the special character, I'm going to get the output as false. So these two methods, they are going to give you an indication whether the given input data is available or not. But there is other flavors of searching a value as well. The other flavor that we have is startsWith() and endsWith(). Sometimes you may want to understand whether your String is starting with a specific word or ending with a specific word or a specific letter.

The requirement can be anything you are more concerned about the starting value or ending value. In such scenarios, you can use these instance methods that are available inside String class, which are starts with and ends with to the startsWith() method If you provide an input, it is going to check whether the original String is going to start with your input data. If yes, it is going to give a boolean value. Very similarly, endsWith() method is going to look at the end of the string if it is ending with the given input data.

Apart from these three approaches, we also have fourth approach which is matches() method. This matches() method can be used for more complex search operations. To overcome this challenge, we have a printf() method available inside Java. So how to invoke the printf() method? Let me show you that it is going to be very similar, like I'm going to mention first System post that I'm going to invoke out, and after the out, I need to invoke the printf() method and this printf() method first it is going to accept the format string like I can pass this entire content directly to the printf() method. Post that it is going to take care of printing the given string onto the console. I can show you the demo of this line as well by executing the program. lectures.text:
For the next few lectures, we are going to talk about the string immutability concept. I already gave a quick introduction in the previous lectures. That string is an immutable object. What is the meaning of immutable? Something cannot be changed once it is created. Whatever objects that we are going to create with the help of String class, they are always going to be immutable. Just like how we can't change the tattoos once created. Similarly, once a string object is created in Java, we cannot change the content of that String object.

If needed, we can forcefully remove the tattoos with the help of some laser. But altering the String object is impossible in Java. Does that mean we don't have any option inside Java to create mutable string content? No. We have certain companion classes for the String class. The classes like StringBuilder and StringBuffer. Using these classes, we can modify the content of the string data, and we can make the string data mutable. Before we try to discuss about how to create a mutable string data with the help of StringBuilder and StringBuffer.

First let me share you more details about the immutability concept of string. Here I have an example like you can see first, I'm trying to create a s1 string object, and inside this string object I'm trying to store the string data, which is hello. In the very next line by using the same String object, I'm trying to assign a new data, which is Hello World! This may give an illusion to you that we are able to change the content of the String object data, but that is not going to happen.

Let's try to understand what is going to happen behind the scenes. Then you're going to agree with me that String objects are always immutable like you can see here. First we are going to have a heap memory. The heap memory is going to be empty before you try to start your program. Now think like I'm trying to execute a Java statement which is String s1 = Hello. As soon as we try to execute this Java statement, a String object will be created inside the Heap memory and the same will be stored in a memory location.

How we can access that memory location with the help of s1, which is the object reference name or the variable name. Now think like I'm trying to execute the next Java statement, which is s1 = Hello World. So to the same object reference, I'm trying to assign the new String content. If we try to execute this second statement, let's see how the Heap memory is going to look like. Like you can see here a new String object behind the scenes is going to be created inside your heap memory at a different location.

And this new object is going to hold the new content, which is Hello World to this new object or to this new memory location. Your object reference are your String variable is going to refer. So whatever object which was previously created, it is going to become an orphan object. At some point of time, my Garbage collector is going to collect it and destroy it. With this, it should be pretty clear for you when we say string immutability, the immutability applies to the String objects that are stored in a memory, not the reference variable, which means we can use the same reference variable for the new string content as well.

But behind the scenes, the same reference variable is going to be pointed to a new object which is stored in a new memory location. If you are looking for an option where you don't want to give any flexibility to other programs to change the content of your String object, then you can use the final keyword whenever you are trying to create your String object. Here I have an example where when I'm trying to declare and initialize my String object, which is s1, I have mentioned final keyword with that in future if someone is coming, if they're trying to change my Java program by trying to assign new content to the s1 object, then they are going to get a compilation error.

I can quickly show you this in the demo as well. For the demo I have created a Java class which is StringImmutableDemo. Inside the class we have a main() method and inside the main() method you can see first I have created a String object which is s1 and to this I'm trying to assign a hello and post that I'm trying to assign Hello World. With this, I'm getting an illusion that I'm able to change the String data, but like we discussed, we cannot change the String object behind the scenes a new String object is going to be created with the new content, and the previous old object will be deleted or destroyed by the Garbage collector.

So if I try to run this program, you can see I'm getting an Hello World as an output. Now let me show you how to use a final keyword and how to avoid changing the string content inside our Java programs. For the same, I'm going to create a new string object with the name s2 for the same s2 I'm going to assign the content which is high. So this is the normal syntax that we usually follow. If I keep a final keyword just before the string, then this object, whatever we have created is going to become final and no one can alter the content, and at the same time they cannot reuse the s2 object reference name to create another String object.

For example, for the same s2 object reference if I'm trying to assign a new content, which is Hi World, I'm going to get a compilation error if let me show you the error details by hovering on to this, you can see I'm getting an error message saying that cannot assign a value to final variable s2. So this is one of the smartest way to avoid reusing the same object reference of string for the new data. So let me remove this compilation error and I'm going to check in this file for your reference into the GitHub repo.

With this, I'm assuming you are clear about the immutability concept of String. So now you should be able to answer any questions around the String immutability concept. As a next step, let me show you how to create the mutable string data with the help of StringBuilder and the StringBuffer. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: How to create mutable strings in Java
lectures.text:
We know when we create objects with the help of String, they are going to be immutable. So how to build a mutable String data. There are three different approaches to build a mutable string values inside Java. The very first approach is with the help of StringBuilder. Using this class we can create, update, delete, insert string data, whatever update operation that you are going to do with the help of StringBuilder. The string data is going to keep changing on a single StringBuilder object.

Unlike string, the StringBuilder object reference is always going to point to the same object. Here you can see I have given an example whenever you want to store String data with the help of StringBuilder, you need to first create an object of StringBuilder with the help of new operator and a constructor of the StringBuilder, and to the constructor of StringBuilder. You can either invoke the default empty constructor or to the constructor of the StringBuilder.

You can also pass the input string data. Here inside the example, I'm trying to pass the hello as an input string data, so by the time my StringBuilder object is going to create, it is going to hold hello string data inside it. Later on, if I want to append new information to the same StringBuilder object, I can invoke the method which is append() available inside the StringBuilder. Using append(), I can try to update my original string with the new string.

Here I'm trying to invoke the append() and I'm trying to add new content, which is space world. And with that, whenever we try to print out these StringBuilder object by converting into string, we are going to get the output as Hello world! This way we can always update the String data with the help of StringBuilder object. Once you feel like that, you are done with the update operations of your string data. At last, you can invoke the toString() method to convert your StringBuilder into a String object.

Just like StringBuilder we also have another option which is StringBuffer. StringBuffer is also going to work very similar to StringBuilder. The way you create the objects, the way you append the data to the StringBuffer object, everything is going to be same as StringBuilder. But the reason why we have two options in the form of StringBuilder and StringBuffer is StringBuffer objects are thread safe, whereas StringBuilder they are not thread safe.

Whenever you are trying to run your Java programs, you can run them in an multi-threading environment. We are going to talk about what are threads and what are multi-threading environments in the coming sections. For now, please note that thread is like a process that is going to accept the request from a single user. So if your Java code is deployed into a production server and if there are many end users, they are trying to access your Java code, then each end user they are going to get a thread.

So using the threads the Java program is going to be executed in an isolated environment. So if your program is going to be executed in an multithreading environment, it is always advisable to use the StringBuffer. Because whatever objects that you are going to create with the help of StringBuffer, they are thread safe, whereas StringBuilder objects, they are not thread safe. So if you ask me when to use StringBuilder and when to use StringBuffer, I would say you can always use the StringBuilder.

If you know that your code is going to be deployed in a single threaded environment, and if you are looking for a higher performance and thread safety is not a concern, then in all such situations you can use StringBuilder. Otherwise, if you are looking for an option where your code is going to be deployed in a multi threading environment, and you want to make sure that thread safety is always followed in that scenario, always go with the StringBuffer.

As of now, we are able to update the content of the StringBuilder and StringBuffer objects with the help of append() method. Apart from the append() method, these classes, they have many instance methods using which we can try to update the string content that we are trying to store inside the objects of Stringbuilder and StringBuffer . Apart from these mutable operations methods, StringBuilder and StringBuffer, they also have an important method which is reverse() method.

Whenever you invoke this reverse() method, with the help of the objects of StringBuilder and StringBuffer whatever content that you stored inside the objects of these classes will be reversed and stored as a new content. lectures.title: Converting String to primitive data type values - Theory
lectures.text:
Few lectures back, we discuss on how to convert a primitive data into an String value. Do you remember this? I hope you remember this concept with the help of the valueOf() method, which is available inside the String, we can convert any primitive data into an string representation. For example, here I have an int value 42. If I give this 42 as an input to the valueOf()method, which is a static method inside String, I am going to get an string representation of that 42.

So what is the string representation of 42? A 42 with a double quotes value is a string representation. So this is a scenario where we want to convert a primitive data type into a String object. Sometimes we may want to convert a String object into a corresponding primitive data type. So let's try to understand how to achieve the same. The process of converting a String data into a primitive data type. We call that process as parsing. Parsing involves converting a string representation of a value into its corresponding primitive data type.

So how to perform this parsing operation? I may have an int value in the format of String, but I want to convert that into a normal into primitive value. So for this kind of parsing scenarios we need to use a wrapper classes. Do you remember long back I told you that every primitive data type it has a corresponding wrapper class. For example, for into primitive data type, we have a wrapper class with the name Integer. Inside this Integer wrapper class, we have a static method which is parseInt().

This parseInt() method is going to accept a String object as an input, and inside this String object, we need to make sure we are providing only the int values like numeric values. If you try to be oversmart and try to provide some alphanumeric values to this parseInt() method, it is going to throw an NumberFormatException. But if you give a proper int value using a String object, this pass int is going to give you an int value as an output. That's why here you can see for the parseInt() method, I'm trying to pass the string number as an input, and the return type that I'm receiving from this method is of type int primitive data type.

Very similarly, if you are trying to convert a String object which has a double value into the double primitive data type, then you need to use a corresponding wrapper class which is Double. Inside the Double wrapper class, we have a method which is parseDouble(). To this parseDouble(), if you give a String object, it is going to convert your double number from string to primitive data type. For the float, it is going to be very similar. The wrapper class is going to be Float, and inside this wrapper class we have a method which is pass float that we need to invoke.

After the float, we can see the example of Long. If you want to convert a Long string value into a primitive long value, you can use a wrapper class long. And inside this Long class we have a parseLong() method which we need to invoke, and this parseLong() method is going to convert your string data into a long primitive data type. In case if you are looking to convert your boolean string value into the boolean primitive data type value, then Boolean has a wrapper class with the name boolean where b is capital.

Inside this Boolean wrapper class, we have a method which is parseBoolean(). To this method, you need to pass your string representation of your boolean value. So here I'm trying to pass the true. So the output is going to be the true which is in the form of Boolean data type. If you try to be smart and if you're trying to send some values other than true and false, you're always going to get the output as false from this method. For example, I can pass my name as an input to this parseBoolean().

If I pass my name as an input, then obviously that will be converted into an false value. So anything other than true and false always going to be converted into a false. Otherwise, if you are going to send the true value, you're going to get the true as an output. And similarly, if you send the false as an input, you are going to get the false as an output for the number scenarios like int, long, float, and double. If you try to send some invalid values, like maybe you're trying to send a alpha value.

In such scenarios like we discussed, we're always going to get number format exception. So using the wrapper classes and invoking the static methods like parseBoolean(), parseLong(), parseInt() int parseFloat(), parseDouble(). So this is one approach there is also another approach which you can achieve with the help of constructor of your wrapper classes. So here you can see I'm trying to create an object of wrapper class Integer. During the same process I can pass the String object as an input to the constructor.

And with that, I'm going to get an object of Integer object. From this Integer object, we can fetch the actual valueOf() int, but this approach is deprecated from the Java 9. So what is the meaning of deprecated, Java team regularly they are going to deprecate some methods, some functionalities, some features. The purpose of deprecate is, in future versions they may remove these options. So here you may have a question like why Java team deprecate some features or some methods.

The answer is very simple due to some performance issues are some security concerns, the reason can be anything Java team. Whenever they found some issues, they're going to make the features or the methods or classes deprecated. So when you try to use this deprecated approach inside our projects, it is considered as a bad practice. That's why always don't use that deprecated approaches. The reason why I'm sharing this information is you may work in an project where they are using Java 8, since inside the Java 8 this is not deprecated.

You don't know that, but from Java 9 this method or this approach is deprecated. So all of a sudden a valid code inside the Java 8 is going to become invalid from the future versions like Java 9. So that's why regardless of which version you are using, please don't use this approach. As of now, we discussed the parsing process for the primitive data types like int, float, double long, boolean. How about the char value, for the char it is going to work differently because what is a String?

String is a sequence of characters. For that reason, whenever you are looking to convert your String data into an char data type, you have two different approaches. One is with the help of charAt() method. We already discussed this method. Using your String object, you can invoke the charAt() method and you can mention what is the index number. Based upon your index number, you're going to get the char as an return type value. So this is the very first approach.

And the second approach is using your String object you can invoke a method called toCharArray(). And with that you are going to get an char []. So what is an array? In the previous lectures I gave a small hint. Array is a collection of elements. So in this scenario the array is going to have multiple car elements. Suppose if you're trying to fetch a specific char element from the given array, you need to pass your index value to the array. So here you can see first I'm trying to invoke that toCharArray().

And with that I'm going to get an char []. That's why after the char I'm trying to mention square brackets using this charArray object I can pass the index which is one. So with that I'm going to get the second char, which is e, because the index I have mentioned as one. So this is the second approach. If this is not clear don't worry because this is going to make more sense to you when we discuss about the arrays in the coming sections. So this is all about the parsing process for all the primitive data types except a car data type, you can simply use the corresponding wrapper class and invoke the corresponding static parse methods like parseInt(), parseBoolean().

Whereas coming to the char, you need to invoke the methods like charAt() and toCharArray(). I hope you are clear with these three discussion in the next lecture. Let's see the demo of all these examples. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, let's try to discuss about the Logical Short-circuit AND operator and Logical AND operator. The syntax to use the Logical circuit operator is, It's very simple. First you need to mention what is your operand1 followed by you need to mention two ampersand symbols, and after these symbols you need to mention your operand2. So both operand1 and operand2 they have to be of type boolean. You have various options to mention the operand values.

You can directly mention the literal values, or you can mention the variable values, or you can mention the Java expressions. Or if needed, you can invoke a Java method as an operand, but your Java method has to return a boolean value, otherwise you're going to get a compilation error. So let's try to understand how these Logical Short-circuit AND operator is going to work. This operator in Java returns true value only if both operands are true.

If any one of your operand is false, it is going to result in false. The reason why it is referred as Short-circuit AND operator is, if the left operand, which is the operand1, evaluates to false, then this operator simply ignore operand2 or the expression inside the operand2, because anyway, even if it evaluates the operand2, the output is going to be false only. That's why to achieve some performance, this operator is always going to ignore the operand2 if your operand1 is giving the output as false, I have a table showing you the combinations of operand1 and operand2, and what will be the result when we use this Logical Short-circuit AND operator.

So you can see if both of your operands are true, then you're going to get the output as true. If one of your operand is false, then you're always going to get the output as false. In the third scenario and the fourth scenario, since the very first operand, which you are going to use on the left hand side is false, then the operand2 is not going to be evaluated. My Logical Short-circuit AND operator simply going to give the output as false and false without looking at the operand2 values.

I hope this clear. Now let's see some code examples. Here you can see I have declared a num1, num2 and num1 holds nine and num2 hold six. lectures.text:
As of now, we discuss on how to write the conditional Java statements with the help of if statements. On the very similar lines we can also use switch case statements to write conditional statements inside Java. So there are two approaches for the developers. One is with the help of if statements and the other one is with the help of switch case statement. Here you may have a question, which is why we have two different approaches inside Java and when to use which approach.

To explain you about the same. First, let me give you a problem. Think like there is a supermarket and inside this supermarket they are going to sell lot many fruits like banana, apple, grapes, pineapple, mango. So for each of the fruit the price is going to be different. So the owner of the supermarket, he asks you to develop a Java logic to determine what is the price that he has to charge to the customer based upon the fruit selected by the customer.

To solve this problem, if you go with the if statement approach, your logic is going to look like this. Like first I'm going to check if the fruit name is equal to banana if yes, I'm going to print a statement, $1 is charged and post that I can write else if statements to check apple, to check grapes to check pineapple and to check mango. And at last I can have an else statement if my fruit name is not equal to any of the valid fruit names, I'm going to print a statement which is pick a valid fruit with the help of else statement.

This may look very good for you, but if you closely observe this Java program that we built with the help of if statements, we are trying to evaluate the condition at multiple places at each if block and else if block, I'm trying to check whether my fruit name is equal to so and so value. So the condition is getting evaluated multiple times. On top of that, my code also is looking very lengthy and clumsy. So as the conditions that you have to evaluate is going to increase, the amount of code that you are going to write is also going to be increased.

On top of that, you need to evaluate the condition for each and every if and else if blocks. So to overcome this challenge we have switch case statement inside Java. So whenever you have these kind of scenarios where you have to evaluate lot many conditions, in such cases you can use more efficient approach which is switch case statement. I hope you are clear when to use switch case statement. As a next ste, let's try to understand the syntax of the switch case statement.

The syntax of the switch case statement is going to be very simple. Like you can see first we need to start the switch statement with the help of switch keyword. And after that inside the parentheses you need to write an Java expression, which is going to be evaluated only once based upon the outcome from the expression one of the case that we have defined inside the switch block is going to be executed. You can see I have so many case statements.

With the help of case, I have defined a label1, label2, label3. So if my expression is evaluated to a value which is equal to label1, then whatever statements I have written under this case is going to be evaluated. Similarly the same is going to happen for label2 and label3. If my Java expression is not evaluated to any of the label values in such scenarios, the default block is going to be executed. So under default I can write some Java statements.

And if you closely observe the syntax, we also have a break keyword used inside each of the case, including the default. The purpose of the break is whenever your expression is evaluated to one of the label, whatever Java statements that you have under that label case are going to be executed. Once these execution of this statements is completed, you want to break the flow and come out of this switch expression. If you don't have this break, then your switch case is going to execute the next case labels as well.

So this break is completely optional. If you don't mention this break keyword inside all your case labels and default block, then in such scenarios you may get an unexpected results. For example, think like this expression is evaluated to a label2. In this scenario, you might be expecting only the case label2 to be executed, but in the scenario where you are not mentioning the break, all the next label cases and the default block also is going to be executed.

So as soon as this case label2 is executed, since there won't be any break, the execution will jump to the label3. And if the label3 also does not have break statement, it will go to the last block which is default block. So to avoid this kind of behavior always make sure you are mentioning the break keyword inside each of your cases, including the default one. So we have an expression after the switch keyword. So the value that is going to be derived from this expression has to be of type byte, short, char, int, enum or String.

Remaining data types are not allowed. For example, the boolean is missing from this list and float, double, long all these values are missing from this list. That means you cannot write an Java expression, which is going to result as a boolean, or a float, or a double, or a long, whenever you are using the switch case statement. On top of that, one more important point that you need to take care is whatever label1, label2 values that you are going to define against each of the case.

They have to be compile time constant expressions. You can't define a variable or an expression against these labels like label1, label2 and label3. . I'm going to show you all these in demo. Then it is going to make more sense to you. So whenever you are trying to build a switch case statement, by following this syntax, all these steps are going to be executed. First the Java expression is going to be evaluated and based upon the value derived, one of the case label will be selected and all the statements inside the case label block will be executed by the switch statement.

So this way with the help of switch case statement also, we're able to control the execution of the Java statements. Let me show you an example on how to write the switch case statement by taking the same supermarket example. Here you can see first I have a fruit name as mango. So this fruitName variable I'm trying to send as an expression to my switch statement. At runtime, my switch statement is going to look what is the fruitName value that I have under the variable fruitName.

Accordingly, it is going to select one of the case label. For example, here we have a mango as an value. So it will go to the mango case block. And inside the mango case block we have System.out.println() which is $3 charged. Post that we have a break statement. You can see this time the code is looking very neat and we are not evaluating the condition at the multiple places. We are simply evaluating that Java expression only once and based upon the value from the Java expression, we are going to execute one of the case.

I hope you are clear. Now let me share more important details about the switch case statement. Like I said before, whenever you are trying to use the switch case statement, please make sure that your expression is not going to evaluate a value of type boolean, long, float, and double. Even if you try to pass a variable of type boolean, long, float and double to your switch statement, you are going to get an compilation error. And the second point that I want to highlight here is the break statement, like we discussed is used to exit the switch statement once the corresponding code segment is executed.

Otherwise all the following cases will be executed. That's why always make sure you are mentioning the break statement inside your switch case statement. If you closely look at this switch case statement, the last case that we have is default. So default also has a break statement. And here you may have a question which is anywhere below the default we don't have any other cases to be executed with that assumption you might be thinking why should we mention break statement inside the default?

I agree with you. Technically the final break is not required because the flow anywhere falls out of the switch statement, but using a break statement is strongly recommended so that in future, if any of the other developer he's trying to add more number of cases after the default case in such scenarios, if the new developer forget to mention the break statement, then in such scenarios you are going to get unexpected result that's why always make sure you are maintaining the break statement in all the case statements, including the default.

As of now, you can see inside my switch case statement, I'm using an expression which which is going to be evaluated as a String object. So using the String object inside the switch expression is allowed only from the Java 7 version. Before Java 7 version, we are only allowed to use int, byte short, but from Java 7 even the String objects are also allowed to use as part of the switch expression. Let's see what do we have as a next point? The next point is related to that default label that we have.

So here inside the program, I have mentioned the default label at the end, but it is not mandatory. You can always build your switch case statement without default label as well. On top of that, whenever you are defining the default label, you don't have to be the last label. You can use this default label even at the starting or in the middle of the switch case statement. And please note that at max we can only define one default label inside switch case statement.

I hope you are clear about that default label. Now moving on to the normal case labels. Whenever you are trying to define case labels inside a switch statement, we cannot define two case labels with the same value. For example, here I have a case banana, I can't create one more case with the same banana that is not allowed, and I'm going to get a compilation error that is very obvious. Why do we want to maintain duplicate cases or conditions inside our program?

And the last important point that I want to highlight here is, what our case labels that we have defined inside our switch case statement we need to make sure these values like banana, apple, grape. So all of them they should be compile time constant. Like I said before, I can't define a String variable or String object or a Java expression as a case label. I should always make sure I'm mentioning a compile time constant value otherwise I'm going to get a compilation error.

I hope you are clear with these points. Now very quickly let me show you the same program with a different flavor. Here my requirement is for both banana and apple, I should charge the same $1 in this kind of scenarios, where you want to have a common logic for different cases, you can achieve that easily by following these kind of syntax. You can see first I have mentioned the case banana. Immediately I have mentioned a different case, which is case apple.

And at these two cases I can define my Java statements which are going to be executed if my fruit name is banana or apple. So whenever you have this kind of common business requirements, you can also try to have a common Java statements for multiple case labels. So whatever we are discussing right now this is a switch case statement. But from Java 14 a new syntax of switch statement is introduced. And the name of that switch statement is switch expression.

Obviously there are some drawbacks with the switch case statement, that's why Java team they have introduced a new form of switch statement which is with the name switch expression. So the switch expression is more convenient to use compared to the switch case statement. So we are going to discuss about the switch expression as well in the coming lectures. But here you may have a question then if there is a more convenient way which is switch expression is available inside Java, why are you teaching us about the switch case statement?

The question is very valid, but let me clear your question. Though a new switch expression is introduced inside Java. The Java team did not removed or deprecated the switch case statement. Even today from the latest versions of Java, you can use either switch case statement or switch expressions. Both of them are valid and many Java projects which built before Java 14 they will have lot of these switch case statements inside the Java code. So that's why as Java developer, you should know the both flavors of the switch statement.

Once you understand both flavors of the switch statements, it's up to you which one to use based upon your business requirements. You may work in an legacy project or a world project where they might be using a Java version which is less than Java 14. In such scenarios, you don't have any option. You have to use the switch case statement. Whereas if you are going to work on a Java project where they are going to use the version which is above or equal to Java 14, then obviously you're going to always go with the switch expression, because that supports more convenient syntax.

I hope you are clear with this very quick introduction about the switch statement in the next lecture, first, let me try to build a Java program with the help of switch case statement. Once we are clear about everything about the switch case statement, we can explore the switch expression as well. Thank you bye.

lectures.title: break statement - Theory
lectures.text:
Branching statements inside Java helps to jump the flow of the execution from one part of a program to another part. Inside Java there are three branching statements. One is the break statement and the second one is continue, and the last one we have is return statement. So for the next few lectures we are going to focus on these branching statements. And we are going to learn in detail about these branch statements when to use them, what are the rules that we need to follow.

So all these kind of discussion we are going to do for the next few lectures. Inside this lecture, first let's try to focus on the break statement. We already saw how the break is going to help to terminate the flow of the execution inside the switch case statements. Very similarly, if you use these break statements inside a loop that you have developed with the help of for loop or while loop or do while loop, this break statement is going to help you to prematurely exit a loop based upon the condition that you have defined.

So there are two types of break statements that we can define. The very first one is labeled break statement and the second one is unlabeled break statement. So let's try to understand more details about the break statement by looking at few examples. Here I have a simple example. I have written a for loop. If I don't have break statement inside this for loop this for loop is going to run total ten number of times. It is going to print all the numbers right from 0 to 9.

But if you closely observe my for loop inside my for loop business logic, I have written an if condition. Whenever the I value become five I'm trying to use the break statement, and with that, my entire for loop execution is going to be stopped, and any other further iterations that is supposed to run will not be executed. Because with the help of this break statement, we are coming out of the for loop execution, regardless of how many more iterations it's supposed to run.

Here, you may have a question, we are trying to break the for loop as soon as the I value become five. Why can't we control the same inside the for loop definition? Maybe instead of i < 10, I can define i less than five so that whenever the i value become five, the System.out.println() is never going to execute. I agree with you to make you understand. I have given this small example, but in real projects you will face more complex problems. For example, your method may receive 100 different numbers as an array.

So from these array of numbers, maybe you are looking to find a specific number. So you will keep looping all the elements of the array one by one. At certain point of time whenever you identify the given searching number inside the array, you don't want to continue the for loop iteration because you already found the result that you are looking in such scenarios, you can simply break out of the for loop. I'm also going to show you a demo of these example in few minutes.

So whatever break we are using right now here it is an unlabeled break. So whenever we use a break statement inside a for loop, when the given condition is met, it is going to break the execution of the for loop. And the execution will be continued with the statements that we have outside of the for loop. Now let me show you an another example where we are trying to use the labelled break statement. Here you can see I have two for loops, one is outer for loop and the second one is a nested for loop.

For both these for loops I have given a label. So for the first outer for loop I have given a label as outerForLoop. So after mentioning this label you can give the colon. And with that this entire outer for loop is going to have a label or a name which is outerForLoop. Very similarly for the inner for loop also I have given an label which is innerForLoop. So I have a logic here inside my inner for loop and whenever a condition is met like i == 3 , I'm trying to mention the break.

If I simply mention the break, the inner for loop only is going to be stop. The outer for loop is not going to be impacted. So from my inner for loop, if I want to stop the outer for loop also, then in such scenarios I can use this label. After the break, I am mentioning the label which is outerForLoop. So whenever I mention this break with the label, my JVM is going to look for the for loop with a given label. So the label that we have given is outer for loop.

And with this label we have an for loop which is outside of my inner for loop. So with this, my JVM is going to stop the iteration of the outer for loop. And whenever the execution of the outer for loop is stopped, obviously the inner for loop execution is also going to be stopped. So this is how we can use the labeled break statements as well based upon our own requirements. I hope you are clear with these quick introduction about the break statement.

If something is not clear, don't worry. In the next lecture, I'm going to show you a few examples on how to use these break statement. As of now, I'm trying to explain everything with the help of for loop, the same kind of behavior you can also achieve inside the while loop or do while loop as well. So any loops where you are trying to use the break statement, the syntax is going to be the same and the behavior also is going to be the same. The break is going to help you to prematurely exit the loop based upon the condition that you have defined.

Let's see the demo of this break statement in the next lecture. Thank you, bye.

lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, let's focus on the continue statement. With the help of the break statement, we can prematurely exit from the loops of for while or do while, whereas with the help of continue statement, we can only skip the current iteration. We can't skip or exit the entire for loop our entire while loop or do while loop. We can only bypass or we can only skip the current iteration. So let's try to understand more details about the continue statement.

Like I said before, a continue statement can be used inside the for loop while loop and a do while statement. Whenever you are trying to use a continue statement, you have two options. One is with the help of labeled continue and the other one is with the help of unlabeled continue. First, let me show you an example of unlabeled continue. Like you can see here, I have written an for loop, which is going to print the numbers from 0 to 9. But if my requirement is to print only the odd numbers but not the even numbers, I can write a small logic inside my for loop.

The logic is if i exactly divisible by two, then in such scenarios I can simply mention continue. So since there is a continue statement, the current iteration will be skipped. That means the System.out.println() is not going to be executed. Simply, my for loop is going to run the next iteration. So this is one of the way of using the continue statement with the help of unlabeled form. Because here we're not giving any label. If you have scenarios where you have written nested for loop or nested while loop or nested do while loops.

In such scenarios you can use the labeled continue statement. Here you can see I have two for loop. For the outer for loop I have given the name as outer, whereas for the inner for loop I have given the label name as inner. If I simply mention continue, the continue statement is going to skip the current iteration of my inner for loop. But if I'm looking to skip the current iteration of the outer for loop, then in such scenarios I need to use the label statement like continue outer.

I hope this is clear. lectures.title: Local variables & Scope - Theory
lectures.text:
As of now we gained knowledge inside this course on how to build a conditional logic with the help of if statements and looping logic with the help of for loop, while loop, do while. So we have done a lot of discussion around the conditional statements and branching statements with this knowledge now you should be able to easily understand about a new concept which is local variables and scope. At the starting of the course, we discussed about instance variables and static variables that we can create as part of the class definition.

But what are these local variables? So let's try to understand the same. Local variables are the variables that are declared inside a method or a block. When I say block, it can be an if block or for loop block or while block, or do while block or switch block. So whenever you define a variable inside a block or a method that variable, we can call it as local variable and the scope of it is going to be limited to the block or the method in which it is declared.

When I say scope, the meaning is we can only access that variable only within the area where we have defined that variable. If I declared a local variable within a if block, then I can access that variable only within that if block. So the scope is going to be limited to that if block itself. And we should not be able to access that variable outside of the if block. Let me give an example to make it more clear. Here you can see I have declared a method with the name my method.

Inside the method I have defined a variable x of type int and this holds a value ten. So here x is a local variable because I'm not defining this variable inside the class definition. Since this is only applicable within this method, we can call it as local variable and this local variable I can access only within this method. Outside of this method or after ending of this method, x is no longer is going to be available. So this is the example of defining a local variable inside a method.

I'm going to show you how to define local variables inside a if block or for loop or switch statement in few seconds. But before that, I want to highlight you that whenever we are defining instance variables, local variables, or static variables inside our Java class, you can use the same name and your compiler is not going to complain anything. Because when I define an instance variable, how can I access that only with the help of the object of the class, whereas a static variable or a class variable I can access only with the help of the class name, and similarly the local variable I can access only within the scope.

With that, since there is a clear difference on how to access all these kind of variables, the compiler is not going to complain anything. Even if you use the same name for an instance variable, static variable and local variable. But it is always advisable to use different and meaningful names for your variables to avoid confusion. We know instance variables are going to be stored inside the heap memory, and the class level variables are static variables they are going to be stored inside the method area or class area.

But coming to the local variables they are going to be stored inside the stack memory. So what is a stack memory? Inside the stack memory only all our method invocations, they are going to be maintained in a stack manner. Whenever we are invoking a new method, a new stack is going to be created and all the local variables related to that method, along with the method parameters, everything, they are going to be stored inside the method stack. So once the method execution is completed, the method stack is going to be destroyed.

And with that, we will not be able to access any of the local variables. As a next step, let me show you on how to declare the local variables inside the for loop. Like you can see here, I have a method with the name my method inside my method I have an for loop. Inside my for loop I have declared so many local variables. For example, i is a local variable which I can access only within my for loop. Very similarly here I have defined an variable with the name x.

So this is also a local variable, and the scope of this local variable is going to be only within the for loop. As soon as we are done with this for loop execution, I will not be able to access this x and i variables even inside the same method like the for loop is present inside a method myMethod(). Even inside this method, once I executed my for loop, I will not be able to access both of these local variables, because the scope of these local variables is restricted to the for loop that we have defined.

Very similarly, let's try to look at an another example where I'm trying to create multiple local variables inside if and else statement. Here you can see into number is equal to ten. This is a variable within the method and outside of the if and else statements. Since my if and else statements are present within the same method, they should be able to access these local variable. But whatever local variables that I have defined within my if block and else block, I will not be able to access them inside my method like outside of this if and else if I try to access one of the local variable which is square, I'm going to get a compilation error.

The same kind of concept is applicable for other kind of loops like while loop, and do while loop. But coming to the switch statement, the local variables that are going to work in a tricky manner. So let's try to understand more details about the local variables inside a switch statement. Here you can see I have an example of a switch statement. Inside my switch statement, under case2, I have defined a local variable i. So int i is equal to number.

So the same local variable I will be able to access in the following cases like inside the default, I should be able to access my i variable without any issues, even if I have other case labels like case 3 and case 4. Under my case 2 block, I should be able to access the local variable that I have defined under case 2 but case 1 will not be able to access it because by the time the case one is going to be executed. Since the i local variable is not declared, that's why if you try to access the i local variable within the case one, you are going to get the compilation error.

On top of that, whatever local variable that we have declared inside. case 2. This variable can only be accessed within the following cases after the case 2, but not outside of the switch statement. Here you can see I'm trying to print the i variable which I have defined under case 2. Since this System.out.println() is outside of my switch statement here also, I'm going to get a compilation error. I hope you are clear about how the local variables are going to work inside the switch block.

Before I try to close this lecture, I want to share the standards that you need to follow whenever you are trying to declare local variables inside your methods and blocks. So let's try to understand those. The very first best practice that you need to follow is whenever you are trying to declare local variables, please try to declare them with the narrowest scope possible. That means if you need a variable within the if block, declare it only within the if block.

Don't try to declare the local variable outside of your if block within the method, because with that, you are going to increase the scope of your local variable from if block to the method. So this best practice is going to help you in preventing the naming conflicts, and reduces the risk of the accidental modification of the variable values. And the next best practice is, try to give some meaningful variable names for your local variables, so that your code can be easily understand by other developers.

Moving on to the next best practice, always make sure to initialize the variables whenever you are trying to declare them. For primitive data types, you don't have to initialize anything because all the primitive data types, they are going to have a default value. Whereas if you are trying to declare a Person object or a String object, don't try to leave them by just declaring them. At least try to initialize them with a null value so that it gives an indication to the other developers that so and so variable object is going to hold a null value, and they need to be very careful while trying to access it, since it may result into NullPointerException.

If they don't perform the null check the next standard is, always make sure you are declaring only one variable per line. So Java allows you to define any number of variables in a single line. It's not a good practice because for other developers it is going to be super tough to read your code. So to make your code more readable and maintainable, always try to declare one variable per line moving on to the next best practice, which is avoid declaring unnecessary variables.

If you don't need a variable inside your business logic, then don't declare it so this is the simple thumb rule that you need to follow. Otherwise you will have so many unused or unnecessary variables inside your business logic, which will make your code complex to understand and clumsy. And the last, best practice that we have is keep a variable declarations close to their first use. For example, think like your method has 1000 lines of Java code and you are going to use a local variable at the line number 900.

Instead of defining this local variable at the line number one of the method, you can simply do the same just before the 900 line. That way you are going to reduce the scope of the local variable. When I say scope in this scenario, all the lines below 900 line, they will not be able to access your local variable because you have not declared it otherwise if you declare it at the very first line, then your local variable can be accessed to write from line number two.

So to avoid these kind of situations or error prone scenarios, you can always try to declare local variables close to their first use. With this, I'm assuming you're clear about what are local variables and the scope of them. I know you may have some questions. Let's try to see the demo of this local variables in the next lecture. Thank you bye.

lectures.title: Introduction to packages & benefits of them
lectures.text:
What is a package in Java? With the help of packages, we can organize the Java code like Classes, Interfaces, Enums and Annotations into namespaces. In other words, a package is a collection of related Classes, Interfaces, Annotations, and Enums grouped together in a single unit. Why should we group our Java code with the help of packages? Because we do have certain advantages when we use packages inside Java projects. So let's try to understand what are those advantages.

The very first advantage is with the help of packages, we can organize large code bases into logical units, making it easier to manage and maintain code. In the previous lecture, I showed you some videos where the fruits and plants they are organized into logical units or logical groups. Very similarly, inside real projects. We have thousands of Java classes. Since we are going to have lots and lots of classes inside real projects, it is always advisable to organize them into logical units.

For example, think like you are working in an application related to a bank inside this bank related projects. You may build a business logic to handle functionality related to saving account, current account, credit card, debit card, home loan, personal loan, vehicle loan. So there are lot many functionalities that you are going to build inside your Java project. So when you are creating a Java class or an interface, Annotation or Enum, it is always advisable to create them in the package associated to their business logic.

Maybe you're trying to build a business logic inside a Java class which is related to a credit card. So all credit card related business functionality. You should try to group together in a separate package so that it is going to make your life easy in future, whenever you want to manage and maintain your code, the next advantage that we have is Encapsulation. Packages provide a way to encapsulate the classes and interfaces. When I say encapsulate with the help of packages, we can hide the business logic or implementation details from other packages or from other parts of the Java application.

So encapsulation is a mechanism to hide the business logic from other packages or from other modules or other Java projects. The same we are going to achieve with the help of packages. The very first approach is whenever you want to define packages inside your Java project. You can do that by considering your business functionality.

Think like you have a Java project, and inside this Java project, you're going to build a business logic around the Employee, Vehicle, User. So in these kind of scenarios you can create packages focusing Employee, Vehicle and User. For example here you can see I have a package which is com.eazybytes.employee. The second approach is based upon the Architectural patterns. Usually any Java project, when they're trying to build a business logic for a production application, they're not going to write all the business logic inside a single method or inside a Java class.

Instead, they are going to build the logic in different layers. For example, we may have model layers, service layer, utility layer, control view layer, and presentation layer. So these are the most commonly used layers inside the Java applications. For example, inside the model layer we are going to create all the Java classes which are going to hold the data of an application. Here I can also give an example. Think like you have an UI application, and there is a back end logic written with the help of Java.

If the UI application wants to send the data of a person from UI browser to the backend, it is going to send that with the help of a Java class. Like we can create a Java class with the name Person. And inside this Person we can create all the fields related to the person, like what is his firstName, what is his lastName, and what is his mobileNumber. So we are going to have simply fields, but no other Java methods. So these kind of classes we are going to call them as Pojo classes are entity classes.

When I say Pojo, Pojo, plain old Java objects, we are going to discuss about Pojo classes in the coming lectures, but for now, please note that Pojo classes are entity classes which you are going to write inside the model layer. They are simply going to have the fields to hold the data that we get from the UI. And similarly, whenever the back end layer want to send the data to the UI in such scenarios also we are going to use these kind of Pojo classes, all these Pojo classes we are going to write inside the model layer.

Similarly we also have service layer. Service layer is responsible for implementing the actual business logic, processing the data received from the model layer. It typically contains classes and methods that performs data validations, transformation of the data, and other business logic. In the similar lines, we also have utility layer. Utility layer is a layer where we are going to maintain all the common functionality that can be reused across the application by all the Java classes.

It typically contains helper classes, constants, helper methods. So all these kind of helper classes, helper methods we are going to maintain inside a utility layer. And after the utility layer we have controller our view layer. So this layer is responsible for handling the user input that we are going to receive from the UI. And similarly from this layer only we are going to send the data to the UI. So it typically contains classes that handles and accept the HTTP request map the URLs that are invoked to the service methods and the render views for displaying to the end user.

So all such logic we are going to write inside the controller view layer. And at last we also have presentation layer. Presentation layer is responsible for presenting the data to the user in a format that can be easily understand. It typically contains the HTML pages or HTML code that is going to help to display the mobile web pages or mobile app screens. So if you see here there are multiple layers where we are going to separate our business logic for easier maintenance or better maintainability.

So based upon these layers also you can create the packages. For example here I have created three packages co.eazybytes.model. lectures.title: Important points about packages & imports
lectures.text:
Now let's talk about a few important points that you need to be aware while you are trying to use the import statements. The very first important point is import statements inside Java they don't support or allow recursive imports. What do I mean by recursive imports? Let me show you a demo here. For example, think like I'm trying to import the package which is java.util. And inside this util I'm mentioning the wild card. So with this I'm trying to import all the classes present inside the util package.

So if I open this util package you'll be able to see under util there are so many classes, but inside the same util package there are other sub folders or other sub packages. For example, I have a reject sub folder a sub package under the util package. With this statement, please don't assume that you're going to get all the classes present inside these sub packages as well. That is not going to happen. You will be only able to access the classes present directly under this util package.

Like for example, there is a class which is ArrayList. You should be able to access it without any issues, but if you try to access a class which is present inside regex, which is like Pattern or Matcher, you're going to get a compilation error. In this kind of scenarios, you need to specifically import the classes present inside the sub package of regex as well. Like just after the util you need to mention rejects.*. I hope you are clear about the point, which is Java does not allow recursive imports.

On the similar lines java also does not support nesting package structure. Like I said before, this util package is completely different from the regex package, which is present as a sub package inside the util. You should not be under the assumption that regex and these util they both are related to each other. They are not going to be related. They will have completely different classes based upon the business requirements. Always note that Java does not support nesting package structure.

Now to explain you about the next important point, let me create some classes inside the packages that I have created.
