lectures.title: Introduction to access modifiers
lectures.text:
As of now, whenever we are trying to create a Java class or a Java method or a Java field, in all these scenarios we are using the public access modifier. But apart from public access modifiers, there are other access modifiers also available inside Java. Since these access modifiers are tightly coupled with the concept of packages, I have not discussed about them as of now. But now since we know everything about the packages, it is the right time to discuss about the access modifiers in Java.

So what is our purpose of access modifiers in Java? With the help of these access modifiers, we can specify what is the visibility of our Classes, Methods and variables or fields, which means I can control who can access my class or who can access my methods and variables. In Java there are four access modifier. The very first access modifier that we have is public. We are using these public access modifier a lot. as of now. Whenever we are using these modifier as part of the class definition or method definition or variable declaration.

In those scenarios we are letting to access our class, our method, our variable from anywhere. When I say anywhere within the class or outside the class, or from any other class which is present inside another package. There are no restrictions anyone can access our class, method or variable. The next access modifier that we have is private. So this is completely opposite of public. Whenever we are defining a private access modifier for a class, method or a variable, it can only be accessed within the same class where it is declared.

Here you may have a question which is how can I access a class within a class for that the answer is very simple. Java allows you to declare inner classes as part of a outer class. That means your Java class can contain other Java classes. When you make your inner class as an private class, that class can be only be accessed within the same class, whereas for methods and variables, it should be pretty clear for you. If you define a private method or a private variable, the method or variable can only be accessed within the same class.

So understanding public and private should be pretty simple. The third access modifier that we have is protected, when we define a class, our method or variable as protected. In such scenario, the class or method or variable can only be accessed by the classes in the same package, and subclasses which are present inside or outside of the same package. So what is a subclass? Subclass is a concept that we are going to discuss as part of the inheritance concept.

Using the inheritance concept, a Java class can inherit another Java class. That means a Java class can act as a parent to the child Java class. In this kind of scenarios, the child class we can call it as subclass. So more details about subclasses inheritance we are going to discuss in the coming sections. For now please note that when we define a access modifier protected, all the classes in the same package can access our class, method or variable.

But if one of the class which is outside of the package is trying to access them, they will be able to access only if the class is a subclass of the given class where we have defined the protected access modifier. I know it may be confusing to you to understand about protected. Don't worry, when we discuss about inheritance it is going to be super clear for you. For now, please focus on that definition. Next, moving on to the last access modifier which is default.

If you are not mentioning any access modifier for your class, method or variable, then behind the scenes Java is going to consider that default access modifier. Whenever we are using the default access modifier, it is going to provide package private access that means any class, method or variable which are using default access modifier they can only be accessed within the same package, but not from the outside of the package. I hope you are clear with these definitions.

Always make sure you are using the access modifiers to control the access to your classes, methods and variables. You should not build a business logic by using completely public access modifier or private or protected or default. You should use a mix of these modifiers based upon your business requirements. If there is a method which is going to be accessed to only within the same class, then in such scenarios it is always makes sense to make that method as private instead of public.

Why do you want to unnecessarily expose your method to the other classes or other packages? So these kind of restrictions you can achieve with the help of access modifiers in Java. Let me show you a very quick example here. Like you can see here, I have a class which is MyClass. For the class I have given the access modifier as public and inside my class there are multiple variables that I have defined like publicVar, privateVar, protectedVar. So for these variables I have mentioned the access modifiers like public, private, protected.

Whereas for the last modifier I have not mentioned any access modifier. That means the last variable which is defaultVar, it is going to have the access modifier default behind the scenes. In the similar lines, we can also define any number of static or non static methods by using these access modifiers. The very first method is using the public access modifier followed by private access modifier in the second method, and the third method is using protected access modifier.

Under class, we have a method where we have not mentioned any access modifier. Since we have not mentioned any access modifier for the last method, it is going to follow the default access modifier behind the scenes. So this is the syntax on how to use this access modifiers as part of the class definition or method definition or variable declaration. Inside these examples, like you can see, since publicVar and publicMethod has a access modifier public, they can be accessed from anywhere inside your project, even from other packages, whereas privateVar and privateMethod they can only be accessed to within the same class.

Now coming to the protectedVar and protectedMethod, they can be accessed within the same package by any class or any subclass of the MyClass, which is present even if it is present outside of the package. So what is the class name here? MyClass. So any class which is extending or inheriting my class, it is going to become a subclass. So the subclass can be present in the same package or in other package. So such subclasses, they can access my protected method and protected variable even though they are present in other packages.

And at last coming to that default variable and default method, they can only be accessed within the same package. Here I want to highlight one important point though. I made my class as public the content of the class I'm not trying to allow to access by others with the help of the private access modifier. Similarly, think like I might have declared the class as default in such scenarios, even if I have public methods and public variables inside my default class, the classes present inside another packages they cannot access my public method and the public variables.

The reason is, whenever they want to access any of the methods or fields of a class, first, they should be able to access the class without accessing the class they cannot access the method and variable even though they marked as a public. So always class is the very first entry. Once you are able to access the class post that only you should be able to access the Java fields and Java methods based upon the access modifiers defined. I hope you are clear.

I know you may have some questions around these access modifiers. In the next lecture, let's try to create some examples to clear our understanding around the access modifiers. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: Introduction to Inheritance in Java
lectures.text:
Let's try to understand what is an Inheritance. Before I try to explain you about Inheritance in Java first for a second, let's imagine we are all non-technical people. And with that assumption, let's try to answer what is an Inheritance according to a common man or a non-technical person. The meaning of Inheritance in a non-technical world means passing down of the attributes or the wealth from parents to the children. Like each one of us, we get our genes and DNA from our parents and similarly, children they will also inherit the wealth of parents if they allow.

So this is the meaning of the Inheritance in a non-technical world. The same kind of definition or concept applicable inside Java as well. So let's try to understand what is an inheritance in Java, why should we care about Inheritance inside Java? Think like you have multiple classes and in all these multiple classes you have multiple methods and fields. Sometimes you may have a requirement to maintain a same business logic, or a same method or a same field across multiple classes.

So in this kind of scenarios, what you are going to do, you are going to copy the same method or same code from one class to other classes where you want to maintain the same code. But do you think this approach is the best approach ? Off course not, because in future, whenever you want to make a small change or a new change inside this common code, then you need to change the code or the business logic in all the classes where you have copied the same code.

For example, let's imagine you have three different Java classes, and inside these three different Java classes, you have a requirement to write a same Java method or to maintain the same Java fields. As a developer, first you are going to define the logic or the fields or the methods in one of the class and the same set of code you are going to copy into the two other Java classes. But the problem comes when you have a requirement in future to make some changes inside this common code.

In such scenarios, you have to make changes in all the three places, which can be a challenging task. So to handle these kind of scenarios, we have an Inheritance concept inside Java or in any object oriented programming languages. So instead of you copying the same code to the different places, you can create a class with the common code that you want to maintain and the other classes where they want to maintain the same code they can inherit that code from the parent class or the class where you are maintaining all the common code.

This way, all your common logic is going to be present always in the parent class, and all the child classes who are inheriting the parent class they should be able to access the methods and fields with the help of Inheritance concept. We have some jargons or terminologies that we need to aware whenever we want to implement the Inheritance in Java. These jargons are like superclass subclass so there are some good amount of jargons. So let's try to understand what are those.

So the class where you are going to maintain all your common logic, whether it can be methods or fields, we can call that as a superclass or a base class or parent class, and all the remaining classes which are going to inherit from the superclass or parent class or base class, we can call such classes as subclass or derived class or child class. So this is the definition of Java Inheritance and the purpose of Inheritance in Java. I know you may have some questions around the Java Inheritance.

In the next lecture, let's try to take a scenario to understand about Inheritance in a more clear manner. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: Deep dive on Inheritance - Theory
lectures.text:
In the previous lecture we talked about Inheritance on a high level. So what is an Inheritance? Inheritance is a mechanism that allows one class to inherit the properties and behavior of another class. This is very similar to real world scenario on how a child inherits certain physical attributes and characteristics from their parent. As a next step, let's try to take a scenario and try to solve it with the help of Java Inheritance. The scenario is going to be super interesting.

This scenario revolves around the superheroes that we have in the Marvel universe. You might have seen lot many movies from the Marvel universe. So inside the Marvel Universe we have so many heroes like Iron Man, Spider-Man, Doctor Strange, Hulk, Wonder Woman. So there are many great heroes that we have inside this Marvel universe. So now let's try to take a scenario around this, and let's try to build the Java classes for each of our superheroes.

Like think like, I want to build a Java class representing three different heroes from the Marvel Universe. So these three different heroes can be IronMan, SpiderMan, and CaptainAmerica. So if you look at the three classes, they have a logic which is very similar. Like every hero, they should have a name and age attributes. So that's why these two attributes are repeated in all these three classes. And similarly all these heroes, they have the behaviors like eating, walking, sleeping and using the power.

So to reprint these behaviors I have methods like public void eat() that is going to accept the food as an input. Similarly, I also have a walk() method which will make my superhero to walk, and after the walk we have sleep() method and after the sleep() method we also have usePower() method. So if you look closely at all these methods, the same methods are behaviors are repeated in all the three classes. Do you think the behavior is going to change from one hero to other hero, off course not.

They will all eat with their own mouth. They will walk in a similar manner, they will sleep in a similar manner. Maybe using the power can be different from one hero to other hero. Like for Iron Man, he will use the power from his suit, whereas for the Spider-Man he will use the power with the help of Spider Web, for Captain America, he will have his weapon to use it as a power. So the only difference between all these three classes is on how they are going to use their power.

Remaining all the attributes and the behavior is going to be same. So with the current Java classes that we have, there is a lot of duplicate code across all the classes. So how to handle these kind of scenarios? I'm pretty confident you know the answer here. The answer is Java Inheritance. Let's try to understand how we can solve this problem with the help of Java Inheritance. Like you can see here first I'm going to create a super class with the name Person.

When we are creating a super class, we don't have to take care of any special syntax. It can be a normal Java class like you can see here. I have created a super class with the name Person by using the public class Person and inside this Person class body I have all the common code like the name age fields and the methods like eat(), walk() and sleep(). I have not put the use power() method inside the Person, because the uses of the power can be vary from one hero to other hero.

So once you define your super class like this as a next step, you need to create all your different subclasses or child classes. Like first you can see I have created the IronMan, followed by SpiderMan, followed by CaptainAmerica. If you closely look at these classes after the class name I am using, the keyword extends, with the help of extends keyword we are trying to inherit the attributes and the methods from the super class. So what is the super class that I have here, Person.

So extends Person, I need to mention immediately after my child class name or subclass name our derived class name. So the same I have done after the SpiderMan and CaptainAmerica. Now if you closely look at the child classes inside the child classes, I don't have all these common code because anyway, they are going to inherit from the parent. The only logic that I have inside my subclasses are child classes is the method usePower(). So inside this usePower() I can write different logic based upon to which hero that subclass belongs to.

I hope you are clear with this explanation. Inside Java, we are always going to return that child and parent relationship by using these upwards arrow mark. Like you can see when we use this upwards arrow mark, this indicates that this child is inheriting the properties or the methods from the parent class, which is Person. So usually inside a Java class we'll be having the Java fields, methods and constructors. Since the constructors are not the members, they are not going to be inherited by the subclasses or by the child classes.

But if needed, a constructor of the superclass can be invoked from the subclass. We're going to discuss how the constructor invocation is going to change based upon this parent and the child relationship in the coming lectures. But now, please note that constructors are not going to be inherited by the subclasses from the superclass. I know you might be learning these Java Inheritance very first time, and it might be still be confusing for you. That's why let me show you another example like you can see here we have an Interface diagram related to Animals.

So for all the animals that we have on the earth, they are going to have the common attributes and behaviors such as name, age and the ability to move from one place to other place. So all these common attributes and behaviors we can keep inside a superclass with the name Animals. And this superclass can be extend by the subclasses or the child classes like mammals, reptiles and birds. So again each of these child classes, they can have their own behavior like birds.

They'll have their unique behavior which is they can fly. So this kind of unique features are unique variables or behaviors the subclasses they can still have or they can still build. But all the common logic or the common attributes and the common behavior, we can always keep and maintain them inside the superclass like Animals. So what are the advantages that we get with these Inheritance? We are getting a flexibility to maintain all the common code in a single class.

And in future, whenever we want to make a change inside this common code, the change has to be done at a single place, which is the superclass. So as soon as you make a change inside the superclass, the updated business logic is going to be immediately reflected inside all the child classes and the subclasses. On top of that, if needed my child classes, they can overwrite the behavior or they can override the properties provided by the superclass.

I'm going to explain the concept of overriding in the coming lectures, but for now, I'm assuming you are clear about the Java Inheritance. So one more time, if you try to understand the syntax that we need to follow whenever we want to implement the Java Inheritance is, first you need to mention what is your access modifier. It can be a public or default and after that you can keep the class keyword followed by what is your subclass name or child name or derived class name, and after your subclass name you need to mention the extends keyword.

So extends is very important here. This is going to enable the Java Inheritance. After the extends keyword, you need to mention what is the superclass name. For example, think of a scenario where we have a superstar in dance. So if the superstar is trying to teach some dance moves to another fellow or to another subclass, in such scenarios we can have these kind of class definition where my subclass name is going to be funky subclass, and this is going to extends the parent class, which is superstar class.

So all the dance moves that my superstar knows, it is going to be inherited by my funky subclass. And whenever you are trying to mention the parent class just after the extends keyword, you need to be very careful about mentioning the import statement as well. If your superclass is present inside the same package, then obviously you don't have to mention any import statement. Otherwise, if your superstar class is present inside another package, then in such scenarios, definitely first you need to mention an import statement.

Once the import statement is mentioned, then only you can mention your parent class. Otherwise, if you don't want to mention the import statement, you can mention the complete qualified name of your parent class after the extends keyword. I hope you remember all the import and packages concept that we have discussed in the previous lecture. With this, we discussed about Java Inheritance theoretically. Now in the next lecture, let's try to create some super classes and subclasses and try to implement the Java Inheritance with the help of extends keyword.

Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: Inheritance Demo - Part 2
lectures.text:
In the previous lecture, we implemented Inheritance inside our Java project and we also validated all our subclasses. They are able to inherit the methods and fields from the parent class, which is Person. So what is the advantage that we're getting with Inheritance here? The advantage is we are maintaining all the common logic or the common Java fields in a single place. So this is going to give a great advantage to the developers. Think like in future, if someone wants to change the logic that we have written inside the each method, they need to change at a single place which is inside the Person parent class, and the same is going to be reflected in all the subclasses.

So this brings reusability as an advantage. You can write your code at one place, and you can reuse that in many other places like subclasses. And here you may have a question which is I do understand that my subclasses are child classes they are able to inherit the properties and the behaviors from the parent class. But does that mean that my child classes they have to live with this behavior off course not. In case if your child class, if they want to override the logic present inside the parent method, they can do that happily by defining the same method inside the subclass.

And similarly they can also override the Java fields as well. So all the overriding logic we are going to talk in the coming lectures. For now, let's try to focus on the basics of Java inheritance. So in the previous lecture, I showed a demo from the Marvels main() method that my IronMan class is able to access the all the methods that are present in the parent class. There is also a another shortcut that you can use to validate what are all the methods and fields that are derived or inherited by a subclass from its superclass.

The shortcut is you can go to any of your subclass like I'll go this time to the SpiderMan. Here I'm going to look for the list of methods and fields available inside my given class. So inside my given class, like SpiderMan, I'm trying to press a shortcut which is command F12, and inside windows the shortcut is going to be control F12. So here there are three checkboxes like inherited members anonymous classes or lambdas. So if I try to uncheck these inherited members you will be able to see only the methods and fields available inside these given class.

But if I select these checkbox which is inherited members, I'll be able to see all the methods and fields that are inherited by my subclass from its superclass. So you'll be able to see other methods like eat(), sleep(), walk(). So these are all the methods that are inherited from the person superclass. There are other methods also which are inherited from the object. We'll discuss about the object superclass in the next lecture. For now, let's focus on only the person superclass, because we are explicitly inheriting the properties and behaviors from the Person superclass.

So if you select any of the method like eat() method, you'll be able to see that this method is inherited from the Person. That's why you are able to see these arrow marks as well. Whereas for the usePower() method, you're not able to see any of the arrow marks or any of the superclass name, because this method is directly defined inside the given subclass. And similarly, if you go to the fields like age and name, you'll be able to see that these are also inherited from the Person superclass, and for them, the icon you'll be able to see there is a lock icon, which means these are defined as protected variables.

Whereas for the methods like eat() and sleep() and walk(), you are able to see an icon which is open lock. Since we define the methods as public, so that's why we have this symbol. So this is one of the shortcut that you can use to always understand what are the methods and fields that are derived by my subclass from its superclass. Can we validate the same for CaptainAmerica as well. So I'm trying to press command F12 here. So here also we have all the methods from the Person superclass.

And we also have the fields. So the same you can also validate inside the IronMan as well. So let me press F12. So here also we have the fields and methods. If you try to select any of the method which is inherited from the Person, it will take you to the Person superclass where this method is defined. So this is the beauty of intelliJ. That's why in real projects it is always advisable or mandatory to use IDE's like IntelliJ, Eclipse, NetBeans.

They are going to make our life super easy. So as of now we are only inheriting from one of the class which is Person. But here you may have a question which is can I inherit from more than one class? The answer for this question is no. In Java, a single subclass cannot inherit the methods or fields from multiple Java classes. So if I try to put one more class name like MarvelsMain, you can see here I'm getting an compilation error saying that class cannot extend the multiple classes.

So always please note that in a single subclass you cannot inherit or extends from multiple classes. We are going to talk more about these in the coming lectures. But now I just wanted to share this important note. So as of now my Person is being inherited by my IronMan, so can any other subclass can inherit my IronMan, off course it can inherit. For example, if I go to the MarvelsMain here, I can try to add the extends and mention any of the subclass like IronMan.

So this way the inheritance can go to up to any level, like a parent will have a child, and a child can have its own child. So that kind of chaining of inheritance is always possible in Java. I hope it is clear. Let me remove this extends keyword inside this MarvelsMain because it is not necessary here. As a next step, let me go to any of the subclass and press command F12 to see my class structure. You can see there are good amount of methods are being inherited from the class called object.

So the methods like clone(), equals(), finalize(), getClass(), hashCode(), notify(), notifyAll(), sleep(), wait(). This confirms that our class is also inheriting the behavior from the object superclass. But we know where given the object to superclass inside our extends keyword. If you go to any of the class like MarvelsMain here also there is no extends keyword and we are not inheriting any of the class including object. But if you still press the command F12, you will be able to see the all the methods that are inherited from the object superclass.

So why is this happening? Let's try to understand the same in the next lecture. Thank you bye.

lectures.title: Object class is the default Superclass
lectures.text:
In the previous lecture, while we are seeing that demo of the Inheritance, we saw the methods from the Object class are also being inherited by default. This is because inside Java, every class is going to have a default superclass which is Object. So this object class is present inside the package, which is java.lang package. Since this class is present inside the java.lang, we don't need to use any import statement as well. So behind the scenes, the Java is always going to add these object as a superclass for each and every class that you are going to create.

So this is going to happen implicitly. As a result, any class that you create will inherit the instance methods of the Object class. So this Object class has many important methods related to the Java objects. So these methods are like clone(), using clone we can create another copy of an given object. And after the clone we have equals() method using equals() method, we can validate whether the current Java object is equal to another Java object, and after the equals() we have finalize() method.

Using these finalize() method, we can write a logic that can be executed whenever our object is going to be garbage collected. So just before removing our object from the heap memory by the garbage collector, we can try to execute some logic with the help of this finalize() method. And we also have getClass() method, which is going to give the what is the class name or the class data type of an given object. And with the help of hashCode(), we can calculate the hashCode() value of an object.

And at last we have toString() method here So using the toString() method we can return an string representation of the object. So apart from these method, there are many other methods also available inside Object class. So we're going to talk in detail about the all the object class related methods in the coming sections. For now, let's try to understand why this Object class is made as the default or implicit superclass for all the Java classes.

The reason is very obvious, since we are going to create objects for all our Java classes. So while dealing with all these Java objects that we create, we may have some requirements like creating the copy of a Java object, or checking the equality of the Java object, or knowing the class name of the Java object, or calculating the hashCode value, or printing our object content in an string representation. So since every Java object may have all these common requirements, so all these kind of object related functionality has been developed inside a Object class.

And the same are being inherited by default by all the Java classes. I hope it is clear. Now, if you try to understand more details about the Object class. Like you can see here on the left hand side, I'm trying to create a Java class which is Person and on the right hand side I'm also trying to create the same class which is Person, but this time I have mentioned the extends Object. So both of these class definitions, they are same. Regardless I'm mentioning the extends Object or not.

The behavior is always going to be same, which is we will be able to inherit the methods from the Object class. For example, in all the earlier sections that we have discussed, nowhere we have not used the extends keyword to inherit the Object class, but still behind the scenes we are quietly inheriting the Object class. That's why any class that you have created so far without using the extends keyword. When you try to create the object of those classes, you will be able to invoke the methods from the object class like hashCode() and toString().

So this means we are using our writing the Inheritance train since the very first Java program that we have created, but we never realized it the reason is behind the scenes, the Object superclass is going to be inherited implicitly by each and every Java class. Let me try to show you the demo of hashCode() and toString() methods for the same inside my Marvels main() method, I can try to create an object of any of the classes. For example, here I can try to create an object of Person class.

For the same I need to mention Person, what is the object reference name followed by equal to followed by new operator followed by Person() default constructor. If I open this Person Java class. As of now, you can see this is not extending any of the superclass. But if I go to the MarvelsMain and try to mention that dot operator after the object reference, you will be able to see all the methods from the Object class. Like for example, I can try to invoke the hashCode() method, and this hashCode() method is going to give an output in an into format.

So that's why I'm going to assign the output to a variable which is int hc, hc indicates hashCode(). Very similarly, I'll try to create one more variable of type String. And the variable name I'm going to give here is str. And to this I'm going to assign the output from the toString() method. So you can see I'm trying to invoke the toString()method by using the object reference of the Person class. So I can keep a breakpoint here and try to debug this program.

You'll be able to see the what is the value inside the hc at runtime. So this is the hashCode value for this object. And very similarly this is the string representation of the Person object that we have created. So this confirms that all our Java classes implicitly inheriting the Object class. And inside this Object class what do we have, we have all the important methods related to the object related operations. So these are Object class, Object.java and it is present inside the package java.lang.

That's what you can confirm here. And it has so many methods related to the Java objects. So all these methods we can try to invoke based upon our business requirements. We are going to talk in detail about the purpose of these methods in the coming sections. I hope you are convinced with our discussion that Object class is the default superclass. So with this information, if you try to check the class hierarchy relationship, this is how it is going to look like.

Inside Java are in any object oriented programming language we can use is-a relationship or has-a relationship to represent our established relationship between different classes. Inside your Java interviews or inside your Java related exams. Definitely sometimes you may hear questions about what is a , is-a relationship or has-a relationship in Java. So let's try to understand what are those. Using is-a relationship we can express Inheritance relationship between two classes.

So whenever we use extends keyword that means we are establishing Inheritance relationship between a superclass and a subclass. For example, here I have a superclass with the name Animal, and I also have a subclass that is extending the Animal superclass, and the subclass name is Dog. So both of these Dog and Animal, they have a relationship which is established with the help of inheritance concept. So this kind of relationship that is established with the help of inheritance, in other words we can call it as is-a relationship.

So how this is an is-a relationship. So let's try to understand the same. So if someone asks you what is a Dog, you will say Dog is a animal. Very similarly, we can also say SpiderMan is a Person, Car is a Vehicle, Orange is a Fruit. So this way using is-a relationship, we can always express our establish Inheritance relationship between two classes. If you can't build a sentence like Dog is-a Animal, you should not be establishing the Inheritance.

Though your compiler is not going to stop anything around this, but it is a best practice to make sure that you are establishing the Inheritance only when a is-a relationship is established between different classes.

I hope you are clear. What is an is-a relationship? Now let's try to understand what is a has-a relationship. lectures.title: What a subclass inherits from its superclass
lectures.text:
Based upon our discussions in the previous lecture. Now, you should be pretty clear about the basics of the inheritance. So what is the purpose of inheritance? Whenever we implement inheritance, a subclass can inherit Java fields and Java method from its superclass. But usually inside a superclass we can write lot of other types of members as well. Like static fields, static methods, instance methods, instance variables, constructors. So there'll be different kinds of members, usually inside a Java class.

And we should not be under the assumption everything inside the superclass is going to be inherited by the subclass. So that's not going to be the case. There are certain limitations, our rules and regulations that you need to be aware. So let's try to understand what are those inside this lecture. Like I said before, it is important to note that a class does not automatically acquire or inherit everything from its superclass class. It is going to selectively inherit Non-private members from the superclass.

That means the members of the class that are declared with the public, default, and protected, they are going to be passed down or inherited to the subclass, whereas private members they are going to be remain confined within the superclass, and they are not going to be accessible to the subclass. I'm going to talk in detail how access modifiers are going to influence the inheritance process in few minutes. But before that, let's try to understand few general rules and regulations and thumb rules that we need to be aware around inheritance.

The very first rule is the constructors and the initializers that we are going to write inside a superclass. They are not going to be inherited by the subclass. A superclass can have any number of constructors, and it may also have a static initializer or a instance initializer. So since these are not fall under the category of the members within a class, they are not going to participate in the inheritance process. Moving on to the next rule, all the static members that you are going to define inside your superclass, they are going to be inherited by the subclass.

When I say static members, what are those? It can be a static field or a static method. So these static methods and static fields, they will be inherited by the subclass without any issues. We're also going to see the demo in few minutes. Apart from static members like static fields and static methods, we can also define instance method and instance variables. We know that these instance methods and instance variables they are also going to be participate in the inheritance process regardless whether a method is static or non static, whether a field is static or non static.

So all of them, they are going to participate in the inheritance process. But they are going to be greatly influenced by the access modifiers. For example, if you define a class member with a private access modifier, its accessibility is going to be restricted solely to the class in which it is declared. That means private class members are not going to be passed down to the subclasses, and they are going to be remain exclusive, but the superclass alone. After the private we can also define class members by using the public access modifier.

So when we use the public access modifier, all of your class members, they are going to be inherited to the subclass. That means a subclass inherits all public members of its superclass, whether it is a method or a field. If it is a public, the same is going to be inherited by the subclass. On the similar lines, when we define a class member with a package level or a default access modifier, then in this kind of scenarios, if the subclass is present inside the same package, then these default are package level class members they are going to be inherited by the subclass, whereas if your subclass is belongs to a different package compared to the superclass, then in such scenario, the subclass does not going to inherit package level members or default members from its superclass.

So to resolve this challenge, we can use protected Access modifier. When we use the protected access modifier, your subclass always going to inherit that class members regardless your subclass present inside the same package of superclass or a different package compared to the superclass. So these are the guidelines or the rules that you need to be aware to understand. What is subclass inherits from its superclass. As a next step, let's see that demo of these rules very quickly inside the intelliJ, inside my IntelliJ as of now, you can see we have a superclass with the name person, inside this super class, I'm going to define a private method by mentioning private void and the method name I'm going to keep it as calculateEdge().

To this method, we are going to accept the input parameter which is int year. So based upon the year, we want to calculate the age. But in order to calculate the age based upon the year, first you need to be aware about the dates concept inside Java. As of now, we have not discussed on how to represent a date inside Java, since we are going to discuss about all these concepts in the coming sections, for now, I'll keep the logic of this method very simple by writing a System.out.println() and to this println() method, I'm going to pass an input which is age() method.

So with this we successfully created a private method inside my Person super class. Now if I go to any of my subclass of the Person like IronMan here, if I try to look for the list of methods and fields that are available inside this class by pressing the command + F12 shortcut, you will not be able to see any method with the name calculateAge() because calculateAge(), we marked it as private and all the private members of a super class they are not going to be inherited by the subclass.

I hope it is clear now I'm going to change this private to default. So how to do that? lectures.text:
What is downcasting ? downcasting is the exact opposite of upcasting. Inside the upcasting, we are going to assign the object of a subclass to the superclass, but if you try to do the exactly opposite of it, which is assign an object of superclass to the object reference of subclass, then we are going to call it as downcasting. First, let me show you a demo of downcasting. Later on, we can discuss more details about downcasting. For the same here inside my app package, I'm going to create a new Java class with the name DownCastingDemo.

Inside this DownCastingDemo. First I'm going to create the main() method inside my main() method first I'm going to create the object reference of superclass which is Animal pose. This Animal object reference I want to create the object of Dog class. So let me create it with the help of new operator and default constructor of Dog class. So now you can see we have a object reference of superclass. And we also have an subclass object. So if you try to type anm = dog.

So this is perfectly acceptable inside Java because this is upcasting because we are trying to assign an subclass object to the superclass object reference. But if you try to do the opposite of it, we are going to get a compilation error. So let me type dog = anm. So you can see I'm getting a compilation error because inside Java by default downcasting is not allowed. So to resolve this compilation error we need to tell specifically to the compiler.

I'm aware of the fact that I'm trying to downcast, and I'm sure that these Animal object reference is holding the Dog object, so we need to give an assurance to the compiler to resolve this error. So how to give that assurance just before your anm object reference we need to mention parentheses. And inside the parentheses we need to mention the subclass name which is Dog. And with that you can see the downcasting right now it is allowed. So here we are trying to assign a superclass object reference or superclass object data type to a subclass object to reference.

So this is called downcasting. So why Java is not allowing this automatically is by default we can't say that every Animal is a Dog. It is going to be invalid because under Animal we may have cat, we may have horse, we may have elephant. So since it is invalid to call every Animal as a dog, your compilation is going to stop you with a compilation error. So you as a developer, you need to give a assurance or confidence to your Java compiler saying that that these anm is holding the object of Dog.

So how to give that confident or assurance by mentioning the subclass name within the parentheses just before this name. So the same kind of syntax we also followed for primitive data types casting as well. So with this syntax we are able to manually perform the downcasting. But whenever we are trying to perform the downcasting we need to be very careful. We need to perform the downcasting only if we are 100% sure that these anm is going to hold the object of Dog.

Otherwise we are going to get a RuntimeException which is ClassCastException. So let me show you a demo around this. For the same I'm going to first create the object reference of Cat subclass, followed by I'm going to assign the a anm object reference. And with that I'm going to get a compilation error because by default downcasting is not allowed. So to resolve this issue I can simply say Cat within the parentheses and my compilation error is resolved.

But if I try to execute this program at runtime, I'm going to get a ClassCastException. I can show you that as well by running my program in a debug mode. You can see I got a ClassCastException saying that inside my anm object reference we are holding the Dog object, but we are trying to assign that to the Cat. So since they are representing two different classes, the casting is not going to be allowed. That's why we are getting the ClassCastException at line number 16.

So that's why always please make sure you are 100% sure that your object reference is holding the actual object of your subclass whenever you are trying to perform that downcasting. Otherwise, you're going to get the surprises like we discussed. I hope you are clear what is downcasting. I know you may have a question here, which is what is the advantage of downcasting? lectures.title: Static Binding and Dynamic Binding in Java
lectures.text:
Inside this lecture we are going to talk about the concept of "Binding" and what are the types of binding available. Usually inside a Java class will be having fields and methods. and these methods and fields can be invoked with the help of class name or with the help of object. So there won't be any confusion if you have a single class which has its own static methods, instance methods and variables. But if you try to bring inheritance into your Java project, then there will be lot many scenarios like Upcasting, Downcasting.

So in this kind of scenarios, your compiler sometimes it has to take a decision which method has to be invoked. For example, inside your superclass you may have a method which is method one and inside your subclasses also, you might have overrided that method with the same method name. In the case of Upcasting we saw we can upcast a subclass to a superclass. So when these kind of upcasting happens and if you try to invoke the method one with the help of object reference of superclass, then your compiler has to take a decision which method has to be invoked, whether it has to invoke the method present inside the superclass, or it has to invoke the method present inside the subclass.

So the same kind of decision it has to take for the variables as well. So the effort that is going to be put by your Java to determine which method to invoke or to which variable to invoke is called as binding. In other words, we can say binding is the decision making process that establishes the connection between the code and the specific method or field it is trying to access. This binding process can happen at two stages during the compilation time and runtime.

If the binding is happening at the compilation time, we can call that as Static Binding. In other words, we can also call the Static Binding as Early binding or compile time binding. So static binding or early binding indicates that decision that has been taken by the Java or Java compiler, to which method, or to which variable it has to invoke during the compilation time. Maybe this decision will get override during the runtime, but it has to take a decision at compile time about which method or which field it is going to invoke.

Just like Static Binding, we also have Dynamic Binding. The other name for this Dynamic Binding is late binding or runtime binding, because as part of this dynamic binding, the decision is going to be taken at the runtime. At runtime, Java is going to check which object is being hold by an object reference. Using the same data, it is going to decide which method or which variable to invoke at the runtime. So if your Java class has private methods, or private variables, or static methods, or static variables, or final variables or final methods.

So in all these kind of scenarios, the decision is going to be very simple. The Java always going to follow the Static Binding because private variables, private methods, static members and the final members, they're all going to be exclusive for a given class. There won't be any confusion in these kind of scenarios, only in the scenario of non private instance methods or instance variables. The compiler or Java is going to have a confusion due to inheritance.

Let me show you an example and with that you're going to be pretty clear here I have a Java program. Let's try to understand the same. First I have a class with the name A. And inside this class I have a method show(). So this class A is going to act as a superclass for my class B. So B is a subclass and the A is a superclass. We can also confirm the same by looking at these extends keyword followed by A.

So inside my subclass also the same method which is inherited from the superclass is Overrided with the logic specific to the subclass. So inside my superclass the logic is show() method. Inside class A is going to be printed, whereas the subclass change the message to show method in class B. . I hope you are clear. We have a superclass and a subclass, and both of them has the same method which is show(). Now if you see there is a Main class and inside this Main class I have a main() method.

First, I'm trying to create the object of A and B without any typecasting or Downcasting it's a simple object creation of the A class and a B class. So object reference we have is a and b. So if I try to invoke the a.show() there won't be any confusion to my Java compiler, because on the right hand side we have a and on the left hand side also we have a. So since there is no confusion to my compiler, the static binding is going to happen at this point of time, the compiler is going to take a decision that it is going to invoke the show() method available inside the a superclass.

So that's why we are going to get the output as show() method in class A. Coming to the b.show(), even for the b.show() also, there won't be any confusion to my Java compiler because on the right hand side we have B constructor and on the left hand side also we have reference to the B class. So since this is going to be pretty straightforward in this scenario, also the compiler is going to take a static binding decision and the same it is going to follow even at the runtime.

That's why we are getting the output, which is show() method in class B up to this point I'm assuming you are with me now the fun starts. So here you can see I'm trying to do the upcasting. I'm trying to assign the object of subclass to the object reference of superclass, which is a. So this obj object reference, it belongs to the class A which is a superclass. But inside this object reference I'm holding the object of B which is a subclass. So in this kind of scenarios, definitely my compiler is going to have a confusion because I'm trying to invoke the show method with the help of obj.

So here my compiler does not know whether to invoke the show() method present inside the A or inside the B. So first, during the compilation time, the Java at the compiler is going to perform the static binding, and with the static binding, it will be under the assumption that it is going to invoke the show() method present inside the a superclass, because this obj belongs to the class A, but at runtime the Java is going to check this obj object reference points to the which object.

So this obj object reference is pointing to the object of B subclass. So that's why at runtime, based upon the dynamic binding are based upon the dynamic decision taken, the show() method present inside the subclass is going to be invoked. The sme you can see I have confirmed here the output we are going to get is show() method in class B. I hope you are clear. What is a static binding and dynamic binding? lectures.title: Method Overriding - Theory
lectures.text:
Before I try to explain you about what is a method overriding inside Java inheritance, first let me ask you a question. Think like you have inherited a property from your parents. Are you going to keep that property forever without making any changes? Off course you're not going to do that maybe at some point of time, if you have your own requirements or if you want to change it, you will go ahead and change the property. Maybe you will go for repainting or renovation based upon your taste, though the property is inherited from your parents. Very similarly inside Java, also, if a subclass is inheriting a method from the parent class, it is not mandatory to accept the same method and to follow the same logic given by the parent forever.

If a subclass has a requirement to override the behavior provided by the superclass method, then it is perfectly allowed inside Java. So this concept we call it as method overriding. So what is a method overriding? Method overriding is a feature of Java inheritance that allows a subclass to provide its own implementation of a method that is already defined in its parent class. So this is the simple definition that you can tell if someone is asking what is a method overriding?

While we are trying to perform the method overriding inside a subclass, we need to make sure we are defining a method with the same method name, same return type, and same method parameters, as mentioned in the parent class method, the access modifier or the access level of the overriding method can be different from the superclass method, but you need to make sure the access modifier is not more restrictive than the method being overridden. In few minutes I'm going to show you a demo around this, so don't worry if something is not clear for you.

So when you have a method both in the parent class and a subclass, and if you're trying to invoke the method name with the object reference of the parent class like we discussed in the Upcasting in such scenarios, first your JVM is going to look if there is any method in the subclass which is overridden. If yes, the same is going to be invoked at the runtime. Otherwise, whatever method defined inside the superclass or the parent class is going to be invoked.

So the concept of method overriding inside Java provides great flexibility and customization in the behavior of objects in the subclass. If we don't have method overriding concept inside Java, then inheritance is not going to be a great feature, because if you inherit something, then you have to live with that. There is no option of changing. Are you going to accept such kind of behavior? Off course not. Each one of us, we always want our own freedom, our own thinking though we inherit the properties or the characters from our parents.

Very similarly, inside Java, also, with the help of method overriding, we are giving the flexibility to the subclasses. If they want, they can override the business logic provided by a method inside the superclass. But whatever method overriding that we are discussing right now, this applicable only to the non-static methods. Static methods we can't override them because static methods are only applicable at the class level. It is not belongs to a specific object.

With that reason, we cannot perform the method overriding. Instead, whenever we are dealing with the static methods, we can call that concept as method hiding. We are going to talk about what is method hiding in the coming lectures, but for now, please note that method overriding concept is applicable only for the non-static methods and obviously the private methods which are present inside the superclass. They can't be overridden by a subclass because the private methods present inside the superclass, they are going to be never inherited by the subclass.

So let's try to take an example around method overriding. Like you can see here, I have a parent with the name Person. So that's why I'm trying to extend the same Person superclass inside my IronMan subclass. So inside my Person superclass we created a method with the name walk(). But the IronMan, he's not going to walk like other persons. He's walking style is going to be something different, maybe due to his iron suit. So since he has his own style of walking, it makes very sense to the IronMan to override the method that he's inheriting from the Person.

Whereas for the CaptainAmerica, you don't need to override the walk() method, because CaptainAmerica is going to walk very normally like humans, whereas for the IronMan, since he has iron suits, sometimes he's going to fly and sometimes he's going to walk. And when he's walking, we're going to get a lot of sound like tuck, tuck, tuck. So since he has his own walking style, I'm trying to overwrite the walk() method inside the IronMan class. So when we are overriding, we need to make sure we are mentioning the same method name, same method return type, and same method parameters along with the access modifier.

So that's why I'm trying to mention the same, which is public void walk(). And inside this method I can write my own business logic and whenever we are trying to do a method overriding, it is always advisable to mention an annotation which is @Override on top of your overridden method inside your subclass. So here I have mentioned an annotation which is at symbol followed by Override. Inside Java all annotations they are going to be represented with the help of this at symbol.

With that you may have a question here, why should I mention this annotation? Because I said it is an optional. But the question you may have is since if it is optional, then why should I mention this annotation? What is the advantage that I get? So I perfectly understand your question. Let me try to answer that. Whenever we mention these Override annotation on top of your overridden method, your compiler understands that you are trying to override the walk() method present inside the superclass, and if you try to miss one of the rule of method overriding, maybe you're trying to give a different return type or maybe you're trying to accept a different method parameters, in all such scenarios, since your Java compiler knows that you're trying to override a superclass method, it is going to throw a compilation error and it is going to warn you saying that hey, you didn't follow so-and-so rule while you are trying to override so on and so method from the superclass.

Whereas if I don't have these Override annotation, then my compiler does not know and it will simply treat it as a normal method, and it is not going to guide me in the process of method overriding. On top of that, one more advantage we have with the @Override annotation is, if you mention these @Override annotation on top of a overridden method, and if there is no method with the same name inside the superclass in such scenario also you're going to get a compilation error saying that hey buddy, you're trying to override a method with a so and so name, but I don't find such method inside the superclass, so please do check your method name.

So this kind of guidance is going to be provided by the compiler when we follow the Override annotation. I hope you're clear. Now the next question you may have here is I'm hearing the annotation very first time from you, can you please share more details about what is an annotation in Java? Let me try to answer the same inside Java, annotations are a form of metadata that provides information about a program's code, particularly its classes, methods, fields, and parameters.

I know this definition does not make any sense, but let me try to make it more simple to you. So whenever you are using an annotation inside Java, we are going to convey an information to the compiler or runtime or other tools that process the program. For example, here I have a method and this is going to be processed by my compiler, by my JVM or other tools of Java. So if I mention these @Override annotation, so there'll be a meaning assigned to this annotation behind the scenes.

So using the same meaning, my compiler can guide the developers on how to override a method. So very similarly we have lot many annotations inside Java. So inside Java, please note that all these annotations they are going to start with at symbol. So whenever you see an annotation being used inside Java programming language, first you need to understand what is the purpose of that annotation and under which scenarios we need to use that annotation.

So throughout this course we are going to talk about lot many annotations. So if you are clear about these most commonly used annotations you should be good. Once you become an advanced Java developer, maybe after five years or six years of Java programming experience, you can also create your own annotations. So that is also possible inside Java. But for now, since you are getting started just now, I would advise you to get comfortable with the most commonly used annotations, which I'm going to discuss throughout this section.

I hope you are clear about what is a method overriding inside Java inheritance. In the next lecture, let me show you a demo of method overriding. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: Method Overloading - Theory
lectures.text:
As of now, we understand what is an method overriding in Java. As a next step, let's try to understand what is method overloading and how we can achieve static polymorphism with the help of method overloading. Inside Java, whenever we want to perform the method overloading, there is no mandatory that you need to implement inheritance even in a normal and independent class also, you can implement method overloading. So first I'm going to show you an example where I'm not following any inheritance post that I'll also show you another example on how to perform the method overloading.

When we implemented inheritance between two classes. Coming to that definition of the method overloading, it is a feature in Java that allows a developer to define multiple methods with the same name in the same class. However, the methods must have different parameters list. Though the method names are same, but they are going to hold the different number of parameters or different data types of parameters, or both of them the return type and the access modifier and the Throws class of a method they are not going to play any role in making an method overloaded, and at the same time using different names for the method parameters does not going to make the method overloaded.

I have an example class and this class it is not inheriting any superclass. If you closely look at the class body inside this example class, we have three different methods with the same name print and all of these methods they have different parameters as an input. For example, for the first print() method, I'm having the input parameter as int followed by double and at last for the last print() method, we are accepting the String data type as an input parameter.

So this is a perfect example of method overloading. Though the name of the three methods is same, but they are having different method input parameters. So in this kind of scenario the Static Binding or compile time binding is going to happen. And that's why whenever we are implementing method overloading we are going to achieve Static Polymorphism. Here you can see I have given an example. First I'm trying to create the object of this Example class, followed by I'm trying to invoke all these three methods.

When I'm trying to invoke these three methods, I'm passing the method input parameter value as per the method definition. If I pass the int value, the very first method is going to be invoked, whereas when I pass the double value, the second method is going to be invoked. And when I pass the String data, the last method is going to be invoked. So the compiler, it is going to take the decision about which method to invoke at the compile time itself.

So you can see here the same print() method it is trying to behave differently based upon different input that we are passing at the compile time itself. That's why we can call this kind of Polymorphism as Static Polymorphism. So there won't be any confusion to the compiler to which method it has to call, because all your overloaded methods always they are going to have different method signatures. Now let me show you another example where we have the inheritance implemented.

Here you can see I have a Person superclass and inside the Person superclass I have an eat() method and it is going to accept a String food as an input parameter. Now inside my subclass which is IronMan first I have a override method because you will be able to see that I have used the annotation at symbol followed by override. On top of that, this method signature is exactly same as the method signature that we have inside the Person superclass.

Now coming to the last two methods inside the IronMan, you can see they are maintaining the same name like eat(), but the input parameters to these methods are different. For the second method, we are not accepting any method input parameter, whereas for the third method we are accepting String and the int as an method input parameters. So the last two methods that we have inside the IronMan, they are overloaded methods because they have different method input parameters compared to the parent method are inherited method inside the IronMan subclass.

So whenever you have confusion to understand whether a method is overloaded or not, you can follow a simple rule. First, you can write down the method name followed by a separator like comma or percentage, whatever works for you. After mentioning the method name, you can also mention the data type of your method input parameters. So each of the data type also you can separate them with the help of a separator like comma. So once you have written all this method names and parameter data types.

Using a separator, you can compare all of them. If they are having different values, then obviously it indicates method overloading. Otherwise it is going to indicate there is no method overloading inside your class. And here I also want to highlight a very important point. Think like inside your class you have a private non-static method or private instance method. This private methods they can always be overloaded by only a non-static method inside the same class.

I hope you are clear about what is method overloading. I'm going to show you a demo of method overloading in the next lecture. Thank you, bye.

lectures.title: Method overriding vs Method overloading
lectures.text:
Since method overriding and method overloading concepts are very important inside Java, let's try to put more efforts on trying to understand what is the difference between these two concepts. People may get confused very easily at these concepts and inside interviews. Also, the interviewer, he or she can try to confuse you very easily. So to avoid these kind of scenarios, let's try to put some efforts on understanding the differences between method overriding and method overloading.

The very first difference is method overriding always happens if a class declares a method that shares the same name, along with the same number of method parameters and same parameter data types in the same order as specified by its superclass, whereas the method overloading is going to happen if multiple methods inside a class have a same name, and all these methods which are sharing the same method name if they have difference in at least one aspect, like it can be a number of method input parameters or their data types are in their order.

So in such scenarios the method overloading is going to happen. So these are the definitions of method overriding and a method overloading. Moving on to the second difference. Whenever you want to perform the method overriding, you should always have followed the inheritance. That means you should always have at least two classes, one is superclass and the other one is subclass in order to implement method overriding concept. On the contrast side, you can try to implement method overloading in a single class without worrying about the inheritance.

The third difference is the return type of the overridden method must be same as the superclass method, or it should be compatible with the return type of the superclass method. When I say compatible, it should be one of the subtypes of the return type mentioned inside the superclass, whereas inside the method overloading the return type of the method is not going to be considered, and it is not going to influence method overloading concept. On the similar lines, while you are trying to implement method overriding, you are not allowed to include any additional throws class compared to the overriding method.

If needed, you can get rid of all the checked exceptions defined inside the superclass method, or you can maintain the same number of checked exceptions or less number of checked exceptions or if needed you can also maintain a different checked exception, but you need to make sure it is one of the subclass of the checked exception, which is defined inside the superclass method on the method overloading side the Throws class is not going to play any role, and it is not going to impact the process of overloading.

And the last difference that we have is the method overriding is always applicable for the instance methods or non-static methods, whereas method overloading is applicable for any type of method, whether it is an static method or a non-static method, I can define multiple static methods in a same class with the same name, but with a different method input parameters. So that is perfectly possible with the method overloading. Whereas if you try to overload a static method present inside a superclass in the subclass, then it is not allowed or we cannot call that concept as method overriding.

So there is a different concept called method hiding, which you are going to discuss in the coming lectures. And at last I want to highlight you that method overloading is always going to be resolved at compile time based upon the static binding or compile time binding or static polymorphism. And the other side method overriding is always going to be resolved at runtime based upon that dynamic binding or dynamic polymorphism. With this, I'm assuming you are clear about what is method overriding and method overloading.

My humble request is please create some classes and inside these classes you can try to define multiple methods with the same name and in the same process, you can try to implement method overriding and method overloading so that you will get used to these concepts easily. Thank you, bye.

lectures.title: this and super keywords in Java
lectures.text:
As of now we discussed enough details and examples around the this and the super keyword in Java. But still, I want to spend more time around these keywords inside this lecture explaining you about the differences between them and when you should use them. Because this is the most common topic where students may feel some complexity and they may get confused very easily inside the interviews. So let's try to understand difference between them and when to use them.

The very first basic point that you should be knowing is, both of them are two reserved keywords inside Java, we are going to use the this keyword whenever we want to access a member of a current object, whereas super keyword we need to use if we want to access a member of a super class object. For example here you can see I have given two different examples. On the left hand side, I have a class of Person inside this Person class I have a constructor that accepts two input parameters.

Since the parameter names to the constructor and the variable names inside the class since they both are same, I need to use this keyword to point to the variable present inside the current object. Like you can see with the help of this this.name, I'm trying to refer to the instance variable that I have created at the top of the class, whereas with the other name variable, we are trying to refer to the parameter that we have received as an input to this constructor.

So with this, it should be clear for you. Whenever we want to access a member of a current object, we should be using the this keyword. Whereas super keyword will always come into picture in the scenarios of inheritance. Without inheritance, you will not be able to use the super keyword. Here I have an example where I have a Animal superclass and a subclass with the name Dog. Both these superclass and subclass, they have a same method which is makeSound().

That means my Dog subclass overridden the method makeSound() with its own logic. But if my subclass has a requirement to access the method present inside the superclass, then in such scenarios, my subclass should use the super keyword to access the makeSound() method available inside the superclass. We can also use these, this and super keywords while we are trying to invoke the constructors. For example, I can use the this keyword along with the parentheses to invoke the other constructors from a constructor inside the same class.

And whenever we are using the this keyword to invoke the other constructor, it should be the very first statement inside a constructor. On the similar lines we can also use the super keyword to invoke the constructors of the super class. Just in the previous lecture, we have discussed this scenario. Even in the scenario of using super keyword to construct an invocation in this kind of scenario also, we need to make sure that super constructor invocation is a very first statement inside your subclass constructor.

At last, I want to highlight you that both these this and super keywords. They are reserved keywords inside Java. We can't use them as an variable identifiers or method name identifiers. And there is also a restriction or limitation on where we can use these these and the super keyword. We can only use this and super keywords in an non-static area like inside the non-static methods or inside the constructors. We will not be able to use these keywords inside the static methods or inside the static initializers.

The reason is these keywords are specific to the objects of a super class or objects of a current class. Since the static method and the static initializer they belongs to the class, we will not be able to use these and super keyword in the static areas. And like I said, we can use that this keyword without the involvement of inheritance concept. Whereas in order to use a super keyword, you need to make sure there is a inheritance involved and there is a superclass and there is a subclass.

So the most common use case of super keyword is to eliminate the confusion between the superclass and subclass methods that have a same name. I hope you are clear with this discussion. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.text:
As of now, we discussed about the three pillars of object oriented programming, which are Encapsulation, Polymorphism, and Inheritance. As a next step, let's try to understand what is an Abstraction and how to implement it inside the Java programs. Both the Polymorphism and Abstraction, they are tightly coupled with the Inheritance like we saw in the previous lectures, Polymorphism can be easily achieved with the help of Inheritance. Very similarly Abstraction also we can only implement along with the Inheritance.

That's why whenever you are trying to implement Inheritance inside your Java project, you should also try to take care of implementing and balancing other pillars of object oriented programming, which are Polymorphism and Abstraction. With that, now let's try to understand what is an Abstraction. As of now, all the super classes that we have created, they have the methods along with the business logic. That means the super classes, they are giving an option to the subclass you can inherit my business logic which is present inside my methods.

If you want, you can change that business logic by overriding the methods defined inside the superclass. So this is what happening right now. But with Abstraction, the developers, they are going to have an option to have some methods inside their classes without any business logic. That means a super class can simply define a method without any business logic, and it will be the responsibility of the subclass to define the actual business logic based upon the subclass requirements.

I know this might be a super confusing. Let me show you an example. First, I'm going to create a class inside the base package. The class name is going to be Subject. So this Subject is going to act as a superclass for many other subjects. Inside this superclass of Subject, I can create normal methods with the business logic, or I can also try to create methods without any business logic. Let me show you how to do that. That's a compilation error right now we are facing. So to resolve this, first we can go to the Student subclass and here I can simply mention extents followed by Person. Let me do the same for Employee as well. Here also I'm mentioning the extents followed by Person.
