So if I update these Student class as final, you can see the compilation error is resolved. So with this we are telling that Student class is not going to be inherited by any other subclasses. So this kind of confirmation we need to give to the compiler by either mentioning final sealed or non sealed.

Let me go to the Employee here also, you can see I have three options to resolve this compilation error. So let me go to the more actions. The very first option is marking the class as final like we did for the Student class. The second option is I can mark the Employee subclass as sealed. If I mark my Employee class as sealed, then immediately it is going to ask me to provide the what are the permitted subclasses. If I don't have any intentions to allow these Employee class to act as a superclass for other subclasses, then there is no need of defining the sealed here.

We can roll back and with that we are going to left with the final option which is non sealed. If I mention this non sealed keyword inside my class definition. In that scenario, I am making this Employee class to be inherited by any other class inside my Java project. That means when we use this non sealed, we are not going to restrict any restrictions. Whoever want to inherit my Employee as an superclass. So these are the rules that you need to follow.

The rule number one is inside your superclass you need to make sure you are mentioning the sealed keyword, followed by permits and the list of subclasses. The subclasses they need to make sure the class is marked either as final sealed or non sealed. If they mark themselves as sealed classes then again, my subclass also need to define permits keyword followed by list of other subclasses. So these are the basic rules that you need to be aware when you are trying to build sealed classes.

Apart from these rules, there is also one more rule that you need to be aware, which is if you didn't build your Java project with the help of Java modules, then you need to make sure all your sealed classes and its subclasses are present inside the same package. As of now, we are only using the packages to build the Java classes inside our Java project. We are not using the Java modules which are introduced in Java 9, but if a given Java project is implemented with the help of Java modules and packages, in such scenarios, the condition is your sealed class and subclasses can be in different packages, but all these different packages they should be present inside a single module.

I hope you are clear with all the explanation around the sealed classes. Just like how we have sealed the classes, we also have sealed interfaces. Even for interfaces also the sealed mechanism or the sealed concept is going to work in a very similar fashion. But for now, please note that even for the interface also we can use the same keyword sealed, permits. Using these permits and sealed, we can also build a selective inheritance for interfaces as well. And overall, if you ask me, what is the advantage that we are getting with the sealed class and sealed interfaces is, they are going to provide an useful tool for designing more secure and flexible class hierarchies inside Java, particularly if you are going to work in an enterprise Java project where they are going to have thousands of Java classes and interfaces, in such scenarios, it is always advisable to go with the inheritance selectively with the help of these sealed classes and the interfaces.

We use USB drives or pen drives a lot on our day to day basis. The same pen drive or USB drive, we should be able to connect to various brands of laptops, and even we should be able to connect the USB drive to the smart TV. So how is this is possible? This is because there is an international standard body which takes care of publishing the standards or specifications or a guidelines to build an USB drive or a pen drive. So any company who are manufacturing the laptops, smart TVs, they should stick to the same specification or the guideline which is published by the international standard body around the USB drives.

That's why the same USB drive were able to connect across devices without any issues. The same kind of specifications or the guidelines is usually published by many organizations to bring some consistency in the implementing. For example, in the covid time, the World Health Organization, it published the guidelines at the protocol or the specifications that every hospital in the world that has to follow to treat a Covid positive patient. Along with the treatment, they also published the specifications or the guidelines on how to clean the surrounding of the hospitals or the surroundings of the Covid affected person.

Why I'm telling about all these right now. This is because whatever I have discussed just now, they are very closely related to the interfaces concept in Java. So what is an Interface, in Java Interface provides a way to define a contract that a class must follow in order to implement a certain set of behaviors. For example, think like you have a scenario where you are going to build a group of classes around that business scenario. So in this kind of scenarios to bring some consistency in all these group of classes, we can define a contract or a guideline or the specifications with the help of an Interface.

So inside an Interface we can define all abstract methods without worrying about the actual implementation logic. And all the classes who are trying to implement these Interface, they need to adhere to the contract or the specifications that we have defined with the help of abstract methods. In simple words, an Interface always going to provide method, signature, return types and parameters that the implementation classes must follow. Here you might be clear about the definition of interface and you may say okay, I understand what is an Interface and what's the definition of it.

But the question you may have here is what are the advantages that I am going to get with Interfaces? And why should we define Interfaces first of all inside a Java project. So it's a very great question and a valid question. So let's try to discuss more details about Interface by taking a scenario. Think like you have a business requirement where you want to build a multiple Java classes that portray different heroes that we have inside the Marvel Universe.

Like inside Marvel Universe, we have IronMan, SpideMan, CaptainAmerica. This way we have many other superheroes inside the Marvel Universe. So the task that you have right now is you need to build the Java classes representing each of these superheroes. In real projects obviously, a single developer is not going to develop all the Java classes, so the task is going to be divided among the multiple developers. Think like you, as one of the developer received this task and your team manager or team lead, he has given a day time to implement these business logic since three developers, they are going to work on these three different classes.

This is how the final result from three different developers. You can see every developer he created a class representing his superhero like IronMan, SpiderMan and Captain America. All these superheroes, they have a common behavior, which is they have a special power using which they can kill or stop a villain. So these two behaviors is implemented by using different method names, different method signature by different developers. For example, inside the IronMan, the method name is usePower(), which is not going to return anything, whereas inside the SpiderMan the method name is applyPower() with the return type of int, and in the Captain America we have the method name as throwPower() with the return type of String.

Similarly, regarding the behavior around the stopping the villain or killing the villain, we have different method names with the different method signatures. So from this, it should be pretty clear for you that there is no consistency though all the superheroes have the common behavior. So to handle these kind of scenarios, only we can have an interface in Java. Before we try to understand how to resolve this problem with the help of Interfaces in the coming lectures.

First, let me more details about the disadvantages that we have if we don't follow Interfaces in Java, like we discussed in the previous slide, three different developers, they develop three different classes representing three different superheroes from the Marvel Universe. The very first disadvantage with this approach is each developer has written the classes methods inside them based upon their own understanding. Though all these heroes have the common functionality.

The method names the return type, and the accepting parameters are different, so there is no consistency like we discussed. So what is the problem if we don't have any consistency? Think like you want to go with the war with Thanos, and you may want to call all your superheroes and invoke their powers, issue commands to kill the villain. So in this kind of scenarios, since we have no consistency inside the superhero Java implementation classes, the code that you are going to write to invoke all the methods present inside these superheroes is going to be super clumsy, and you need to write a lot of code handling different, different superheroes in a different manner.

For example, if you want to invoke the method related to the power inside the IronMan, you need to invoke these usePower() method. And we can't use the same logic to invoke the power related method present inside the SpiderMan, because the method name is different. So these kind of problems you will face due to inconsistency code. And here you may also have a question why can't we solve this problem by defining a super class? And inside the super class we can have all these common functionality.

I agree with you. To some extent we can follow that approach, but the problem with the super class is whenever you are trying to define a super class, the developer has to provide some implementation logic and the subclasses. Either they can follow that implementation logic, or they can override the super class methods with their own implementation logic. For example, think like you have 100 different methods representing 100 different common functionality between multiple classes.

In such scenarios, why should we force a developer to define a super class and inside the super class, he need to write 100 different methods, and inside the 100 different methods, he need to provide some default common implementation. So to avoid such kind of pain points, we can follow the Interface approach. When we use the Interface approach, we don't have to provide any implementation logic. The Interface can simply define the specifications or the contract, or the guidelines that all the superhero related classes has to follow.

So the advantage that we get when we use Interfaces is, we are going to build a more maintainable, reusable and modular code. So just like how a subclass can inherit from a super class, very similarly, with the help of Inheritance, a class can inherit the specifications from the Interface. Once the Inheritance is established between an Interface and a Java class, the Java class has to take care of implementing the business logic in all the abstract methods which it inherited from the Interface.

I hope you got a clarity around what is an Interface, what are the problems that we may face without interface. From the next lecture, let's try to understand how to create an Interface, how to define a contract or specification with the help of Interface, and how to use an Interface to provide an consistency behavior across multiple classes. Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.text:
In the previous lecture, we have created multiple superhero Java classes and in all these classes we implemented a common interface, which is superhero. Now let's try to understand what is the advantage that we are getting whenever we are trying to implement a superhero. We already know about one advantage, which is we are getting a code consistency in all the classes where a particular interface is being inherited. From this consistency advantage, we will have many other advantages.

So let me show you what are those? To demo you the same I'm going to create a new package and the package name is going to be com.eazybytes.marvel.hero.app. Inside this package I'm going to create a Java class which is MarvelHeroDemo inside this class first let me create a main() method. And inside this method first I'm going to write a logic to invoke the methods available in one of the superhero class. Think like we are going a war with the Thanos or any other villain.

In this kind of scenarios, we need to alert our superheroes by invoking their methods. So let's try to understand how to do the same. First, I'm going to create the object of IronMan using IronMan new Ironman() and post that I'm going to invoke the method IronMan.usePower() and whatever we are trying to return from this method, the same is going to be printed onto the console. So let me try to do the same for the other method where I'm going to invoke the method which is top villain and to this I will send the value n as an input.

So if I try to execute this logic, you'll be able to see an output saying that IronMan using his power and IronMan stop the villain. Let me try to do the same for other two superheroes I have. So I'm going to create the object of SpiderMan and by using the SpiderMan class, the object reference also, I'm going to change to SpiderMan. Now using the SpiderMan Object reference, I'm going to invoke the methods which are usePower() and stopVillain(). And at last let me try to create the object of Captain America by using the class of Captain America.

Now, using the same object reference of Captain America, I'm trying to invoke the methods, usePower() and stopVillain(). So if I try to execute this method, you can see I'm getting all the output like we expect. So here you can see there is a lot of code is being repeated. Like whenever we want to invoke a SuperHero related methods, we are trying to repeat the same statement multiple times. The only thing is changing here is object reference name.

We can try to solve this problem by using the interface type as an object reference name. For example, here instead of IronMan IronMan, I can try to use the interface name, which is SuperHero. So the casting is always acceptable because every IronMan is a superhero. So here, right now, the IronMan object variable, it is trying to refer to the type SuperHero. Whereas on the right hand side we are trying to create an object of IronMan. So inside these variable IronMan, the IronMan object is going to be stored.

So let me try to do the same for remaining objects like SpiderMan and CaptainAmerica. And to this method I'm going to pass the object of type SuperHero interface. After this I'm going to mention the curly braces. And inside this new method I'm going to mention the business logic with the help of superhero variable name.

So now you can see I have an static method which is going to hold the common logic that is required for my all superheroes. So instead of writing this logic at multiple places, I can simply try to invoke the method invokeSuperHero(), and to the same I can try to pass the object reference of my superheroes. So let me do the same for SpiderMan as well. So instead of IronMan, I need to mention the SpiderMan, and at last let me do the same for CaptainAmerica as well.

So this way you can see now the code is looking very short and concise, and in future, whenever we want to make any changes, the change is always going to be inside a single method. So here you can see the other advantage that we are getting from the interface is, we are encouraging the reusability. And we are also building the common logic in a separate method. So this is also kind of Polymorphism. The same method is trying to act differently based upon the input that you are trying to send.

So this kind of discussion we also did when we are discussing about the superclass and subclass in the previous section. So the advantages are always going to be similar to the subclass and superclass scenario. But here you may have a question which is, if you are able to achieve the same with the subclass and superclass, why should I go with an interface? It's a great question. The answer is very simple. With interface we are not taking the headache of providing the implementation logic, we are just defining the standard or the specification or the contract which all my implementation classes has to follow.

I hope you are clear with the demo. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: Constant Field Declarations in interface
lectures.text:
As of now, inside our interfaces, we just declared the abstract methods. Apart from abstract methods, we can also declare constant fields inside interfaces. So whenever you are trying to declare a constant value inside an interface, it is going to be by default public static and final. That means you don't have to mention public static final. For example, like you can see here, I have two different examples where I'm trying to create the same constant, which is UNIVERSE_NAME.

On the left hand side example, I'm trying to mention public static final before my constant declaration, whereas on the right hand side I simply mentioned String UNIVERSE_NAME as MARVEL So both of these examples, they are going to be work very similarly because like I said, inside interfaces, all your constants, they are going to be implicitly public, static and final. So whenever we define a constant inside an interface, we can access these interfaces with the help of interface name.

So please note that we can only define a static fields inside interfaces. We will not be able to define instance variables inside interfaces because the interfaces are mean to be defined a contract a specification, but they are never meant to be to create an object from them. That's why the instance variable declarations inside interfaces is not allowed. And since by implicitly, every static field that you're going to create inside interface is final, you will not be able to change the value of these constant values at later point of time.

So whenever you are trying to declare during the same time, you should also assign an initialize value. And this initialize value is going to be final forever. If you try to change this initialized value at later point of time, it is not going to work because all the constants that we define inside an interface, they are going to be final. On top of that, if you are trying to simply declare an constant without initialization, it will also not allowed and it may result into compilation error.

For example, here I have a variable name which is UNIVERSE_NAME. I'm trying to do only the declaration, but not the initialization. That's why I'm going to get a compilation error. The next important point that you need to be aware here is, whenever you are trying to define constant fields inside an interface, please make sure you are mentioning the variable name in all uppercase letters, and each of the word inside your variable can be separated by an underscore value.

Following this naming convention is only optional. Java is not going to enforce this specific naming convention rules, but I would always recommend you to follow this naming convention. So what is this naming convention called? It is called as snake case Naming convention, where we can mention all the letters or characters inside a word in completely capital letters, and each word can be separated with the help of underscore. The next rule that you need to be aware is, interface fields are always public, but their accessibility from outside the declaration package depends on the interface scope.

For instance, if an interface has a package level or default scope, then in such scenarios the interface fields won't be accessible outside the package, even though the fields themselves are public. So if you want to make your interface constant to fields to be accessible by everyone across all the packages, then you need to make sure you are declaring your interface with a public access modifier. lectures.title: Different method declarations allowed in interface
lectures.text:
Let's try to understand what type of methods we can declare or define inside interface. Inside interface in total, we can try to create four different kinds of methods. The very first one like we saw previously, abstract method followed by default method, static method and private methods. But please note that the default methods and static methods we can only create inside an interface from Java 8, and similarly the private methods we can only create from Java 9 version.

So before Java 8 inside an interface, we can only create abstract methods, but from Java 8 it is allowed to create static default methods. And from Java 9, like I said, we can also create private methods. So there is a strong reason why these default static and private methods are allowed from Java 8 and later onwards, I'm going to explain you what is the strong reason in the coming lectures. For now, I just wanted to highlight you that before Java 8 we can implement 100% of abstraction using interface, because before Java 8 only abstract methods are allowed inside an interface, whereas from Java 8, since default and static methods are also allowed inside an interface.

That's why from Java 8, the difference between abstract class and interface is almost negligible. Using both of these options, we can achieve 0 to 100% abstraction. I hope you are clear with this quick introduction about what kind of methods that we can create inside an interface. Since we already discussed about the abstract methods previously, let's try to quickly revise about these methods. Whenever you are trying to declare an interface. The primary goal of an interface is always to outline an abstract blueprint or concept or a guidelines.

So that's why most of the times in real projects developers, they will create interfaces to define multiple abstract methods. So we can have an interface with the zero abstract methods or more abstract methods as well. And whenever we are trying to declare a method inside an interface, by default it is going to be considered as abstract and public unless specified otherwise with the static or default keywords. So you can see here I also gave two examples on the left hand side for the abstract method walk() and sleep().

I have mentioned the public abstract void and this is completely redundant and not required. So regardless whether you are using left hand side example or right hand side example to create a abstract method, it is going to have the same effect. And how to declare an abstract method, it is very simple. You can have a method name along with its return type, followed by method input parameter and any Throws class to throws to mention any Exception handling.

After mentioning all these details inside your method signature, you can simply mention the semicolon without any method body and curly braces. So these kind of methods are going to act as a abstract method. And the last point that I want to highlight here is, whenever you are trying to create an abstract method inside an interface or an abstract class, we can't make the method as final, since it is against to the concept of interface and abstract classes.

It is not allowed to define an abstract method as final inside Java. Because if final is allowed on top of abstract methods, then no other class or no other subclass can override the abstract method. And with that, the final abstract method declaration is going to become useless. I can also show you a quick demo around this. For example, here we have a SuperHero interface. If I try to mention final, you can see I'm getting a compilation error saying that modifier final not followed here.

Why it is not allowed because this method usePower() is an abstract method. I hope you are clear with all the discussion that we have done inside this lecture. Thank you, bye.

lectures.title: [JAVA 8] Why we need default methods in interfaces
lectures.text:
What are default methods in interface? Let's try to understand the same. Before I try to explain you about what are these default methods, please note that that these default methods are allowed only from Java 8, because inside Java 8 or JDK 8 version only the default methods are introduced, and from this version only we should be able to create default methods in interface. Any version that we have before Java 8 like Java 7, if you try to create default method in these old versions, then definitely you're going to get a compilation error.

So in summary the default methods inside interface, they are not available from day one of Java. They are introduced only from Java 8. And with that you may have a question here like why Java people they introduced this default method from Java 8. What made them to introduce these methods? To explain the same, let me try to create a same superhero scenario that we have. Think like all of a sudden the Marvel company decided to introduce a new specification or a new abstract method in SuperHero interface.

Maybe after 2 or 3 years of introducing this interface, the Marvel team, they decided to add one more specification by introducing a just new abstract method. And this may look very simple or straightforward from interface perspective, but when you introduce a new abstract method inside an interface, it is going to have ripple effect on all the implementation classes. Think like your interface has hundreds of implementation class. In all these hundreds of implementation classes, you're going to get a compilation error immediately saying that a new abstract method is introduced inside the super interface.

Please overwrite the same by providing some business logic. So this kind of errors you may get if you try to evolve your interface with the new requirements. I can also show you an example here you can see we have a SuperHero interface. Initially, when we started implementing the SuperHero interface, we used to have only two abstract methods like usePower() and stopVillain(). But later on, after 2 or 3 years down the line, if the super hero is going to have a new abstract method which is trackLiveLocation(), immediately it is going to have compilation error in all the implementation classes. Like you can see for IronMan, SpiderMan, CaptainAmerica we are having a compilation error.

Though this new abstract method is going to help to evolve the SuperHero interface, but it is creating problems on the implementation class. The same kind of problem even Java team faced when they tried to update the thousands of interface available inside the Java library before Java 8, there are thousands of interfaces inside the Java library. Java team when they decided to introduce new features into these interfaces, they immediately faced the problem in all the subclasses with the compilation error.

And all these Java interfaces might be being used by many of the organizations in their own business logic. So if there is a change in one of the library interface, it may have ripple effect in all the organizations where they are trying to use these interface. So it will force them to update their code. And updating a code for many organizations may not be a simple task. They may have to do a lot of research testing. That's why Java team, they did a lot of research and brainstorming and analysis on how to handle these kind of scenario.

And at the end they choose the solution which is default method. So with the help of default methods, what is going to happen is, whenever a new feature want to be introduced inside an existing interface, instead of creating the method as an abstract method, they are going to create a default method with some default business logic inside it, and with that, the implementation subclasses they'll have various options. The very first option is they can completely ignore this new feature introduced inside the interface, and they can continue to work the same way like they used to work before.

And the second option is the implementation classes they can accept the default behavior provided by the interface and continue to work with the help of default business logic. And the third option is the implementation classes if needed, they can override these default methods with their own business logic. So with these three kind of options the implementation classes, they can take some time to choose one of these option and make the changes inside the implementation classes.

I hope you are clear with the discussion around why we need default methods in interface, why they are introduced in Java 8. In the next lecture, let's try to see the demo of default methods. Thank you, bye.

lectures.title: Multiple Inheritance using interfaces - Part 1
lectures.text:
In the previous section, when we are talking about types of inheritance, we briefly talked about why Multiple inheritance is not allowed with the help of superclass and subclass. So we are going to have a diamond problem that's why Java is not going to allow you to inherit more than one class in the same class, but the same Multiple inheritance is not going to be a problem when we are trying to inherit multiple interfaces, we are going to get this diamond problem.

But there are some approaches to solve this diamond problem whenever we are dealing with the multiple inheritance with the interfaces. So first let's try to understand how to build a multiple inheritance with the help of interfaces like you can see here, we have implementation classes like IronMan, SpiderMan and CaptainAmerica. Inside these classes, we are trying to implement our inherit more than one interface at the same time. For example, I have a interface name, SuperHero and Person.

So this is one of the classical example of multiple inheritance using interface. So just like how a class can inherit multiple interfaces with the help of implements keyword, very similarly a interface can extend multiple other interfaces. Here I also gave an example. I have an interface with the name SuperHero and it is trying to extend multiple other interface the interface names are Person and Hero. I hope you are clear how to achieve multiple inheritance using interface.

It's very simple. You can mention your list of interfaces by using comma as a separator, but when you try to achieve multiple inheritance with the help of interfaces, sometimes you may get a diamond problem or a ambiguity to your compiler. So let's try to understand what kind of ambiguities your compiler may face and how to solve them. Inside the scenario one I'm going to give some tricky questions around the multiple inheritance. Here you can see I have an Interface A and B, and inside both of these interfaces I have the same abstract method with the name m1().

If another interface, which is C, is trying to extend both A, B. In this kind of scenarios, which m1() method is going to be inherited by my Interface C. So this kind of ambiguity your compiler may get. So this is one typical scenario that may arrive during multiple inheritance using interfaces. Let's see other combinations as well. If you take the same combination of interfaces A, B and C, this time you can see one of my interface which is A it has m1() method defined as a default method.

So since it is an abstract method, obviously the class C, it has to provide the implementation logic. Now coming to the m2() method here also the same rule is going to apply.

The same m2() method is present inside A and AB but inside A we have it as an abstract method, whereas inside AB we have it as an default method. So in this scenario also AB interface is going to be most specific super interface. The reason is inside AB we are trying to override the m2() method with the help of this override annotation. That's why my class C is going to inherit that default m2() method. lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, let's try to understand what are Marker interfaces in Java. You won't be creating are going to use marker interfaces a lot inside your real projects. But I still want to cover about this topic because inside interviews people may ask about these Marker interface, what is the purpose of them and how to create them. That's why let's try to spend few minutes around these Marker interface. So what is a Marker interface? Just like you can see, this tin is an empty tin or empty box.

Similarly, inside Java, a Marker interface is an interface that does not contain any methods and it is completely empty. Marker interface are also sometimes referred as tagging interfaces. Immediately you're going to get a question here, which is if Marker interfaces are empty interfaces, then what is the purpose of creating them and using them? Let me try to answer the same. Using these Marker interfaces, we are going to provide some metadata about a class indicating that some special behavior of the class to the compiler.

In other words, whenever a class is going to implement a Marker interface, we are communicating to the compiler that my class. Since it is implementing so and so Marker interface, it is going to have a special behavior or a special characteristic that my compiler should aware. For example, inside the Java library we have two important Marker interfaces clonable and serializable. Let's quickly validate these interfaces inside IntelliJ. Inside IntelliJ, you can press the shortcut command O for the Mac operating system.

Otherwise, for windows, you can use control O. Here inside the search box if you can type clonable, you will be able to see an interface inside the package java.lang. That's what I can see here, it is of type interface. So let me open this. If you can closely look at these interface. It is just an interface without any content inside its body. So this is a perfect example of Marker interface. If you try to read the documentation about this interface, there are clear instructions given that whenever an class is implementing these Marker interface, which is clonable, that class object can be clonable.

For example, if I have a class which is Employee, to this Employee, if I'm trying to implement Clonable interface, then I'm telling to my Java compiler, since I have implemented Clonable interface inside these Employee class, the object of Employees can be Clonable. So it is an indication to the compiler and to other developers as well. What is a cloning? Inside Java, cloning means we want to create an exact copy of an object. After the cloning is completed, we are going to have two different objects which are copy of each other.

So if I'm not using these implements Cloneable, then I will not be able to do the cloning. My Java compiler is going to throw an exception. Apart from implementing this Clonable, my Employee class should also override a method available inside the object superclass. Like you can see here I have a clone() method from the Object class, which is going to be inherited by my Employee class. The same needs to be overridden by my Employee class, so that whenever someone is trying to clone my object, whatever I have written inside this clone() method, the same is going to be executed. For some reason if I'm not implementing this Clonable interface, then I'm always going to get these CloneNotSupported exception even though this method is overridden inside the Employee class.

So you can see there is a special purpose to this Clonable interface. So for all these kind of interfaces where they don't have any logic inside them, such interfaces, we are going to call them as Marker interface. Let me show you other interface that we have which is Serializable. So this Serializable interface is available inside the package java.io. If I can open this interface you can see this interface is also empty. The purpose of this interface is whenever I am implementing these interface inside any class, it is an indication to the compiler that the object of these Employee class can be Serialized.

So what is a serialization in Java serialization is a process of converting an object into the stream of bytes data, so that these streams of byte data I can save into a disk space, or I can send to some other application over the network. So whenever we have these kind of requirements where if I want to send the my entire data object data into some other application, I can follow the serialization. And similarly, deserialization is a process of converting stream of byte data into an object representation.

So whenever an object of a class needs to be serialized or deserialized, the very first basic requirement that it has to follow is it has to implement the Marker interface, which is serializable. Otherwise compiler at runtime it is going to throw an RuntimeException. I hope you are clear about the purpose of Marker interface and the examples that we have discussed around this. Like I said before, in real projects you may never create the Marker interfaces, you may never have such requirements.

But if you want to understand how to create a Marker interface, it is going to be very simple. First you need to mention public followed by interface keyword and what is your interface name and post that you should have empty curly braces and with that you will be able to successfully create your own custom marker interface. If you want to use the same inside any other class, just like any other normal interface you can using the implements keyword, you should be able to inherit or implement your My Marker interface.

But like I said these days Marker interface are not being used frequently inside Java because alternative mechanisms like annotations came into picture and they become more popular. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

So what is a Functional Interface? Any interface with only one abstract method is commonly referred as Functional Interface. You can also recall this concept using the acronym or short form which is SAM.

Sam means Single Abstract Method. So whenever an interface has an SAM, we can call such interface as Functional Interface. Apart from having a single abstract method inside and Functional interface, we can have any number of static methods and default methods. There are no restrictions around static methods and default methods, because default and static methods, they are not going to play any role in determining if an interface is a Functional interface or not.

The concept of Functional interface is introduced only from the Java 8 before Java 8, there is no concept of Functional interface, so inside the Java library there are some interfaces with the single abstract method, but still we never used to call them as Functional interface, because the concept of Functional interface came into picture from Java 8 only. lectures.title: Class Vs Abstract Class Vs Interface
lectures.text:
As of now, we discuss everything about what is a class, what is a abstract class, and what is an interface. Inside this lecture, I want to spend a few minutes explaining about the differences between these three different components. Understanding them is very important, otherwise you may get confused very easily. First, if you start with the inheritance, both the class and abstract class, they support a single inheritance, whereas with the help of interface we can achieve multiple inheritance.

The next point that we have is, around the implementation or the creation of the object. Can we create an object of a class? Off course we can create. That's why I have mentioned can be instantiated. Whereas both abstract class and interface, we cannot instantiate them or we cannot create an object of them. Coming to the constructor, both the class and abstract class, they can have constructors, whereas inside interface constructor eaters are not allowed.

And here you may have a question. We said abstract class cannot be instantiated. Then why abstract class can have constructors? Because constructors can only be used during the object creation. If we will not be able to create an object of abstract class, then why constructors are allowed inside an abstract class. So that's a question you may have here. Let me try to answer the same. Like we discussed in the previous sections, whenever a abstract class is inherited by a class inside the subclass constructor, the compiler automatically is going to add the super keyword to invoke the abstract class constructor.

Why Java compiler is going to do that automatically? Because abstract classes, they can have some instance fields the same are going to be inherited by the normal subclass. So when we are trying to create an object of a normal class, all the instance fields present inside the class and the abstract class, they're all going to be initialized or created as part of the object creation of the subclass. So to support these initialization, abstract class also should have an its own constructor, which is going to be invoked from the subclass constructor with the help of super keyword. Coming to the methods and fields inside class, we can write all kinds of methods except abstract methods.

Like we can write a concrete method, static method, and we can have non static and we can have static fields, instance fields. The only limitation inside a class is we cannot define an abstract method. Coming to the abstract class it can have an abstract method, concrete method, static method and all type of fields are allowed inside abstract class, whereas inside interface we can only have constant static fields, default method, abstract method, static methods and private methods. Even abstract class and normal class also they can have private methods coming to the purpose.

The purpose of classes is to create the objects and define behavior as part of the class definition. Whereas abstract class purpose is to provide a base for all the derived classes or for all the subclasses and define some common behavior. Whereas interface main purpose is to define a contract or a behavior in a more abstract manner. If you want to simply define a contract and don't worry about providing any implementation logic, then always interface is a good choice, whereas abstract class can be a good choice if you want to provide some base functionality as some common functionality with the help of concrete methods followed by.

You can also define some abstract methods inside abstract class. Coming to the access modifiers, we can use public, protected and private access modifiers for the methods in class, and the same applies for the abstract class. Whereas inside interface by default all methods are going to be public if needed we can define default methods and private methods as well. And the last point that I have here is relationship to the subclasses. If a class is being inherited by another subclass, then the superclass is going to act as a blueprint for that derived class.

Whereas coming to the abstract class, like I said, it is only going to act as a base by providing some implementation details. And with an interface, we can define a contract for all the implementation classes. I hope you understand all these differences, all the points that we also discuss. I mentioned inside the slide for your reference. I also have a couple of memes around interfaces, abstract classes and inheritance. Like you can see, this is a funny definition of abstract class in a nutshell, the combination of interface and inheritance we are going to get the abstract class.

I hope you like this funny meme. Moving on to the second meme, someone is trying to identify the differences between interface and abstract class. But from Java 8, since the default method static methods, private methods, everything is allowed. The difference between these interface and abstract class is reduced drastically. That's why, on a funny note, we can say slowly interface is trying to become an abstract class. That's why this lady here, she's also telling they are the same picture.

I'm not able to identify any differences between them. It is true to some extent, but like we discussed just now, there are some minute differences between an abstract class and interface. On a funny note, we can always say they both are same. Before I try to close this lecture, I want to highlight about the Sealed interfaces. Like we discussed in the previous section, there is a concept of Sealed classes using which a superclass can select its own subclasses.

Very similarly, using Sealed interfaces also, we can permit list of implementation classes that can inherit your Sealed interface. Here you can see first we need to mention sealed keyword followed by interface, followed by your interface name and after the interface name with the help of permits keyword you can mention the list of classes. Like here I'm trying to mention Dog and Cat, and with that, only these two classes will be able to inherit or implement this sealed interface.

I hope you are clear. Thank you, bye.

lectures.title: Iterate elements of Array using for-each loop
lectures.text:
When we are discussing about the loops inside Java, I told you that there is a for each loop available, which is an enhanced version of traditional for loop this for each loop we can only use with arrays and collections. Collection is an another advanced topic similar to arrays. But now let's try to focus on how to use this for each loop to iterate the elements of an array and how it is going to be a better version of traditional for loop. For each loop, which is also known as enhanced for loop, is a loop that is used to iterate over elements of an array or a collection.

This is introduced in Java five to provide a simplified way to iterate through the elements of an array or collections. Whenever we are using these for each loop, we don't have to worry about how to use an index to iterate the elements. First, let's try to understand what is the syntax to use the for each loop. Like you can see here, whenever we want to use this for each loop, we need to mention the same for keyword followed by parentheses and curly braces.

Inside traditional for loop, we will write three different kinds of expressions, whereas inside the for each loop we are going to write only two expressions, which are separated by colon. On the right hand side to the colon we need to give the variable of an array or the variable of an collection. In other words, to the right hand side of the colon, we need to mention what is the array, or what is a collection that we want to iterate with the help of for each loop, whereas on the left hand side we need to mention what is the data type of the elements that we stored inside an array or collection.

For example, inside an array, if I store all elements of type int, I need to mention the data type as int followed by a temporary variable name. If you follow this syntax during the iteration, this for each loop, it is going to extract the element from the array one by one in each iteration, and during the same process, the value of the current element or the current iteration is going to be assigned to this temporary variable that you have mentioned.

Using this variable only inside your for each loop, you can write the business logic. I can also show you an example here. Here you can see we have an array of type int. The array name is numbers. And inside this array we are storing five different int values. So whenever we want to use for each to iterate this array first we need to mention what is the array name. The array name is numbers and to the left hand side we need to mention what is the data type.

The data type that we have considered during the declaration of numbers is, int the same I need to mention here. And what is the temporary variable name? So the temporary variable name that I have given is num. This temporary variable num is going to be used to refer to the current element in each iteration. And the same we can use as part of the business logic. If you see inside my for each loop, I have written a business logic which is to print each element inside my array.

That's why I'm simply passing this num variable as an input to the println() method. Here you can see I'm nowhere worrying about the what is the length of my array? What is the current index? Since these for each loop is making our life easy, most of the developers on day to day work. They are going to use this for each loop, only to iterate over the elements of an array or a collection. Let me show you very quickly what is the difference between a traditional for loop and an enhanced For each loop. You can see the same input I have taken, like numbers, which is an array.

In the case of for loop first we need to check what is the length of my array, and similarly we should start the index value at zero. By using this int i is equal to zero, and apart from initialization and this conditional check, we should also take care of updating the index variable after each iteration with the help of these i++ and inside the business logic if you want to access the current element for the current iteration, you need to use this syntax, which is numbers.

And inside the square bracket we need to mention the current index value which is represented by this i variable. Whereas with for each you can see how simple it is. We just have to mention what is the array variable and what is the data type of the element which is int and what is the temporary variable? Using this temporary variable, we can easily write the business logic inside the for each loop. So like I said, most of the times for each loop is a preferred approach for the developers to iterate the elements of an array.

But that does not mean we don't have any use case to use the for loop. There are certain scenarios where using for loop is preferred approach compared to the for each loop. For example, think like inside your business logic you need to modify the array or collection elements during the iteration itself. So in this kind of scenarios we need to use the for loop. Because using for loop we should be able to know what is the current index number. After modifying the current array element value, we can update the same back into the current index number.

The same we can't achieve with the help of for each loop, because inside for each loop, developers will not be able to get hold on to the current index number. I hope you are clear with this theory discussion. Let me show you an example on how to use for each loop very quickly. To demo you about the for each loop, I'm going to create a new Java class. The Java class name that I'm going to give here is ArrayForEachLoopDemo inside this class first, as usual we need to create the main() method, followed by I'm going to create an array of type int with the name numbers.

And inside this array I'm going to store the values like 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. As a next step, let's try to use the for each loop to iterate these elements. For the same, first I need to mention for followed by what is the data type of my array elements. The data type is int followed by what is that temporary variable name that I want to give to the current element of each iteration. After providing the variable name, you can mention space followed by colon.

After colon you can mention the space again and at last you need to provide your array as an input. Since our array is represented with the help of numbers variable, I'm trying to provide the same followed by curly braces. Now inside my for each loop, I'm going to use the num variable name to print each element available inside my numbers array during the iteration. So let me keep a breakpoint here. And if I try to execute this program, you can see during the first iteration the breakpoint stopped.

And during the first iteration, what is the value stored inside the num, it is one because at the very first position we have the value one. If I try to keep debugging, the num variable is going to keep change to 3, 4, 5. During each iteration, the current focused element is going to be assigned to this variable. The same variable we can use inside the for loop to perform the business logic. So you can see inside our console we have the output 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Let me do the same for one more array. For the same this time I'm going to define an array of type String, and inside the String I'm going to store three different names. The names are Madan followed by John, followed by Lucy. Now I have my names array ready, so let me use the for each loop by mentioning for followed by parentheses. After the parentheses, I can mention the curly braces. Inside the parentheses, this time I need to mention the data type as String and the temporary variable name as name, followed by what is the array variable name.

So the array variable name is names. Now let me try to write the business logic inside this for each loop. The business logic is just to print the name value. If I execute this program, you will be able to see three names that are being displayed inside the console as well. As the next step let me show you under which scenarios we cannot use the for each loop. Suppose think like, I have a requirement to convert each of my name value to a completely capital letter.

So in this kind of scenario, I want to first read the element from the array. Post that I need to current the element value into a complete capital value, and update back into the array. In this kind of scenarios, whenever we want to update a value back inside an array, we need to know what is the current index number, since for each loop is not going to provide you, what is the current index number during the iteration? We cannot use for each loop in this kind of scenario.

So that's why I'm going to use the traditional for loop. Inside the traditional for loop, we are going to first mention int i is equal to zero, followed by a less than names.length, followed by i++ and post that inside the curly braces. I'm going to write a business logic, which is names followed by square brackets, and inside the square brackets I'm going to mention what is a current index number is equal to followed by names and inside the square brackets i and dot toUpperCase().

So what do I get from these names off I I'm going to get a String object because my names array is going to hold the objects of String. So with the help of a String object, I can invoke the method toUpperCase(), which is going to convert the content of my String object into completely capital letter, the same I'm trying to assign back into my names array. So after executing this traditional for loop, all the names inside the names array is going to be converted into completely capital letters.

We can also confirm the same by keeping a breakpoint at the end. Let me execute this method. You can see the breakpoint stopped at the line number 22, and the values inside the names are completely converted into uppercase letter. So when you have these kind of scenarios where you want to modify the elements of an array or a collection, in such scenarios, definitely you need to go with the traditional for loop, but not with the for each loop. Whereas if your scenario is only to process each element by having a business logic but not modifying or but not updating back into the array, then in such scenarios you can happily use the enhanced to for loop, which is for each for loop.

I hope you are clear with this discussion. Thank you, bye.

lectures.title: Arrays advantages and disadvantages
lectures.text:
Let's try to understand what are the arrays advantages and disadvantages. Before we try to focus on advantages and disadvantages. First, we need to understand how arrays are stored behind the scenes inside memory. Whenever you try to create an array behind the scenes, all the elements of an array are stored continuously inside memory. What do you mean by continuously or consecutively? So let me show you an example. Think like I have declared an array which is going to store the int numbers.

That's why I have defined that type of this array as int. So inside this you can see we have five different int values. So when these statement is being executed behind the scenes my JVM or Java they are going to look for a space where five continuous are consecutive memory locations are available. For example think like my JVM identified a space which is of type five continuous memory locations. The memory location they are going to start from 3415 to 3419.

So this is just a random memory location value that I'm trying to mention here. So if you see all the contents of my array like 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 they are stored at the continuous memory locations. The behavior will not be the same if you try to create an array which is capable of storing an object of String or other custom data type. For example, think like I have an array which is capable of storing three different Person objects. In this scenario, whenever we try to create an Person object, we know it is going to be created inside the heap memory.

If we end up creating three different Person objects, the same three different objects, they are going to be created at some random location inside the heap memory. lectures.title: Introduction to multidimensional or nested arrays
lectures.text:
As of now, we discussed about simple arrays. Using these simple arrays, we can store a group of elements which belongs to a same data type. For example, by using a simple array, I can store a group of into values or a group of String object or a Person object. Apart from these simple arrays, Java also supports multi-dimensional or nested arrays. So what is this multi-dimensional or nested array? In simple words, we can call them as array of arrays, which means each element of an array can be also be an array.

So that's why anytime if someone asks you what is a multi-dimensional or a nested array, you can simply answer them it is an array of arrays. The most common multi-dimensional array that we are going to use in real projects is two dimensional array. If needed, we can build a three dimensional array, four dimensional array, five dimensional. We can build any multi-dimensional arrays or nested arrays based upon our business requirements and complexity of the data that we are trying to store inside arrays.

So these are simple definition about the nested arrays and multi-dimensional arrays. Let's try to understand what is the syntax that we need to follow whenever we want to simply declare an nested array or multi-dimensional array. Like you can see here first, as usual, we need to mention what is the data type which is going to be supported by your array, followed by you can mention the square brackets, usually as part of simple arrays we will only mention a single square bracket, but here we can mention any number of square brackets.

For example, if I want to create a simple array, then we are going to mention a single square bracket. Whereas if you have a requirement to store the data using the two dimensional array, then I need to mention two square brackets. Like the same way we can mention any number of square brackets based upon how many number of dimensions that we want to consider while building the nested array. And at last you can mention, as usual, what is your array variable name followed by semicolon.

So here we are just declaring the nested array. We are not initializing it, or we are not assigning any size or length to my multi-dimensional array. As an excerpt, let's try to understand how to initialize and multi-dimensional or nested array. In the very first syntax you can see first, I am trying to use the same variable name that we have created in the above step. After the variable name as usual, we need to mention is equal to followed by new operator, followed by data type, and after the data type, you need to mention the same number of square brackets that you have defined during the declaration.

Inside these square brackets, you can define the length values like length one, length two. If you want to combine both these declaration and initialization into a single statement, then you can look at these last syntax that I have mentioned. Like I said before, using these multi-dimensional array we can build a 2D array 3D array 4d array. So based upon our business requirements we can go to any nesting level. But most of the times in real projects people will end up using only 2D or at a max they will use 3D arrays.

The higher number of dimensions you are trying to consider for your nested array, the more difficult you are going to face. To access and store elements inside a multi-dimensional array, you're going to understand the same when we are going to discuss few examples around the two dimensional array and the three dimensional array. Whenever we are using simple arrays to store the data, it is going to be super simple to access an element or to store an element at a particular index, because we just have to provide what is the position number or the index number.

And providing such information with simple arrays is going to be super easy. But like I said, if you try to create two dimensional or three dimensional arrays, then you need to mention multiple index values along with their correct combinations. Otherwise you will end up accessing an invalid element. When we see examples around multi dimensional array, it is going to make more sense to you. The last point that I want to highlight here is, whenever we want to convert a nested array into a String representation, so that we can print the nested array onto our console.

In this kind of scenarios, we need to use the deep toString() method available inside arrays. Whereas for simple arrays we used toString() method which is available inside arrays. The same toString() method is not going to work for multi-dimensional or nested arrays. That's why whenever you want to convert your multi-dimensional or nested array into a String object, please use the deepToString() static method available inside the Arrays class. I'm also going to show you a demo around this method in the coming lectures.

I hope you are clear about what are multidimensional and nested arrays in Java. If something is not clear, don't worry, I'm there for you. From the next lecture, we are going to start discussion around the 2D arrays and the 3D arrays. And in the same process I'm going to show you many examples. And with that you're going to have a clear understanding around the nested arrays inside Java. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: Comparison of BufferedReader and Scanner
lectures.text:
Let's try to understand the differences between BufferReader and Scanner approaches. Most of these differences we already discussed in the previous lectures, but there is no harm in revising one more time. The very first difference is whenever you are trying to use a BufferReader, it is only capable of reading the sequence of characters in a String format. Once the reading operation is completed, it is going to be the responsibility of the developer to convert that String object data into an corresponding output format like int, double, float based upon the business requirements of the developer.

Whereas with the scanner we have various methods which are going to start with a prefix and next. So based upon the type of input data that we are trying to accept, we can invoke these next methods to get the output in various formats like int, short, byte, float, long, double, String, boolean. So please use them based upon your business requirements. The second difference, like you know, BufferReader is present inside the Java right from day one, whereas Scanner is introduced only from the JDK 1.5 release.

So why Java team release Scanner? Since there are some drawbacks, and since there is some complexity in using BufferReader, they want to make the life of developers easy. That's why they have introduced Scanner under the java.util package as part of the 1.5 version. The next major difference that we have is BufferReader has a capability to hold the large buffer size, which is by default eight kilobytes, whereas with the Scanner the buffer size is going to be only 1kb.

Apart from these buffer size differences, BufferReader allows you to customize this buffer size based upon your business requirements. If these 8kb is not sufficient, you can try to create the object of BufferReader with a buffer size of 16 kb or any amount of large buffer size, and the other side the Scanner. It is not going to provide you that flexibility. It is always going to allow you to create an object of Scanner with the default buffer size, which is 1kb.

With these differences, it should be pretty clear for you when you are dealing with the large amount of data, like you're trying to read the data from a huge file. In such scenarios, the BufferReader is the most suitable one compared to the Scanner, because BufferReader at a time, it can load the data of around 8kb, whereas Scanner is only capable of 1kb. So due to these size differences, Scanner always has a disadvantage whenever you are trying to deal with the large files or large input data, whereas for a short input data or a small input files, you can happily use Scanner and there won't be any performance issue.

The next difference is around the synchronization. Inside Java, there is a concept of multithreading. We are going to discuss in the coming sections. What is multithreading? Multithreading is a concept where your program is going to be executed at a single time by multiple threads, or by multiple requests, which are invoked by multiple end users. In such scenarios, it is always safe to use BufferReader because it is a synchronized class, which means you can share the same BufferReader object across multiple threads.

Whereas Scanner is not a synchronized class, you cannot share this Scanner object across multiple threads. So if you are developing a business logic for a multithreading environment, always consider BufferReader. The next difference we have is around the exception handling. BufferReader always force you to handle the IOException, either by mentioning the throws statement inside the method signature, or with the help of exception handling techniques, which you are going to discuss in the coming sections.

Whereas scanner does not force the developer to handle the IOException, it is going to hide it and behind the scenes it is going to handle this exception. And at last we can say BufferReader is faster and efficient because it supports larger buffer size of 8KB and if needed we can further increase it, whereas Scanner is slower and less efficient. That's why always please note that if you are dealing with a small input data, you can happily use the Scanner.

Whereas if you are trying to deal with the large input data like large files, like 1MB, 2MB files, then in such scenarios always go with the BufferReader. I hope you are clear with these differences. These differences are very important from interview perspective. So people can always ask you what are the differences between them and under which scenarios. We should use BufferReader and Scanner. So these kind of questions you should be able to easily answer with the discussion that we had throughout this lecture.

Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: Don’t use System.out.println in Production code
lectures.text:
As of now, we discussed a lot of concepts and topics inside Java. With all the knowledge that we have gained so far by this time, you might have became a fan to the System.out.println(), and you may have intentions to use this a lot inside your real projects as well. But I want you to stop there and I want to give you a cautious note here, which is it is not recommended to use the System.out.println() or any other print methods inside production code.

What is the meaning of production code? Whenever you are building the Java logic or any code for a real application which will be deployed eventually into your production environment in the form of website or in the form of mobile application, or in the form of a API service. Regardless of how your code is deployed, it is always considered as a production code because your code is going to be served to the actual end users. So in all these kind of production related scenarios, we are not allowed to use a System.out,.println().

We should only use this during learning Java, or whenever you are trying to debug your code, or whenever you are trying to test your code. In those scenarios only we are supposed to use this, but not in the production code. With that definitely you might have surprised and you may have questions. Why should I not use a System.out.println() ? Let me try to explain what are the drawbacks that we have. If we use the System.out dot.println(), your compiler is not going to stop you.

You can always mention System.out.println(). In fact, even today there are many developers who use these System.out.println() unknowingly inside their production code. But inside the projects where a strong review process is established. In this kind of projects, the lead or the senior developer who is trying to perform a code review of a junior developer if he sees this System.out.println(). Which is trying to get pushed into the production code in such scenarios, they will definitely blame you and they will give a code review comment saying that remove these System.out.println().

So I don't want you to be into that embarrassing situations. That's why let's try to understand why we should not use them and what are the alternatives that we have. The very first drawback using System.out.println() is, performance degradation. If you write a small program with the System.out.println() are two different places, nothing is going to happen. It is not going to impact your application in any way, but in real projects there will be thousands of classes and inside these thousands of classes, there will be millions of lines of code in all these millions of lines of code.

If each developer end up using System.out.println(), wherever he wants will be, end up having thousands of System.out.println() statements. And with that, it is going to have a performance degradation problem inside your application, especially while we are trying to print the a large message. Why there will be a performance degradation. Because whenever you want to print a big message onto your console like we discussed previously, first it has to get an object of PrintStream.

So when this object of PrintStream is getting created, a connection to your console will be opened behind the scenes. And with that connection, only the message will be printed onto the console. And at last, the connection with the console, which is established by the PrintStream object, has to be closed behind the scenes, since these kind of operations are happening behind the scenes, so there is a good chance that a performance degradation can happen.

The second disadvantage is lack of flexibility. Whenever you are trying to print a message to the console, you will have very limited control on how you can format your message. Especially you can't add the details like under which method, under which class the printing of the statement happened, at which point of time, and using which thread. So all these kind of information you will not be able to print with the help of System.out.println() statements.

Believe me, in real projects the logging requirements are even more complex. When I say logging. What is the meaning of logging? Logging is the process of printing a value onto the console or onto a file, which we can use at later point of time to debug what happened inside our program. So in real projects, the logging requirements are going to be super complex. All such complex requirements can't be achieved with the help of System.out.println().

And the third disadvantage is inability to disable logging. When I try to print a message with the help of System.out.println(), there is no way for me to disable that printing other than deleting the entire line of System.out.println(). Whereas with the alternatives that we are going. To discuss in the coming lectures. They're going to provide you an ability to disable your logging if it is on. The logging is going to happen if it is off. In such scenarios, the logging is not going to happen.

So it is a kind of having a control to disable the logging whenever you want. Whereas with System.out.println() we will not have any such control always the only option to disable the logging with the help of System.out.println() is to delete the code itself and at last using the System.out.println() will have some security risks, especially if you try to log the sensitive information such as passwords, personal data, health data. So all these details if you try to print into the console, it can pose a security risk as anyone who has access to your console can see the information.

So using System.out.println(), we can only log the output into the console. So anyone who has access to the server where it is deployed, they will be able to easily see the sensitive information that is logged. So with all these we should always not use the System.out.println() inside production code. Instead we should look for the advanced options. So what are these advanced options? We should use the logging frameworks. So what is a framework?

A framework is a project or a library which is focused to solve a given problem with less effort. So to overcome all the drawbacks of System.out.println(), there are good amount of logging frameworks available inside the Java ecosystem. The Java library itself. It has a package with the name java.util.logging. Inside this package we have logging related classes which we can use to perform the logging, and apart from these basic support of logging from the Java, we also have dedicated logging frameworks like Log4j, SLF4J.

So these are the most advanced logging frameworks. And they allow you to configure logging levels, log rotation, log aggregation and more. So what is logging levels? I'm going to discuss about logging levels in the coming lectures. Log rotation and log aggregation is a process where these frameworks, they will allow you to log your output data into a log file. So if you keep appending the log data to a single log file at some point of time, it can become 2GB, 5GB or 1TB text file and you will not be able to open such files.

So that's why these frameworks to avoid these kind of challenges, they provide you log rotation and log aggregation. So whenever we are using these logging frameworks we can configure these frameworks such a way that every one hour or every five minutes you can create a new file. And the logging is going to happen in the new log file that got created. I'm not going to focus a lot about the logging frameworks inside this course, because these are super advanced topics and since right now we are focusing on the Java programming language, I'm just giving some hints around what are the best practices that you need to follow so that you can become a good developer inside your projects.

Once you master Java, obviously, as a next step, you're going to learn frameworks like spring spring boot microservices. During your advanced journey inside the spring ecosystem, you should also learn one of the logging framework. For example, inside my Spring Spring Boot related course, I have discussed in detail about the logging framework, so when the time is apt, you can also learn this logging frameworks. For now, let's try to understand how to achieve the logging with the help of java.util logging library available inside JDK, so that we can avoid using the System.out.println() from now onwards, wherever is possible, we can use the logging.

I hope you are clear thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.
