Agenda of the section
lectures.text:
Life is full of surprises regardless of how carefully we are planning our life, sometimes it is going to do unexpected things. In similar lines, regardless of how carefully you are developing our programming, your Java programs, sometimes your programs may throw unexpected results due to an invalid input from an end user, are due to some network issue, or due to some system error, or due to some invalid input path are due to some invalid input values.

So the reason can be anything but there is a good chance that your program may not work like you are expecting. So all these kind of situations, we call them as error scenarios or exception scenarios. Whenever we are writing a risky Java method. When I say risky Java method, this Java method may have lot many operations. Like for example, you're trying to read the data from a file. You should always think about both happy ending and not happy ending scenarios.

Happy ending scenario is the file is properly present. Your Java program is able to open it, read it and close it. This is a happy path scenario. In this scenario, everyone is going to happy because your program executed like everyone expecting, whereas coming to the unhappy scenario, think like the file is not present in the mentioned path or mentioned folder. In such scenarios, obviously your code will throw an error or exception. So to handle these kind of unhappy scenarios, we should always build some safety mechanisms inside our Java program so that we are handling these kind of exception scenarios or error scenarios gracefully and accordingly we are acting on them.

Safety measures is very common even in the real life scenario also. For example, whenever we are trying to perform some adventurous activities like bike racing or bungee jumping. So in all these kind of scenarios, we'll make sure there is some safety mechanism as safety measures have been taken, so that even in the unexpected scenario also, we are not going to get harmed a lot. I can also show you some videos around this. For example, you can see this person is doing the bungee jumping right now, and there are enough safety measures for him so that he won't get harmed even in the unexpected scenario.

Very similarly, this person is doing bike racing or bike riding, so he has a proper helmet and there'll be a first aid kit as well along with him. So he's ready to face any kind of scenario. On the similar lines, you can see these persons, they are doing the cycling and they have a proper helmet, and they have taken enough safety measures so that even if they fall down, there won't be any injury, especially for their head. On the similar lines, while we are trying to drive our car, the very first safety measure that we are going to take care is, to have the seatbelt locked around us, so that even in an unexpected scenario, this seatbelt is going to protect us.

Even the car manufacturers as well they will have some inbuilt safety mechanisms inside the car, like there'll be air balloons, which is going to help the passengers in an unexpected results. Just like how we are taking safety measures whenever we do some activity inside real life. In very similar lines, whenever you are writing a Java program, you need to make sure your code is always ready to handle any kind of situations. Especially the error situations are the exception situations.

Here you may have a question which is I agree with you boss, but how do we know if a method is a risky and where do we develop the code to handle the exceptions or any risky situations? So you may have all these questions floating inside your brain. So don't worry. We're going to put a lot of efforts throughout this section to understand how to properly implement exception handling inside any Java program. I hope you are clear with the agenda of this section.

Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, let's try to discuss about a special try block which is try with resource statement. In the previous lecture we discussed about finally block and what is the purpose of finally Block. We need to use these finally block in the scenarios where we are dealing with the IO resources like Scanner, BufferReader, Files or database connections in all such scenarios, the developer has to make sure he's writing a finally block and he's making sure to close the resources.

But what if developer forgets to close the resources or if he's not closing properly to handle these kind of scenarios? A special form of try statement introduced inside java7. This special try block is try with the resource statement. So the syntax to use this is whenever you are trying to create a try block inside the parentheses. After the try keyword, you can try to declare the object of your resources. For example, you can see inside the try block parentheses itself.

I'm trying to declare the object of Scanner and the same Scanner object I can use inside my try block. The advantage that we get with these try with resource statement is the developer. So that's the beauty of this try with resources statement.

This is introduced in java7. Let's see the demo of this statement very quickly. I'm going to create a new Java class. If you try to be oversmart and try to write a piece of code in between your try and catch or try and finally or catch and finally, in all such scenarios we are going to get compilation error. The third rule is, try should always be followed with a catch, or finally, or both. We need to have at least either catch or finally is present. If needed we can define both of them as well. lectures.text:
Inside Java all the exceptions and errors. They are categorized into two categories. One is checked and other one is unchecked exceptions. Inside this lecture, let's try to put some efforts to understand more details about these checked and unchecked exception. First, we are going to focus on checked exception. If you ask me what is the definition of checked exception? It is very simple. Whenever a compiler is forcing the developer or programmer to handle a specific exception.

So such exceptions we call them as checked exceptions. So why we call them as checked exceptions? Because your compiler is checking whether the programmer handled a particular exception or not. Examples of checked exceptions are IOException, SQLException and a FileNotFoundException. These are the most commonly faced checked exceptions by developers on day to day work. So whenever you are writing a code inside a Java method that is going to deal with the input and output operations like accepting an input.

In all such scenarios, your compiler knows that you are writing the code related to input and output processing. That's why it will force you to handle the IOException by saying that hey buddy, you're writing lot of input and output processing business logic. It will always be a wise decision to handle these IOException. Similarly, whenever you are writing a Java program which is going to run some SQL queries on top of a database by connecting to it in such scenarios, Java compiler knows that you are trying to write some SQL related business logic.

That's why it will force you to handle the SQLException. And similarly, whenever you are trying to read a file, there is a good chance the file may not be available at a given path. So what should happen in this kind of scenarios? Since compiler is going to worry about these kind of scenarios, it will force you to handle the FileNotFoundException as well. So if someone asks you what is a checked exception, we can simply say, checked exceptions are the exceptions that the Java compiler is going to perform the validation at the compilation time, and if we don't handle them inside our code, it is going to simply throw an compilation error.

lectures.title: Differences between throw and throws keyword
lectures.text:
There are a good amount of differences between throw and throws keyword. Let's try to understand one by one. The very first difference is using throw keyword we can manually throw an exception when an error or unexpected situation arises, and we can use this throw keyword only inside a method body. Whereas coming to the throws keyword, throws keyword is used in the method signature to indicate that a given method may throw list of exceptions due to certain statements or actions within its body.

So please be very clear about the placements. Throw can always be used inside the method body, whereas throws can be used only in the method signature. Now coming to the syntax on how to use these keywords whenever we are using the throw keyword, after mentioning the throw keyword, we need to provide an object or an instance of an Exception class. That means always the throw keyword should be followed by the instance variable containing the Exception object.

For example, here, immediately after the throw keyword, I'm trying to create the object of the ArithematicException class by using the new operator. If I don't mention this new operator, you can see I'm going to get a compilation error. That means my throw keyword always going to expect a object of a class, which is a subclass of Throwable. If I try to create an object of String, I'm going to get a compilation error because String is not a subclass of Throwable class, which is a superclass for all the exceptions and errors inside the Java library.

That's why always make sure you are creating the object of a subclass of Throws class. I hope this is clear. Coming to that throws keyword syntax, it is very simple. Whenever you are trying to mention throws keyword inside a method signature. After the throws keyword, you need to mention the list of class names of the exceptions that may be thrown by the method. So all these list of exceptions, they need to be separated by comma. The next difference is using the throw keyword, we can only throw one exception at a time, whereas with the help of throws keyword, we can declare multiple exceptions that are separated by commas.

The last difference is somewhat complicated to understand. That's why let's put some good amount of efforts to understand these last difference. Whenever we are throwing unchecked exceptions with the help of throw keyword, there won't be any issues. The unchecked exception it is going to be propagated very easily to the parent classes as well. Whereas if you try to throw a checked exception using the throw keyword, in such scenarios, the Java compiler will make sure that a method is either handling that checked exception or it added the checked exception details to the method signature with the help of throws keyword.

Let me show you a demo around this. As of now here you can see I'm trying to throw an ArithmeticException which is unchecked exception, whereas if I try to throw and check it, exception things will change a lot. For example, let me try to throw one of the checked exception which is FileNotFoundException. As soon as I tried to throw an FileNotFoundException, you can see I'm getting a compilation error saying that that this method is not handling these checked exception.

So to resolve this issue I need to have a catch block or I need to add the throws statement to the method signature by mentioning the file not found exception to the list. That's why whenever you are trying to throw an unchecked exception, the unchecked exception, it is going to be propagated very easily to the invoking methods as well. Whereas when you try to throw a checkered exception, your Java compiler will make sure that a given method either it is handling it or it is throwing to the caller methods with the help of throws keyword I hope you are clear.

Let me revert back to the normal unchecked exception, which is ArithmeticException. In the similar lines, whenever you are trying to use a throws keyword to throw the unchecked exceptions, the propagation is going to be super easy. Like here you can see inside the ThrowsDemo. As of now I have a try and catch block. Even if I remove these try and catch block, nothing is going to happen because these are unchecked exceptions and whoever is invoking these method, they will not be forced to handle them.

Whereas if I try to throw one of the checked exception which is like FileNotFoundException, then immediately a compilation error may arise in all the classes where this divide() method is being invoked. You can see the compiler is trying to force the developer to handle the exception, which is FileNotFoundException because it is a checked exception. So that's why always please note about these checked and unchecked exceptions when ever you are trying to use them as part of the throws and throw keyword.

So that is what the last point is trying to highlight with this. I hope you are clear with all the differences between throw and throws keyword. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: Exception Propagation
lectures.text:
Let me explain about what is an Exception Propagation Inside this lecture. We know whenever an exception is being thrown from a method, and if the same is not being catched or caught within that method, then the exception will try to propagate to the calling method. So this process continues until the exception is properly handled with the help of a catch block or it reaches the top level method. So what will be the top level method inside our Java programs?

It is main() method in the case of an unchecked exception, being trying to propagate to the caller methods or the parent methods, then in such scenarios, there is no mandatory to have a throws statement or to have a catch block, so the unchecked exception eventually it will propagate to the top level method or a main() method. Whereas in the scenario of checked exceptions, since the compiler is going to force the programmers to handle the checked exceptions either with the help of throws or with the help of catch block.

In the case of checked exceptions, the exception will try to propagate to the nearest catch block, or it will keep propagating to the main() method or the top level method. Let me show you a example here. Like you can see inside my method stack at the bottom we have the main() method. main() method is invoking method1() followed by method2(), method3(), method4(), method5(). Think like there is an exception occurred inside the method5(). In this kind of scenario, my method5(), first, it will check if there is any catch block handling a given exception.

Then the exception will not be propagated to the parent methods or the caller methods inside the method stack, whereas if the exception is not handled with the help of a catch block, in such scenarios, the exception will be propagated to the method4(), and this process will keep on continue until there is a catch block inside a method where the exception is being handled, or it reaches to the main() method. lectures.title: final, finally and finalize
lectures.text:
Inside Java, there are three different similar jargons that you may hear a lot many times these are final, finally, finalize. Though they are looking very similar, but there is a lot of difference between them and the scenarios where we are going to use them also vary a lot. Since this is a topic where students can easily get confused, I want to spend a few minutes explaining you about the differences between final, finally and finalize, and this is also a favorite question for the most of the interviewers.

That's why please be attentive to this lecture, and with that, any confusions that you may have around these jargons will get cleared. The very first jargon or the keyword that you can see here is final. So what is the purpose of final inside Java? Using final we can declare final constant values or final methods under final Java class. Whenever we are using this final keyword to declare a variable or to declare a constant value, such variables are such constants we can't update them, or we can't reinitialize them with a different value at later point of time inside the program. Whatever you are going to provide during the initialization, the same value is going to be final.

For example, inside this program you can see I'm trying to declare a variable x along with the final keyword, and inside this x I have stored the value five. With that, I will not be able to update these x variable with some other value inside the program at later point of time. The compiler is not going to allow this. Similarly, whenever we are defining the final keyword as part of the method signature, then such methods behavior or the logic cannot be overrided by the subclasses.

All the subclasses they have to simply accept whatever business logic defined inside the final method of a superclass. And at last we can also mention this final keyword as part of the class definition. Whenever we are mentioning the final keyword as part of the class definition, then in such scenarios, your class is not going to support any inheritance, no other subclass. they can extend your class as a superclass. So we are trying to completely disable the inheritance behavior with the help of final keyword inside the class definition.

Now moving on to the next jargon, which is finally. We just now discussed inside this section where we talked about how to perform the exception handling. Whenever you are trying to define, try and catch blocks in such scenarios, we can define the finally blocks using finally keyword we can build the finally blocks we already discussed what is the purpose of finally block? With the help of finally block, we can specify a block of code that is going to be executed regardless of whether an exception is thrown or caught in the try or catch blocks.

This finally block ensures that the code that you have written inside them, such as closing a database connection or releasing a lock. So all these kind of code, it is always going to be executed in both kind of scenarios like happy scenario and exception scenario. Now moving on to the last jargon which is finalize. Finalize is a method available inside the object superclass. We know inside Java there is a garbage collector which is responsible to clean up the object that are no longer being used.

So with the help of garbage collection, the memory occupied by the unused objects inside the heap memory is going to be cleaned or retained regularly. So whenever a garbage collector is trying to remove an unused object from an heap memory. In such scenarios, if you want to perform any cleanup operations, or if you want to release any resources before the object is destroyed in such scenarios inside your class, you can override the method finalize() that is provided by the object superclass.

So whatever logic that you are going to write inside this Overrided finalize() method, the same is going to be executed whenever the garbage collection is happening. But please note that JVM is not always going to invoke your finalize() method. It is not going to guarantee that it is always going to invoke the finalize() method that you have defined whenever a class object is being destroyed. In fact, this finalize() method is deprecated. In the previous lecture, we discussed that the default behavior of the hashCode() method inside Object class is to calculate the hash code value based upon the memory address of the object where it is stored. But sometimes we may want to override these hashCode() method to have our own logic to calculate the hash code. In such scenarios, if equals is returning output as true, then whatever hash code logic that we have written, it should give the same hash code value both for object to one and object to two.

We are ready to discuss about the equals() method. We are going to discuss about the same in the next lecture, but I want to highlight here that both hashCode() and equals(), they are tightly coupled. They are like sister twins or brother twins. So there is a good history why this hashCode() and equals() are tightly coupled with each other, which I am going to discuss in the next lecture. But now please note that whenever you are trying to invoke the equals() method by using two objects like obj1.equals() and to the equals() method, I'm trying to pass obj2 as an input object.

So behind the scenes this equals() method it is going to compare the content of these two objects. If they are same it is going to return true. Otherwise the equals() method is going to return false. So whenever this equals() method returns true in such scenarios, the hashCode() method of object one and object two, they should return the same hash code value or same Integer value. In other words, if two objects are equal using the equals() method, they must have the same hash code value.

So that's a very first rule that you need to take care whenever you are trying to implement your own hash coding logic. The second rule is if the hash code values are same, that is not going to guarantee the equality of the objects. So this is the reverse of the rule number one, but in a negative way. Think like the object to one hash code and the object two hash code return the same integer value at the same hash code value. That doesn't mean both object one and object two they are equal and your equals() method is going to return true.

So there is a good chance, even if the hash code values are same, the objects content may not be the same. So this is what rule number two conveys. Coming to the rule number three if you are trying to invoke the same hashCode() method on top of the same object multiple times in the same execution or in the same operating system or in the same mission, your hashCode() method should always give the same hash code value or same integer value as an output.

For example, think like you are having the same execution environment, which means same laptop, same operating system, same Java project. With this kind of environment, if you are trying to invoke the hashCode() method on top of an object ten different times, in such scenarios, you should always get the same hash code value or same integer value as an output. Whereas if the execution environment changes like in a different laptop or in a different operating system, the hash code may vary.

But generally, if you're trying to invoke the hash code method in the same execution environment multiple times, it should always give the consistent hash code value as an output. And at last, the rule number four says whenever you are trying to overwrite the hashCode() method inside your subclass, you should also make sure you are overriding the equals() method as well, because they both are closely tied with each other. So whenever you are trying to invoke the equals() method, you're going to use an object reference. So the object that you are trying to invoke your equals() method, that is going to be considered as the object one. And whatever object you are trying to pass an input to these equals() method that is going to be considered as the second object by default this is the logic that equals() method is going to have behind the scenes. So it is going to simply compare the current object with the object that we are trying to pass as an input with the code.

Like you can see this is equal to is equal to object. So this default code is going to check if both objects they are referring to the same memory location. In such scenarios it is going to give the value as true. Otherwise it is going to give the value as false. But this default behavior may not be useful if you have your own custom requirements, because with this default behavior will only get the output as true if you're trying to compare the same single object with the help of equals() method.

Because we know whenever we are using the new operator inside Java to create an object, it is definitely going to create at a different memory location. With that, we are always going to get the output as false with this default behavior, but sometimes we may have requirement to not compare the objects by referring to their memory location. lectures.text:
We talked briefly about the finalized() method in the previous section when we were trying to compare with the final keyword and the finally block. But now let's try to discuss in detail about the purpose of this finalized() method. In Java, it is very normal that an Java object. Sometimes it may consume some resources, or it may open some connection with resources like files or a database. So in all these kind of scenarios, whenever an object is trying to consume a resource, it is always a good practice to release these resources whenever it is no longer needed by your object to achieve the same.

The Java language offers a mechanism to perform the cleanup or resource releasing just before the object is destroyed or discarded by the garbage collector. We know inside Java, we as a Java developers, we are only allowed to create the objects and there is no need of manually destroying the objects or destructing the objects inside the heap memory. We are not allowed to do that because behind the scenes, the Java virtual machine, it is going to employ a low priority process known as garbage collector to identify and eliminate all the objects that are no longer needed.

So whenever an object is being destroyed or removed by your garbage collector, it is going to give an opportunity to execute some cleanup code in the form of finalize() method. The purpose of the finalize() method is whatever logic that you are going to write Inside these finalize() method, the same is going to be executed by the garbage collector. Just before your current object is going to be destroyed. You can see by default the finalize() method in the object class does not going to do anything, it is an empty method.

If needed, we can override this method based upon our business logic inside our class. But there is a caveat or important note that you need to be aware, which is the garbage collector does not guarantee that it is going to invoke the finalize() method. Whenever the object destroying is going to happen, it is going to invoke your finalize() method randomly based upon its own calculations. That means this makes using this approach as undependable or unpredictable for programmers to write cleanup logic.

That's why since this method has all these limitations, and it is also not advisable to use this method to clean up the resource due to security reasons. With all these reasons and limitations, this finalize() method is deprecated from Java 9. That means the Java team itself is encouraging not to use this method to clean up the object related resources. Instead, there are better alternatives or better approaches that we have. Like we discussed previously, there is a try with resource or you can write a try with the finally block, which is going to automatically close the resources or the connections that a specific object has opened.

lectures.text:
Now let's try to discuss about an interesting method available inside the Object superclass. The method is clone(). In layman language or in non-technical language clone is a process of making a copy from a original. So the same definition you can consider even for Java cloning process as well. Why do we need a clone() method inside Java? Because inside Java, there is no automatic mechanism for cloning an object or creating a copy of an object. With the help of this clone() method, we should be able to easily create a copy of an given object.

And here you may have a question which is as of now, we are able to assign a object to other object reference with the help of is equal to operator. But I want to highlight an important note here. Whenever you are trying to assign an object to another object to a variable with the help of is equal to operator. In that scenario, you're not going to physically copy the data from one object to other object. Instead, the same physical object is going to be referred by two different object reference variables.

Let me show you a demo around this very quickly. Here inside my package, I'm going to create a Java class with the name CloneDemo. Inside this class, as usual, first we need to write the main() method to execute our program. Post that, I'm going to create a person p1 object by invoking the constructor, and to this constructor I can pass data like John, followed by 25, followed by gender, which is Madan at last I can also mention his ssn number. Let me type some random SSN number.

So these are random SSN number. With this code, a Person object is going to be physically created behind the scenes inside the heap memory. With the data that we are trying to provide the same Person object, memory, location is going to be pointed with the help of these p1 object reference variable. As a next step, I can try to assign the object to p1 to another object to reference variable, which is p2. With this, you might be under the assumption that we are able to copy the p1 object into the p2 object, the reference variable, but this is not going to copy the p1 object into the p2 reference variable.

Instead, they both point to the same physical Person object present inside the same memory location. I can also confirm you this by writing a small logic. Think like I'm trying to change the name of the person with the help of p2.setName(). And here I'm trying to change the name to John Doe. Later on, I'm going to print the name of the person using the p1.getName(). You can see the change happened inside the p2, but the same change is going to be reflected inside the p1 object as well.

The reason is both the p1 and p2 objects. They are pointing to the same object inside the same memory location. Let me try to execute this program. You can see we are getting the output as John Doe, so there is no direct automatic mechanism inside Java to physically copy the contents of an object from one object to other object. So to efficiently copy an object into another object, we have clone() method. So let's try to understand how to use the same to copy an object to enable cloning of an object belong to a class.

First we need to manually re-implement the clone() method within the class. For example, if you want to clone the objects of Person, then inside the Person class, you need to override the clone() method. So that whenever someone is trying to clone() the Person object, whatever overridden clone() method that you have written inside your class, the same is going to be invoked. By default. the clone() method that is provided by the Object class. It is going to have all the logic that is required to clone an object physically.

So all the logic of cloning is going to be written in the native code format. That's why we are able to see the native keyword inside the method signature of clone. As a developer, you just have to override this clone() method, and from your clone() method, you need to invoke the clone() method in the superclass with the help of super.clone(), you're not going to take the responsibility of copying the content by writing your own code. Instead, you just have to invoke the clone() method available inside the Object of super class from your own class.

The actual copying process is going to be taken care by the Java library. Apart from overriding this clone() method inside your Person class or inside your any other class, you should also take care of implementing a Marker interface which is Clonable. What is a Marker interface? Marker interface is an empty interface, which is not going to have any body inside the interface. The purpose of this Marker interface is to communicate about a special information, or about a metadata information to the JVM.

With the help of Clonable Marker interface, we are communicating to the JVM. Please allow the cloning of my objects belongs to a given class. If you don't implement this Clonable Marker interface inside your Person class, and if you try to perform the cloning with the overridden method that you have implemented, in such cases, you are going to get the CloneNotSupportedException. Since these CloneNotSupportedException is a checkered exception. Whenever you are trying to perform the cloning process, you need to either handle these checkered exception with that try and catch block, or you can propagate the exception by using the throw keyword.

I hope you're clear. Let's try to implement these clone() method inside our Person class. Inside our Person class, I'm going to mention override annotation followed by public, and the return type from this method is going to be object, and the method name has to be clone followed by throws CloneNotSupportedException. So inside these method I need to invoke super.clone() method and the return type from the super.clone() method. I can return from these method as well, which I'm trying to override.

With this, we have implemented our own clone() method inside the Person. As a next step, let me try to do the cloning process inside the CloneDemo class. I'm going to assign the return type that I'm going to get from the clone() method, which I'm trying to invoke with the help of p1. With this code, whatever data that we have inside the p1, the same is going to be copied into the p3, and they both will point to the two different objects inside the memory location as well.

We are getting a error saying that we have not handled the CloneNotSupportedException. Like I said before, since this is a checked exception, we need to either handle it with the help of try block, or we can simply add throws statement to the method signature. For now, let's try to add exception to the method signature with the help of throws, and with that, the compilation error related to the checked exception is resolved. But we still have one more compilation error, which is the casting from object to person is not allowed by default.

So let me execute this program. You can see we are getting a runtime exception which is CloneNot SupportedException. lectures.title: Details about Shallow cloning & Deep cloning - Theory
lectures.text:
In Java there are two types of cloning that we can perform. The very first one is Shallow cloning and the second one is Deep cloning. Let's try to understand what are these cloning and how they work. These are the very important topics. If you go to any Java related interviews, anyone can answer questions around the clone() method. But if someone wants to test your deep knowledge inside Java, they can ask some difficult questions around shallow cloning and deep cloning.

That's why, my friend, my request is please pay attention and try to understand what is this Shallow cloning and Deep cloning. This shallow cloning and deep cloning only come into picture if a given object has some other embedded objects. In the previous lecture, we have a Person class, and inside this Person class we only have primitive data type instance fields along with that String object. Other than that, we don't have any other complex objects, but in real projects we always have embedded objects as an instance.

Variables inside your own class, I'm going to show you what do I mean by embedded objects in few seconds. But before that, let's try to understand what is a shallow cloning. Whenever you're trying to perform cloning with the help of shallow cloning, it is going to create the new copy of your outer object only, but it is not going to create the copies of the embedded objects referenced by the original object. Instead, it is going to simply copy the reference of the embedded objects.

For example, like you can see here, I have a Student class, and inside this Student class I have instance variables name and course. So this course is a instance variable which belongs to other class with the name course. So inside this course class I have another instance variable which is courseName. So with this code my Student class object it is going to have an embedded object of Course class. If you try to override the clone() method inside the Student class like you can see here, we simply override the clone() method and we are trying to invoke the clone() method with the help of super.clone().

So this is a classical example of shallow cloning. So with this shallow cloning, what is going to happen behind the scenes inside the heap memory is you're going to have an original student. And if you try to clone this original student object, you're going to get another cloned student physical object. They both are stored in two different memory locations, but coming to the embedded objects, like course, both these original student object and the cloned student object, they are going to point to the same course object, because shallow cloning is not capable of copying the embedded objects.

Instead, it simply copy the reference of the embedded objects into the objects of original student and the cloned student. This is because we are trying to go with the simple invocation of super.clone(). With this, it should be pretty clear for you whenever your class has instance variables, which belongs to other class. In such scenarios, if you are going with the default logic of cloning, you are always going to end up with the shallow cloning.

I can also show you an example of shallow cloning based upon these two classes, Student and Course. You can see here inside the main() method. First, I'm trying to create a Course with the variable name as math. Inside this math course, I'm trying to store the course name as math and post that I have created an original student by passing the student name and the course object later on if I try to perform the cloning with the help of original Student object, I'm going to get another object with the name cloned student.

So both these original student and the cloned student, they represent two different physical objects. That's why if I try to compare the memory locations of these two objects with the help of these double equal to operator, I'm going to get the output as false because they point to the two different memory locations. Whereas if you try to check the memory location of the Course object which is present inside the original student and the cloned student, you're going to get the output as true, because the same course object is being maintained in both the original student and the cloned student object.

I hope you are clear about the shallow cloning. Now let's try to understand what is deep cloning, which means whenever you want to copy the even the embedded objects, then in such scenarios, you need to override the clone() method with a different logic like you can see here first, I'm trying to invoke the super.clone() method, which is going to give me the cloned student object later on I should also perform the cloning of the Course object, which is available inside the same object.

So that's why I'm trying to invoke the course.clone(), and the same I'm trying to assign to the clonedStudent.course(). And with that, we will end up performing the deep cloning. And this is how it is going to look like inside the heap memory both the original student and the cloned student. They will point to the two different course objects. But before you try to perform this deep cloning, please make sure you also implement Clonable interface inside your Course class.

On top of that, you should also overwrite the clone() method with the help of super.clone(). Otherwise, when you invoke these clone() method with the help of Course object, you are going to get the CloneNotSupportedException. Let's try to understand the example of deep cloning like you can see here. When we try to perform the cloning of the original student, the student details along with the embedded course details, both of them, they are going to be copied into separate physical memories.

That's why for these two statements, we are going to get the output as false because they are pointing to the two different memory locations. I hope you are clear about these theory discussion around the shallow cloning and deep cloning. In the next lecture, let's see the demo of these shallow cloning and deep cloning. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.text:
Since we are discussing everything about the objects inside Java inside this section, I think it would be a wise decision to discuss about one more important concept around objects, which is creating mutable and immutable objects in Java. So what are mutable and immutable objects ? In java mutable and immutable terms refer to describe the ability of an object to be modified after it has been created. Immutable objects are the objects whose state or whose data cannot be changed once they are created.

If you need to modify an immutable object, it is not going to be possible. The only option is you must create a new object with the required modified state or with the required new data. Whereas on the other hand, we have mutable objects whose state or data can be changed once they are created. With mutable objects we should be able to add new data, modify the existing data, delete the existing data inside the objects without worrying about creating a new instance.

So these are basic definition about mutable and immutable objects. First, let's try to understand how to create mutable objects. Later on, we can focus on the immutable objects. Like you can see here whenever you want to create a mutable object, you need to create a Pojo class. And inside this pojo class you can create any number of instance variables. But please make sure your instance variables are of type private. So to access that data inside your object and to update the data inside your object, we should always use the getter and setter methods.

So that's a standard approach. And similarly, whenever you are trying to create an object of your mutable object, you should be using the constructor. And just like how you have these fields, getter and setter methods, it is also recommended to have a constructor inside your class that is going to accept the required number of input parameters. These kind of Pojo classes we have created a lot throughout this course, so whenever you are following this approach to create a Pojo class inside Java, you are going to end up creating the mutable objects because once the object of this class is created, anyone can change that data by invoking the setter method.

For example, like you can see here first, I'm trying to create a Person object with the help of new operator and with the help of constructor. To the constructor, I'm trying to pass the name as Elmer Raymond and the occupation as Software Engineer. So once this object is created, I'm trying to change the occupation of this person by invoking these setOccupation() method. So to the setOccupation() method, I'm trying to send the occupation name as chef.

That means with the help of setName() and setOccupation() methods, we should be easily able to modify the values of the properties present inside the Person object. So this makes the Person class or the Person object as mutable, because it is allowing us to change the data inside it once the object is created. You can see here I also have a representation about the mutable objects. Think like there is a person initially we created this Person with the occupation as software engineer.

Later on, we can change the occupation to whatever we want like a chef, pilot, nurse, doctor, It's up to us. This way based upon your own business requirements, you can keep on changing the data inside your objects. But please note that your class should have the setter methods, along with the other guidelines that we have followed here. Now let's try to understand how to create immutable objects. To make the same Person class as immutable. We can make few changes inside the Person class.

The very first change that you need to do is you need to remove the setter methods. With that, no one will be able to set new data inside your object once it is created. And after removing the setter methods, you should also make your properties as final. Like you can see here just after the private. I'm trying to mention the final keyword with this once the data is assigned to this name and occupation with the help of this constructor, during the object creation, no one will be able to change that data inside them.

The only way to change the data is to create the new object with the required new data. So this is the approach that you need to follow to make your class as immutable. This time if you try to see the sample code that I'm trying to provide, I'm trying to create the object of the Person with the name as Chitra mansi and the occupation as doctor. With this, an immutable object of Person is going to be created and no one will be able to change the data present inside this object, because there is no way for others to change the data, either with the help of setter method or by accessing the variables directly.

No other class or method they should be able to access my instance variables, because we have defined them as private. And on top of that, we also declared these instance variables as final. Apart from removing the setter method and making your instance variables as final, it is also a good practice to mark your class as final, because this is going to prevent any other subclass from modifying the behavior of your class. When we mention the keyword final in the class definition, no other subclass can extend your immutable class.

And with that, we will be closing the loophole of inheritance as well, so that no other subclass can modify the behavior of my immutable class. So you can see this Person object right now it is an immutable object. No one can change her designation or name. I hope you are clear on how to create immutable objects in Java. Here you may have a question which is why should I create immutable objects? What is the advantage that I'm getting by making my object as immutable?

That's a great question. There can be some scenarios where you don't want your object to be modified at later point of program. Maybe think like you have created an object inside method1(), and you are trying to send the object as an input for the other methods like method2(), method3(), method4(). So regardless of how many methods your object is going to be passed, you don't want the other methods to change the content of your object. In such scenarios, we can go with the immutable objects and apart from this, we also have another great reason on building the immutable objects.

The reason is due to security reasons. Think like inside your Java application, you are dealing with some sensitive logic or sensitive information. You don't want any other method or any other API inside your project to be able to modify a given object once that is created. If the object can be modified, then you may have some serious implications inside your business logic. So to handle these kind of scenarios, we can also use immutable objects. These immutable objects in other words, we can call them as data carrier classes.

The reason why they are called as data carrier classes is, they primary purpose is to store the data and provide the methods to access the data. So how others can access the data inside an immutable object using the getter methods. But there is no way to change the data. That means this is going to act like a post card. Once someone returns something on the post card, it can be only be carried or sent over to other person and the other person he should be able to read the post card, and he will not be able to update any content inside the post card.

Similarly, immutable objects are also going to work in the similar fashion. Think like your frontend layer or frontend application. It is trying to send some data from browser to the backend server. So these kind of data can be sent in the form of immutable objects. And the backend it can simply accept the data and process the same based upon the business logic written inside a Java program, or if needed, the same data carrier object or immutable object can be transferred between multiple layers of the backend system.

Inside backend system we are going to have multiple layers like controller layer, service layer, persistent layer or DB layer. To all these layers, we can try to send the same immutable object, and since it is an immutable object, we can happily sleep with an assumption that no one will be able to change the data inside this object. Now let's try to understand the differences between mutable and immutable objects very quickly. The very first difference between mutable and immutable objects is mutable objects requires synchronization whenever they are trying to be used inside a multithreading environment.

So what is a synchronization? Synchronization is a process that developer has to implement that at a time a single thread can access a given object. If you don't implement the synchronization, then different threads inside your Java program. They will be able to manipulate the data inside mutable objects very easily. And with that you will end up race conditions. So what is a race condition? Race condition is a scenario where different threads have different set of data in their own hands.

So one thread may have the designation as doctor, whereas other thread may have the designation of software engineer. And at the same time one more thread can come into picture and it can also try to manipulate the data. So with all these simultaneous manipulation of the data inside a mutable objects, it will result into the inconsistent state of your object. So that's why to overcome these kind of issues inside multi-threading environment synchronization has to be implemented.

Whereas with immutable objects we don't have to worry about the synchronization, race conditions. Regardless of how many threads I have inside my program, all of them, they will be able to access the data inside these immutable objects without the need of synchronization. Since all threads they can only read the data. I don't have to worry much because no thread can change the data inside a immutable object. So that's why we can call these immutable objects as thread safe.

So whenever you're trying to build a logic for multi-threading environment, you can consider the immutable objects. We are ready to discuss about what is a thread, what is multithreading inside Java ? This advanced topic we are going to discuss towards the end of the course. The next difference is mutable objects are going to provide more flexibility and they are going to be more efficient. The reason is once the object is created, the same object can be used multiple times by changing the data any number of times.

Since we are not going to create the object from scratch with the new data, they are going to be efficient because already the object creation might have happened long back inside your program. But these mutable objects require careful handling to avoid issues related to concurrent access, especially in the multi threading environment. Whereas immutable objects may require more memory and potentially they may work slowly compared to the mutable objects.

The reason is, every time you want to store new data, you need to create a fresh objects. And as you are trying to create more and more immutable objects, you're going to occupy more memory and it may potentially slow the performance of your application compared to the mutable objects. That's why most of the times Java developers, they will end up creating only the mutable objects. But if they have some special requirement where they don't want the object content not to be modified once the object is created in such scenarios, they are going to build the immutable objects.

So the choice between mutable and immutable is always going to depend on the specific use case and the performance requirements of your application. I hope you are clear about mutable and immutable objects. In the next lecture, let's see the demo on how to create a mutable and immutable object. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.text:
Are you going to live with a single goal throughout your life? Off course not your goals will keep changing from time to time based upon how you are progressing inside your life. For example, while you're studying in a college, you may have a goal to get a job in a decent company with a decent pay. And once you settle down inside this job, your goal may change this time, you may have a new goal like you want to buy your own car, or you may want to buy your own home, or you may want to get married and settle with your own family and children.

This way, as you're trying to progress inside your life, the goals are going to keep changing from time to time. In the similar lines, when you're trying to build and run a Java program, the requirements from your program may change from time to time. Maybe initially, you might be under the assumption that your program may need only certain space to execute, but later on during runtime, your program may demand more space to store more new elements or more new objects.

As of now, inside this course, we discussed about arrays. Using arrays, we can store any amount of data or collection of objects or collection of items, but with arrays there is a problem. Whenever you want to use arrays inside your program, you have to be very clear about your memory requirements of your array. For example, if you want to store ten different objects, then you need to be very clear about the same while you're trying to build your Java program later on during runtime.

If your program is demanding more space inside your array, then in this kind of dynamic scenarios arrays, they are not going to work like you expect. They are not going to grow based upon your program requirements. I can also show you an example here. Think like you have started your own startup, which has its own mobile application and a web application. Inside your startup, web application or mobile application. You might have used Java because you are a Java developer.

Initially, you might be under the assumption that your startup is not going to work, you're not very confident. That's why you have written a small piece of logic inside your web application, with an array that can hold up to 50 Customer objects. Because you don't want to waste memory unnecessarily by buying a big server, you just wanted to go with a minimum budget. So with the array that is capable of holding 50 customers, your program is going to work without any issues, up to 50 customers.

But the moment the 51st customer is added into your application in such scenarios, definitely you're going to have a surprise from your arrays. They are going to throw ArrayIndexOutofBoundsException because inside an array which is capable of storing 50 customer objects, you are trying to add 51st customer. And since arrays can't grow dynamically, your program will fail. So to fix this issue immediately, you increase the size of your array from 50 to 100.

This time also, you are not very confident that not more than 100 people will use your application. But to your surprise, a lot many people are liking your application and more and more customers are being onboarded into your application. So the story is keep repeating like every time you're trying to onboard more and more customers into your application, you need to continuously increase the size of the array. So with this, you may feel frustrated and you may ask a question yourself.

Is there any alternative to this array? Should I live with this array with these pain points. So these kind of questions you may ask yourself or you may ask your friends or senior developers in the Java community. They will simply answer, saying that you don't have to live with these arrays. If you have a dynamic scenarios where the amount of size needs to be very runtime based upon how many objects you are trying to store at runtime, then in this kind of scenarios, we can go for the collections in Java.

I'm going to give an introduction about collections in the next lecture. But before we try to close this lecture, let me also highlight you about other disadvantages that we have with arrays. We know one of the greatest disadvantage of arrays is they support only a fixed size. On top of that, whenever an array is getting created, they are going to be created in a continuous memory location. In future, whenever you want to add a new element, then in this kind of scenarios, your JVM is going to look for new space in the same continuous memory location.

If it is not finding any new space in the same continuous memory location area, then obviously it has to move to some other location inside the heap memory where the continuous memory location is available, including with the new element. On top of this limitation, arrays also has another limitation, which is they are only capable of storing elements of a single data type. This means you can either only store the int numbers or String objects, or Person objects or Customer objects, but you can't store different data type objects within the same array.

So all these limitations we are going to overcome with the help of Java collections. But before that, let's see one more example to understand the limitations of arrays like you can see here. Initially I have created an people array and inside this People array I'm trying to store the name of three different persons. Since I have provided three different names, the size of these array is going to be three with the index number zero, one and two.

So once I have created these array, think like in the upcoming methods or in the upcoming lines of code, I have a different requirement which is to add one more person name. So in this kind of scenarios definitely I can't straight away go ahead and add a new name to the existing people array. Instead, I should create a new array with the size of four. Once the new array is created, I should copy the three names from the old array with the help of arrays.copyOff() method or with the other approaches that we have discussed previously.

And at last I'm trying to populate a new name Sita at the index three. So if you see here these are very cumbersome or complex process that needs to be followed whenever we want to resize the array, as it is not going to grow automatically. So to overcome all these limitations, we have collections in Java. So let's start the journey of collections from the next lecture. Thank you, bye.

lectures.title: What are Collections & why they accept only objects
lectures.text:
What are collections in Java? You may have this question, so let's try to understand the same inside this lecture. From many years computer scientists they are trying to address the drawbacks of arrays with their research computer scientists they are not able to identify a single universal solution. Instead, they have identified various clever techniques that can be used or incorporated in any programming language to store multiple elements that can grow dynamically based upon the elements that we are trying to add and remove.

The same clever techniques are incorporated inside Java collections as well. With the various names. Like you can see we have various data structure or data types under the name collections these are List, Stack, Map. Set, Queue. All these data structures, they have their own use cases, or they have their own style of storing the data. Based upon our own business requirements, we need to choose one of them. For now don't worry about which one to use and what are the scenarios that you need to consider for each data structure or each data type that we have under collections, we are going to discuss about them in detail in the coming lectures.

So when we say Java collection, it is not a single interface or a single class. It is an concept or it is an ecosystem under which we have many classes and interfaces that implement all the collection data structures that you see on the left hand side. So what are collections? They are very similar to arrays which are capable of holding the any number of objects. But the only difference between collections and arrays is, collections they can dynamically increase or decrease their size based upon the objects that we are trying to store or remove.

On top of that, Java collections they support various data structures for storing and accessing the elements inside a collection. These data structures are like List, Set, Map, Stack and Queue. All the classes and interfaces around the Java Collections framework they are grouped under the same package, which is java.util package. So based upon our business requirements, we need to choose one of the data structure like List or Set or Map or Stack or Queue.

Once we discuss everything in detail about these data structures, then you will be in a position to choose one of them based upon your business requirements. For example, I'll try to leak some information around these data structures very quickly. Whenever you are looking to maintain that data inside a collection, ignoring the duplicates, then you can always go with the Set. Whereas if you want to maintain the order of insertion into your collection, in such scenarios, you are going to use the List.

Similarly, if you want to store your data in a dictionary format like key and value, then in such scenarios you can use the Map data structure. And similarly, if you want to follow the principle which is LIFO last in first out, then in such scenarios you can go with the Stack data structure. Whereas if you want to follow the first in first out principle, which is in short form, we can call it as FIFO. In such scenarios, you can obviously go with the Queue data structure.

So data structures itself is a very big concept. We're not going to talk everything about the data structures, but instead we are going to discuss most commonly used data structures and their classes and how to use them and how to store the data inside them. So all those important concepts around the Java collections we are going to discuss inside this course. But whenever we are trying to use the Java collections, there is an very, very important point that you need to be aware, which is Java collections they will only allow you to store the objects.

You can't store the primitive data type values like I can't store a primitive data type value like int, double, float, boolean, char because they are not objects, they are simply primitive data types. But with that, don't feel sad that we can't store the numbers and characters and boolean values inside the collections. There is a workaround we're going to discuss in the coming lectures. For now, please note that collections they will only allow you to store the objects inside them.

Now you may have a question, which is why collections, they accept only objects. Why they are not accepting primitive data types. The reason is very simple Java team when they are trying to build a collections library with the help of lot many interfaces and classes, they have a problem which is inside Java we know we can store the data in two forms. One is with the help of primitive data types like int, float, double, char, boolean, short, byte, long.

So these are the primitive data types which we can use to store the data. And the other side we can also store data with the help of objects. For example, with the help of a String object, I can store alphanumeric data. Similarly, with the help of a Person object, I can store all the person related information. So since there are two different ways to store the data inside Java Java team, they have a problem, which is they need to develop the collections framework considering the primitive data types and the objects.

Since it is not going to make sense to develop the same library for two different purposes. What they have done is, they came up with a thumb rule, which is whenever someone wants to use the collections, they need to make sure they have their data stored in the form of object. Especially this rule came into the picture by considering the primitive data types. Developers they are not allowed to store that data with the help of primitive data types.

But there is a workaround, which I'm going to discuss in few seconds on high level the reason why collections accept only objects is to keep these collections library more flexible and generic. On top of that, using only objects allows collections to support polymorphism that can operate on different types of objects. When we start using the collections, we can write some generic code that can be worked for any kind of objects that you are going to pass as an input.

So based upon the input that you are trying to feed to your program, the program is going to behave differently. So that's a concept of polymorphism which we discussed long back. We are going to see a more powerful polymorphism by following collections in the coming lectures. Overall, like I said, the decision to accept only objects in Java collections is it was a design choice made to increase the flexibility and generosity, enabling them to store and manipulate a wide variety of objects.

But with this discussion, you may have $1 million question which is running behind the scenes, which is how to store the primitive data types data using collections. So whenever we want to store a primitive data type value, we need to wrap that primitive data type as an object. And similarly, whenever you want to retrieve data from the collections, you need to unwrap the value from the object that you stored previously. So this wrapping and unwrapping process we are going to do whenever we are trying to store the primitive data type values inside collections.

But this may look very complex to you, but don't worry, there are good amount of wrapper classes inside Java library to make our life easy. So from the next lecture, let's try to understand how to wrap and unwrap the primitive data type values while we are trying to deal with the collections inside Java. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: Autoboxing and unboxing - Theory
lectures.text:
As of now, we are performing the boxing and unboxing manually with the help of the methods available inside the wrapper classes. For example, we are leveraging the valueOf() method to perform the boxing, whereas to perform the unboxing with the help of the wrapper objects, we are invoking the instance methods like intValue(), doubleValue(), and longValue(). But here you may have a question which is boxing and unboxing seems to be a very most common scenario inside Java.

Is there any better approach or is there any automated way of boxing and unboxing? It's a very great question and a valid question as well. When Java introduced the collections very first time Java team, they made these boxing and unboxing as manual process, which means that Java developers, they have to perform the boxing and unboxing manually with the help of these methods. But in the Java five version, the Java team, they made these boxing and unboxing automatic.

So that's why from Java five there is a new concept came into picture which is auto boxing and auto unboxing. So let's try to understand how these boxing and unboxing is going to happen automatically. Like I said before, the Java is capable of performing automatic boxing and automatic unboxing from Java5 version. That's why these concept is commonly known as auto boxing and auto unboxing. First, let's try to understand how to perform the boxing automatically. Like you can see here, first, I have created the inter primitive data type variable with the name num and to the same variable I'm trying to assign the numerical value, which is 16.

As a next step, I'm trying to assign this num variable directly to the object of Integer wrapper class. So this is auto boxing. So whenever I'm trying to assign a direct int literal value or a variable in such scenarios the boxing is going to happen automatically behind the scenes. We don't have to manually invoke the valueOf() method. So this is auto boxing. Whereas coming to the unboxing even this is also work very similarly. You can see first I'm trying to assign the 16 directly to the wrapper object of Integer.

So at the very first line auto boxing is going to happen. Whereas in the second line I'm trying to assign these num object to the primitive data type variable which is num. So at the second line the unboxing is happening automatically. Did you see how easy it is with this auto boxing and unboxing? We never have to do the boxing or unboxing manually with the help of valueOf() method or intValue(), doubleValue(). . or longValue() methods. We can use this auto boxing and unboxing feature only from the Java5 version.

Do you know when Java five released? Java5 released a long back in 2004. In 2004, most of us might be in school, which means this feature is introduced long back, and right now we can happily use the auto boxing and unboxing without any manual code. Let's try to understand more details about auto boxing and unboxing these auto boxing and unboxing it is going to be performed when we compile the code. The JVM is completely clueless of the boxing and unboxing performed by the compiler, which means when we try to assign a primitive data type value to the wrapper class object, the auto boxing is going to happen behind the scenes.

So by the time my JVM is trying to execute the bytecode of my Java program behind the scenes, the compiler will use the valueOf() method to convert that primitive data type value into the wrapper class object. The same applies for the unboxing as well. Here I want to share a very important note. So as of now everything seems to be good. Like you might be liking these auto boxing and unboxing a lot, but you need to be very careful whenever you're trying to use these auto boxing and and unboxing feature.

While you are trying to deal with the null values. Like you can see here first, I have created an object of Integer wrapper class, and to the same I'm trying to assign the null value later on. If I try to assign this wrapper class object directly to the primitive data type variable, I'm going to get a NullPointerException. Do you know why? Because behind the scenes the compiler is going to write a code which is with the help of these n wrapper object it is going to invoke the intValue() method available inside the Integer wrapper class.

So anything that we try to invoke on top of the null object, what do we get? We get our favorite exception which is NullPointerException. That's why whenever you are trying to deal with the wrapper objects that have null values, please do enough null checks and do enough unit testing to avoid these kind of surprises. I hope you are clear about the process of autoboxing and unboxing how it is going to work. As of now, we just discussed this concept using the slides.

In the next lecture, we can try to write a Java program, and in the same program I'll show you how these autoboxing and unboxing is going to happen automatically. I hope you are fine with the plan. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

Instead it is going to create a single object and both your references like obj1 and obj2, they are going to point to the same object inside the heap memory. Since our number is just above 127, this obj3 and obj4 will be created as two separate objects inside the heap memory. So why Java is doing this? The reason is very simple.

According to the Java team, most of the times Java developers end up creating the objects with small numerical values, which may fall in the range of -128 to 127. In both these scenarios, this caching mechanism is going to come into picture. Whereas if you try to create the wrapper objects with the help of deprecated constructor approach, then in that scenario, regardless of what kind of value you are trying to store, you're always going to get a fresh new object.

Whereas if you are trying to implement autoboxing or if you're trying to use the Integer.valueOf(), method or value of methods inside other wrapper classes like Long, Byte and Short.

In those scenarios, always JVM is going to check what kind of data you're trying to store. lectures.title: Java Collection Framework Hierarchy
lectures.text:
Finally, we discussed everything around the wrapper classes, autoboxing and unboxing, which is a prerequisite concept for Java Collections framework. Now we can happily get started with the Java Collections Framework. From now onwards, I'm going to use the framework jargon most Oftenly. With that you may have a question which is what do we mean by framework? Anytime if you hear the jargon framework, it means it is an ecosystem of libraries or classes or interfaces, which is going to help you in solving a problem.

What are we trying to solve with the help of Java Collections Framework? Under these collections framework, we are going to have list of interfaces and classes, which is going to help us in storing the multiple elements with a single data type on top of that, we can overcome that disadvantages of arrays with the help of Java collection framework. I hope you are clear. Now let me show you the Java collections Framework hierarchy. You can see these are the most important interfaces and classes that we have under the Java Collections Framework hierarchy.

I'm not trying to show you each and every class and interface inside this framework because it is unnecessary. And these framework also have hundreds and hundreds of interfaces and classes. I'm just trying to show you the most commonly used or most important interfaces and classes inside this slide whatever you see inside the green color, they represent the interface. Whereas whatever you see in the form of light pink or light peach color, you can call them as Java classes.

First, let's try to understand what is there on the right hand side. On the right hand side we have an interface at the top which is iterable. The same is going to be implemented by collection. The collection interface is again implemented by List, Queue and Set. So using this List, Queue and Set we will be able to store any amount of elements or objects. But each of these interfaces and their implementation classes, they provide certain characteristics which you need to consider whenever you are trying to decide one of their implementations.

For example, if you are trying to use the class of ArrayList to store your objects or elements, then you need to convince yourself why you are trying to use this class, but not the Set or Queue or Stack. I'm going to explain you what are the special characteristics of all these data structures. So based upon these special characteristics, you should use them to solve your business problem. So each of these interfaces classes like List, Queue and Set, they have good amount of implementation classes.

We don't have to remember all of them because we're not going to use all of them on day to day basis throughout this course. Whatever is super important and whatever developers they are going to use on day to day basis, those classes and interfaces, I'm going to discuss them in detail in the coming lectures. So on the right hand side we have these kind of interfaces. But on the left hand side you can see we have a Map interface. So Map interface also has its own implementation classes.

You may have a question which is why Map is not included inside this family under collection and Iterable. The reason is very simple. Map follows a different structure to store the data Map, always follow with the help of key and value format. When we discuss about Map in detail, it is going to make more sense to you. Whereas whatever you see on the right hand side, they always follow the same format. But all these interfaces, they have their own unique characteristics or features, which we need to consider while we are trying to use one of their implementation classes.

Inside the next slide, I have mentioned all the important points around the Java Collections Framework hierarchy. From this slide, I just wanted to reiterate a few important points. The very first one is Collection. The Collection is the root interface for all the collection classes. So these Collection interface, it is going to have some abstract methods supporting the basic operations, such as adding an element, removing an element, and checking for the presence of an element inside a Collection implementation.

So any implementation class that is implementing Collection interface, they should provide implementation logic on how to add an element, on how to remove an element, and on how to check for the presence of an element inside a Collection object. After Collection we have List interface. You should use List and its implementation classes only if you have a requirement where you want to maintain the order of insertion of the elements inside your Collection object, and on top of that, if you want to maintain the duplicate elements inside your Collection object.

In such scenarios, you should use the List and its implementation classes. Whereas coming to the Set it is going to behave completely opposite to List. Set is not going to maintain the order of insertion, which means all the elements will be inserted at random positions in an unordered manor. On top of that Set it does not allow duplicates. Whenever you have a requirement where you don't want to maintain the duplicate elements, then in such scenarios, you can happily use the Set and its implementation classes.

Coming to the Queue you need to use these interface or its implementation classes whenever you want to follow the principle which is first in, first out. So inside these Fifo principle, all the elements which are added first, they are going to be processed first, whereas Stack it is going to follow the completely opposite principle of Fifo which is lafoe last in, first out. So whenever you have a requirement where you want to process the last element first, in such scenarios, you can go with the Stack and its implementation classes.

And at last we have a Map interface. You should use a Map and its implementation classes whenever you want to store the data in the form of key and value pairs. For example, if you want to store the numbers of your friends, definitely you first need to have a key, which is what is your friend name followed by value, which is what is his number. In such scenarios, we should use the Map which will allow us to store in the format of key and value, all these interfaces and classes they are going to present inside the package java.util.

Like I said before, there will be hundreds of classes and interfaces discussing about each and every interface and class require a separate dedicated course. That's why what I am going to do is to make our life easy. I'm going to discuss most of commonly used collections and the implementation classes throughout the course. With that, you will be in a very safe hands by the time you are done with this course. I hope you are super clear and super excited to start the journey of collections.

I'm also super excited to teach you about these complex concepts. Without learning collections, you can't climb yourself as a Java developer. That's why my humble request is please practice as much problems as you can around the Java collections. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.
