lectures.title: ArrayList performance
lectures.text:
Performance is the important parameter that you need to consider whenever you are trying to select a particular data structure available inside the Java Collections framework. Based upon your business scenario, you may need to select various data structures available inside the Java Collection framework. That's why inside this lecture, let's try to understand under which scenarios ArrayList is going to perform better and under which scenarios. It is going to cry a lot to understand about the ArrayList performance.

First, let's try to consider an ArrayList example like you can see here I'm trying to create an object of ArrayList, and this ArrayList object is capable of storing the Integer objects or int wrapper objects. You can see here with the help of add() method I'm trying to add various int values like one, two, three, four. And here if you can recall, I'm not doing any boxing. Like I'm not trying to convert this primitive data type values into a wrapper object.

But behind the scenes, the auto boxing is taking care of converting my primitive data type values into the Integer wrapper objects. I hope you remembered the wrapper classes discussion that we have done previously. So based upon the data that I am trying to add, this is how the data is going to store inside the memory location. So at the zero index the value one is going to be stored followed by two, three and four. ArrayList is going to store the data very similar to array which means ArrayList also is going to store all your elements in an contiguous locations.

With this clarity, let's try to understand how various operations is going to work inside the ArrayList. First let's try to talk about random access operations. So what do I mean by random access operation? Using random access operations, I want to randomly access any element inside my ArrayList object. So in this kind of operations, whenever you are trying to randomly fetch an element or randomly set an element inside an ArrayList object, it is going to work super fast.

You're always going to have a constant time, regardless whether you're trying to fetch the first element or the thousand element or the 1 million element inside your ArrayList object, it is always going to have same time to fetch the element, or to set the element at a random given index location. Do you know the reason why the random access operation is always going to have a constant time, and why it is going to work super fast? It's very simple.

If you try to think about it, think like you have 1000 elements inside your ArrayList object. If you are asking for the 999 element behind the scenes, Java is not going to look for each and every index location. Instead, from the first index, it will try to jump directly into the 999 location by adding zero plus 999, and with that, the memory location is going to be jammed very quickly. lectures.text:
Sometimes we may have a requirement to create immutable list objects, just like how we can create normal immutable objects. Very similarly, inside Java, we can also create immutable collection objects. Here you may have a question which is what is the use case or the requirement to create an immutable list object? The answer is very simple. Sometimes you may pass on your list object or any other collection object to other methods to process the elements inside them.

While you are trying to hand over your List object, you want to make sure you don't want the other methods to manipulate the data or to manipulate the elements present inside your List object or inside Collection object. In this kind of scenarios, we need to create the immutable List object. Let me show you an example so that it is going to be clear for you. For the same, I'm going to create a new Java class. The class name is ImmutableListDemo. Inside this class first let me create the main() method here first, I'm going to create an normal List object.

Maybe using the ArrayList for the same I'm going to type List integer and the variable name I'm going to mention as accountNums. So I'm trying to store List of account numbers inside these ArrayList object. So using these account nums variable I'm trying to add various account numbers. Maybe I'll try to add some random account number. Think like this is a bank account number. Very similarly let me add few more account numbers. In total I'm trying to add three different account numbers.

Now think like you are trying to hand over this List object or ArrayList object to some other method to process these account numbers. You may have a business logic which is to credit some amount into these bank accounts for the same. Let me write the private method like private static add $10. So this is the method name and the return type from this method is List of integer. Whatever List I'm trying to send, I want to return the same as an output from this method.

So to this method the input obviously it is same as List of integer and the variable name I'm going to keep it as same, which is account names. So inside this method, as of now, I'm going to write a simple logic which is using for each I'm going to iterate all the elements inside my ArrayList object, and for each account number I'm going to credit $10 into their bank account. We're going to talk in detail about how to iterate the elements inside an ArrayList in the coming lectures.

For now, let's try to use for each you know how to use for each to use the for each. First we need to type for and inside these first we need to mention Integer account : what is your collection object? Account numbers is the Collection object. So now this for each loop it is going to iterate all the account numbers inside my accountsNum Collection object inside my for each loop for each iteration, I'm going to simply have a System.out.println(), saying that $10 credited into the account colon, followed by I'm going to append the account number, and at last I want to return the same account numbers as an output from this method.

So this private method I'm going to invoke from my main() method by invoking at $10 and passing the account numbers as an input. So if I try to execute this program, you will be able to see that the $10 is credited into these three different account numbers. Now think like some bad developer, he added his own account numbers so that he will get free $10 into his account number. Maybe he will add a account number which is 545634. Now if you try to execute this program, you will be able to see that $10 is credited into his account as well. So do you see the intention is getting changed because someone is able to change the list elements. To avoid these kind of problems, we need to make sure we are creating the immutable objects are immutable collection objects before we hand over them to the other methods inside your Java project, we can create immutable list objects inside Java in two ways.

The very first approach is I can try to invoke the collections. Collections is an utility class which is present inside the java.util package. Inside this CollectionsUtility class you can look for the method which is unmodifiable list. So we have other methods also to create UnmodifiableCollection, UnmodifiableList, Map, Set. So since we are right now looking to create an immutable list object, I'm trying to invoke these unmodifiable list method. To this method I'm going to pass the account numbers as an input and the output from this method I'm going to catch into the same account numbers List object.

After invoking this method, I can try to pass the same account numbers to the add $10 method. So this time if I try to execute this program, hooray! We are getting an exception saying that unsupported operation exception. That means if someone is trying to perform some alter operations on top of my unmodifiableList like add(), set(), delete(), remove() anything that they are trying to do which will alter the elements inside my unmodifiableList. They are going to get a runtime exception. My Java at runtime it is simply going to throw an error message saying that I'm sorry dude, I cannot change that.

I'm not allowed to do that. How it is conveying it is conveying the same with the help of UnsupportedOperationException. So this is one approach of creating UnmodifiableList. But from Java 9 there is more easier approach is introduced. So let me show you how to do that. To create an unmodifiable list from the Java 9 version, you can straight away invoke of() method available inside the List interface. To this of() method, we can pass any number of elements as an object.

This time I'll try to pass same account numbers by comma separated. So this is one of the easiest way of creating the List object. Behind the scenes, this of() method, which we are trying to invoke to pass various elements. It is going to give the object of one of the implementation of list class and this List object it is going to be immutable. So the output from this of() method I can try to catch on the right hand side, either in an ArrayList format or LinkedList format, or I can simply mention List and the variable name as immutableAccountNums.

So now if I try to pass these immutableAccountNums and try to execute this program, you will be able to see the same exception which is UnsupportedOperationException. So whatever of() method that we are trying to invoke, this is introduced only from the Java 9 version. To make developer life easy to create ImmutableList objects with a very short code. So with this List.of() we are trying to do initialization and we are also making our List object as Unmodifiable.

If needed, we can assign these immutableAccountNums to the ArrayList object. Let me show you how to do that. For the same, let me type var arrayListObject. And on the right hand side I'm going to invoke the array list constructor and mention the integer as the data type. And to this constructor I'm going to pass immutableAccountNums as an input. But please note that these ArrayList object which we have created from the immutableList, it is not going to be immutable.

Let me show you the demo as well. If I try to pass this arrayListObject, the method is going to work without any exception. That's why anytime, if you want to pass an immutableList object, please only use these two approaches. One is with the help of List.of() and the other one is with the help of Collection.unmodifiedList() method. The same kind of concept applicable for other data structures also like Set, Map, which we are going to discuss in the coming sections.

Whatever we discussed around the immutableList I have highlighted in this slide for your reference, the most preferred way is to use the of() static methods available inside the List interface, but please note that this option is only available from Java 9. I hope you are clear. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.text:
When you are dealing with the ArrayList of objects, or any other List objects, one of the primary requirements that you may have on day to day basis is processing the elements inside the ArrayList object or inside the List object. That's why it is very important to understand what are the various options that we have to iterate the list of elements inside a Collection object. There are three most commonly used different approaches. I'll try to show you all of them one by one.

The very first approach is with the help of for each loop. That's why I'm trying to mention the class name as ArrayListForEachExample. So this is the class name inside this class first, as usual, we need to create the main() method post that inside this main() method, I want to create a ArrayList object that is capable of storing various String objects. For the same, let me go to the ArrayListDemo here we already have a code related to creating an ArrayList object and storing various country names, so let me copy these code and paste it inside the ArrayListForEachExample class.

First, let me remove this String data type because we don't need to mention on the right hand side if we are already mentioning on the left hand side this is called diamond operator, which we already discussed previously. Post creating these ArrayList object I'm trying to add various country names into my ArrayList like India, Canada, USA, Germany and India. The process of iterating the elements with the help of for each is very similar to what we have done with the arrays.

We just have to mention for and inside the for we need to mention colon and to the left hand side of the colon we just need to mention what is the data type of your element which is String. And after that we can give a variable name which is going to act as a temporary variable name for each element that we are going to iterate with the help of for each loop. And after the colon, we need to provide what is your List object name or ArrayList object name.

It is going to be country names, and inside this for loop we can write any kind of processing logic it can be converting your country names into and capital letters or it can be simply printing and country name. The business logic can be anything, but I just wanted you to understand the process that you need to follow to iterate the elements of an List object. So here I'll just go with the simple business logic, which is to display the each element that is available inside my ArrayList.

So if I try to execute this program, you will be able to see the list of countries that I have printed. The elements are going to be printed based upon the same order that we have inserted. On top of that, duplicate elements are also going to be allowed inside ArrayList. That's why we're able to see this India as a very first element and the last element. So these are very first approach which is the basic approach. Now let's go to the second approach.

For the same I'm going to create a new class. The class name I'm going to mention as ArrayListIteratorExample. . Inside this class let me copy the code that we have inside this ArrayListForEachExample. I'm going to copy the entire main() method here instead of for each loop this time I'm going to use the iterator. So whenever you want to use the iterator to iterate the elements of your Collection object, first using the Collection object which is country names, you need to invoke the iterator() method.

This iterator() method is available inside the List. It is going to give the Iterator as an output, which is capable of iterating a given data type elements. That's why on the left hand side, I need to make sure I'm catching the output with the help of iterator and mentioning the element data type, which is String. And after that I'm going to give the name to my iterator, which is iterator itself. This is just like a variable name. Now using these iterator I can invoke various methods to identify whether I have the next element to invoke with the help of hasNext().

And similarly, whenever I want to fetch the next element inside the iterator, I need to invoke this next() method. So whenever you are trying to use this iterator, you have to use the while block using the while block first, we need to make sure to define a condition which is iterator.hasNext(). So this condition is going to check during the each iteration whether your iterator has any element in the next index. If there is an element, then only the logic inside the while loop is going to be executed.

So inside my while loop I can try to fetch the element with the help of next() method. But before that, let me try to create a variable country and invoke the next() method post that I can try to print out the country details. If I try to execute this program, you can see I'm going to get the same output here. You may have a question which is if for each also capable of doing the same. Then why should I use the iterator and why should I use these hasNext() and fetching the element manually with the help of next().

I agree with your question. It's a great question. Whenever you have a simple requirement just to iterate your elements, you can happily go with the for each loop. But compared to for each loop, iterator has one more advantage, which is with the help of iterator. You can remove the element inside your List at runtime. For example, here, if you try to remove with the help of like countryNames.remove() and providing these country name as an input.

In this kind of scenario, you're going to get a runtime exception. Let me confirm you that by running the program you can see we are getting ConcurrentModificationException. So this exception you're going to get while you are trying to iterate. And at the same time you are trying to delete or modify the elements inside your ArrayList object. But there is a workaround to remove the elements with the help of iterator. What you can do is you can invoke the remove() method with the help of iterator.

So here I can mention iterator.remove(). Maybe what I can do is I can write a condition, which is if country.equals() India I'm going to invoke the iterator.remove(). This if condition is capable of removing the element if it is matching with the name India, maybe what I can do is to prove you that the element is removed outside the while loop. I can try to print out the ArrayList object with the name countryNames. So if I try to execute this program this time, I'm not going to get any runtime exception.

You can see first I have displayed all the elements and after the while loop is executed my ArrayList object. It has only three countries and all the elements with the name India are removed. lectures.text:
When we try to store multiple objects or elements inside an Collection object, sometimes we may have requirement to sort them based upon ascending order or in a descending order. You might be storing simple primitive data type objects like Integer, String, Character, Double, Float, or you may also store complex data types like Person, Employee. Regardless of what kind of data that you're trying to store inside your Collection, object sorting is one of the common requirement that you may see inside your projects.

That's why let's try to understand what are the options that we have to sort the elements inside an Collection object. To show you the demo of sorting, I'm going to create a new Java class inside the package com.eazybytes.List. The class name that I'm going to give here is SortingDemo. Inside this class, first we need to make sure we are creating the main() method post that I'm going to create an object of ArrayList, which is capable of storing the Integer objects.

The variable name I'm going to mention as numbers followed by new ArrayList with the help of diamond operator. Now inside these numbers ArrayList object, I'm going to add few integer values for the same I'm going to paste few lines of code. You can see I have added multiple elements of type Integer. If I try to print out all these elements with the help of System.out.println(), and by passing these numbers as an input, I'm going to get the output in the same order of insertion that I have followed.

But like I said, we need to look for options on how to sort these elements. There are multiple approaches. Let's try to understand what are those one by one. The very first approach is with the help of a static method available inside the Collections class. Inside this we have a sort() method. So there are two overloaded methods of sort(). First, let's try to see the demo of very first sort() method which is going to accept the object of List. Here you can see I'm trying to pass the numbers object as an input to the sort() to static method, which is available inside the Collection class.

So with this line of code behind the scenes, all the elements inside the same numbers object, they are going to be sorted in an ascending order after this line. If I try to print out all the numbers inside the Numbers Collection object, I will be able to see the output in an ascending order. You can see this is the original list. Later on, after the sorting is completed, you'll be able to see all the Integer elements they are sorted using ascending order.

But what if you have a requirement to sort your elements in an descending order? The default order that is going to be followed by the collection framework is ascending order. If you want to follow that descending order, you need to invoke the same sort() method, but this time you should invoke the sort() method that is going to accept the two method input parameter. The very first input parameter is the Collection object itself, followed by you need to invoke the Comparator interface, and inside these we have a reverseOrder() method.

You need to invoke the same with this extra input parameter, which is Comparator.reverseOrder(). I'm telling to the collection, please sort my elements in an reverse order which is descending order. After this last statement, if I try to print out the numbers again this time, you should be able to see the numbers sorted in and descending order as a next step. This time, let's try to sort the list of String objects. As of now we are trying to use the numbers for sorting, so ascending order.

Descending order for the numbers is very common. But coming to the Strings or Characters, you may have a question which is how the String objects are characters. They're going to be sorted all the String objects and the Character objects they are going to be sorted by using the lexicographically order we know inside English the very first letter is A, followed by B, followed by C, and it will continue till the end of the alphabetic letters using the same order A is going to be considered as the smallest compared to the B.

Behind the scenes collections framework also is going to follow the same format or the same formula to sort the String objects or characters by using the Lexicographically order. So let me show you one demo on how to sort the String objects. For the same this time also, I'm going to create one more ArrayList object this time I'll use the var keyword and with the variable name as countries. And to this I'm going to assign the new ArrayList of type String.

Inside this ArrayList object I'm going to store various country names like India, USA, Japan, France and Canada. If you try to print out all these elements without sorting whatever the order that you have followed, the same is going to be consider. While displaying these elements into the console, we should be able to sort the Countries object also by using the Collections.sort(). So let me copy these lines of code and paste the same here. Instead of numbers, I'm going to pass countries in all the places so that we can see the output in the console.

So you can see these are default insertion order. Later on when we try to sort based upon ascending order, you can see the very first character is C followed by F, followed by I, j and u. Whereas in the descending order, the very first element has the character as u, followed by j, I, f, and c. And here you may have a question which is what if two elements have the same first character? In those kind of scenarios, the Java collection framework is going to look at the second character.

If all the characters in both the elements are same, then there won't be any sorting. The elements will be displayed next to each other, which is expected in any kind of sorting mechanism. So as of now, you can see we are trying to use the same approach, which is with the help of sort to static method available inside the Collection class. But there is one more approach let me show you the second approach. In the second approach, you can directly invoke the instance method available on top of your object.

So the object here is Country. So on top of this I'm trying to invoke the sort() method. So whenever you are trying to invoke the sort() method using your List object, you need to make sure you are passing the comparator value as an input. So that's why after invoking the sort(), I need to invoke the Comparator followed by I need to invoke the method which is naturalOrder(). So when we say naturalOrder, we are referring to the ascending order. The same kind of logic I can write by removing these line of code here.

This time, instead of naturalOrder(), we are going to mention reverseOrder(), since we want to sort the country elements based upon the descending order. So let me execute this program and you'll be able to see the same output inside the console. So this is very simple data where we are trying to store numerical values and String objects. And we are simply invoking the sort() related methods available inside the JDK. But sometimes we may have some custom requirements to perform the sorting.

So let's try to understand how to implement our own custom sorting requirements in the next lecture thank you, bye.

lectures.title: LinkedList performance
lectures.text:
Let's try to understand about the performance of LinkedList objects. We need to understand under which scenarios LinkedList is going to work better and under which scenarios it is going to have some performance issues. We all know that arrays, they are going to store the objects or elements in an consecutive memory location. The same applies for the ArrayList as well. But coming to the LinkedList, we know that each object it is going to stored in a separate link or node.

Inside this link or node, we are going to store a reference to the next link or the next node, and similarly to the previous node or the previous link as well, if it is not a first element. That's why, in other words, inside the Java programming language we can say all LinkedList are actually double linked. The reason why we call them as double linked is, each link or node it is going to point to the two other nodes. One is the next node and the other one is the previous node.

One of the drawback of ArrayList or array is they are going to have lot of performance issues. If you try to do the random addition operation or remove operation, since they are going to store the elements in a contiguous memory location. If you try to remove the element from the middle of the ArrayList object in those scenarios, all the subsequent elements has to be shifted either to the left side or to the right side based upon whether you are trying to perform delete() operation or add() operation.

But with the LinkedList we can overcome these drawback of ArrayList. Whenever we are using LinkedList, removing an element or adding an element from the middle of the linkededList or from any location, it is going to be an inexpensive operation. When I say inexpensive, it is going to be fast. Let's try to understand why it is going to be fast inside LinkedList. lectures.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
lectures.text:
Let's try to discuss about the differences between ArrayList and LinkedList. With this discussion, you should get a clarity under which scenarios you should use ArrayList and LinkedList. The very first difference is we know ArrayList is an implementation of List interface, and it is going to store the elements in an contiguous block of memory or contiguous memory locations. Since the elements are going to be stored in a contiguous memory location, accessing an element or reading an element is faster compared to the LinkedList.

Coming to the story of the LinkedList, LinkedList is also an implementation class of List interface, but it is going to store all the elements as nodes with a reference to the next node and the previous node. Since LinkedList is going to store the elements with the help of nodes, it is going to allow faster insertion and deletion of elements from the middle of the LinkedList or from any index inside the LinkedList . Do you know the reason why? The reason is very simple.

The LinkedList has to update only the references of the affected nodes, whereas with the ArrayList all the subsequent elements, they are going to be affected and there needs to be moved either to the right hand side or to the left hand side to maintain that continuous memory location. The next difference is around the performance time whenever you are using the ArrayList, regardless of which index element you are trying to access, it can be 10,000 index elements or 1 million index element.

You're always going to have a constant time off performance. For example, if the time taken by the ArrayList to read the very first index element is one millisecond, then the same one millisecond time is also required to read any element. It can be 10,000 element or 1 million element. But coming to the LinkedList, whenever you are trying to perform the read operation, it is going to take the linear time, which is O(n), which means if the LinkedList is going to take one millisecond to read the very first element, and if you are trying to read the 10th index element, then your LinkedList is going to take one into ten milliseconds, which is ten milliseconds.

So based upon the index element that you are trying to access inside your LinkedList, the performance also is going to increase. ArrayList they are going to be slower than LinkedList only in the scenarios of adding or removing elements, especially from the middle of the List. That's why LinkedList is going to be a good choice whenever you need to frequently add or remove elements from the middle of the List, or from any location inside your List object.

Overall, if you ask me what is the summary from this lecture, I would request you to remember one important point, which is always use ArrayList. If your code is going to do a lot of reading operation, whereas if your code is trying to perform lot of writing and deleting operations, please always use the LinkedList. If you are just dealing with the 100 elements or 1000 elements, you don't have to worry about ArrayList or LinkedList. You can use any of them.

The performance issues only come into picture if you try to store thousands and millions of elements. I also mentioned few pictures here. You can see on the left hand side a person is trying to read the book. So please always remember this picture whenever you are trying to refer to the ArrayList. So remember this picture whenever you are trying to recall about LinkedList. So for writing and removing scenarios, always LinkedList is the best option. lectures.text:
Sometimes inside interviews, people may try to trick you by asking a question like create an array, List object or any Collection object and store different types of objects like a String object, Integer object, Boolean object, Float object. This kind of peculiar requirement they may try to give to you, to confuse you, and you might be under the impression that we can use collections only with the generics, and it may not be possible to store multiple data type objects around this scenario.

I want to provide a clarity, which is we can use the collections without generics as well. That is perfectly possible inside Java. In fact, when Java started, all collections are not developed with generics. Generics came into picture in the later versions. So to provide that backward compatibility, even today, Java allows you to create the collection objects like ArrayList, LinkedList or any other collection object without any generics as well.

Let me show you a demo around this. For the same, I'm going to create a new Java class which is WithoutGenericsDemo. Inside this class, first let me create the main() method, followed by I'm going to create an ArrayList object here the variable name I'll keep it as List followed by new operator followed by ArrayList constructor. You can see here I'm not using any generics. With this now, my collection is capable of storing any kind of objects. So this is one more difference between an array and a collection.

With array we can only store the elements belong to a particular primitive data type or a particular object. Whereas with collections, if you don't use generics, you will get a flexibility to store any kind of object elements here inside this List, first I'm going to add a String object, which is hello, followed by next time I'm going to add into value. When I invoke the add() object, you can see it is trying to accept an object as an input parameter.

Whenever we are not defining an generic while we are trying to create an ArrayList object or any List object, by default, all the methods are going to accept a object of type Object class. So that's what happening here. Now here let me try to send an input value which is 1, 2, 3. So though I'm sending the input data in a int primitive data type format, this is going to be converted into an Integer wrapper object with the help of Autoboxing. Next I'm going to add one more element which is Boolean value true.

This way we can add any data type object into this ArrayList. But the problem with this approach is though, you are getting a flexibility to store any kind of object while you are trying to read these objects, you need to typecast them otherwise, you can't use these elements inside your business logic. For example, from this List, if I try to get the element which is present at the first index by mentioning zero on the left hand side, if I just mention object greeting as a variable name, you'll be able to see that I'm not going to get any compilation error, but with this object, I will not be able to invoke any String related methods, because as of now I got an object which belongs to Object class.

But I know at the zero index I stored a String object. That's why I should be doing String typecasting. In order to convert this object as a String object. Post that I will be able to use a String related methods like toUppercase() or toLowercase(). It's up to me what business logic I want to write. Similarly, let me try to copy the same code inside the second element we know we stored the Integer object. That's why I'm trying to typecast to Integer.

And on the left hand side I'm going to mention int and the variable name as number. Similarly, in the next line I'm going to typecast this to boolean and the data type I'm going to mention as boolean on the left hand side. The variable name I'm going to mention as flag. So this way you need to do the manual typecasting instead of boolean. If you try to mention double, you are going to get a ClassCastException on the left hand side also, let me change this to double.

If I execute this program, definitely I'm going to get a ClassCastException. So with this it should be pretty clear for you though generics they are giving an advantage or power to you to store any kind of objects. Along with this power, you're also going to get a drawback, which is around the casting. Whenever you are trying to do this casting, you need to be very careful and you need to do the proper casting. Otherwise you're going to get a ClassCastException.

Whereas if you try to use generics in the same code, you can see it is going to be super safety and clean. So here after the ArrayList I'm going to mention String. And on the right hand side I'm going to mention a diamond operator and the variable name. I'm going to change it to List one, the same list one I'm going to mention in the next set of lines. This time you can see when we are trying to add the Boolean object and the Integer object, we are getting a compilation error.

We are getting this compilation error due to a concept called type safety. Whenever you are using generics inside your code, the compiler will make sure that no other data type objects are being added into your Collection object or into any other object. So if anyone asks you what is the advantage that we are getting with the generics? The very first answer that you need to tell is type safety or compile time check, which is going to save us from manual casting and ClassCastExceptions.

So let me comment these two lines of code just for your reference post that I'm also going to comment the last two lines. Now here I don't have to do these casting. I can directly read the element. Let me rename this variable name to greeting one here. Instead of List, I need to mention List one so that this compilation error is going to get resolved. If I try to execute this program this time, you can see I'm still getting a exception. Let me see what is the problem here?

We are getting a ClassCastException at this line of code because we forget to update this index to 2. So this time they should not be any problem. Let me execute this program. You can see this time the program executed without any issues. I hope you got a clarity around the point, which is we can build a Collection object even without generics as well, and that is going to give an advantage to store any data type objects. But this power comes with a responsibility, which is you need to do a lot of casting, and you need to be very careful around the ClassCastException.

The details that we discuss inside this lecture I have mentioned in this slide for your reference. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.text:
As of now, we are building the generic classes or generic methods which are capable of processing any kind of data type objects. But in reality, the developer life is not going to be so easy and simple. Sometimes we may have a requirements to build a generic classes or generic methods which are capable of accepting or processing the objects which are inheriting from a particular superclass, or which are implementing from a particular interface. So these kind of complex requirements, you may get around the generics inside the real projects.

As of now, we discussed the simplest flavor of generics, where you just mention the generic type as T and U, and with that, you are good to accept any kind of object. But there are more flavors around generics which are going to help you to impose some restrictions around that data type objects. We are going to discuss about those flavors in the coming lectures. But for now, before we try to explore about the other flavors of generics, first I want to teach you about an important concept inside this lecture, which is Covariance.

For the same, I'm going to create a new Java class inside the same package that we have created previously. The class name I'm going to mention as CovarianceDemo. So Covariance is a concept inside Java which you need to understand to further explore about the other flavors of generics that we have inside Java. Let me create this class inside this class, first I'm going to create a main() method, followed by I'm going to write a static method which is capable of printing the array elements.

So I'm just going to mention the method name as printArray(). Before that, I want to create some model classes inside a new package. First, let me create a package with the name com.eazybytes.generics.model inside this model package, I'm going to first create a class with the name Employee.

The same class I'm going to extend by other subclasses like first I'm going to create a Java class with the name Developer and this class it is going to extends the Employee superclass. In the similar lines, I'm also going to create one more Java class this time the name of the class is going to be manager and this manager class also going to extend the Employee superclass. For now, let's not worry about the code inside these classes. They can be empty classes.

We don't have to implement any code inside them. Now let me go to the CovarianceDemo class here I'm going to update the printArray() method to accept an method input parameter of type Employee[] array and the parameter name I'm going to give as employees. Inside this method, I can write a logic, which is to iterate all the employees that we received inside the array employees the same I'm going to print them with the help of System.out.println().

For now, let's not worry about what is the output that we are going to get. As of now, we are not storing anything inside these employee objects. That's why we are not going to get much useful information on the console when we try to print these objects. Now, inside the main() method I'm going to create an array of Employee[]. First let me type employee followed by square brackets and the array name I'm going to mention as employees. And with that I'm just going to get these statement whenever I try to print the object of Employee. So the same kind of logic I can try to do inside that developer as well. So let me try to generate the toString() method. And this time also I'm going to click on this okay button. Similarly I'm going to generate the toString() method inside the Manager class as well.

Now if I go and execute this CovarianceDemo this time we are going to get some meaningful data. So it is an empty. You can see I'm able to invoke the printArray() method with the developers as an input. In the similar lines, I should be able to do the same for manager as well. If I execute this program, you can see I'm going to get a proper output based upon whatever I'm storing inside my objects.

So this concept is called as Covariance. Inside the Java, whenever we write the code with a parent supertype, the same code can be used by the subtypes as well. So here I'm sending a subtype which is Manager and Developers. Still my code is working this kind of concept we call inside Java as Covariance. This Covariance exists throughout the Java. It's not only applicable for arrays. For example, I can try to create an String object with the name s and inside this I can try to store a value which is generics.

Post that the same String object I will be able to assign to the variable of type object by using the code like you can see here, Object o = s, so this is perfectly is going to work inside Java due to the concept of Covariance. lectures.title: Supertype or Lower Bound Wildcards
lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, let's try to understand another flavor of generics, which is Supertype are lower bound wildcards. This syntax is exactly opposite to what we have discussed in the previous lecture. Just like how we have covariance in the similar lines, we also have contravariance. Contravariance refers to the ability of a type to accept a more generic, broader types. With the help of Upper bound wildcards that we have discussed in the previous lecture, we are going to restrict the unknown type to be a specific type or a subtype of that type, whereas with the help of lower bound wildcards, we can restrict an unknown type to be a specific type or a super type of that type.

How to define this lower bound wildcards. It's very simple. Inside the angle brackets after the question mark, you need to mention super, whereas for the upper bound wildcard we used to mention extents, but coming to the lower bound of wildcards, we need to mention the super. And what is the generic type. So here I'm trying to mention the type as A. We can only specify either an upper bound for a wildcard or a lower bound, but we can't specify both of them.

So that's an important note that you need to be aware. Now let's see an example to understand more details about the lower bound wildcards usage. Like you can see here, there is a method with the name addNumbers. This method is going to help me to add the elements inside a List object. My business requirement is to add the integer numbers inside this, but I want to make this method more flexible by making these. To be able to add elements that belongs to Integer object are its super class.

Integer class has super class like number and the number has a super class object. Since I want to have a flexibility to store the objects of integer or number or object, I can use lower bound wildcards like you can see here. First I need to mention the question mark, followed by super followed by integer. With this now my List is going to allow me to add the objects of Integer or number or Object class. lectures.title: How HashMap Store Key, Value
lectures.text:
So whenever you try to attend an interview around Java and if the question is around HashMap, the toughest question that you can expect around the topic, which is how a HashMap stores the data internally. In the case of List and Set, or any other data structure where they store a single element or a single object with respect to to those data structures. The storage mechanism is very simple. They will be stored somewhere in the heap location. But coming to the map, this is going to be something different every time.

Whenever we are trying to store an entry inside the HashMap, the entry has to be stored in a key and the value format. And if we ask the HashMap by providing a key, it has to return the same value object that we initially stored. To make this work, behind the scenes, HashMap is going to do a lot of work. As a Java developer, you need to understand the internal working of HashMap. That's why inside this lecture, let's try to understand how HashMap store the key and the values inside the memory location are inside the heap memory.

Whenever we try to create an object of HashMap behind the scenes my JVM, it is going to create few buckets like you can see here. The JVM has created 16 different buckets. Each of these buckets are going to be represented by an index number right from 0 to 15. So this is just a sample representation. With the sample representation. Don't be under the assumption that all the indexes and all the buckets, they are going to be stored in a SequencedManner.

It's not going to happen that way the HashMap can create the buckets and indexes in any order. So once these buckets are created and the index numbers are tagged to these, each of these buckets inside these buckets and index numbers, only the key and values that we are trying to store inside a HashMap will be eventually stored. But here you may have a question which is how HashMap determines which bucket it has to store, or which index number it has to consider to store a particular key and value.

So that's a great question. Let's try to answer the same behind the scenes HashMap is going to use the hashing principle or hashing algorithm, the HashMap. First it is going to calculate the hash code value of a given key. For example, here, if you try to store a key and a value which is India and New Delhi, first my HashMap . It is going to calculate the hash code of India String by invoking the hashCode() method present inside the String class.

We know that String class has overridden the hashCode() method, which is inherited from the Object class. The same is going to be invoked by the JVM to calculate the hashCode() of a given string. In the case if your string is of type Person or Employee object, then definitely JVM is going to look. If you have any hashCode() method overridden inside your respective data type. Otherwise it is going to simply leverage the hash code present inside the Object superclass.

Based upon our previous sections discussion, we know the default behavior of the hash code is to calculate the value based upon the memory location where it is stored inside the heap memory. So the memory location will be feed as an input to the hashing algorithm, and the output from this hashing algorithm will be the hash code, whereas with the String the behavior is going to change because the String class has overridden the hashCode() method to generate the hash code value based upon the content of the String.

Let's imagine the hash code of the India String is 3492. By taking this hash code behind the scenes, the JVM will try to calculate the bucket index with the help of the hash code and with the length of the HashMap. As of now, you can see behind the scenes the JVM has created 16 different buckets. So that's why it is going to consider the maximum length as 16 by using this maximum length and by using the hash code of the key element, it is going to calculate the bucket index value, which is going to be in the range of 0 to 15.

Think like in our scenario the index is calculated as three. So with this calculation the India and its value which is New Delhi, it is going to be stored at the bucket or index three. The same kind of mechanism is going to repeat for all the remaining keys and values that you are trying to add. For example, think like this time I'm trying to add France and Paris. Based upon the above steps that we have discussed. Imagine this time the index is calculated as seven.

So that's why the France and Paris is going to be stored at the index seven. Similarly, if you are trying to store Japan and Tokyo, and if the index is calculated at 11, the same is going to be stored at the 11th index or 11th bucket. In the scenarios where you are trying to send the key value as null. Then in such scenarios we can't calculate the hash code value. That's why whenever you are trying to pass null as a key, which you can do only once in these kind of scenarios, the key and its value is going to be stored at the index zero.

That's why you can see we are storing the null, which is the key, and its value which is invalid at the zeroth index. As of now, this may look very simple to you, but there is some complex part which you need to understand. Let's try to understand the same. As of now, we have these kind of keys and values which are stored in different bucket index values. But like I said, there is a complex concept present inside the HashMap which is hash collision.

Based upon our discussions around the hashCode() and the equals() method in the previous sections, we know that two different objects may have same hash code value. Ideally, if the hash code implementation inside a class is good, then obviously all the times you're going to get a unique hash code. But sometimes few classes are few data types they may result into same hash code value due to two reasons. One is due to the logic present inside the hashCode() method, or may be due to the reason that finite range of hash codes are available in comparison to the potentially infinite number of keys.

We know hash code has a range which is equal to the range of Integer, but coming to the keys, we can store any number of keys. For example, if you take a String as an element data type using String, we can create infinite number of keys like I can have a string value a similarly b. Similarly, c I can write any number of keys with all the alphanumeric combinations. So with these two reasons, sometimes the JVM may calculate the same index number at the same bucket number for two different keys.

So in those scenarios the hash collision is going to happen. So whenever these kind of hash collision occurs then obviously JVM has to look for a smarter mechanism to store multiple elements at a same bucket location or at a same index location. That's why to handle these kind of hash collisions, HashMap employs a strategy. One common strategy is, to use a data structure, like a LinkedList or binary tree, to store multiple key values in the same bucket.

Let's try to understand the same by taking an example. Think like I have a country which is UK and it's a capital as London for some reason think like the hash code of this key, which is UK is 3492, which is same as for India. Since the hash codes are same, there is a very good chance that bucket index also is going to be calculated as three, where we already storing India. So with this hash collision my JVM, it is not going to override India with the UK.

Instead it is going to convert these single element into a LinkedList. Like you can see here, this is how the UK and London is going to be stored. So this is a LinkedList where this is the first entry of the LinkedList followed by this is the second entry of the LinkedList. So that's why this first element is pointing to the address location of the second element inside the LinkedList in the similar lines think like this time I'm trying to store Brazil and its capital city for this also, let's imagine the bucket is calculated as 11 this time.

Since the bucket index is calculated as 11. This Brazil and Brasilia is going to be stored after the Japan in the format of LinkedList, like you can see here. I hope you are clear about the process that HashMap follows to store a key and value. I also have a flowchart here for your reference. In the very first step, the developer is going to call the Map.put() method with the key and the value. So based upon the key and its data type, the hash code of the key is going to be calculated by invoking the hashCode() method present inside the key data type and using the same hash code behind the scenes, the index number or the bucket number is going to be calculated.

Once the bucket number is calculated, my JVM is going to check if there is any key value pair is already present at a given bucket index. If it is no, then it is a straightforward scenario. The given key and value entries is going to be stored as a first element to node inside the LinkedList. Otherwise, if there is a hash collision, then my JVM first check if the key values are matching. There is a good chance that I may try to overwrite the value of a given key multiple times.

In that scenarios, hash collision is always going to happen, so it is going to check if this is a true hash collision or the collision is happening just because we are using the same key value. lectures.title: [JAVA 9] Creating Immutable Maps
lectures.text:
Sometimes we may have a requirement to create immutable map objects, so that no other business logic or no other method can add or remove entries from a given Map object. To handle these kind of scenarios, you can happily use the static factory methods available inside the map interface. Just like how we have of() static methods inside a List interface. Very similarly, we also have often static factory methods inside Map interface as well. Apart from of() method, we also have another static method inside Map interface which is off entries in few seconds.

We are going to discuss on how to use these static factory methods in order to create an Immutable Map object. But before that, let me highlight these half and half entries. Map static factory methods. They are introduced only from the Java 9. Before, in order to make a Map object as an immutable or unmodified object. This is the process that developers use to follow. First, they will create the Map with the given key and the value data types. Once they populated all the required entries inside the Map, they are going to send the same Map as an input to the method unmodifiableMap(), which is present inside the Collections class.

So this unmodifiableMap() is a static method which is going to return the immutable or unmodifiable version of your Map object. But like you see, this is a two step process. Instead, from Java 9, we can happily use the static factory methods with the names half and half entries to directly create the immutable or Unmodifiable Map object. Let's see a few example on how to use these static factory methods, which are introduced in JDK nine or Java 9.

Here you can see I'm trying to invoke the half static method with the help of Map interface to the same I'm trying to send the same data that we have here, so the very first one is the key one, followed by value one followed by key two value two, Key three, value three. This way there are multiple overloaded half static methods. Using these multiple overloaded methods, we will be able to easily create the immutable Map objects. There is also one more flavor which is off entries, so this is also a static factory method available inside Map interface.

So whenever you are trying to invoke this method, you can pass any number of entries. There is no limit. You can pass thousand or 10,000 because this method, it is going to use the variable arguments as an input. So to this method, whenever we want to send the key and value, we need to invoke another static method available inside the Map interface, which is Map.entry to the same entry() method we need to pass what is the key and the value. So this approach you can always use whenever you have more than ten key value pairs that needs to be created inside a Map object.

Whereas if your requirement is only to create key value pairs which are less than or equal to ten, then you can happily use the half static method, regardless of which approach you are trying to use to create the unmodifiable or immutable Map object. If anyone make an attempt to add a new entry or remove an existing entry, or someone is trying to update the value against a key in all these kind of scenarios, they are going to get a unsupported operation exception because your map right now is a immutable object.

Let's see the demo of these approaches very quickly. Inside my intellig, I'm going to create a new Java class with the name ImmutableMapDemo. Inside this class first let me create the main() method followed by I'm also going to create one more static method which is public static void, and the method name I'm going to mention as processMap(). To this method, I'm going to pass the input of type map with the key data type as String, followed by integer and parameter name.

I'm going to keep it as StringIntegerMap. Inside this Map, I'm going to iterate all the entries that we have inside the Map object that this method is going to accept. For the same, I can try to use for each block. There are many implementations of Set interface.

Inside Java library, we are going to learn about the most commonly used implementation of set throughout this section. So what is a Set? In Java, a set is an interface that extends the collection interface coming to the scenarios when you have to use this Set or its implementation class is whenever you have a requirements to store unique elements inside a data structure. In all those scenarios, you can use Set and its implementation classes. The primary character of Set and its implementation classes is it is going to maintain the uniqueness of your elements, which means it is not going to allow any duplicate elements.

And typically most of the set implementation classes, they are not going to maintain the order of insertion, but there are few implementation classes where they are going to maintain the order of insertion, which you are going to discuss in the coming lectures. But any day, if someone is using set or its implementation class, the primary motivation that they may have is they want to maintain the unique elements, and they are not going to care about the order of insertion.

Let's try to see how to create an object of Set like you can see here on the left hand side, we need to mention the Set interface followed by inside the angle brackets. We need to mention what is the data type of element that you are going to store inside an Set object. On the right hand side, we need to use one of the implementation of Set. Inside this example, I'm trying to use hash set along with the diamond operator. HashSet is a most commonly used Set implementation on day to day basis inside real projects set also stores similar to List.

It is only going to accept a element. If your primary requirement is around the order of insertion, then you can always go with the List and its implementation class.

Whereas if your primary requirement is to maintain the unique elements inside your collection object, in such scenarios, you need to go with the Set and its implementation classes. This HasSet also is going to work based upon the hashing mechanism and the hash table mechanism that we discussed as part of HashMap. With that you may have a question which is here we are only providing a value. There are no key involved. Then how these kind of data is going to be stored with the help of hashing mechanism and the hash table, you may have this kind of question.

Now let's try to understand about one important question that you may have, which is how HashSet is going to maintain the uniqueness of the elements for the same. Inside this lecture, we are going deep to understand how HashSet works internally. And all of these elements are going to have the same value which is present.

I hope this makes sense to you. Now moving on to the next important point, which is HashSet is not going to offer a direct method to retrieve a particular element or object. For example, whenever we are using the HashMap or Map implementations, we can use the get() method, and to the get() method, we can pass the key as an input and based upon the key, the get() method is going to return the value that we stored inside a HashMap. So if I execute this program, you can see we are getting the true from the remove() method and post that from the Set. The Singapore country details are removed.

So this way you can use all these methods based upon your business logic. I hope this all clear to you. Thank you, bye.

lectures.title: Demo of TreeSet in Java
lectures.text:
In the previous lectures, we discussed about HashSet, which is one of the most commonly used Set implementations inside real projects. But has it has some drawbacks or limitations one such limitation is whenever we store elements with the help of HashSet object, we cannot perform the sorting. That's why whenever you have a two primary requirements, one needs to store unique elements and the other one needs to store them in a sorted manner. In such scenarios, you can use the TreeSet.

So this is another implementation of Set which is greatly inspired by TreeMap we know HashSet inspired from HashMap. Similarly tree set inspired from that TreeMap. Internally it is going to store the data in the form of TreeMap we discussed in the previous sections. TreeMap guarantees the sorting order by storing all the elements with the help of red black tree implementation. So let's try to understand more details about these tree set like you can see here, TreeSet is a collection that store elements in a sorted and ascending or natural order by default.

So by default this tree set it is going to use the Comparable interface and the compareTo() method to perform the natural ordering. But if you are looking to perform sorting based upon your custom requirements, then you can define your own comparator implementation and the same can be passed as an input to the constructor of the TreeSet. Since the TreeSet is going to leverage the Comparable and Comparator interfaces to perform the sorting, the null elements are not allowed to store inside the object of TreeSet.

So this is the hierarchy of the TreeSet at the top we have Set interface. The same is extended by SortedSet, followed by NavigableSet, and all these interfaces. They are implemented by TreeSet class. The important methods inside TreeSet are add to add a element clear to clear all the elements contains. To check if the specified element is present inside that TreeSet or not. Since the elements are sorted inside the TreeSet, we have some helper methods like first and last to get the first element and the last element, since by default the tree set is going to perform the sorting based upon the ascending order.

When you invoke the first method, you are going to get the lowest element. Similarly, for the last method, you're going to get the highest element, and using the remove() method, we can remove the specified element from the TreeSet, and with the help of size, we can return the number of elements inside the TreeSet. Let's see the demo of this tree set by writing a Java program inside IntelliJ. Before we try to see the demo, first let's try to see what is there inside that TreeSet.java class.

So this is the documentation and it says it's a NavigableSet implementation based upon a TreeMap. The elements are ordered using their natural ordering or by a comparator provided at a Set creation time depending on which constructor is used. So if you can scroll down, you will be able to see the class definition like this class extends the AbstractSet class and it is also implementing so and so interfaces. The interesting point that I want you to understand here is, if you can open the constructor of the TreeSet, you'll be able to see that whenever we are invoking these default constructor, a new object of TreeMap is going to be created.

This conforms behind the scenes, the TreeSet it is going to leverage TreeMap. That is how it is going to achieve the sorting order of the elements by leveraging the red black tree approach. If you can scroll down, you'll be able to see other constructors as well. Whenever you want to pass your own sorting logic with an Comparator, you can pass your Comparator object as an input to this constructor. The same is going to be used to perform the sorting.

Otherwise, the default comparable sorting logic is going to be leveraged. So let's see the demo of this TreeSet. For the same, I'm going to create a new Java class with the name TreeSetDemo. Inside this class, first let me create the main() method, followed by I'm going to create the object of TreeSet. For the same, I can mention TreeSet or Set I can mention var as well, but here this time let me mention the TreeSet itself and inside the angle brackets I can mention String.

Since I want to store String data type elements inside my TreeSet object the variable name. I'll just keep it as TreeSet only, and on the right hand side I'm going to mention new TreeSet with a diamond operator. Here I'm trying to invoke the default constructor. That means I want to perform the comparison by the default Comparable. Here I'm trying to store the String data type elements. If you can open the String, you will be able to see that these class implementing the Comparable interface.

That's why inside this class, you'll be able to see there is a method which is comparedTo(). Inside this method only we have the logic on how to compare two different String objects. So using this logic only the sorting is going to happen inside my TreeSet object. Now to this TreeSet object I'm going to add the elements. The very first element I'll add here is India which is the country name followed by I'll try to add another country which is USA, followed by Germany.

So first let's try to print out these TreeSet with the help of System.out.println(). If I execute this program, you'll be able to see the output in an default ascending order. The letter G comes first, followed by I followed by u. So this output confirms that my elements are sorted based upon the default natural ordering or ascending order. Let's see that demo of few other methods that we can invoke whenever we are using the TreeSet. This time I'm going to invoke the remove() method and with the help of remove() method, I'm going to remove the country Germany from my TreeSet object.

I can also confirm whether the removal is successful or not by using a System.out.println(). And inside this I'm going to have a statement which is TreeSet after removal. After this statement, I'll just mention colon followed by space and to the same. I'm going to append that TreeSet object. With that we'll be able to see the what elements right now we have inside the TreeSet. After the removal, you can see we have India and USA in an ascending order.

Similarly, we can invoke the size() method to know the size of our TreeSet object. What I can do here is with the help of System.out.println(), I can try to print out the size details by invoking the size() method with the help of TreeSet object. Here I'll try to change the statement to size of TreeSet. So if I execute this program, I'll be able to see the size which is two because Germany is removed as part of our business logic. Similarly, we can also use the contains() method to check whether a given element is present inside your TreeSet. This time also, I can try to copy the System.out.println() and try to update these statement to ease India present in TreeSet.

So to confirm the same, I need to invoke the contains() method and to this contains() method I need to pass the element as India and we are going to get the output as true because as of now my TreeSet object, it has the element India. That's why we are getting the output as true. At last, let me show you the demo of the first and the last methods that you can invoke to get the first and last elements inside your TreeSet object. For the same, let me copy the System.out.println() statement and change this statement to first element of TreeSet to display the first element, I need to invoke the first() method.

Similarly, to get the last element, I need to invoke the last() method. So if I execute this program, I'll be able to see what is the first element which is India, followed by what is the last element which is USA. Since TreeSet always guarantees the same order, we can use the SequencedSet related methods as well. For example, here, with the help of this TreeSet, I'll be able to invoke reversed() method to reverse the element. Similarly, I'll be able to invoke the addFirst() method to add the element at the first location and addLast().

So this kind of SequencedCollection related methods. I can use them happily, because my TreeSet object is always going to maintain the same order. Even if you try to look at these TreeSet class definition, you will be able to see that it is implementing an interface NavigableSet and this Navigable interface it is extending SortedSet and this SortedSet it is extending another interfaces like Set and SequencedSet. So if you can open the SequencedSet it is extending the SequencedCollection.

Under this we have so many methods using which we can perform the operations related to the boundary elements like first andLast(). And we can also use these reverse() method to reverse the elements inside a TreeSet. I hope this makes sense to you. The sample program that we discussed, I have mentioned in this slide for your reference along with the actual output, please refer the same for any questions. You can also find this code inside the GitHub repo as well.

Feel free to refer to the GitHub or to this slide. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: List vs Set
lectures.text:
One of the important question that you may face inside your Java interviews is, people may ask you to explain you about the differences between List and Set, and under which scenarios you need to choose one of them. To answer these kind of questions, you should have a good clarity about the differences between List and Set. That's why inside this lecture, let's put few minutes efforts to understand the differences between the List and Set. We know both List and Set are the interfaces inside the Java collection framework.

However, there are good amount of differences between them. The very first difference is List can contain duplicate elements. If you have a requirement to maintain a collection of elements that can contain duplicates, you need to use a List. Whereas if you are looking for an option which will not allow the duplicates, then in that scenario you can happily use Set and its implementation classes. The next difference is around the order of insertion.

By default List always maintain the order of insertion while Set. They do not maintain. If the order of insertion is important to you, always prefer List. The Set does not maintain the order of insertion by default. If you are looking for the order of insertion within the Set implementations, then you need to go for the LinkedHashSet. The third difference between List and Set is, List allows for positional access to elements, which means we have 1000 elements inside your List.

You should be able to easily pick 200 element or 300 element, or 250 element without any performance issues, because we know by default List is going to maintain the elements in an sequential memory. Locations coming to the Set, Set does not going to provide the positional access. Instead, you can quickly check if an element is present inside a Set or not with the help of contains() method. Off course, List also have contains() method, but whenever you are using contains method on top of a List object, it is going to iterate all the elements one by one, whereas in the scenario of Set it is going to be very quick.

It is going to calculate the hash code of your element and pick the corresponding bucket number inside the HashMap, and straight away will return you whether a given element is present or not. Moving on to the next difference list generally have better performance than sets for positional access. This is because List use an index to access the elements, which is faster than checking every element in a Set for membership. This means if you are looking for an option to randomly access the elements with the help of index, always prefer list because they are going to have better performance, whereas on the other side sets they are going to have better performance than List for testing the membership.

When I say membership, we can test whether a given element is present inside a Set object or not with the help of contains() method. In summary, always prefer using List when you need to maintain duplicates and preserve the order of insertion, whereas you can prefer Set whenever you need to ensure uniqueness or test for membership of an element very quickly. I hope this is clear to you. We finally did it guys! We are done with the collection framework discussion.

We had a very good discussion around the List, Map and Set and generics as well. I know this is a very big concept, but I'm very happy with the progress that we made. With this, we can conclude the discussion around the collection framework and move on to the other important Java concept. But here you may have a question which is, hey Madan there are good amount of other data structures as well inside Java collection framework like Queue, Deque, Stack.

I agree with you, but I just wanted to highlight those are not commonly used by the developers on day to day job. That's why I'm not going to put efforts around those least used data structures. But if there is a requirement comes inside your real projects to use one of those least used data structures. I'm sure with all the knowledge that we have gained throughout this course, you'll be able to explore those data structures, their documentation, their methods, and easily able to use them inside your projects.

I hope you agree with me. We are going to revisit the collections framework one more time when we are discussing about the functional programming, I'm keep telling throughout the course there is a beautiful concept of functional programming. Using the functional programming, we can make our collections framework even more powerful. With very less code we can try to achieve lot. So that's a power of streams and functional programming inside Java.

So hold your thoughts around this. When we start discussing about the functional programming, you are going to become a fan of it, and I would strongly recommend you to use the same inside your real projects as well. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next section, bye.

Instead, printing an urgent or high or medium or low, it is going to make more sense to achieve the same. Then we need to change the contents of these constants, which will bring other problems to handle by the developer.

As of now, as a developer, I know low should be before the medium, and medium should be before the high and the high should be before the urgent. lectures.title: Advantages of Enums
lectures.text:
By this time, it should be pretty clear for you that enums are the clear winner compared to the traditional Java constants. Inside this lecture, let's try to discuss about the advantages of enums so that it is going to help you inside your Java interviews. Because inside Java interviews, many times people may ask you, why should we use enums when we can achieve the same job with the help of Java constants? That's why let's try to understand the advantages one by one, the very first, and a major advantage that we are going to get with the help of enums is type safety.

Enums provide type safety by allowing developers to define a fixed set of named values. So this will stop other developers to use invalid values or wrong data types as an input to the business logic, like we saw in the previous lectures demo. Whenever we are using enum as an input parameter, other developers, they will be able to invoke my method only if they are passing a valid value of enum. The second advantage is around the readability. Enum makes our code more readable by providing a clear and concise way to represent a fixed set of related constants.

I saw many projects in my career where they are not using enums. What they are going to do is, they are going to put thousands of constants inside a single Java file, and it is going to make developers life tough. Whenever someone is looking for a particular scenario constant, they need to end up searching that entire file. And sometimes they may have constants with very similar names as well. Whereas with enums we can build multiple enum data types which are going to hold the constants based upon a particular scenario.

For example, if someone is looking for the constants which are related to the task priority, they can find all the constants related to the task priority inside the PriorityEnum class. As a standard, we know developers they are not going to maintain other scenario constants inside the PriorityEnum class. So that's why using enums is always going to improve the readability of your code. The next advantage is around the robustness enums. They are going to make your code more robust by providing a centralized and consistent way to handle a set of related constants.

If the help of enums, we are going to make our life easy to modify the code in future without introducing bugs. So whenever I want to introduce a new constant, or whenever I want to change a value of my constant or date of my enum constant, the change is always going to be in a single place. We don't have to worry about compiling the multiple dependent files. After robustness, we have the advantage around the code organization. Like we discussed previously.

With the help of enums, we can group related constants together in a particular file. In all the previous lecture, we have created so many enum classes one to store the priority related constants, other to store the day related constants, and the other one related to the size related constants. So whenever you are following enums, you will end up organizing your code and constants based upon your scenario. And the last advantage is around the switch statements we saw in the previous lectures how easily we can use the enums along with the switch statements or switch expressions.

By combining both enum and switch blocks, we can write business logic to handle a set of related cases. So these are the advantages on using the enums. So my humble request always is to implement the constant logic with the help of enums wherever possible. I hope this makes sense to you. And now you have a good understanding around the enum concept. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.
