lectures.title: TimeZone specific Date and Time
lectures.text:
As of now, in the examples that we have discussed so far around the date and time, the value of date and time is getting created based upon the default time zone where I am trying to execute my Java program. Since I am trying to execute my Java program from India, the time zone of India is getting considered in the date and time values that are getting created. But in real projects, we will have specific requirements to create the date and time based upon a different time zone.

To handle those kind of scenarios, you need to understand how to create date and time based upon a given time zone. So what is a time zone throughout the world all the countries they are going to have different, different times. Not every country is going to have morning at the same time and night at the same time. So based upon how the earth is rotating, the time is going to vary from country to country to make our lives easy long back these time zones are introduced in order to use these time zones.

First you need to understand what are the time zones supported by these legacy date API. In order to show you the list of time zones supported by the Legacy Date API, I am going to write a small program with the Java class name as TimeZoneIDsList. So these are class name. Inside this class, I need to create the main() method post that using the class which is time zone. This class is present inside the java.util package. Inside this class we have a static method which is get available IDs.

So I'm trying to invoke the same. So this is going to give all the available time zones in a String array format. That's why on the left hand side I need to catch the output with the help of String array and the variable name as timeZoneIds. Now this array content I'm going to display with the help of our age. So let me first create a temporary variable name which is String timeZoneId. And after the colon I'm going to mention timeZoneIds which is my array variable.

Inside this for each loop, I'm going to print out each timeZoneId during each iteration. So if I execute this program, you'll be able to see there are lot many timeZones that are supported by Legacy Date API. So if you are looking for the time right now in the US eastern, you can use this time zone. Similarly US specific UTC Turkey time. So there are so many time zones available which you can use based upon the country that you are interested to get the time.

I hope you are clear with this logic that I have written now using these time zone values, we can try to create a date and time by providing that time zone details. So first I'm going to show you how to create a time zone specific date and time with the help of java.util.Date. So let me create a class with the name TimeZoneDatesDemo. Inside this class I'm going to first create a main() method followed by first I need to create the object of SimpleDateFormat.

What I can do is, instead of typing, I can copy some code from the CalendarDemo class. So let me copy these code and paste it inside the TimeZoneDatesDemo. So here you can see I just created an Object of DateFormat by providing a format detail post that using the same DateFormat object, I need to invoke the method setTimeZone(). To this setTimeZone() method, we need to pass the object of TimeZone. So to create that TimeZone object, first we need to invoke that TimeZone class followed by we need to invoke the getTimeZone() method.

And to this method I'm trying to pass a timeZone value, which is America/New_York. So these time zone is already available inside my list that I have printed here. You can see using this, I can try to get the what is a current date and time in the new year. Please make sure you are passing one of these values only to the getTimeZone() method. Otherwise things won't work like you expect. Now I have said that TimeZone details to my DateFormat object.

Now using the same DateFormat object, I need to invoke the format() method, and to this format() method I need to pass the object of Date. So if I invoke new date here, it means I'm trying to pass the currentDate and time as an input to this format() method. So on the left hand side I can try to catch the output with the help of String variable with the name formattedDate. So let me try to print out these value present inside the formattedDate. So if I execute this program, I'll be able to see what is the time right now in New York.

So right now the time is 7:39:35 seconds Am. I can also show you by mentioning some other TimeZone details here. So let me execute this program and pick randomly one of the time zone. Maybe this time I'll try to take some country maybe I'll take these Europe/Vatican. So let me mention the same here or maybe instead of replacing, what I can do is I'll try to copy this code one more time and paste it here and copy this Europe, Vatican in the place of America, New York.

And with that I can remove this String. And that content of the formatted date is going to be overwritten. And now I'm trying to print formatted date again. So if I execute this program you'll be able to see right now in New York this is the time which is 7:45 a.m., whereas in Vatican it is afternoon 13:41:06 seconds. So this way you can always get the date and time based upon a given time zone. So the process to get that time zone specific date and time with the help of Date object is very complex.

First, you need to create the SimpleDateFormat object post that you need to set the time zone followed by you need to invoke the format() method by passing the current date time value. So these are very length approach. But if you try to use the GregorianCalendar approach, it is going to be super simple. You just have to first create the object of GregorianCalendar as usual with the help of default constructor. Once you have written this code to the constructor of GregorianCalendar, you can pass the time zone details by invoking the getTimeZone() method, and to these geTimeZone() method.

I'm trying to pass America/New_York, so whenever you have a requirement to create an object of TimeZone, you need to invoke the static method available inside the TimeZone class. To this getTimeZone(), you need to mention what is the time zone for which you are trying to get the Date and Time. So now, inside this GregorianCalendar, the current date and time of New York is going to be present.

Now let me show you the demo on the date and time details created with the help of these GregorianCalendar. So if I execute this program you'll be able to see that right now in New York the time is 7:44:54 seconds and this is the milliseconds as well. If I try to print out the same onto the console, surprisingly you will not see the New York time. You will see the highest time. That's because whenever this getTime() method is invoked behind the scenes, a new Date object is going to be created. And when this object is getting created, it is going to construct the default time zone where the program is running.

In my scenario, it is highest if you want to get the same time zone like in the GregorianCalendar, then you need to follow all these steps like. First you need to create the SimpleDateFormat object pose that you need to set the time zone using the same DateFormat object. You need to invoke the format() method to the same you need to send you a Date object. Then only your Date object is going to have your desired time zone details. Otherwise it is going to carry the default time zone details.

Whereas if you try to read the data individually, with the help of this get() method, you will be able to get the time based upon the time zone that you have provided to this GregorianCalendar() constructor. If you see on a high level with the introduction of Calendar related classes, certain limitations of date are resolved. Like we can directly pass the year, we can use the month constants. There are lot many utility methods and useful methods inside the Calendar, so to some extent the Java team, they try to resolve the issues with the java.util.Date class.

But still, even with the Calendar also there are some design flaws like there is no way for us to store the date and time separately. On top of that, dealing with the time zones is also complex with the help of Date and Calendar. And in fact, this Calendar created more confusion to few developers. That's why many of the developers still they are using java.util.Date. So no worries we have new Date-Time API to our rescue. When we discuss about the new Date-Time API, you're going to see the beauty of the new API, how it is solving all these limitations and complexities.

I hope you are clear with all the discussion that we have done around the Calendar so far. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: [JAVA 8] Introduction to new Date & Time API from Java 8
lectures.text:
I know you might have been scratching your head when this fellow is going to talk about the new Date-Time API. The waiting is finally over. From this lecture we are going to completely focus on new Date-Time API. Inside this lecture, let me give an high level overview and introduction to the new Date-Time API that is introduced as part of Java 8. With all the limitations that Legacy Date API used to have, most of the Java developers they started using lot many third party date and time libraries such as Joda time.

So there is a third party API or library, which is developed by other open source developers with the name Joda Time. This Joda time library it has lot many features compared to the legacy date time API. To overcome all the challenges of legacy Date-Time API. Most of the developers they used to use these Joda time API, which is from third party. So with all these reasons, Java team finally decided to introduce a high quality date and time support within the Java library itself.

As a result, as part of Java 8, a new date time API released under the package java.time inside java.time package and all its sub packages. There are many interfaces, classes, enums. We can't discuss all of them, but I'm going to discuss most commonly used or most important interfaces and classes and enums, which you may need on your day to day work. Like you can see here under that java.time package, we have these important classes with the name LocalDate, LocalDateTime, LocalTime, ZonedDateTime.

OffsetDateTime. Instant, Duration, Period. Similarly, we also have enums with the name DayOfWeek and Month. We are going to discuss about all these classes. Then it is going to make sense to you. Under the java.time package we also have a sub package with the name temporal. Under this temporal package we have so many classes related to temporal with the name like Temporal, TemporalAccessor, TemporalAdjuster and TemporalQuery. And we also have enums like ChronoField and ChronoUnit coming to the formatting of date and time.

In the legacy Date-Time API, we have a class with the name SimpleDateTimeFormat in the similar lines in the new Date Time API as well, we have a class with the name DateTimeFormatter, which is going to help us to format our Date and Time objects. This is present inside a sub package with the name java.time.format. So anytime if you see a class interface or enum under the package java.time or under its sub package, you can simply assume it belongs to the new Date-Time API.

Let's start the discussion of new Date-Time API by trying to understand how to represent Date, Time and TimeZone details with the help of these new Date-Time API. Inside these new Date-Time API, we have a class with the name LocalDate, which is going to useful to strictly represent a Date. There won't be any time involved. If you are looking to store only date, you can simply use these LocalDate to create the Date object. After LocalDate, we have a LocalTime which is going to help us to represent only a time without a date value.

Sometimes you may have a business requirement just to store time of a day without worrying about the dates. In all those kind of scenarios, you can create the object of LocalTime, but if you want a combination of both date and time, you have a class with the name LocalDateTime which is capable of storing the date time details but not the time zone. If you are worrying about the time zone as well, then you have an option in the form of ZonedDateTime.

So with the help of ZonedDateTime class, we can create objects that are capable of storing Date, Time along with the TimeZone. So did you see the beauty here of the new date time API? You have a complete flexibility to choose from what you want. You are simply looking to store only time. Go for the LocalTime if you are looking for the date and time along with the time zone, go for the ZonedDateTime. And the naming convention of these classes also is selected very cleverly.

So whenever someone is talking about LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, they're trying to refer what is the time in your local area. But if someone is looking for the Date and Time based upon a zone or based upon a TimeZone, then they can safely use these ZonedDateTime. It also has the word zoned to convey the purpose of it. So if you try to visualize these four classes, this is how it is going to look like. We know each date and time. It is going to have three different parameters.

lectures.text:
As of now, when we're trying to store that date and time details, we are trying to create the objects of LocalDateTime and ZonedDateTime. But apart from these classes, we also have other class with the name Instant. Using these Instant also, we should be able to create the objects that are capable of storing date and time value. Inside this lecture, let's try to understand more details about this Instance class and under which scenarios we need to use them and how it is different compared to the other classes that we have discussed so far.

We as humans, we use date and time values, but for machines, the time is calculated based upon number of seconds passed from the Unix epoch time. What is the epoch time? The epoch time inside computer is represented by the time which is midnight of January 1st, 1970 UTC. If you try to look at these representation, this zero represents the epoch time, which is the midnight of January first, 1970 UTC. After this epoch time, we have various numbers like 1, 2, 3, 4.

For each of these numbers, they represent the number of nanoseconds passed from the epoch time. So if you try to travel on to the right hand side, all the nanosecond numbers will be positive. Whereas if you try to travel on to the left hand side, which is before the epoch time, all the numbers, they are going to be represented with the help of negative numbers like you can see here. Each of these numbers inside the timeline, they are representing an instant time from the epoch time.

If you take these eight, this is an instant time which represents that eight nanoseconds completed from these epoch time. Inside Java whenever we want to create an object representing these instant time, we can use the Instant class available inside the new Date-Time API. And apart from Instant, we also have Duration class. So what is a Duration? Duration is used to identify the duration of time between two instances. For example between these 3 and 11 if I try to identify the duration, it is going to be 8 nanoseconds.

So whenever we want to represent the duration between two time instance or between two dates, or between two times, in all such scenarios, we can use the Duration object. Inside this Duration object, the difference between two time instances they are going to be stored in terms of hours, minutes, seconds, and nanoseconds. When we see the demo about these Instant and Duration, it is going to make more sense to you. For now, let's try to understand more details about these classes.

This Instant class it is often used for low level operations where precise timestamps are required, such as logging or measuring elapsed time. For example, think like you're trying to calculate the duration between two different events occurred inside your application. In all these kind of scenarios, you are going to create two different instant object representing the start of the event and the end of the event, and the duration between them can be calculated with the help of Duration class.

Here at the end of the slide, I also highlighted all the points that we have discussed. I tried to explain about this timeline and how it is work with the help of these two points here. With this now you may have a question running behind the scenes, which is what is the difference between instant and the LocalDateTime or ZonedDateTime. So let's try to understand the same. We know both Instant, LocalDateTime and ZoneDateTime. They all can be used to represent date and time values inside Java, but they have a fundamental differences in how they work internally.

Here I'm trying to compare between Instant and LocalDateTime. So the same comparison is also applicable for Instant and ZoneDateTime as well. So the very first difference is whenever you are trying to represent a time with the help of Instant, it is going to represent a specific moment in time from the epoch time. Whereas if you try to represent a date and time with the help of LocalDate time behind the scenes, the date and time values are going to be stored without the time zone details.

Whereas if we use ZoneDateTime, even the time zone details are also going to be stored. Coming to the internal representation internally, all the Instant objects, they are going to be represented with the help of seconds and nanoseconds since Unix epoch time, whereas inside the LocalDateTime or ZoneDateTime, all the date and time details are represented with the help of year, month, day, hour, minute and second. And the third difference is instant is independent of time zone.

Instant is not going to worry about time zone. It is only going to worry how many nanoseconds or seconds passed from the Unix epoch time, whereas the LocalDateTime, though it is not going to contain any time zone information. But behind the scenes it is going to consider your local time zone to create that date and time value. If I try to invoke the now() method present inside the LocalDateTime, it is going to give me the current date and time based upon the time zone where I am executing the code. And at last we have use cases you should consider using the instant whenever you are very serious about representing your time with the help of Timestamps, Durations, TimeZone, IndependentTime.

In all those scenarios, you can use the instant. Coming to the LocalDateTime and ZonedDateTime you can use them whenever you want to display the dates and time in an user friendly manner. I also provided more details when to use which class, so you can use Instance when you need to represent a specific point in time, regardless of location or time zone. So this is ideal for Timestamps, Durations and Calculations, whereas LocalDateTime you need to use when you display the dates and times to user in their local time zone or when the specific moment itself is not critical.

I hope you are clear with this initial introduction around the Instant and Duration. In the next lecture, I am going to show you the demo of these classes so that it's going to be more clear for you. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: [JAVA 8] The truncatedTo() method
lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, we're going to discuss about the truncatedTo() method that we can use on top of a Duration object. To show you the demo, let me create a new Java class with the name TruncatedToMethodDemo. Inside this class first, let me create a main() method post that I'm going to create a Duration object with some random duration, so I'll just type Duration.ofDays(). So to this I'm trying to pass 28 days, followed by I'm going to add hours to the days with the help of plusHours(), to this plusHours() method I'm trying to pass 6 post that I'm going to also add minutes with the help of plusMinutes(), to this plusMinutes(), I'm going to send the 56 minutes as an input, followed by I'm also going to invoke plusSeconds() method.

And to this method I'm providing 19 seconds. So with this I'm trying to create a duration of total 28 days, six hours, 56 minutes, 19 seconds. But we know behind the scenes duration is never going to store that duration in a form of days. It is always going to store with the units of hours, minutes and seconds. That's why if I try to see the content of this Duration object at runtime, you'll be able to see the duration as six 78 hours, 56 minutes, 19 seconds.

I can copy this value the same I'll try to mention for your reference here. Just after this line inside the comments, I'm trying to mention the duration value. So how these two 78 hours came. So behind the scenes it is going to multiply 24 hours to these 28 days. And we are going to get the output as 672, to the same 672 hours it is also trying to add six hours. So that's why we are getting 678 hours followed by 56 minutes 19 seconds. Now think like I want to truncate these duration to the number of days, which means I don't want to carry the number of hours and seconds which are beyond the exact number of days.

So in all such scenarios, I can happily use that truncatedTo() method. So with the help of Duration object, I'm trying to invoke the truncatedTo() method. To this truncatedTo() method, we need to pass the TemporalUnit as an input. So what is this TemporalUnit? It is an interface inside the new Date-Time API which represents a unit of date and time. So there is an implementation enum for these interface with the name ChronoUnit. So you can see inside this ChronoUnit we have so many enum constants like NANOS, MICROS, MILLIS, SECONDS, MINUTES, HOURS, HALF_DAYS, DAYS, WEEKS, MONTHS, YEARS, DECADES, CENTURIES, MILLENIA, ERAS, FOREVER.

So these are all the enum constants that we have inside this class. So we need to pass days as an input. Whenever you are trying to truncate your duration to days. So that's why here to this method I'm going to pass the enum constant of ChronoUnit, which is DAYS. With that, all the extra hours, minutes and seconds they are going to be truncated. So let me catch the output inside the variable which is daysTruncated. If I try to see what is present inside these daysTruncated at runtime, you can see I have 672 hours, so the extra 6 hours and 56 minutes 19 seconds they are truncated because these 672 hours will result into the exact number of days, which is 28 days.

So all the extra hours, minutes and seconds beyond a given number of days they are going to be truncated. So here I'm going to get the output as PT672H. We can also truncate hours and minutes as well. So here instead of days if I try to mention hours, then all the minutes and seconds they are going to be truncated. With that we are going to get the output as 678H. So this minutes like 56M 19 seconds, they are going to be truncated, followed by if we pass the constant as minutes, we are going to get the output as 678H56M.

So the seconds they are going to be truncated. So let me change this variable names to hours truncated. Later on I'll mention minutes truncated, if I try to observe these values at runtime you can see we have 678 hours under the hours truncated variable and 678 hours 56 minutes as an value inside these minutes truncated. So based upon your constant that you are trying to pass, the duration is going to be truncated. So especially these truncated methods, they are going to be useful when you want to ignore some duration especially seconds minutes, hours.

One important point that you need to be aware whenever you are using this truncatedTo(). Please make sure you are only using the variables like day, hours, minutes, seconds, and below constants only. Don't try to be smart and use constants like weeks, because we know duration is never going to store the week's information. So if you try to use invalid constants, we are going to get a runtime exception saying that unit is too large to be used for truncation.

So that's why always use a constants like days, hours, minutes, seconds are any smaller constants. These truncatedTo() method is not available inside Period, because we know with the help of Period we represent the differences between dates, and there is no meaning to truncate such a larger values. So that's why truncated is not supported inside the Period. But you should be able to identify similar truncated methods inside the LocalTime class. So inside this class, if you type for truncatedTo(), you have the same kind of method.

Similarly, inside the Instant class also you have this method with with the name truncatedTo(), so please feel free to use them based upon your requirements. If I start discussing all the methods and all the features supported by the new Date-Time API, it will easily take months and months of time. That's why my humble request is to practice more and more around these new Date-Time API. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: [JAVA 8] Non-ISO Calendars in java.time Date and Time API
lectures.text:
The beauty of new Date-Time API is it covered all the possible scenarios around the Date and Time. We know most of the countries in the world they follow the GregorianCalendar. In other words, we can call this GregorianCalendar as ISO calendar or English calendar, but apart from ISO or GregorianCalendar, we have other types of non ISO calendars as well exist in few countries. Such calendars are Thai Buddhist calendar, which is going to be followed inside Thailand.

Hijra calendar which is going to be followed by the Islamic countries. Minguo calendar, which is followed inside the China and Japanese calendar, which is followed inside the Japan. Please pardon me if I pronounce these calendar names incorrectly. The point that I'm trying to highlight here is, the new date Time API that introduced in Java 8. It also supports other types of calendars, which are used only in specific regions. All these kind of calendars we can call as non ISO calendars.

For example, think like you are working for an organization which operates inside Japan. Obviously, if they want to localize their content to the Japan people, sometimes they may have to display that date based upon that Japan calendar. With the legacy Date-Time API, we don't have any option to identify what is the equivalent date for the Japan calendar based upon a given English calendar date, but with the new date time API, it is going to be super fun and easy.

Here you can see I'm trying to use a class with the name JapaneseDate. Using this class, if I invoke the now() method, it is going to give me that today's date based upon the Japan calendar. Whereas if we use our LocalDate.now() it is going to give that today's date based upon the GregorianCalendar or based upon the English calendar. Apart from simply creating the non ISO calendar objects, we can also convert a non ISO date to ISO date and vice versa.

Here you can see with this from() method which is available inside the JapaneseDate. I'm trying to convert my ISO date or English date to an equivalent JapaneseDate. So these ISO now object I'm trying to pass as an input here. Similarly inside the LocalDate class also we have a from() method to this you can pass any calendar object like JapaneseDate class object. If you pass this as an input, it is going to give you the equivalent to date as per the GregorianCalendar or as per the English calendar. For each of the non ISO calendar systems available inside the new date time API.

Usually there will be two pair of classes. So these classes they are going to present inside the package java.time.chrono one class it is going to have a suffix which is chronology. For example, if you take the Hijra calendar, there is a class with the name HijraChronology. So all these chronology classes, they are going to have the set of rules and characteristics belongs to the particular calendar. Whereas using the other class we can represent the date object which belongs to a particular calendar.

Such classes are HijraDate, JapaneseDate. So you're going to have a prefix, which is the calendar name followed by date. I hope you are clear with this quick introduction. Let's see the demo of Japanese calendar so that it is going to be make more sense to you. Inside my package, I'm going to create a new Java class with the name JapaneseCalendarDemo. Similarly, if I try to use the LocalDate, I'm going to get the current date and time based upon the ISO calendar or the GregorianCalendar. So if I try to put a breakpoint here, you'll be able to see in local date today date is February 11th, 2024. But if you see inside the Japanese day today's date, here is some 602-11.

I'm assuming someone who is from Japan it is making more sense to them. So this way you can always create current date and time for any calendar system that is supported by the new Date-Time API. And like we discussed, if needed, we can also convert one calendar date into the other calendar date. So here, with the help of JapaneseDate class, I'm trying to invoke the from() method and to this from() method, I am passing the object of LocalDate, and with that we're going to get the object of JapaneseDate as an output, which I I'm going to catch with the variable name as japaneseDate1.

Similarly, using the LocalDate class as well, we can invoke the from() method and to this from() method we can pass the object of JapaneseDate, and on the left hand side we can catch the output with the help of LocalDate object with the variable name as localDate1. So if I execute this program, you will be able to see and a localDate1. The date is 2024 February 11th, whereas under the japaneseDate1 this is the value that it holds. So this kind of conversion from one calendar to other calendar is also possible.

So if you can open these JapaneseDate class, it is available inside the Java.time.chrono package. Similarly we have other kind of calendars like HijrahDate. So here we have a class with the name type. With this date and MinguoDate also is available, which is going to be used inside China. So please refer to these classes whenever you have a requirement to build the date and time based upon a specific non-iso calendar system. I hope this makes sense to you.

Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

In the history of human mankind, we saw many paradigm shifts. So let's try to understand what is a paradigm shift. A paradigm shift is defined as an important change that happens when the usual way of thinking about or doing something is replaced by a new and different way. I hope this definition makes sense to you. Otherwise don't worry, I'm there for you. I'll give an example to understand about what is a paradigm shift. Long back we as humans we used horse and the carts for the transporting.

If someone want to move from one place to other place. We used to use horses as a mode of transport, but later on in New Paradigm Shift came into picture like steam engine or the petrol engine or the diesel engine. With all these paradigm shift inventions, we as humans started using the vehicles like car, bus, train. But these mode of transports are also not enough for our needs. That's why a new paradigm shift came into picture with the invention of aeroplanes.

So with the aeroplanes were able to travel from one place to other place very fastly. So if you take transport as a field, there are multiple paradigm shifts introduced throughout the mankind history. Similarly, inside every field this kind of paradigm shifts you will be able to see. So why I'm talking about these paradigm shifts right now. The reason why I'm trying to refer paradigm shifts is just like how there are some disruptions introduced inside the transport field, very similarly inside Java programming language as well.

There is a disruption or there is a paradigm shift introduced as part of the Java 8. So from Java 8 a new style of programming is introduced. So this style we call it as functional programming which we can build by using the lambda expressions. Let's try to understand more details about these functional programming. lectures.title: Deep dive on Lexical Scoping of Lambda expressions
lectures.text:
As of now we started writing lot of lambda expressions inside the existing Java methods like main() method. So whenever you are trying to define a lot of lambda expressions inside the Java methods, sometimes you may end up using the same variable names inside your lambda expression and inside your Java method. And with that, you may receive a lot of compilation errors. To resolve these kind of compilation issues. First, you need to understand how the variable scope is going to work inside the lambda expression.

So let's try to understand more details about scoping concept inside the lambda expressions. Like we know there is a similarity between the lambda expression and the method declarations like they both accept the input parameter and they both are going to have body which can be written inside the curly braces. They are going to have return type. So there are a lot of similarities between lambda expression and the method declaration that we need to accept first.

But with these understanding, don't be under the assumption that the scoping is going to work very similarly inside the normal methods and the lambda expressions. The very first thumb rule that you need to be aware is, whenever you are defining a lambda expression, it is not going to create its own scope. Instead, it is going to work within the scope of the enclosing context. When I say the enclosing context, it is the enclosing Java method where you are trying to define your lambda expression.

So this characteristics is referred as lexical scoping inside lambda expressions concept. Let me show you the demo on how the scoping is going to work with the lambda expressions. For the same, I'll go to intelliJ. Inside my IntelliJ, first, I'm going to create my own functional interface with the name Printer. So this is an interface. That's why I need to select the interface option followed by I'm going to mention the annotation which is @FunctionalInterface, followed by I'm going to define a single abstract method inside these interface.

So the method is going to be void print and it is going to accept an input parameter of type String with the variable name as input. So this is my function interface. Now using this function interface I want to show you the lexical scoping of lambda expressions for the same let me create a new Java class with the name LexicalScopeTest. So these are class. Let me create it and post that I'm going to create the main() method inside the main() method first I'm going to create a variable with the name input and to this variable I'm going to assign a String object which is hello world.

Now I'm going to create the lambda expression with the help of Printer functional interface. So let me type input followed by lambda symbol followed by System.out.println(). Followed by to this println() method I'm going to pass the same variable which is input. So if you see here I'm getting a compilation error because variable input is already defined in the scope. So right now we have created these lambda expression inside these main() method.

So the scope of this method is going to be shared by these lambda expression. It is not going to have its own scope, since the same scope is going to be accepted by this lambda expression. And getting this compilation error, because there is already a variable defined with the same name input. So if I update these two, input1 to a different parameter name, and if I use the same, I'm not going to get any compilation error. So now using this Printer.print() method I'm going to pass String object as an input.

So here I have a String object with the name input. So if I execute this program you can see I'm going to get the hello world as an output. So this is one rule that you need to be aware. Don't ever try to use the same variable names that you have declared inside the method as the input parameter names for your lambda expression. But if the String input is present after my lambda expression, I'm not going to get any problem. So these whatever parameter name that you have defined here like input, this is going to be specific to my lambda expression.

And it is not going to be affect other method scope. So that's why I'm able to happily create a variable with the same name input. And still I'm not getting any compilation error. So if I execute this program you can see I'm getting the proper output this time. Let me show you another interesting scenario to show you this scenario. First, let me move back the String input to the first line. With that we are going to get a compilation error. Let me change this variable name to input one in both the places inside my lambda expression.

Now think like I have a requirement to write some good amount of business logic inside my lambda expression. That's why I'm trying to use curly braces to write a body inside my lambda expression. So as of now I have a single statement but think like for these System.out.println(). I want to change the content of input variable which we have declared inside the method. So to this input variable I'm trying to assign a new value which is high. So if you see here I'm getting a compilation error saying that variable used inside lambda expression should be final or effective final.

That means whenever my lambda expression is trying to use the variables that I have declared outside my lambda expression this variable, it is going to act as a implicitly final. Regardless, I am trying to mention final or not inside the variable declaration. Still, this variable whose scope is being shared with the lambda expression, it is going to act as a implicitly final. Do you know why we have this restriction inside Java? It's pretty clear.

Think like once you have created this lambda expression, you're trying to pass this behavior to multiple other methods and each of the other methods, if they are trying to assign different, different values to these input at some point of time, especially inside the multithreading environment, you're going to get unexpected results, because each execution of your lambda expression is trying to have different, different values. And with that, you are going to corrupt the original value which you have defined here.

That's why this limitation is enforced whenever we are dealing with the lambda expressions. We will not be able to change the content of the variables that we have declared outside of the lambda expression, but I should be able to use them without any issues. So here, instead of input one, I can mention input1 + input So the input is defined outside. So if I execute this program you'll be able to see that I'm getting Hello World Hello world two times I hope this makes sense to you.

Now as a next step let me show you another interesting scenario. Think like I have declared this input with this content later on in the next line itself, I'm trying to assign a different value which is high. So these kind of variables where you are trying to assign multiple values inside your method scope. So such variables, you can't use them inside your lambda expressions. The reason is this variable is never going to act as a implicitly final, because first you assign this value later on, you're trying to change with a different value.

So since this variable is never going to act as a implicitly final, we are not allowed to use these input variable inside my lambda expression. That's why I'm getting a compilation error here. So the compilation error says variable used in lambda expression should be final or effective final. I hope this makes sense. So to resolve this compilation error, we need to make sure we are initializing the variables only once, otherwise we can't use them inside your lambda expression.

With this discussion you may have a question which is can I create my own local variables inside the lambda() method? So this can be your question. You can create them without any issues. There is no restriction. You can create any number of local variables inside your lambda expression. For example, inside my lambda expression, I'm going to create a local variable with the name msg. And to this I'm going to assign a content which is high. So the same msg I can try to append to the inpu1, input like you can see here.

So if I execute this program this time you can see I'm going to get the output Hello world, Hi. So this way always feel free to create any number of local variables inside your lambda expression. But these local variables you will not be able to access them outside your lambda() method. So here if I try to access MSG, you can see I'm getting a compilation error saying that cannot resolve symbol msg. I hope you are clear around the lexical scoping the examples that we have discussed inside this lecture.

I have mentioned them in this slide for your reference, please refer them for any questions. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

lectures.title: Funny memes around Functional Programming
lectures.text:
Now is the time to have some fun. As of now, we discussed basics around the functional programming, and we have a very good understanding around the lambda expressions and how to build them. Let's take a break from the serious discussion and have some fun by looking at the funny memes around the lambda expressions and the functional programming. So these are very first meme. I want to show it to you, though it is not related to functional programming or lambda expression, this is the feeling that you are going to get whenever you are trying to learn a programming language.

It can be Java or it can be JavaScript, Python. Regardless of what programming language you are trying to learn, you will always think like there is only a little bit more to learn and master a programming language, but that's not going to be the story. In real scenario the programming languages, they are always going to get updated with the new features, based upon the new trends and the demands from the developer community. We also saw one such example, which is functional programming.

It is such a big feature. Understanding it and learning it itself will take hours and days of time. So that's why never be under the impression that you're going to master a particular programming language by completing a course or by reading a book. It is a continuous process that you need to keep yourself up to date with the new features that are getting introduced inside each version that is going to be released. The next meme that we have is around the functional programming.

You can see here there is a developer who is using Java 1.6 or 1.7. Welcome to the new section. Inside this section we are going to focus on a new concept called Method References. Method references are also introduced as part of Java 8 as a supporting component to build the lambda expressions. Before I try to explain you about method references, first let me explain you the problem that method reference is going to solve. Sometimes there might be already a method defined in a class which has some business logic, and you want to build the same kind of business logic with the help of lambda expression.

So that's perfectly possible because lambda expressions are introduced only from Java 8. Before Java 8, everyone they used to define their business logic with the help of Java methods. So there is a good chance that there is a good possibility that a particular business logic might be already present in an existing Java method. So in this kind of scenario, you might be thinking that there is no option to leverage the existing Java method. We just have to rewrite the entire business logic with the help of lambda expression by duplicating all the code again.

So this can be your initial assumption or initial thought. But my friend Java team, when they released functional programming and its associated new features inside Java 8, they know that these problem may come into picture. That's why they came up with a new feature called Method Reference from Java 8. So what are these Method References ? Method References are a special type of lambda expression, which we can build by referring to the existing methods.

I know you may have too many questions right now. Don't worry when we start discussing in detail about these method references in the coming lectures, it is going to be super clear for you. For now, let's try to understand what are the different types of method references available and what is the syntax that we need to follow. Like you can see here, there are four types of method references introduce as part of Java 8. The very first one is static method reference.

The syntax is first you need to mention the class name, followed by two colons. So you can see you need to mention two colons, not a single one. There is no need of mentioning the parentheses after the method name, and there is also no need of mentioning the details about your input parameters. So this third type of method reference it is going to handle some special scenarios. We're going to discuss about the special scenario in the coming lectures in detail.

So whenever you are trying to use these third type of method reference, you need to mention what is your class name followed by two colons. And after the two colons, you need to mention your instanceMethod and at last we have constructor reference. The syntax for these constructor reference is, you need to mention what is your class name followed by two colons. And after these two colons you need to mention new operator name, which is new itself.

So after new also you can see there is no need of mentioning any parentheses. I hope you are clear with this syntax. As you might have observed, Java has introduced a new operator which is double colon. So this new operator, in other words we can call it as Method Reference Delimiter. So in future whenever you see a Java code with two colons, you can safely assume that particular code is built with the concept of Method References. I hope you're clear with this discussion.

Please note that you can use the method references concept only in the scenarios when you are trying to build a lambda expression, by using the business logic present inside another Java method. I hope you are clear with the agenda of this section. In the next lecture, let's try to discuss in detail about these staticMethod reference. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: DETAILS OF SOURCE CODE AND PDF CONTENT
Introduction to java.util.stream API
lectures.text:
Inside this new section, we are going to focus on streams API that are introduced as part of the Functional Programming in Java 8 release. As of now, we have very good understanding around the collections, how to store the elements inside collections, how to iterate them, how to process them with the help of various data structures like List, Map, Set, Tree. By using all these data structures, we know how to build a business logic. But with the knowledge that we have so far, we are building the business logic with the help of imperative approach where we are giving low level instructions to the collection framework, saying that to iterate the elements with the help of for each or for loop or iterate our while loop during the iteration.

If you have any filtering requirements, we are writing various if conditions or if you want to build any transformation logic. We are trying to achieve everything with the help of low level instructions, but by combining streams API and lambda expressions, we should be able to process the elements inside a collection with a very less amount of code. Once you master the streams API, like I promised before, you are going to love Lambda a lot and you will be using this lambda a lot inside your code as well.

So what are streams API? When I say streams API, there are list of classes and interfaces available inside the package java.util.stream. So all the classes available inside this package, we can construct them as streams API. If you ask a non-technical person about what is a stream, he may answer saying that stream is a continuous flowing of water like in a river. Similarly, inside Java, whenever someone is saying stream, we can consider it as a flow of data, like someone can store their data or their elements inside a collection object.

Using these collection objects, we can build a stream, and from this stream the data is going to flow element by element for the processing based upon the lambda expressions that we are going to write. We are going to discuss in detail about this stream API throughout this section. So brace yourself and hold your excitement around this. Inside this lecture, let's try to understand the basic details of the streams API. Whenever someone says streams API don't get confused with the package java.io, inside java.io also, we have streams, related classes and interfaces which are going to help us to write the data or to read the data from the source like a file.

So this stream, which is available inside the java.io package, is different from the stream which is available inside the java.util. So here io indicates input and output. So that's why if someone is trying to confuse you, don't get confused. If they ask you what is the difference between these two stream related packages, simply answer them if you are referring to the streams API available inside the java.io package, they are going to help us to read or write the data to and fro from the files. Whereas the streams API which are available under the package java.util they are going to help us to process the elements inside the collection data structure objects with the help of lambda expressions.

So that should be your answer. The next important point is, like I said, with the help of collections like List, Set, we will be able to store the data physically, which belongs to a single data type, whereas with the help of streams, we will be able to process the group of objects available inside a collection. We should be able to process the elements inside a collection object without the help of stream API as well. But with that imperative, our old approach, you will end up writing lot of low level code when we start exploring these streams API in the coming lectures, you're going to understand this point in detail.

We should be able to create the streams from the collections or from arrays or from iterators. So it's not mandatory that streams API is going to work only with the collections. The streams can also be created, and the streams API can also be used on top of the arrays are iterators as well. At last I want to highlight whenever we are trying to use the streams API, we are going to write the code in a declarative way. So what is the meaning of declarative way?

Declarative way means we are going to give instructions to the Java or JRE in a more like a English language, but not like a low level instructions with the help of loops with the help of if conditions, with the help of variable names, we're not going to do all that. So this declarative approach, it is going more like a query style, as opposed to specifying how to implement an operation. With the help of imperative approach, you're going to give every detail to the JVM and how to execute your operation.

But with the help of declarative way or with the help of streams API or with the help of functional programming, you are only going to give the high level instructions in a query style are in a declarative style. I hope you are clear with these basic introduction of streams API. If something is not clear, don't worry. As usual, we are going to see a lot of demos around these API. Once we complete the demos then all these points are going to make more sense to you.

I hope you are excited about these streams API. Let's start the journey of streams API from the next lecture. Thank you, bye.

So Stream.of() is another approach that we are going to follow to create a Stream object. After this I want to explain about one of the beautiful concept inside the stream API, which is ParallelStream. We know all our modern day laptops or modern day servers. lectures.title: Demo of Streams limit() method
lectures.text:
Sometimes you may have a business requirement to process only a limited number of elements inside a collection. Maybe your collection may have millions of elements, but you want to process only the first hundred elements are first 1000 elements. In this kind of scenarios, where you want to enforce some business logic to limit the number of elements to be processed, you can use a limit() method available inside the stream API. Like you can see here, limit() method it is going to accept the number of elements inside a stream that needs to be limited, so it is not going to accept any number of lambda expression as an input, because your business requirement is only to limit certain number of elements to be processed.

So that's why if you pass the number of elements to be limited to this limit, it is going to give a new Stream object with only the limited number of elements which you can transfer them into another collection object, or which you can process them further with the another intermediate operations like filter() or map() it's up to you what you want to do. lectures.title: Introduction to Streams reduce() method
lectures.text:
From this lecture, we're going to focus on the terminal operations available inside the streams API. As of now, we know how to create a Stream object to process the elements inside it. On top of that, we also learned what are the various commonly used intermediate operations, which we can use them based upon our business requirements. So the step two, which is the intermediate operations, is always going to be optional inside a streams pipeline.

Inside this step two we can use any number of intermediate operations. But coming to the step three which is a terminal operation, this is always going to be mandatory if you want to derive the output from the elements available inside the Stream object. On top of that, we can only invoke a single terminal operation on a Stream object. We can't invoke multiple terminal operations on top of a single Stream object like intermediate operations. The reason is very obvious terminal means it is going to terminate your Stream, and it is going to give you the output based upon your instructions.

So once you terminate it, if you try to invoke one more terminal operation, it is it is not going to make any sense. That's why inside streams API, we will be able to invoke the terminal operation only once on a given Stream object. Inside this lecture, let's try to focus on one of the most commonly used terminal operation, which is reduce. So what is this reduce() method. Using these reduce() terminal operation which is also known as reduction operation or a fold operation.

We can combine all elements of a stream to generate a single value as an output. So to these reduce operation you're going to provide a lambda expression which is going to be executed on each of the element inside your stream. So this lambda expression, in other words, we can call it as a combining function, because it is going to combine the output from all the elements into a single value, and the same single value is going to be given as an output once this terminal operation is executed completely.

Example of reduce operations include computing the sum, maximum, average count, and similar aggregate operations for a stream of elements like integers, double, long. When I show you the example, it is going to make more sense to you. For now please note that using reduce() operation, we can derive a single value as an output by applying a given combining function on each element inside your Stream object. So if you try to understand how this reduce is going to work is, there are different kinds of reduce overloaded methods available inside the streams API.

But speaking about most commonly used reduce() method is, it is going to accept two types of input parameters. The very first one is what is your initial seed value followed by what is the combining function, or what is your lambda expression into a single value. So here you can see I have various numbers inside my input stream like n1, n2, n3 and n4. Using this stream, I'm going to invoke the reduce() terminal operation. To this reduce() terminal operation, I'm trying to pass what is the initial seed value along with the lambda function.

So with this what is going to happen is behind the scenes my reduce() terminal operation it is going to iterate all the elements during the first element iteration. It will take what is the initial seed value and apply the same to the n1 value based upon your lambda function given. Post that the output from these is going to be fielded as a seed to the n2 element, so this is going to keep on continue till the last element, and at last we are going to get a single value as an result.

Inside streams API there are some specialized reduce() operations that are also available like sum(), max() mean(), count(). So these are specialized reduce() operations you can use directly instead of writing your own reduce() operation. For example, if you are looking to sum all the integer elements inside a stream, then you can directly use the sum() method which is going to give you the output. And similarly, if you are looking to identify a maximum number, minimum number, and the count of the number of elements.

So in all these kind of scenarios you can use these specialized reduce() operations. Only if these specialized reduce() operations they are not able to help you in your business logic in such scenarios you can write your own reduce() operation with your own lambda expression. But please note that these specialized reduce() methods, they are not universally available for all type of streams. For example, if you want to use a sum terminal operation, you can't use it on top of the normal stream object because it is not going to make any sense adding reference type elements like two people are two employees, so that's why these kind specialized reduce() methods they are only applicable for Stream objects of type IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream.

So using these IntoStream, LongStream, DoubleStream, we can only store the elements of int, long and double, which we can add them with the help of some operation. But coming to the count() terminal operation, you can use these on top of any kind of Stream object, because at the end of the day, this count() terminal operation, it is going to give you the output by counting the number of elements available inside your Stream object. We are going to see the demo of these methods in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Finding and Matching methods in Streams
lectures.text:
Streams API has some terminal operation methods, which is going to help you to find an particular element or to match a particular element. So these methods we call them as finding and matching methods. Under this category there are five different types of terminal operations or terminal methods are available. So these methods are allMatch(), anyMatch(), noneMatch(), findAny() and findFirst(). I'm going to discuss in detail about all these methods by providing examples.

But before I try to show you the demo, let me introduce about this method on a high level. So the very first method which is allMatch(), it is going to boolean value true as an output in the scenarios, if all your elements inside your stream are matched with the predicate condition that you have provided. But coming to the anyMatch(), it is going to give the output as true even if one of the element inside your stream is matching with the predicate condition and noneMatch(), it is going to give the output as true.

If none of your elements inside your stream, they are matching with the predicate condition. And at last we have two methods which are going to help us to find an element. So findAny() will find any of the element that matches to your condition. Whereas the findFirst() method, it is going to give the first element present inside your stream that you built based upon some intermediate operation or based upon some business logic. The beauty of all these methods are they are going to work just like how we have logical and and logical or operations.

What do I mean by they're going to work very similar to short circuiting operations. We have certain short circuiting operations like Logical AND and Logical OR when we are discussing about these logical operators. I told you that when you are trying to apply and operator based upon two different operands, if the first operand gives the output as false, then your Logical And operator, it is not going to evaluate the second operand because there is no need of evaluating the second element if the first operand itself is giving the output as false.

Very similarly, in the Logical OR operation, if the very first element is giving the output as true, then it is never going to evaluate the second operand, because in the scenario of our condition, even if one of the operand is true, then the overall output is going to be true. So the same strategy here also these methods are going to follow especially like allMatch() and anyMatch(). So allMatch() what it is going to do is, whenever it find an element which is not matching with your predicate condition, then immediately it is going to return the output as false.

It is not going to evaluate the predicate condition on all the elements. In the similar lines, anyMatch() also it is going to give the output as true as soon as it identify a first element which matches to your predicate condition. The same principle applies to the other methods like findAny() and findFirst(). So both these methods are going to return an element from your stream. In the scenario of findFirst(), it is going to be the first element and all the remaining elements.

It is not going to look and bother about them. And similarly, inside the findAny(), it is going to randomly pick one of the element, and it is also not going to bother about all the remaining elements. So let's see that demo of all these methods. So first I'm going to have a filter() intermediate operation to filter only the odd numbers. lectures.title: Collections Vs Streams
lectures.text:
We almost covered all the details around the stream API. We discussed everything around the intermediate operations, terminal operations, parallel processing. So now we have a very good understanding around the stream API and how to process the elements inside a collection with the help of streams and the lambda expressions. As part of this lecture, let's try to understand what are the differences between collections and streams. We know collections are present inside Java from day one, whereas streams they are introduced as part of Java 8.

So this is one of the famous interviews around the Java Collections and Streams API. That's why let's try to put some efforts understanding the differences between the collections and streams. The very first and most important difference between collections and stream is, collections they are going to hold the elements inside the memory or inside the heap memory, whereas streams, they are not going to store the elements inside any memory, all the elements, they are going to be stored using the underlying collection data source.

We already discussed in detail about this point in the previous lectures. Moving on to the next difference, a collection is going to be eagerly constructed and the elements can be added or removed. So whenever we are trying to build a collection object and try to add all the elements inside each, these operation is going to be done eagerly. That means before you try to perform any operations on top of your collection object, all the elements might have stored inside a heap memory, but coming to the stream, they are going to operate lazily.

For example, if you are trying to run a map() operation with the help of Stream object, it is not going to load all the hundreds of elements inside your underlying collection data source. Instead, it is going to read the element lazily one by one. The next difference is pretty easy collections. They don't use any functional interfaces and lambda expressions, but on the other side streams they are going to use lot of functional interfaces along with the lambda expressions.

We can't imagine streams API without lambda expressions and functional interfaces. The next difference is collections are non consumable. That means collections can be traversed to multiple times without creating again. If you have a List of object, you can try to iterate it any number of times with the multiple for loops and while loops, you're not going to get any exception. But on the other side, streams are consumable, which means you can only traverse them once if you want to traverse or iterate the elements inside stream one more time, the only option that you have is to create the stream one more time.

If you try to traverse the same Stream object multiple times, like we discussed in the previous lectures, we are going to get an IllegalStateException. Coming to the last difference, it says collections are iterated using external loop like for loop and while loop only. So whenever we are dealing with the collections, we need to give low level instructions to the JRE or the Java and how to iterate the elements inside a collection. Whereas with streams we don't have to give any low level instructions, we can follow the functional style of programming as long as we are using intermediate operations or terminal operations to process the elements inside stream, the iteration responsibility is going to be taken care by the Java internally.

We as a developers, we don't have to manually iterate the stream elements. So these are the differences between collections and streams. I hope you are clear. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: How a program or a software executes inside a computer
lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, let's go back to the basics and try to understand how a software or a program is going to execute behind the scenes inside a computer. So let's try to understand the same. Like you can see here inside a computer at the very low level we'll be having the hardware. So as part of this hardware we'll be having CPU. CPU is responsible to execute instructions or to perform any calculations that a software or a program required. So basically CPU is going to provide computing power to a program or a software to execute a specific set of instructions.

Similarly, we'll be having Ram. Ram is going to provide a memory location, which can be used to save some data and retrieve the same whenever required, very fastly. And similarly, we'll be having hard disk, which is capable of storing any amount of data like 1TB or 2TB. We can store any amount of data inside a hard disk, but Ram memory is very limited. It will usually have 16 GB, eight GB or 32 GB Ram. So whatever data that a program or a software needs to access very quickly all such data, it is going to be saved inside Ram.

And whenever the program or a software is closed, whatever data that we stored inside the Ram related to that program, our software is going to get deleted. Similarly, hardware also is going to provide other capabilities, like it is also going to have network related drivers, which is going to help in performing input and output operations. Like if you want to watch a movie inside Netflix or inside Hotstar. So in all such scenarios, the video needs to be streamed from the remote server.

So based upon the data that is being streamed from the remote server, the same is going to be downloaded by your computer. And whatever video that has been downloaded, you will be able to see inside your browser or inside your media player. After the hardware on top of it, we are going to have operating system. Can we start using a computer without operating system? Off course not. With hardware alone the computer is going to be useless. By installing an operating system on top of the hardware, we will be able to perform lot many actions inside a computer.

So what is an operating system? It is a software that manages hardware resources and provides services for other computer programs. So basically operating system, it is going to abstracts the hardware and provides a consistent interface for applications to run on different types of hardware resources. So now think like we have a proper computer with a proper hardware and operating system. As a next step, we will start using this computer. For example, if I want to open a Chrome browser, I will be able to do that and similarly, if I want to open a PDF, I'll be able to do that.

Similarly, if I want to read an email, I'll be able to open the outlook with the help of the Outlook Software or Outlook program. I'll be able to read the emails. I'll be able to send the emails. Similarly, we will be able to invoke so many softwares or programs based upon our needs. Like you can see here. On top of my operating system, there are so many processors are running based upon the type of softwares or programs that I'm trying to run. So here you can see, seems one user tried to open all these softwares like a chrome, pdf reader, email, intelliJ, ppt, zoom, Safari, notion, Dropbox.

So for each of the software or the program that you're going to invoke inside your computer, a dedicated process is going to be created by operating system. So we can say a process is a program in execution. It is an independent unit that runs in its own memory space. So basically, whenever you are trying to use a software like Chrome, when you open the Chrome browser behind the scenes operating system, it is going to create a process for the Chrome browser alone.

So for this process of Chrome browser, the operating system, it is going to allocate some CPU resources, some Ram memory and similarly some disk memory. So whatever hardware resources needed by my process of Chrome. So all those will be assigned by the operating system to the process of Chrome. It is very important to understand that each process has its own address space and system resources. So whatever address, space or resources assigned to the Chrome, it cannot be shared or used by other processes like Intel, Edge or Safari.

I hope you are clear about the process. Now let's try to understand what is a thread ? Before I try to explain you about what is a thread from operating system perspective, let me ask you a question. If you open a Chrome browser, are you going to perform only one action always ? Off course not you'll be opening multiple tabs inside your Chrome browser. In one tab, you might have open the Gmail. In another tab, you might have opened the Netflix where a video is being played.

In another tab, you might have opened YouTube, where also a video is being played, and inside another tab of your chrome you might have open the WhatsApp where you are trying to chat with your friend. So if you see within a software or within a program or within a process, you're trying to perform multiple tasks. So to handle all these tasks efficiently or parallelly or simultaneously, threats are going to be created within process. So what is a thread ?

A thread is a smallest unit of execution within a process. Multiple threats can exist within a single process, handling the various activities of the software or the program that you are trying to run within a process. So all these threats, they are going to be created by the softwares. For example, inside the business logic of Chrome software, someone might have written the code to create a new thread whenever a new tab is being opened by the end user.

So these threads at the end of the day, they are going to request the operating system to provide some resources like CPU time or Ram memory. So based upon these requests, operating system can provide the hardware resources. So all the threads that we are going to create within a process, they are going to share the same memory space allowing for the efficient communication. So the main purpose of creating threads is they are very lightweight compared to the process.

And they can run concurrently behind the scenes. Let me share more details about threads, how threads are going to be created within the process. Like you can see here, I have a process of chrome. So inside this process of Chrome there will be multiple threads, will be created like T1, T2, T3, T4, t5. So all these threads, they are going to be created based upon the actions performed by the end user on the Chrome browser. So each of the thread is going to give some responsibility to execute a sequence of instructions within a process.

So when a thread it wants to execute some instructions, at the end of the day it needs the CPU computing power. So how it is going to get the CPU computing power? The thread will ask the operating system to give some CPU time of a CPU core, and based upon the time provided by the CPU core to a specific thread, it is going to execute all the instructions. You may have a question here, which is what is a CPU core? CPU core is a main hardware component available inside the CPU, which is responsible to execute the instructions that requires computing power. Back in the days of 1990s in those times, computers, they only used to have a single CPU core, but the modern laptops and systems that we are trying to use, they are having four cores, eight cores, 12 cores.

Many times you might have heard, like someone claiming that that my computer is a octa core processor or a quad core processor. So what do they mean? That means their computer have four cores or eight cores. So when a thread request operating system for a CPU time, it is going to assign the CPU time for a limited time like fraction of seconds or it can be one second or it can be two seconds five seconds 10s. So based upon the demand from your thread, the CPU time is going to be assigned by the operating system.

Like we discussed within a process, we can create multiple threads, enabling concurrent execution of various tasks and enhancing CPU resource utilization and ultimately boosting the throughput. So let's try to understand this statement by taking the example. Think like you launched a Google Chrome. The operating system generates a process for this Chrome. And within that process task like showing a web page, downloading a file, playing a video on YouTube, WhatsApp chatting they can all occur simultaneously due to separate threads.

Suppose think like this T4 thread is capable of playing a video on YouTube in one of the Chrome tab, so as soon as the playing of the video is completed, then this T4 is not going to require any CPU time, or it is not going to require any hardware resources. So in all such scenarios, the T4, it is going to sit ideally, and it is not going to ask any time to the operating system for the hardware resources. Maybe after half an hour if the end user came to the same tab and he's trying to play the another video inside the YouTube.

Then again, the thread will try to request the operating system for the CPU time or for the any other hardware resources it requires. I can also confirm all this theory by showing an information inside my system. Inside my Mac I opened a program with the name Activity Monitor. If you are using windows operating system, you will be able to see the same kind of information inside your task explorer. So if you see here under this activity monitor, I selected the memory which will give me the summary around which processes are using my Ram memory and how many threads are created for each of the process.

You can see inside my system I have processes like IntelliJ Idea, PowerPoint, outlook, subline, OneDrive, Safari. So there are many processes running and each of these processes, they have multiple threads created inside them based upon their own requirements. So this should give a confirmation to you that all these processes, they are relying on threads behind the scenes to execute multiple tasks simultaneously or parallelly. So if you see my IntelliJ Idea, it is using right now 2.53 GB Ram memory.

Similarly PowerPoint it is using 442 MB. I can also go to the CPU tab, where we'll be able to see how much CPU time is being used by each of the process. For example, this Microsoft PowerPoint, it has used CPU time of one hour, 48 minutes zero seven seconds with the threads 52. So this way always behind the scenes operating system. It is going to manage the processes and within the processors multiple threads are going to be created. So all these threads, they are going to work with the operating system to get the hardware time like CPU time or Ram memory.

So based upon thread requirements, the same is going to be requested to the operating system. And if there is a free availability of the resource, then obviously operating system will be more than happy to provide such hardware resources. But if you are trying to run too many programs or too many softwares inside your system, then obviously sometimes you may feel some slowness inside your system. Why that slowness is happening, because the operating system does not have enough resources to assign to your software.

That's why sometimes softwares they'll hang or they will behave very slowly. I hope you're clear how a program or a software executes inside a computer. The same kind of explanation is also applicable for a Java program as well, because at the end of the day, Java program is also a software or it is also a program which needs some hardware resources to execute the instructions that we have mentioned as part of the Java program. I'm assuming you are enjoying this discussion.

Let's continue this discussion in the next lecture as well. Thank you, bye.
