lectures.text:
Inside this lecture, let's try to understand how multiple threads they are going to improve the performance and under which scenarios we should not go for the multithreading. Like we discussed in the previous lecture, if you consider a computer which just has four CPU cores at most, these computer can execute four parallel threads simultaneously. However, you may have a question which is then why do applications often create hundreds of threads?

What are the applications that are going to achieve by creating hundreds of threads? Why not limit the number of threads to match the CPU core count? So you may have all these questions. So let's try to answer all of your questions by trying to discuss in detail about threads. So whenever a thread want to execute a task, the task can be categorized into two categories. The very first one is CPU-bound and the other category is IO-bound. IO means input and output, so all the tasks that requires computational power from the CPU, such as Arithmetic operations, logical processing operations, and relational calculations.

So all these kind of calculations and operations, since they need CPU power, we can call these kind of tasks as CPU-bound task. On the other hand, we also have IO-bound tasks which are highly dependent on input output operations. For example, if you're trying to play a YouTube video inside your Chrome browser, it is not a CPU-bound task, it is a IO-bound task because the browser in this scenario it does not require the CPU time instead, it is going to rely on the network of your system to load the video from a remote server.

So any task which which involves communication over a network, or reading or writing operations onto a file or onto a remote server. So all these kind of tasks we can consider them as IO-bound task. So basically whenever a thread is executing a CPU-bound task only in such scenarios, only the thread needed a CPU time or a CPU core time. And while IO task is being executed, the thread is not going to do any job. It is going to sit ideally behind the scenes because IO-bound tasks, they are going to be executed based upon the network of your system.

So let's try to understand more details about the CPU-bound and IO-bound task. So first I'm going to take a scenario where it involves only CPU-bound tasks. Think like I have a scenario where I want to perform some mathematical calculations. Maybe to my program, I might have given a larger data set as an input, and based upon this large data set, the program has to generate some complex statistical models, all without engaging in any input or output operations.

So this is a scenario where it requires only the CPU-bound to task. And the similar lines I'm also going to give one more example. So this time consider a scenario where I have a combination of both the CPU and IO operations. For example, think of a program where it is going to fetch the data from a remote database. So fetching the data from a remote database involves IO-bound tasks because the data has to be transmitted over the network. So once that data is received by my thread, it has to perform some complex calculations.

So since calculations requires a CPU time, we can consider the second step, which is the complex calculations as a CPU-bound task. And after the calculations are completed, we have the final step, which is the results that are derived from the second step. They need to be sent to the other remote server. So when we want to send the results to another remote server, it again involves IO-bound tasks. So this example, it is a combination of both the CPU-bound task and the IO-bound task.

Similarly, you may also have a scenario where you are performing only the IO-bound related tasks. I'm not considering that example, because if you are performing only the IO-bound tasks, your software or your program is never going to create the threads because threads are only required whenever we are trying to execute the CPU-bound task. I hope it is clear. Now let's try to discuss more details by taking these two examples. In the very first example where we are trying to perform only the CPU-bound task.

So to handle this scenario, since I have a large data set and since I need to perform lot many calculations think like 12 different threads are created to execute all my CPU-bound tasks. Since all these 12 threads can't be executed at the same time behind the scenes, the operating system it is going give me the CPU time randomly So here under the CPU core one you can see we have threads like nine, 12, seven. So randomly my operating system, what it is doing is first it is giving some time to the thread nine to perform some calculations, post that immediately it is trying to switch to the other thread.

So the switching from one thread to other thread by the operating system we call that as context switch. So in this example we have purely CPU tasks. And that's why my threads are always busy. But the problem right now I have is my operating system is keep on switching from one thread to other threads so that it can achieve the concurrency, and nowhere it is giving a specific dedicated time to a given thread. It is keep on context switching, and since the operating system is doing lot of context switching, obviously in this scenario, creating 12 different threads may not be super efficient because the more number of threads you are trying to create, if you have only CPU-bound tasks, then the more number of context switches is going to happen by the operating system.

And whenever the context switch is happening from one thread to other thread behind the scenes, it is going to take some milliseconds of time. It can be 1 millisecond or 2 millisecond, so that kind of unnecessary switching is going to happen. That's why whenever you have purely CPU-bound tasks, don't try to create too many threads. We should go with a limited number of threads. But if you follow the same strategy for this example where you have a lot of I o operations, you are going to have some performance issues.

lectures.text:
Inside this lecture we're going to talk about three important methods available inside Thread which are wait(), notify() and notifyAll(). Since these methods are complex to understand, I want to explain them with the help of a example. So first let me explain you what is the problem that I'm trying to solve and how wait() and notify() related methods. They are going to help us. So think like I want to build two different Thread objects. The very first object is Producer.

So the purpose of this Producer thread is it is always going to produce some data like Integers or Strings, whatever you have configured. To make it simple, let's assume that these Producer thread is responsible to always produce an int value like one, two, three, four, five, and so on. On the other side, we'll be having Consumer thread which is going to consume the data that is generated by the Producer thread. So whenever Producer thread generates a int value one, the same is going to be read by the Consumer thread, and it is going to process it based upon its business logic.

For our example, let's assume the business logic of Consumer thread is just to display the data onto the console. Another interesting problem that we have inside this example is Producer whenever it is trying to produce the next value, whatever previous value it generated, it is going to be overrided. So when the Producer generated the value two, the previous value one is going to be overwrite. That means at a time Producer can hold a single value.

So to make this work like we expect, what we have to do is once the Producer produces a value like one, we need to make the Producer thread to wait till the Consumer thread consumes. So when our Producer thread is waiting the Consumer thread, it has to check whether the Producer thread it is generated, any value. If yes, it needs to consume the value generated by the Producer thread. Once the consumption of the data by the Consumer thread is completed, then obviously whatever data that got generated previously by the Producer thread, now my Producer thread has to generate the next value.

So to achieve the same my Consumer thread, it has to notify the Producer thread once the consumption is completed. And the vice versa also should happen whenever the Producer thread is generating a value, the Consumer thread, it needs to be in the waiting state, and once the Producer thread generates a value, it needs to notify the Consumer thread to consume the value. So whenever you want to have a particular thread to wait based upon certain condition, we can use the wait() method.

And whenever you are into scenario where you want to notify other waiting thread to continue its execution. In such scenarios, we need to use the notify() method. I hope you are clear with this initial interaction. If something is not clear, don't worry. When we start building the logic based upon these methods, it is going to be super clear for you. So here inside my intelliJ, let me create a new Java class with the name SharedResource. Inside this class first I'm going to create an instance variable of type int.

So let me type private int and the variable name I'm going to mention as data. Using these variable only the Producer is going to produce a value and store it inside these int variable. And from these variable only the Consumer thread it is going to read the data. After this int variable, I'm also going to create one more instance variable with the name is empty of type boolean. The default value it has is true. So with the help of this boolean I'm going to control the logic of Producer and Consumer.

So whenever my Producer want to produce a new value, it needs to check whether the is empty is true. If the is empty is true, that means the Consumer consume the value and Producer can generate a new value. And similarly, on the Consumer side, the consumer should never try to read the value whenever the isEmpty() is true. It should only try to read the value when the is empty is false. Just to save some time, I'm going to paste a couple of methods inside this class.

Once the code is pasted, I'm going to discuss about them in detail, so I'm just trying to save some time for both of us. The very first method that you can see here is produce(). So there is a new keyword you'll be able to see here, which is synchronize. I'll be talking about the synchronized in few seconds. For now let's not worry about it. So you can see this is a producer() method which is going to produce a value based upon whatever input it has received.

So whatever thread which is executing this produce() method, it is going to execute this while loop. Inside this while loop, what we have written is, while not off isEmpty() that means if the isEmpty() is false, then these condition is going to become true. So whenever an data already has some value and the consumer is ed to read the value in all such scenarios, the thread that is right now executing this produce() method, it will keep on waiting.

So it will be in the wait state, and it will not ask the operating system or the CPU for the CPU time. Instead, it is going to sit idle for the condition to meet. So whenever the isEmpty() become false and with that, this while statement is not going to be executed. Then we have a logic here where we are trying to assign the value that we have received to that data instance variable. So at this line of code, we are producing a value and post that we are setting the boolean as isEmpty() as false.

And we also have a System.out.println() saying that produced a value. After executing all this logic, we are trying to invoke the notify() method. So with this notify() method, what is going to happen is the other Consumer thread which is waiting for these Producer thread to complete its business logic. It is going to wake up and it is going to start asking the CPU and the operating system to provide some CPU time so that it can start executing the Consumer logic.

So here, since we are setting the isEmpty() as false this thread, it is going to become into the wait state. So whenever these Producer thread is in wait state this Consumer thread, it is going to be notified and you can see here while isEmpty() is true this thread, it is going to be in the wait status since we are setting the isEmpty() as false, this while loop is not going to be executed. Instead, it will directly go here and it will try to consume the data by reading the data variable.

So based upon the consumed data we are just trying to print out onto the console post that we are trying to set this isEmpty() variable to true. So whenever this is true, this while loop is going to be executed. And this Consumer thread, it is going to be enter into the wait status. And since this thread it is also invoking the notify() method, the other Producer thread which is waiting, it is going to wake up and it is going to look for the CPU time so that it can start generating the new value.

So if you see here with the help of these, wait and notify two threads, they are trying to communicate with each other and coordinate with each other to achieve a specific business logic. Now let me explain you very quickly about the purpose of this synchronized. So synchronized is a keyword inside Java which you can use in the scenarios of multi-threading environment. As of now, inside our example we are going to generate only a single thread to produce and only a single thread to consume.

But in real projects, you may have hundreds of Producer threads and hundreds of Consumer threads, and at a time you want only one Producer thread and one Consumer thread to execute the business logic of this method. In such scenarios, you can use the synchronized keyword. So whenever we mark a method with the help of synchronized keyword behind the scenes, the JVM will make sure at a single point of time, only a single thread is executing these business logic, and all the other threads which are trying to execute the same method, they are going to keep on waiting until the current thread it entered into the wait status.

We are going to discuss in detail about the synchronized keyword in the coming lectures as well, but for now I just wanted to give this high level introduction. So now we have this shared resource class ready in the next lecture using this class, let's try to build some multi-threading program where we are going to build a Producer thread and a Consumer thread. I hope you are clear with that discussion that we have done so far. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: Introduction to Race condition & synchronized keyword
lectures.text:
Building a Java program with the help of multithreading concept is somewhat complex compared to normal Java program. The reason is very obvious when multiple threads they are trying to execute your business logic parallely. You may need to handle lot many conditions or lot many complexities that your program may face at runtime. One such important complexity is race condition. So whenever you are dealing with the multiple threads, your program may have a race condition.

So first let's try to understand what is this race condition. And later on we can try to understand how to handle these race condition. The race condition happens when two threads which are trying to access a shared variable at the same time. So both these threads like first thread and the second thread, they read the same value from the variable. But at later point of time when these threads, they want to update the same shared variable then a race condition will happen.

Think like when both these threads they are trying to update the shared variable at the same time. They will be racing with each other to see which thread is going to write the latest value into the shared variable. So the value of the thread that writes its value at the end is going to be preserved. For example, think like initially the shared variable has a value as zero at later point of time. The same shared value is going to be updated by the thread one to the number ten.

Here in the race condition, the thread one wins because it is able to first update the value inside the shared variable, though it wins the race, but its value is going to be overrided by the other thread, because thread two is going to overwrite the value present inside the shared variable with the new value at a later point of time. So this is a race condition. Let me give you an example so that it is going to make more sense to you. Like you can see here, I have a map with the name reserved tables.

So inside this map think like we are going to store the table name as a key. And who reserved that table as a value. Think like this Java program that I'm showing right now it is going to be executed in some restaurant web application. So the restaurant has a booking functionality inside their web application. There is a very good chance that two multiple users may try to book the same table at the same point of time. So in these kind of scenarios, what is going to happen is thread one.

It is going to check if these reserved table map contains the key table one. So indirectly it is checking if there is any one reserved that table one. Since these reserved table initially it is an empty map. So this condition inside the if condition it is going to give false. If we apply the Not condition on top of the false, the overall condition of this if condition is going to become true and the logic present inside this if block is going to be executed at the same time behind the scenes.

Thread 2 also, it is going to run the same logic. It is checking whether the reserved tables contains that table one as a key, since initially it read the reserved table which is an empty here also, this if condition is going to be executed and this thread 2 also it is going to update the table one with the user two. So if you see here both these thread 1 and thread 2, they try to update the same shared variable at the same point of time with just a few fraction of seconds difference.

In this scenario, let's assume the thread one wins the race and it wrote the value which is user one to this table. And with that the user one he is going to get a message inside the website saying that hey, congratulations, you reserved that table one. And with that message, the end user will be under the assumption his reservation is completed successfully. But behind the scenes, what happened just after few fraction of seconds? The thread 2 it tried to overwrite the reservation with the new user, which is user 2.

So with this logic, if both these user one and user two go to the restaurant at the given time, only the user two will be able to get the table 1 because the user one data is overriding by the thread 2 . So this is one of the serious problem that you may face while you are trying to implement a logic with the help of multi-threading environment. The problem here we have is, there is a shared variable which is the reserved tables HashMap. Both these threads are trying to update these reserved table at the same time.

When they are trying to update the variable at the same time, obviously they both will not be able to write at the same time, just with a fraction of seconds difference. Both of these threads, they are going to write their values and whatever thread committed the value at the end, its value is going to be maintained inside the shared variable. So how to resolve this race condition? It's very simple we need to take the help of synchronized keyword like we discussed briefly in the previous lecture.

Synchronized keyword is used to control the access of multiple threads to the shared resources. So whenever we are using this keyword, it is going to ensure that only one thread can execute a synchronized block or a method at a time. So the synchronized keyword can be used in two forms. You can use the synchronized keyword along with the block of code. Whenever you have some complex logic which needs to be executed by only one thread at a time. In such scenarios, you are going to keep all such complex logic inside the curly braces.

And just before this curly braces, you're going to mention the synchronized keyword along with the shared object that you're trying to write. So with that, this synchronized block ensures that only one thread at a time can execute the code within the block. So if you try to apply the same synchronized keyword logic with the previous example, what we have to do is we need to keep these shared variable logic inside the synchronized block. And with that, only a one thread will be able to read and overwrite at a time while the thread1 is doing the reading and writing operation on the shared object, the thread2 it is going to keep waiting as soon as the thread1 completes the execution of this synchronized block, then thread2 will enter into the synchronized block.

So this is how it is going to work. So we need to use the synchronized block. Whenever you have some piece of code which needs to be executed by one thread at a time. In the similar lines, you can also apply the synchronized keyword on top of a method itself. If you want your entire method to be executed only one thread at a time, then you can mention the synchronized keyword just before the return type of your method. You can use the synchronized keyword on top of the static methods and on top of instance methods.

So whenever a method is declared as synchronized, it implicitly uses the Object instance at the class object as a monitor. I hope you are clear with this. I also mentioned a picture here, saying that threads are going to wait for their chance to execute this method, or to execute these block. This way we can avoid the conditions like race conditions. Inside the next lecture, we can see that demo of the synchronized block by taking an example so that it is going to be super clear for you.

Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.text:
In theory, multithreading program may look very simple, but when you start implementing multithreading program inside a real Java application, it is going to become super complex because at runtime we need to handle so many conditions. One such condition is race condition, which we discussed in the previous lectures. In the similar way there are many other conditions also which we need to understand. As a Java developer, you can see this meme perfectly conveys the same.

In theory, multithreading is going to be very simple, like like feeding these puppies in a line, but in reality, all these puppies, they are not going to be so disciplined. And the person who is trying to feed them, you need to struggle a lot, because the puppies are going to move from one location to other location. Even the life of the Java developer is going to be like this only when the developer started implementing multithreading inside Java program.

Inside this lecture, I am going to discuss one runtime issue that you may face while implementing the multithreading program. And I'm also going to teach you how to overcome the same. Let's consider FIFA game that we can play inside the play station. Many of you might be playing FIFA game inside the play station, so let's consider the same to understand a scenario inside this FIFA game. Think like the developers are trying to use multi-threading program.

So there is a thread, one which is going to track the goals made by the players inside this thread. Think like we have a logic which is to update the goal boolean variable to true whenever a goal is made by a player. So initially this variable is going to hold the boolean value false. As soon as a player made a goal, the boolean variable is going to be updated to true value and think like this updation is happened exactly at the time nine hours, 32 minutes 18 seconds, 346 milliseconds.

I'll also try to mention Am or PM. So for now let's try to consider am time. I hope you are clear with the job of this thread one. Now let's try to understand the job of another thread which is running inside this program, which is thread two. So this thread two responsibility is to update the score by incrementing the goals value by one inside the thread2 there might be some logic with the help of while loop. So this while loop it is going to keep on monitor the variable which is isGoal whenever this variable become true.

Inside this while loop, we are trying to increment the goals value by one and after the increment happened, the isGoal variable is going to be reset to false. So this way these two threads are trying to coordinate with each other based upon the shared variable which which is isGoal. So as soon as our goal has been incremented by this thread two, the same is going to be visible to the end user, whoever is trying to play the game. So think like this updation of the goals happened exactly at this point of time.

Maybe after delay of ten milliseconds this update happened. So we as a humans, we can't recognize if there is a delay in fraction of seconds or if there is a delay in milliseconds. So this is an ideal scenario which we are trying to discuss in a multithreading environment. But in reality the update is not going to happen so fastly. Sometimes you may have a delay of one second, three seconds, five seconds based upon how busy your system is. So think like there is a three seconds delay in updating the goal.

With that, the end user who is trying to play the game, he or she will be easily able to recognize that the score is not getting updated immediately as soon as the goal happened. So this gives some bad experience to the persons who is trying to play this game. But here you may have a question, which is why there will be a delay as soon as this thread update this boolean variable. My while loop can easily recognize it, right? What is the problem here which may result into 3 seconds or 5 seconds or one second delay.

So this can be your question. So let me try to explain the same inside multi threading environment whenever we are dealing with the instance variables or any other variables, what is going to happen behind the scenes is all the threads they are going to cache the variables. So what is a cache? Cache is a mechanism using which threads they are going to store the variable values in a nearest local memory location, instead of reading them every time from the main memory location, like CPU heap memory.

So what are the threads that are trying to achieve with these caching mechanism? They are trying to achieve some performance improvements by caching the variable values inside the local memory. You might be hearing this caching also very first time. Let me try to explain the same by taking a real life example. Let's go back into 1990s. During 1990s, no one has mobile numbers. Everyone used to use a landline telephone to make a call and not all homes they not have landline phones, only inside few rich peoples house these land phones used to be available. For a common person if he or she wants to make a call to someone else, the person have to walk in into one of the locations where they can make a phone call by paying some money.

So in this kind of setup, think like there is a student with the name Adam. So he is studying somewhere in a different country and he will try to talk with his parents regularly. So here, whenever he want to call his parents landline number, he will walk into the nearest shop where he can make a call, and he's going to look for what is the landline number of his parents. So there are two approaches for him to look for the landline number. The very first approach is, he can write it on a piece of paper, and he can carry the same piece of paper every time he's trying to make a call to his parents.

So this is one approach. And the second approach is, he can memorize that number inside his mind. So these are the two different approaches. So which approach do you think is faster and efficient. Off course the approach2 itself is efficient because if he memorize them number, he will be able to easily recollect whenever he wants very quickly. And he will not have any dependency on the paper and he don't have to carry it as well. So the caching also is going to work very similarly.

If a thread stores a variable inside the local memory, it is like its brain, where it can read the variable very quickly without relying on the CPU main memory. But here you may have a question which is, when this thread2 to initially try to execute this logic, it is going to read the isGoal variable from the main memory, and the main memory is going to have the value as false and this false value my thread2 it is going to cache it inside its local memory. With this local cached value this while loop is never going to be executed.

And with that there is no meaning for my thread2 to continuously run behind the scenes with a local cached value. So this can be your question. So it's a great question. Let me try to answer the same. Whenever a thread is trying to cache a value, it is not going to retain it forever. Instead, at a regular intervals of time, it is going to recheck the variable and its value inside the main memory location. If there is a change inside the value, then obviously it is going to copy the same into the local cache value.

So, based upon how frequently a thread is trying to read the value from the main memory location accordingly, there can be a delay between this thread1 and thread2 output. So if there is a delay of five seconds by this thread2 to read this variable value from the main memory location, then obviously the five seconds delay will happen in incrementing this goal. And the same delay is also going to happen in displaying the latest goal value onto the screen.

So think like this thread one also cached. This is goal value into the local memory location. If it is trying to update these variable to true in its local memory location at this point of time, and maybe after three seconds if it is trying to write the same into the main memory location, then obviously the time at which the latest value is going to be available will be plus three seconds to these initial time. It will be 9 hours, 32 minutes, 21 seconds and 346 milliseconds.

So this is the time at which the main memory location variable value is going to be updated. Now think like my thread2 it is taking five seconds regular interval of time to read the value from the main memory location and update the same into the local memory. So with that there will be five more seconds delay will be added in reading this variable inside the thread2 and to this, if you try to add five seconds, it will be 9hours, 32 minutes, 26 seconds, 346 milliseconds is going to be the time, and if it is taking ten more milliseconds to update this counter, then obviously the time at which this counter is going to be updated is 9hours, 32 minutes, 26 seconds, 356 milliseconds.

So if you see here the actual goal happened at this point of time, but due to the fact that all these threads, they are trying to cache the variable value inside the local memory, this delay happened. So total there is a delay of around eight seconds here. So this is some scenario that I'm trying to mention here. But in reality the delay can be one second or two seconds or point five seconds, regardless of whatever is the delay the problem that we have right now here is the threads whenever they are dealing with the variables which are stored inside the local memory location, there is a very good chance that the outputs may get delayed by some seconds.

So if you have these kind of there were multiple threads that are trying to use a common shared variable. In all such scenarios, you can use the volatile keyword. So whenever you're trying to declare an instance variable that can be leveraged by multiple threads instead of defining it normally you can mention the volatile keyword inside the variable declaration code. So with that, what is going to happen whenever a variable is marked as volatile, then the threads, they are never going to cache that variable.

They always going to read the variable value from the main memory location only. Even the visibility of the thread is going to be immediately, because there is no caching involved. When it is trying to update the boolean variable immediately, it is going to overwrite the value inside the main memory location and post that immediately the thread2 since it is reading the value from the main memory itself, there won't be any delay, and with that, the output is going to be visible to the end user immediately.

So please use this volatile keyword in the scenarios where an instance variable is being shared across multiple threads. But don't try to over use it because you know, the drawback of using the volatile keyword is the threads are not going to cache the variable inside their local memory, and with that you may see some fraction of seconds performance issues. I hope you are clear with the scenario and the purpose of volatile keyword. In the next lecture, let's try to understand how to define a volatile keyword, and we can also see the demo of the volatile keyword.

Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: Introduction to Deadlock
lectures.text:
Inside this lecture let's talk about deadlock scenario that may happen in multi-threading Java programs. So what is a deadlock? Before I try to explain you about what is a deadlock, first let me provide you some basics on how threads they are going to work behind the scenes. Whenever a thread want to execute some business logic, or whenever a thread wants to leverage the instance variable available in a object first, the thread will try to get a lock on the object so that no other threads there will be able to modify the same object.

So this is what we discussed and implemented with the help of synchronized block or synchronized methods. This deadlock whatever we are going to discuss inside this lecture, it is going to happen in the scenarios when threads they are trying to acquire the lock of a object. So let's try to understand in detail about this Deadlock. Deadlock is a scenario where one of the thread is waiting to acquire the lock of an object currently held by another thread.

That means a thread which is t1, it is waiting for a object which is already locked by another thread, which is t2. So the fun is not going to stop there. The actual fun start now. Now the second thread is waiting to obtain the lock of a different object held by the first thread. So consequently, both these threads find themselves in a state of mutual waiting. Expecting each other will release the lock and this will result into a deadlock situation.

Let me show you this with the help of an image, so that it is going to be super clear for you. So here I have a thread which is t one and I also have thread t2. So initially t1 locked on a object which is r1. You can think r1 is a resource, it can be an object or it can be any other resource that t1 right now have a lock. And similarly t2 is having a lock on top of r2 object or resource 2 object. As a next business logic, my t one thread it want to get the lock on the r2 resource.

So that's why t1. What it is going to do is, it is going to request CPU to provide me the lock onto this resource r2, and it is going to wait for the r2. So during this wait period it is not going to release the lock on r1. The same applies for t2. So t2 right now have a lock on r2. But it is waiting for the new object lock which is on the r1. So in this scenario t2 will go and ask operating system that I want to obtain a lock on r1. And I'm going to wait for the same once I got a lock on r1 obviously the lock on r2 is going to be released.

So whenever a thread gets a lock on a new object, the old lock will automatically released. But the problem here is t1 has a lock on r1 and it is expecting the lock on r2 until the lock of r2 is achieved by t1, it is not going to release the r1 object, whereas on the t2 the story is different. The t2 it is having a lock on r2, but it is waiting for a lock on r1. So if you see they are waiting forever like t1 is never going to release the lock on r1 until it receives the lock on r2.

And similarly r2 is never going to release the lock on r2 until it receives a lock on r1. So this is a deadlock scenario in multi-threading environment. In the next lecture, I'll show you a program where a deadlock will happen and whenever a deadlock will happen, there won't be any progress inside the Java program. So once we saw the demo of deadlock, I'll also show you how to fix a deadlock. And what are the possible options that we have to avoid the deadlock inside multi threading program.

Deadlock can be one of the toughest question that you may face in Java interviews. So having a good understanding around these is going to help you to clear your Java interviews. I hope you are clear with what is a deadlock. And I'm assuming you will be able to answer a definition of deadlock to anyone. Before I try to close this lecture, let me show you a couple of memes around deadlock so that it is going to be super clear for you. So this is one of the real life deadlock that may happen in some interviews.

So if you see the interviewer, she is trying to ask the candidate saying that, explain me the deadlock and I will hire you. The programmer who attended the interview. This fellow is saying you first hire me, then I'll explain deadlock to you. So this is one of the perfect example that you can say around deadlock scenario, but don't do this inside interview. I'm just trying to shed this on a fun note. Let me show you next deadlock meme. So this you might be seeing lot many times in US city as well.

If you see there is a signal and all the roads inside the signal, they are completely blocked and there is no way for the cars to move back. So this is kind of deadlock scenario. In the similar lines we also have another deadlock meme. So this is my favorite one. And in fact it happens many times to me as well. So think like you went to some supermarket to buy some groceries. So here, this woman, she's looking at these fish and she's trying to buy these fish.

The catch woman, she's thinking, I need that thing which is sold by her. So she's thinking that in the meantime, she's also telling to her, I'll pretend to look at these until she moves. She don't need these bananas, but she's trying to pretend as if she's looking at them. And she's continuously waiting for this lady to leave from these fish section. But in the third picture, if you see, there is one guy who is waiting for this cat lady to leave because this guy, he wants to buy these bananas.

Now, coming to the first lady who is standing at the fish grocery section, she is waiting on this guy. So if you see all three of them, they are waiting for others to move. So this is a funny example of deadlock. Off course, there won't be waiting infinitely in this scenario, but in real multithreading Java programs, the objects that are going to wait infinitely in deadlock scenario and that will result your program to run infinitely. I hope you're clear with the definition of deadlock in the next lecture let's see the demo of deadlock.

Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

The latest buzzword in Java multithreading concept is virtual threads. So what are these virtual threads? Virtual threads are the new feature introduced as part of Java 21. They are introduced very recently. These virtual threads are going to be a game changer for all the applications where they are using lot many threads as part of their business logic. As of now, we're just trying to create an object of Thread class and using the same. We are trying to invoke the start() method join() method.

Everyone is happy with the thread, but it has some drawbacks which we are going to discuss in the coming lectures. But if you ask me on a high level, what is the difference between a normal thread and a virtual thread? The answer is very simple. Virtual threads are lightweight in nature. With that, you can create millions of virtual threads inside your Java program. There won't be any restriction, whereas with a normal thread, since they are not lightweight like virtual threads, you will be limited with how many threads you can create inside your application based upon your Ram, memory and CPU cores.

Oracle team they are working on these virtual threads from many years under the project name Loom. So Loom is a Oracle's initiative aimed at tackling the complexities associated with the developing, maintaining and monitoring high throughput concurrent applications. Finally, after doing a lot of research and testing, virtual threads are introduced in Java 21. So to understand in detail about what is a virtual thread and how it is different from a normal thread, first we need to understand some basics of operating system and threads.

So let's try to understand the same. Inside operating system there are two types of threads that you can create. The very first type is kernel threads. So these threads in other words we can call them as operating system threads. These kernel threads are OS threads they are going to be overseen and scheduled by the operating system kernel. These threads are relatively heavyweight in terms of resources and requires system calls for their creation, scheduling and synchronization.

So these kernel threads, they are going to be created strictly for the operating system purpose. That's why whenever you try to start your operating system like Windows or Mac, it is going to take some 30s or one minute based upon your computer and operating system. So during all these 30s or one minute behind the scenes, your operating system taking enough time to boot up and create all these kernel threads. The other type of threads are user level threads.

So what are user level threads? If you try to run any software, or if you try to execute any program like Java so these softwares are Java programs they can be able to create the threads. All such threads we can call them as user threads. Throughout this section we are able to create the threads inside a Java program with the help of Thread class. So all these threads, we can call them as user threads, because a particular library or a particular software is trying to create these threads, but not the operating system.

Compared to the kernel threads, the user threads are lightweight in nature, and creating and destroying these user threads is faster compared to the OS threads. So when we are creating a thread inside Java program, we never side delay. The threads are getting created instantly, but OS threads are kernel threads they are not going to be created instantly. That's why during the startup of the operating system, they are going to take few seconds of time.

In simple words, whenever a program or a software want to create the threads first, it is going to start the process with a default thread to run the applications entry point. In the case of Java, the applications entry point is main() method. That's why behind the scenes it default thread is going to be created by the Java libraries. Following these main() thread java are any other program they have the flexibility to generate the extra user threads as per their requirement.

So all these user threads, they are going to be executed indirectly by the operating system threads or kernel threads, which means each of the user threads that we are trying to create with the help of a Java or any other program, they need to be mapped to some kernel thread so that the kernel thread is going to take care of executing the user thread by getting the CPU time from the operating system. So basically, whenever you have many number of user threads and kernel threads, the mapping has to be done between user threads and kernel threads.

And there are multiple approaches to perform these mapping. So let's try to understand those approaches. In the same process we can try to evaluate the evolution of threads inside Java the association between user. And kernel threads can be done in three approaches. The very first one is, M : 1 model, which means all user threads they are going to be linked to a single kernel thread. So here you can see U indicates user threads and K indicates kernel threads.

So in these many to one thread model all the user threads they are going to be mapped to a single kernel thread. The next model is, one is to one model in this model each user thread is going to be mapped to one of the kernel thread, and at last M is to M model, and inside this model, all user threads are mapped to a pool of Kernal threads. That means a user thread can be mapped to a many kernel thread, and similarly a kernel thread can be mapped to many user threads.

So these are the three models that are available inside operating system based upon which mapping a particular program or a particular library is leveraging accordingly, the performance is going to be impacted inside multi-threading program. Since we are talking from Java perspective from the next lecture, let's try to understand how these three models are going to affect the multi-threading Java program execution. I hope you are clear with all the discussion that we have done so far, we simply discussed there are two types of threads which are kernel threads and user threads.

The mapping between these two types of threads can be done by using all these three models. The mapping has to be done because at the end of the day, a user thread has to coordinate with the kernel thread to get some CPU time and to execute its instructions. I hope you are with me. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

lectures.title: [JAVA 22] Unnamed Variables & Patterns - Theory
lectures.text:
Java 22 released a new feature with the name Unnamed Variables and Patterns. Inside this video, let's try to explore what is this new feature, why it has been introduced, and under which scenarios we need to use this new enhancement. Many times inside our Java code, we end up writing lot many unused local variables, and deleting these unused local variables may not be an option, because we will have some tricky scenarios where we can't delete these unused variables from our code just because Java syntax forcing us defining them.

Or there might be some dependency on these unused variables inside our business logic as a side effect. So in these kind of scenarios where deleting an unused variable is not an option, we can simply use the unnamed variable so your unused variable name can be anything. The name can be replaced with underscore symbol. So that's a simple purpose or explanation about these unnamed variables. So what do we get by using these unnamed variables and patterns?

Developers know more they have to worry about giving some names to the unused variables many times we scratch our head what name we should give to these unused variable name. Can I give temp or I can give some x or y. So these kind of thought process we don't have to go because all these unused variable names which we can't delete can be replaced with an unnamed variable which is underscore. On top of that we also have one more advantage, which is many times IDE's like IntelliJ or eclipse and static code analysis like sonar cube, they will always complain about there is an unused variable inside our code, but we know we can't delete them because there are some tricky scenarios which we are going to discuss in few minutes.

So all these false positive alarms by the IDE's and sonar cube can be resolved with the help of unnamed variable. So whenever we are using unnamed variable, we are indirectly telling to IDE's and static code analyzer saying that I know it is an unused variable, but I have some dependency on it, or I have to declare it just because Java syntax expects that. So this kind of communication we we can give to the tools so that they no more going to throw any warnings.

So on a high level, if someone asks you what is an unnamed value and pattern, just tell them it is introduced as part of Java 22. All the unused local variable names and pattern variable names can be replaced with a symbol called underscore. So these are simplest definition that you can give. But it is important to note that that these unnamed variables and patterns cannot be applied to the instance fields or class level fields, like static fields or instance fields that you are going to create inside your class body.

lectures.title: [JAVA 24] Parallel Gatherers - Theory
lectures.text:
So far we discussed the basic concepts of gatherers API. As a next step, let's try to understand how to build the Parallel Gatherers. In the same process, we're also going to explore about the combiner optional component that we can provide while we are building an intermediate operation with the help of Gatherers API. By using Parallel Gatherers, we should be able to process our elements inside our intermediate operation in multiple threads. Java provides different ways to define parallel gatherers depending on whether we want to use internal state inside our business logic.

If you're not using any internal state inside your business logic, then building parallel gatherers is very simple. Otherwise, you need to take care of merging all the internal mutable states that you are receiving from multiple threads before pushing the output to the downstream. On a high level, there are three different flavors that we can use to build the parallel gatherers. The very first flavor is ,when you are invoking the of() factory method of gatherer.

If you are passing only the integrator logic, then all the elements from the upstream, they are going to be processed parallelly by executing your intermediate operator logic. When you are using this flavor, it means you don't want to use any mutable state inside your business logic, there won't be any finisher and this kind of parallel gathers, they are simple and safe for parallel execution. Whatever logic that you are going to define inside your integrator, the same logic will be executed parallelly for all the elements that is being received from the upstream.

Here I also have an example. I created a gatherer with the name eventFilter. Inside this gatherer logic, I'm just checking whether given input element is divisible by two. If yes, then only push the element to the downstream, otherwise don't push the same. Here, the logic inside my intermediate operator can be executed parallelly and independently. Since there is no dependency on the mutable state, I don't have to provide any combiner as well. We already saw the demo of this flavor, please remember always the thumb rule is if you are using the of() factory method from the Gatherer interface behind the scenes, the gatherer logic is going to be executed parallelly by using multiple threads.

In case if your business logic does not support parallel processing, and if you want to make sure to run the logic sequentially one by one. Under such scenarios, you need to make sure you are using the ofSequential() factory method. Let's move on to the second flavor, the second flavor is, along with the integrator. You can also pass the finisher logic as well. Sometimes you may have a requirement to execute some finitial logic once you are done processing all the elements parallelly.

For example, after invoking a Rest API for 100 different input elements parallelly, at the end, you may want to send an email or confirmation message to someone else. Under such scenarios, you can use this flavor. While using this flavor, also, there won't be any mutable state involved if there is no mutable state is involved, you don't have to, provide any combiner component. Here I have mentioned a simple example. My Gatherer, It is going to simply push the elements whatever it receives from the, upstream.

Apart from pushing the elements, it is not going to do anything else. Once, pushing all the elements to the downstream is completed at the end. I'm, going to execute my finished logic where I'm trying to push a message to the, downstream saying that all items are processed. These are simple flavors. I hope you are clear with these examples. Now let's try to look at the complex flavor where we are going to use some mutable state as well while we are trying to process the elements parallelly.

As you can see this flavor, it is going to accept an initializer using which you can provide an initial mutable state value followed by integrated logic. As a third parameter, you should also provide combiner component logic. I'll explain the purpose of this combiner in few seconds and towards the end, we should also provide the finisher logic as well. We need to use this flavor when you want to inspect or transform elements parallelly by using a mutable state value.

Here I have an example where I'm trying to provide an initial int value zero with the help of the object of AtomicInteger. Whatever initial value that I'm trying to provide with my initializer. The same initial value will be fed to all the multiple threads that are going to execute my integrated logic. For example, if your integrator logic is being executed by three different multiple threads, the same initial mutable state value like 0 ,0will be set to all the threads.

By using these initial state value, all the threads they are going to execute the logic present inside the integrator. Inside my integrator logic, I'm trying to simply add the given input number to the initial state value. So if you see I'm trying to invoke add() and to get() method and to the same, I'm passing the input received element which is number. The output will be saved into this some state object. And towards the end I'm trying to return the true.

So this is my integrator logic. After the integrator logic I have provided the combiner logic. What is the purpose of combiner component? This combiner component, it is going to combine the different intermediate state values into a single value. The logic of combiner component needs to be provided by using a lambda expression that adheres to the Binary operator functional interface. I'll share more details while we are trying to build this example inside our IntelliJ.

So this combiner, it is always going to accept two different intermediate state values as an input. And based upon these two different intermediate state values, it is going to combine them based upon the logic that we have defined. And at the end it is going to return a single state value. For example. Let's imagine initially there are four threads started executing our intermediate logic. There will be T1, there will be T2, T3, and T4. These are the multiple threads that are processing integrator logic.

Every thread they're going to have their own intermediate state value. In our scenario it will be zero. So let's imagine this is S1, S2 and S3 and S4. As soon as two different threads that are done with their execution, the intermediate state values like S1 and S2, they are going to be passed to our combiner. These S1 and S2 will be combined to a value. Let's imagine this is S5. The same applies here as well. These intermediate state values are also going to be combined with the help of combiner components, and a new state value will be S6.

Now we have two more intermediate state values S5 and S6. These will be again combined to get an and final state value. The same final state value will be feed to the finisher component. If you see, at last we are trying to define a finisher. So this sum represents the total sum value that is calculated by all the multiple threads along with the combiner component. This sum we are trying to push into the downstream with the help of this code. So if you see here, the actual pushing of the data into the downstream is happening only inside the finisher.

As a thumb rule, you need to make sure to provide the combiner component. If you are trying to use an mutable state value inside your business logic while you are trying to implement parallel gatherers. In case if you don't want to combine the state by using a combiner component, then you can't run the gatherer in parallel, you just have to go with the ofSequential() option. Inside this slide, I have mentioned a table which is going to give you a summary on how parallel gatherers and sequential gatherers are going to work.

The parallel support will only possible if you are using these of() factory method. That's why for the first three rows. The Yes is mentioned here. Whereas for the ofSequential() factory methods the parallel support will be no. Let's try to understand about other components as well. If you are using of() factory method with simple integrator logic, there won't be any mutable state, there won't be any finisher, and there won't be any combiner. Whereas for the next flavor where you're trying to provide finisher as well in this scenario, also, there won't be any mutable state, there won't be any combiner, but there will be a finisher.

Whereas if you are using this third flavor mutable state finisher, combiner, parallel support all of them, they are going to be present. Now coming to the ofSequential() factory method, there is an option for you to use an mutable state or not, that's why here I have mentioned yes or no. The same applies for finisher also, but combiner and parallel support. They are not applicable when you are using ofSequential() factory methods.

lectures.text:
When we are processing data with the help of Gatherer API. It is also going to give an flexibility or an option to the developer to interrupt the stream processing whenever developer wanted, based upon certain business logic.We know that the integrator logic that we are going to define at the end of the day, it has to return a boolean. Based upon these boolean that we are trying to return from our intermediate operation. The upstream is going to decide whether to send the next value or not for the intermediate operation.

We already saw a demo previously where when I'm trying to return a false, the upstream is not sending any new values. That is one option of interrupting a stream when you are processing the data with the help of Gatherer API, based upon your business logic, If you feel some condition is met and you don't want to process any further elements, you can simply return false from your integrator logic. But sometimes we may not have any requirement to interrupt the processing in between.

In this kind of scenarios, we are always going to push the elements to the downstream. If your downstream is accepting a limited number of elements. In this kind of scenarios, It is always a wise decision to return whatever boolean value that you are getting from the push() method to your upstream as well from the integrator logic. If you always try to return true from the integrator, then you're going to miss these kind of scenarios where your downstream is accepting only a limited number of elements.

Here I have an example where I have built an upstream, which is going to hold 1000 integer elements. If I use this as an upstream and invoke the gather() method to the gather() method, you'll be able to see I'm passing limitGatherer implementation. Inside the limitGatherer, I'm simply trying to push the elements to the downstream from the upstream, but you can imagine in your real applications you may have some complex business logic before you try to push the element to the downstream.

The main important point that I'm taking care here is I'm trying to return whatever boolean value that I'm receiving from the push() method of the downstream. Since I also have another intermediate operation limit which is going to accept only 10 elements. This is going to act as my downstream. After accepting 10 elements. The downstream it is going to return false as an output from the push() method. If I pass the same false as an output from my integrator logic, only the first 10 elements inside my upstream, they are going to be processed.

And with that I can have some performance improvement inside my program. In this scenario, instead of returning the output from the push. If you try to return manually a true value always, then you will end up keep pushing the elements from the upstream though they won't be any exception happening. If you try to push an element into a rejecting downstream, but still you will have some performance issues. Let's see the demo of this example. I created a class with the name G _ InterruptGatherer, and here inside the main() method I am trying to pace few lines of code.

All this code you can get from the GitHub repo. I'm trying to do this just to save some time. Since we already discussed everything about this logic. They should not be any confusion. But I'll try to discuss one more time, let me print the result with the help of System.out.println(). At the very starting of the main() method, I'm trying to create a list that is going to hold 1000 integer values. To the gatherer() method I'm trying to pass limitGatherer. Inside the limitGatherer I have written the logic just to push the elements to the downstream. I'm not trying to execute any other logic. After the gather intimate operation, I'm trying to invoke one more intermediate operation with the name limit. So this is going to act as a downstream, since this downstream has some restrictions to accept only 10elements. This downstream will start sending the Boolean value as false after 10 elements.

If you return the same to the upstream, we will save some performance. I'm going to execute this program since I had the System.out.println() statement inside my integrator. We can easily identify how many elements are being processed by my integrator logic. Let me execute this as you can see, only the 10 elements are processed and towards the end all these 10 elements are pushed to the downstream, that's why we are seeing this list as an output.

In case if you have a requirement, you can also manually check whether downstream is accepting any elements or not. How to do that? With the help of these downstream, you can invoke a method isRejecting() If this isRejecting(), is returning true, it is a confirmation to you that downstream is right now in the rejecting mode. Always remember three thumb rules. The first rule is downstream is always going to start in an non rejecting state. The second rule is once the downstream is entered into the rejecting state, it cannot come back to the non rejecting state.

The last rule is the state of the downstream from non rejecting to rejecting, It is going to only happen when you are trying to push an element into the downstream. So these are the three thumb rules. Please make a note of them. I'm going to mention these rules as it is inside this class in a commented form, for your reference. As a next step, let's try to understand how to chain multiple gatherers. Inside Gatherer interface, there is an method with the name and then with the help of these andThen() method, we can chain multiple gatherers.

These are simple gatherers that I'm trying to create just for our demo purpose, the first gatherer, It is going to accept integrator logic. Inside the integrator logic, I'm trying to simply push the element to the downstream after converting the string element to an completely uppercase value.

I also have another gatherer, which is going to check whether the element is starting with a value J. . If yes, then only push the element to the downstream, otherwise the element is not going to be pushed. Let's try to understand how to chain both these gatherers. Against to these upper gatherer, I need to invoke andThen() method to this andThen() method, I'm going to pass one more gatherer as an input. What is that second gatherer that we have? It is filter. And towards the end I'm going to invoke that toList() method. So here I'm trying to perform the chaining of gatherer by using these andThen() default method. Let me catch the output ,the output we can also try to print out with the help of System.out.println().

Let me execute this program. As you can expect, we received JAVA as an output because all the remaining elements, they are filtered by the second Gatherer.

lectures.title: [JAVA 24] fold(),scan(),mapConcurrent() methods in Gatherers
lectures.text:
Inside Stream Gatherers API, there is a utility class with the name Gatherers. This is very similar to collectors class inside collector API. Just like how Collectors class provides some factory methods or utility methods to perform some terminal operation very similarly this Gatherers class It is having five factory methods with the name fold(), scan(), mapConcurrent(), windowFixed() and windowSliding(). By using these factory methods if your business scenario is matching with the logic that these methods are going to handle, then you can happily use these factory methods instead of writing your own intermediate operation with the help of Gatherer API from scratch.

As of now, this class has only these five methods, but I'm assuming this list is going to grow in the future versions based upon the recommendations from the developer community. Let's try to understand the purpose of each of these methods, under which scenarios we can use them instead of writing the Gatherer API implementation from scratch. fold() is like a reduce() method in streams. This fold() is also accumulates value from a stream into a single result, but there is a difference between fold() and reduce().

fold() is going to support the execution in an ordered and sequential manner. It is not parallel friendly. You need to use the fold(), especially when combining the values cannot be parallelized. The same points I also highlighted here. You need to use the fold() when you want to combine all elements into one result, and you can't use a combiner in order sensitive operations, and you only need a single output at the end of the stream. How to use the fold().

You just have to invoke the same with the help of the Gatherers class and this fold(), it is going to accept two input parameters. The first one is going to represent the initial starting value for your fold logic, and the second parameter is on how to fold the elements that are receiving from the upstream. What is the meaning of folding? Folding is nothing but accumulating the values into a single value. Let me show you an example so that it is going to make more clear to you.

Here I have an upstream with the elements like 10, 200,3 and 45. I don't want to calculate the sum of these elements. Instead, I want to check how many numbers are there in each element. And by the time I execute my entire gatherer logic, I want to display the total numbers. For example, this 10 has two numbers, 200 has three numbers, and this has one number, and this has two numbers. The output that I'm expecting is eight. Let's try to understand how to achieve the same with the help of fold() method.

As you can see here, first, as usual I need to invoke the gatherer() method. To this gatherer() method, I need to assign the return type of the fold() method. So that's why I need to invoke gathers.fold(). To this fold() as a first parameter, I'm trying to pass the initial value as 0. The same 0 is going to act as a mutable state value inside my gatherer logic. Initially, this count will be zero, and this num indicates the element that you are going to receive from the upstream.Inside the folding logic, what I have defined is I'm trying to add the given count value to the number that I'm going to get by executing this piece of logic.

First, I'm trying to convert the number to a string, followed by I'm trying to check the length of the string. So for the 10 I'm going to get the length as 2. So 0+2 will be 2. During the second element processing the count will be 2. Followed by this logic is going to return 3. With that, the overall count will become 5. 5+1 will be the calculation that is going to happen during the processing of the third element. And at last, while processing the last element 45, the count will be 6 to the same 6, It is going to append the length of 45, which will be 2.

With this, the final outcome that we are going to get is eight. The same we can try to catch by invoking these findFirst() method. If you try to print out these total digits, you're going to get optional of 8 as an output. I'm not going to show you the demo of all these programs that I'm going to discuss inside this lecture, because all these are self-explanatory. In case if you are interested, you can find these examples inside the GitHub repo that I have shared.

After the fold we have scan() method scan is like very similar to fold, but instead of producing only final result this scan(), it is going to emit intermediate result at each step. You can think this as an running total or a progressive reduction. Let's imagine I have an input stream that is going to hold 1, 2, 3, 4. I'm trying to build an output where each element is going to be calculated by adding to the previous element. This example we already discussed by building Gatherers API logic from scratch. But let's try to understand how to build the same with the help of scan() method.

By the time my program executes. The first element will have 1, whereas the second element, for these two one will be added, which is the previous element. With that, this value will become 3. Similarly, this will become 6, followed by 10. As usual, first, with the help of these Stream object, I need to invoke the gather() method. To this gather() method, we need to assign the return type from the scan() method. So once you invoke this Gathers.scan().

This scan() method is also going to accept two input parameters. As part of the first parameter, you need to provide what is the initial mutable state value. The second parameter will be a lambda expression using which you need to define your scanner logic. This is my lambda expression, which I'm trying to pass as a second parameter. As you can see here, the first parameter sum, it is going to represent the state value that my Gatherer API is going to use during the processing of the elements.

The second parameter, which is next, it represents the element that is being injected from the upstream, Inside my lambda expression logic, I'm trying to simply add sum, and next the output of this addition will be returned from this lambda expression. Since a scan is going to emit the intermediate results at each step behind the scenes Gatherer API, It will take care of pushing the elements to the downstream. So here what is the downstream? By using the scope to values, we should be able to share immutable data between a method and its colleagues without explicitly passing that data as method parameters.

We know inside Java, a thread is responsible to handle a request, and as part of the request business logic, multiple methods will be executed. We have various options inside Java. These scope to values is a modern approach to share the data between the methods without explicitly passing as a method parameters. Local thread locals are available from last few decades inside Java, but they have their own complexities and drawbacks.

By using these scope to values the Java team, they're trying to overcome the challenges around the thread local. But before that, let's try to understand what are the various options that we developers has to pass the data in between multiple methods. If you closely understand there is a process order method and this method it is internally calling other methods like validate order, calculate price and save order. Again, there is another method invocation with the name check user permissions.

So this method requires the context details to check the user permissions. The same applies for the apply user discount method as well. This method also requires user context details to apply the discount. So if you see the drawback here, though, the in-between methods like validate order and calculate price. They are not using these context details anywhere in their business logic, but they are forced to accept this information as method parameter just for the reason that they have to pass the same information to the other methods that are being invoked in these methods.

When we declare this constant. Under this user context, we may have some initial details or null details, but inside the business logic we can update these context details. For example, under this process order. Since this process order is going to receive the user context details from the caller method inside the same method, we can invoke the set method by using the context variable of type thread local. So here we are setting the user context details that we have received.

So at the top method we can update that data inside the thread local object. And the same can be accessed anywhere inside any method which is being executed as part of the same thread. So when a thread start processing these process order method so the same thread, it is going to invoke the validate order, calculate price and save order. Let's imagine I need these user context details inside one of the method with the name validate order. So to this method we're not passing any context details as an input, but still this method can access that context information available inside the thread local object by invoking the get method against this context variable.

So when this Get method is invoked, it is going to get the user context object, which we stored inside this variable. And the same context details can be passed to other methods or can be used inside any business logic. So the advantage that we are getting with the thread local here is we don't have to manually pass the context details to each method by using the method parameters. So with that, a major problem is solved and most of the senior developers who write the enterprise code and framework code like Spring spring Boot.

They are using these thread locals to a great extent. Once the developer feels like that, all the business logic is executed and no more wanted the details stored inside the thread. Local object. Towards the end, the developer has to invoke the remove method by using the same context variable. So this is going to remove the data that we stored inside the thread local. So invoking this remove method is super important. Otherwise the same data is going to be stored inside the thread unless the thread is shut down or unless the thread is died.

The data that we stored is going to be stored forever. So this thread local approach is working for developers, but it has some serious drawbacks. Let's try to understand what are those?
